1-01_What_is_Machine_Learning.source: Lecture 1 examples — robot arm sorting fruits (video), MNIST handwritten digit recognition, cat-image classification network.

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Machine Learning (ML) is a subfield of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in which a system improves its performance on a task through experience (data) rather than being explicitly programmed with fixed rules for every possible situation. 

 Formally (Tom Mitchell's definition, standard in ML courses): A computer program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some task T and performance measure P, if its performance at T, as measured by P, improves with experience E. 

 The lecture illustrates this with two examples: 

 Robotic sorting arm : A robot arm on a conveyor belt distinguishes an apple from a tomato and sorts them — the "task" is classification of fruit type, "experience" is prior labeled images/examples of fruits, and "performance" is sorting accuracy. 
 MNIST digit recognition (Artificial Neural Network example) : A network takes an input of 784 pixels (a 28×28 grayscale image of a handwritten digit), passes it through a hidden layer of 25 neurons with sigmoid activation , and outputs a predicted digit (0–9). The dataset is split into 50,000 training images, 10,000 validation images, 10,000 test images — this is the classic supervised learning setup. 
 Cat image misclassified as "rabbit" : shows that ML models are not perfect — they can make wrong predictions, especially early in training or with ambiguous inputs. This illustrates the core ML workflow: input → network → prediction → compare with truth → adjust. 

 Key idea: instead of a programmer hand-coding "if pixel pattern X then digit is 5," the model learns the mapping from data by adjusting internal parameters (weights) until its predictions match the correct answers as closely as possible.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Machine Learning is a way of teaching computers to do a task by showing them lots of examples , instead of writing step-by-step instructions for every case. 

 Example 1: Imagine trying to write code that tells a robot "if the object is round and orange, it's a tomato; if it's round and green/red, it's an apple." This breaks quickly — colors, sizes, lighting all vary. Instead, you show the robot thousands of pictures of apples and tomatoes labeled correctly, and it learns the pattern itself. 
 Example 2: To recognize handwritten digits (like a "5" someone wrote by hand), you can't write a rule for every possible way someone draws a "5." Instead, you show a computer 50,000 example images of digits with their correct answers, and it learns to guess the right digit for a new image it has never seen. 
 Sometimes the computer gets it wrong — like predicting "rabbit" instead of "cat" for a cat photo. That's normal in early learning; the model improves as it sees more examples and gets corrected. 

 So, Machine Learning = learning patterns from data , not being told the rules directly.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Machine Learning (ML) kya hai? 
Simple shabdon mein — ML matlab computer ko examples dikha dikha kar kaam sikhana , bina har cheez ka rule likhe. 

 Socho aapko ek chhote bachche ko sikhana hai ki "seb" aur "tamatar" mein farak kaise pata karein. 

 Purana tarika (traditional programming): Aap likhoge "agar gol ho aur laal ho to tamatar, agar gol ho aur crunchy ho to seb" — lekin ye rule har situation mein fail ho jaayega (kabhi seb bhi red hota hai, kabhi tamatar green hota hai). 
 ML ka tarika: Aap bachche (yaani computer) ko hazaaron photos dikhate ho jisme bataya gaya hai "ye seb hai", "ye tamatar hai" — aur bachcha khud pattern samajh leta hai. Agli baar naya fruit dikhe to wo khud bata dega. 

 Lecture mein 3 examples diye gaye hai: 

 Robot arm jo fruits sort karta hai — conveyor belt pe seb aur tamatar aate hai, robot camera se dekh kar unhe alag-alag dabbe mein daalta hai. Ye seekha hua hai, hardcoded nahi hai. 
 Handwritten number pehchanna (MNIST example) — ek image 28x28 pixels ki hoti hai (matlab 784 chhote-chhote boxes/dots), computer in pixels ko dekh kar batata hai ye number "5" hai ya "3" hai. Isme:
 
 Training data (jisse computer seekhta hai) = 50,000 images 
 Validation data (jisse check karte hai theek se seekh raha hai ya nahi) = 10,000 images 
 Test data (final exam jaisa, naye images pe check karna) = 10,000 images 
 
 Billi ki photo ko "rabbit" bol dena (galat prediction) — ye dikhata hai ki ML models hamesha sahi nahi hote, khaaskar jab wo puri tarah seekhe nahi hote. Jitna zyada aur achha data milega, utna better guess karega. 

 Yaad rakhne wali baat : ML mein hum computer ko rule nahi batate, hum data (examples) dete hai aur computer khud pattern dhoondh leta hai.

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
In a supervised machine learning dataset, each sample / instance / observation (a single row of data, e.g., one flower) is described by two categories of variables: 

 Features (x) : the independent/input variables — measurable properties (attributes, dimensions) that describe the object. In the Iris dataset: Sepal.Length , Sepal.Width , Petal.Length , Petal.Width . 
 Target (y) : the dependent/output variable — the value the model is trying to predict. In the Iris dataset: Species (Setosa, Versicolor, Virginica). 

 When the target column is filled in (observed), the corresponding value is called a label . Formally: 

 Labeled data : samples where the target y is known/observed. 
 Unlabeled data : samples where the target y is unknown (marked ? ). 

 The dataset is structured as a matrix: rows = samples, columns = features (+ one target/label column). The core assumption of supervised ML is that there exists some relationship f such that y ≈ f(x) — i.e., features determine (or strongly correlate with) the target — and the learning algorithm's job is to approximate this function f from the labeled data, so it can later predict y for new, unlabeled x . 

 Analogous terms used interchangeably across ML literature: target = label = response variable = dependent variable = ground truth. Features = attributes = predictors = independent variables = input variables.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Imagine a spreadsheet (table) about flowers. Each row is one flower. Each column is a piece of information about that flower. 

 The columns that describe the flower's measurements (like the length of its petal) are called features — these are the "clues" the computer looks at. 
 The column that tells you what species the flower actually is (Setosa, Versicolor, or Virginica) is called the target — this is the "answer" the computer is trying to guess. 
 When we already know the answer for a row (we know the species), we call that a label . So "label" and "target value" mean basically the same thing — the label is just the specific value written in the target column for that row. 
 Sometimes we don't know the answer yet (maybe nobody identified the species of that particular flower) — those rows are called unlabeled data , marked with a "?" in the target column. 

 Simple analogy : If you're guessing someone's job based on their clothes, height, and the tools they carry — those are the features . Their actual job (doctor, chef, engineer) is the target/label you're trying to predict.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Socho ek Excel sheet hai jisme 150 flowers (phoolon) ki information hai. Har row ek flower hai. Har column ek jaankari hai us flower ke baare mein. 

 Features kya hote hai? 
Features matlab wo measurements/properties jo hum flower ko dekh kar naap sakte hai — jaise: 

 Sepal Length (bahar wali patti ki lambai) 
 Sepal Width (bahar wali patti ki chaudai) 
 Petal Length (andar wali petal ki lambai) 
 Petal Width (andar wali petal ki chaudai) 

 Ye sab "clues" hai jinse computer guess karega ki flower kaunsi type ka hai. 

 Target kya hota hai? 
Target matlab wo cheez jo humein predict/guess karni hai — is dataset mein target hai "Species" (yaani flower kaunsi kism ka hai: Setosa, Versicolor, ya Virginica). Isko humesha y letter se represent karte hai, aur features ko x se. 

 Label kya hota hai? 
Jab kisi row ka target/answer humein pehle se pata hai (kisi expert ne bata diya "ye Setosa hai"), to us value ko label kehte hai. Matlab label = target ka actual pata hua answer . 

 Labeled vs Unlabeled data (chhota preview) : 

 Labeled data : jinme species pehle se pata hai (jaise "Setosa", "Versicolor") 
 Unlabeled data : jinme species pata nahi hai, table mein "?" laga hota hai 

 Yaad rakhne ka easy tarika : 

 Features = Sawaal ke clues (jo hum dekh sakte hai) 
 Target/Label = Sahi jawaab (jo hume predict karna hai) 

 Jaise agar aap kisi insaan ko dekh kar uska profession guess kar rahe ho — uske kapde, uske paas ka saaman, uski height — ye sab features hai. Uska actual profession (doctor/engineer/chef) jo aap guess kar rahe ho, wo hai target/label .

1-03_Iris_Dataset_Case_Study.source: Lecture 1, slides 8–11. Enriched with web research (GeeksforGeeks, Guvi).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
The Iris dataset is a classic, canonical benchmark dataset in statistics and machine learning, introduced by statistician and biologist Ronald A. Fisher in his 1936 paper on discriminant analysis. 

 Composition: 

 150 total samples (instances/observations) 
 3 balanced classes, 50 samples each: Iris setosa , Iris versicolor , Iris virginica 
 4 continuous numeric features, all measured in centimeters:
 
 Sepal length 
 Sepal width 
 Petal length 
 Petal width 
 
 1 categorical target: Species 

 Why it's used pedagogically: 

 Low-dimensional (only 4 features) — easy to visualize (scatter plots, pair plots). 
 Small (150 rows) — fast to load and compute on any machine. 
 Clean — no missing values, no noisy/corrupted entries, already balanced classes. 
 Well-separated classes — setosa is linearly separable from the other two; versicolor and virginica overlap slightly, making it useful for demonstrating both easy and moderately-hard classification boundaries. 
 Available built-in in most ML libraries ( sklearn.datasets.load_iris() in scikit-learn, datasets::iris in R). 

 Caveat emphasized in the lecture : This dataset is "small, clean, low-dim... very easy to classify; this is not necessarily true in the wild." Real-world datasets are typically larger, higher-dimensional, noisy, imbalanced, and contain missing/incorrect values — so strong performance on Iris does not guarantee a technique will work well on real, messy data.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The Iris dataset is like the "Hello World" of machine learning — the very first example almost every beginner uses to practice. 

 It's a table of information about 150 flowers, collected long ago by a scientist named Fisher. There are three kinds of iris flowers in the data (Setosa, Versicolor, Virginica), and for each flower, four simple measurements were taken with a ruler: how long and wide the sepal (the green leaf-like part under the petal) is, and how long and wide the petal (the colorful part) is. 

 The goal: given these four measurements for a new flower, can a computer program guess which of the three species it is? 

 This dataset is popular for teaching because: 

 It's small enough to load instantly. 
 It has no messy or missing data. 
 The three flower types are fairly easy to tell apart using just the measurements. 

 But the lecture gives an important warning: real-world data is usually much messier — bigger, noisier, with missing values — so just because a method works great on Iris doesn't mean it will work great everywhere.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Iris Dataset ML seekhne walo ke liye ek "starter dataset" hai — jaise programming seekhte waqt sabse pehle "Hello World" likhte hai, waise hi ML seekhte waqt sabse pehle log Iris dataset try karte hai. 

 Ye dataset ek scientist Fisher ne 1936 mein banaya tha. Isme 3 tarah ke iris phool hai: 

 Iris Setosa 
 Iris Versicolor 
 Iris Virginica 

 Total 150 flowers hai — har type ke 50-50 flowers . 

 Har flower ke 4 measurements liye gaye hai (scale/ruler se naapkar, cm mein): 

 Sepal Length (bahar ki patti ki lambai) 
 Sepal Width (bahar ki patti ki chaudai) 
 Petal Length (andar ki petal ki lambai) 
 Petal Width (andar ki petal ki chaudai) 

 Goal kya hai is dataset ka? 
Given ye 4 measurements, computer ko guess karna hai ki ye flower Setosa hai, Versicolor hai, ya Virginica hai. Yehi classification problem kehlata hai (yaani categories mein baantna). 

 Iris dataset itna popular kyun hai beginners ke liye? 

 Chhota hai — sirf 150 rows, turant load ho jaata hai kisi bhi computer par. 
 Saaf-suthra hai — koi missing value nahi, koi galat entry nahi. 
 Aasan hai classify karna — teeno types mein achha farak hai (khaaskar Setosa baaki dono se bahut alag hai). 
 Har ML library mein already available hai — jaise Python ki scikit-learn library mein sirf ek line code se load ho jaata hai. 

 IMPORTANT WARNING jo lecture mein di gayi hai: 
Iris dataset "chhota aur saaf" hai, isliye is par classify karna easy hai. Lekin real duniya ka data aisa nahi hota — real data bada hota hai, messy (ganda/incomplete) hota hai, values missing ho sakti hai. Isliye sirf Iris pe kaam karne se ye guarantee nahi milti ki wahi method real-world data pe bhi achhe se kaam karega. Ye ek chetavni (warning) hai ki practice ke liye Iris theek hai, lekin real projects zyada challenging honge.

1-04_Labeled_vs_Unlabeled_Data.topic_title: Labeled vs Unlabeled Data (and Supervised vs Unsupervised Learning)
1-04_Labeled_vs_Unlabeled_Data.source: Lecture 1, slide 12 ("Observation Labels"). Enriched with web research (GeeksforGeeks, Toloka).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Datasets are categorized based on whether the target/label is observed: 

 Labeled data : each sample's target value y is known and recorded (e.g., a flower row where Species = Setosa is filled in). Producing labeled data typically requires manual annotation effort (human experts assigning the correct category/value), which makes it costlier and scarcer than unlabeled data. 
 Unlabeled data : the target value is missing/unknown (denoted ? in the lecture's example table). Unlabeled data is abundant and cheap to collect (e.g., raw sensor readings, unannotated images) since it requires no manual annotation. 

 This distinction directly maps to the two dominant paradigms of machine learning: 

 Paradigm 
 Data used 
 Goal 

 Supervised Learning 
 Labeled data (x, y pairs) 
 Learn a mapping f(x) → y to predict labels for new, unseen data. Includes classification (discrete target, e.g., species) and regression (continuous target, e.g., price). 

 Unsupervised Learning 
 Unlabeled data (only x) 
 Discover hidden structure without predefined answers — e.g., clustering (grouping similar points), dimensionality reduction (e.g., PCA, mentioned later in the course syllabus), anomaly detection . 

 In the Iris example: rows with a known species (Setosa/Versicolor/Virginica) are the labeled training set; rows marked "?" simulate new flowers whose species we don't yet know — the supervised model trained on labeled data is used to predict labels for these unlabeled rows. 

 There's also a middle ground, semi-supervised learning , which uses a small amount of labeled data together with a large amount of unlabeled data — useful because labeling is expensive but raw data is plentiful. This isn't explicitly named in the slide but follows directly from the labeled/unlabeled distinction shown.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Think of a table where one column shows the "correct answer" for each row. 

 Labeled data = rows where we already know and have written down the correct answer. Example: a photo of a flower where someone already wrote "this is a Setosa" next to it. 
 Unlabeled data = rows where we don't know the answer yet — it's blank or marked with a question mark. Example: a new flower photo nobody has identified yet. 

 Why does this matter? Because it decides how a machine learning model can be trained: 

 If you have labeled data (question + correct answer pairs), you can train the model like a student with an answer key — this is called supervised learning . 
 If you only have unlabeled data (no answer key at all), the model has to find patterns on its own, like grouping similar things together without being told what the groups mean — this is called unsupervised learning . 

 Getting labeled data usually takes more effort (someone — a person — has to look at each example and label it correctly), while unlabeled data is often lying around for free (raw photos, sensor logs, text, etc.).

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Socho ek table hai jisme har row ek flower hai, aur last column mein uska "sahi jawaab" (species) likha hai. 

 Labeled Data kya hai? 
Jin rows mein "sahi jawaab" pehle se pata hai aur likha hua hai — unhe labeled data kehte hai. Jaise: "Ye flower Setosa hai" — ye already kisi ne check karke bata diya. 

 Unlabeled Data kya hai? 
Jin rows mein jawaab pata nahi hai — matlab "?" laga hai — unhe unlabeled data kehte hai. Jaise: ek naya flower mila hai lekin abhi tak kisi ne uski species confirm nahi ki. 

 Ye kyun important hai? 
Kyunki iske hisaab se decide hota hai ki ML model kis tarah train karenge: 

 Supervised Learning (Labeled data use karte hai): 

 Jaise ek student ko answer-key ke saath practice questions diye jaayein — student sawaal aur sahi jawaab dono dekhta hai, aur pattern seekhta hai. 
 Example: Iris dataset mein flowers jinki species pehle se pata hai, unse model seekhta hai. 
 Isme 2 type hote hai: Classification (category guess karna, jaise "kaunsi species") aur Regression (number predict karna, jaise "price kitna hoga") 
 
 Unsupervised Learning (Unlabeled data use karte hai): 

 Jaise ek student ko sirf sawaal diye jaayein, answer-key na ho — student khud similar cheezon ko group karne ki koshish karta hai. 
 Example: Bina species bataye, sirf measurements dekh kar flowers ko groups mein baantna (jaise similar flowers ek saath rakhna) — isko clustering kehte hai. 

 Labeled data banana mehnga kyun hai? 
Kisi insaan ko baith kar har example dekh kar sahi answer likhna padta hai — isliye labeled data kam hota hai aur mehnga hota hai . Lekin unlabeled data (raw photos, sensor data) bahut zyada aur free mein milta hai kyunki usme label lagane ki mehnat nahi lagi. 

 Yaad rakhne ka tarika : 

 Labeled = "Answer-key ke saath" → Supervised Learning 
 Unlabeled = "Answer-key ke bina" → Unsupervised Learning

1-05_Introduction_to_Neural_Networks.source: Lecture 1, slides 14–16 (MNIST digit example, generic layered network diagram, cat-image misclassification example). Enriched with web research (GeeksforGeeks, Codecademy).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
An Artificial Neural Network (ANN) is a computational model loosely inspired by biological neurons, composed of layers of interconnected units ("neurons"): 

 Input Layer : receives the raw feature values. No computation happens here — it just passes values forward. In the MNIST example shown in the lecture: input = 784 values , because each handwritten-digit image is 28×28 pixels , and 28 × 28 = 784, with one input neuron per pixel intensity. 
 Hidden Layer(s) : intermediate layers that perform the actual computation. Each neuron computes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias, then applies a non-linear activation function . The lecture's example uses 25 neurons in a single hidden layer with a sigmoid activation function (which squashes outputs into the range 0–1). Deeper networks (as previewed in the multi-layer diagram on slide 15) stack multiple hidden layers to learn increasingly abstract representations — this is the basis of Deep Learning , covered later in the course. 
 Output Layer : produces the final prediction. For MNIST digit classification, this would be 10 output units (digits 0–9), and for the cat-vs-rabbit example, the output layer collapses to a decision about the object class. 

 Data split shown for the MNIST example (standard supervised-learning practice, previewed here and formally covered later under "Notion of training, validation, and testing"): 

 Training set: 50,000 images — used to fit/adjust the network's weights. 
 Validation set: 10,000 images — used to tune settings and check the model isn't overfitting during training. 
 Test set: 10,000 images — used only at the end, to measure how well the model generalizes to unseen data. 

 Forward propagation : data flows left→right through the network (input → hidden → output), each layer transforming the signal using its learned weights, producing a final prediction. 

 The cat image misclassified as "rabbit" example (slide 16) illustrates a key ML reality: predictions can be wrong, especially with an under-trained network, similar-looking classes, or insufficient/unrepresentative training data. The arrow pointing backward (←) in that slide foreshadows backpropagation — the algorithm (covered later in the course) that uses the size of this error to adjust the network's weights so future predictions improve. 

 This is only a preview ; the course syllabus lists many related topics to be covered in depth later: loss functions, gradient descent, perceptron/delta learning, MLP, backpropagation, regularization, CNNs, RNNs, GANs, etc.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
A neural network is a computer system designed to loosely mimic how brain cells (neurons) work together — lots of small units connected in layers, passing signals to each other. 

 Using the lecture's example of recognizing a handwritten digit (like the number "5"): 

 Input layer : The picture of the digit gets broken down into 784 tiny pieces (because it's a 28×28 grid of pixels = 784 pixels total). Each pixel's brightness becomes one input number. 
 Hidden layer : These 784 numbers get combined and processed by 25 "neurons" in the middle. This is where the network tries to detect patterns — like curves, lines, loops — that are typical of certain digits. 
 Output layer : Finally, the network gives its best guess — which digit (0 through 9) it thinks the picture shows. 

 To teach the network to be good at this, we show it 50,000 example images with known correct answers (training), check its progress on 10,000 more (validation), and finally test its real skill on 10,000 images it's never seen (testing). 

 Sometimes the network makes mistakes — like looking at a photo of a cat and confidently saying "rabbit!" That's completely normal for a network that hasn't learned enough yet, or when two things look kind of similar. The whole point of training a neural network is to keep correcting these mistakes over many rounds until it gets things right most of the time.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Neural Network kya hota hai? 
Ye ek computer system hai jo thoda-thoda hamare dimaag ke neurons (brain cells) ki tarah kaam karta hai — bahut saare chhote-chhote units aapas mein connected hote hai, layers mein arrange hote hai, aur ek dusre ko signal pass karte hai. 

 Lecture mein diya gaya example: Handwritten number pehchanna (jaise kisi ne haath se "5" likha ho aur computer ko pehchanna hai ki ye "5" hai). 

 Isme 3 tarah ki layers hoti hai: 

 Input Layer (shuruaat) :
Photo ko chhote-chhote pixels mein todte hai. Photo hoti hai 28x28 pixels ki (yaani 28 rows aur 28 columns ke chhote boxes) = total 784 pixels . Har pixel ki brightness ek number banti hai — ye sab 784 numbers "input" ke roop mein network mein jaate hai. 
 Hidden Layer (beech ki layer, jaha "jadu" hota hai) :
Yaha 25 neurons hote hai jo un 784 numbers ko process karte hai. Ye layer patterns dhoondhti hai — jaise curve, line, loop — jo kisi particular number (jaise 5 ya 3) mein hote hai. 
 Output Layer (aakhri jawaab) :
Yaha network apna final guess deta hai — ki ye image kaunsa number hai (0 se 9 tak). 

 Data kaise divide kiya jaata hai training ke liye? 

 Training Data (50,000 images) : Isse network seekhta hai, jaise practice questions. 
 Validation Data (10,000 images) : Isse check karte hai ki network sahi disha mein seekh raha hai ya nahi, training ke beech mein. 
 Test Data (10,000 images) : Ye final exam jaisa hai — bilkul naye images jo network ne kabhi nahi dekhe, unpar check karte hai ki wo kitna achha kaam karta hai. 

 Galat prediction ka example (Billi ko "Rabbit" bolna) :
Lecture mein ek example diya hai jisme ek billi (cat) ki photo di gayi, lekin network ne galti se "rabbit" bata diya. Ye bilkul normal hai — jab network abhi poori tarah seekha nahi hota, ya do cheezein dikhne mein similar hoti hai (billi aur khargosh dono chhote fluffy jaanwar hai), to galti ho sakti hai. 

 Iss galti ko sudharne ke liye ek process hota hai jise backpropagation kehte hai (isko detail mein baad ke lectures mein padhenge) — isme network apni galti ka size dekh kar apne andar ke numbers (weights) ko thoda-thoda adjust karta hai, taaki agli baar sahi jawaab de. 

 Yaad rakhne wali baat : Ye sirf ek preview/jhalak hai. Neural networks ka detailed padhai (jaise loss function, gradient descent, backpropagation, CNN, RNN) course ke aage ke lectures mein hogi. Abhi sirf itna samajhna hai ki network layers mein data process karta hai aur galtiyon se seekh kar improve hota hai .

1-06_Course_Syllabus_Roadmap_and_Resourc.source: Lecture 1, slides 5–6, 13 (Course Schema, Recommended Reading, Kaggle).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
The course syllabus (Credits: 4, L-T-P: 3-0-2) is organized into a logical progression across three broad phases, previewing the entire semester: 

 Phase A — ML Fundamentals & Classical Supervised Learning: 
Introduction to ML → Dimensionality reduction (PCA) → Nearest Neighbours / KNN → Linear Regression → Decision Tree classifiers → Generalization, Overfitting → Train/Validation/Test split methodology. 

 Phase B — Additional Classical Algorithms: 
Ensembling & Random Forests → Linear SVM → K-Means clustering → Logistic Regression → Naive Bayes. 

 Phase C — Neural Networks & Deep Learning: 
Loss functions & optimization → Gradient Descent, Perceptron/Delta learning → Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) → Backpropagation → MLP for classification/regression → Regularization, Early Stopping → Kernels with SVM → Bayesian methods, Generative methods, HMM, EM, PAC learning → Deep Learning intro → CNNs (and popular architectures) → RNNs → GANs & generative models → Advances in backpropagation/optimization → Adversarial learning. 

 Evaluation weighting (Minor 25%, Quiz/Participation 15%, Major 40%, Lab 20%) reflects that hands-on lab performance (20%) and continuous assessment (15%) together carry more weight (35%) than a single exam, encouraging consistent practical engagement throughout the semester rather than last-minute exam cramming alone. 

 Recommended resources: 

 Textbooks span both classical ML (Géron; Müller & Guido; Murphy) and Deep Learning (Goodfellow, Bengio, Courville) — matching the two-phase structure of the syllabus (classical ML first half, deep learning second half). 
 Kaggle (kaggle.com), referenced on slide 13, is the world's largest online ML/AI community and platform — it hosts public datasets, code notebooks, and competitions, useful for hands-on practice, benchmarking against other practitioners' solutions, and applying course concepts to real datasets beyond the classroom labs.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
This slide is basically the "map" of the entire semester — what topics come first, what comes later, and how your grade gets calculated. 

 Roughly, the course goes in this order: 

 Basics first : what machine learning is, how to reduce the number of measurements you're working with (PCA), simple ways to classify data by "nearest similar examples" (KNN), simple line-fitting (linear regression), and tree-based decisions. 
 More classical techniques : combining many models together (ensembling/random forests), support vector machines, grouping data (K-means), logistic regression, and naive Bayes. 
 Neural networks and deep learning (the more advanced, modern part): how networks learn from mistakes (gradient descent, backpropagation), building bigger networks (MLP), preventing them from memorizing instead of learning (regularization), and finally powerful architectures used in today's AI — CNNs (great with images), RNNs (great with sequences like text), and GANs (used to generate new images/data). 

 Your final grade is a mix of a mid-term test, quizzes/participation, a final big exam, and lab work — so consistent effort throughout the course (not just exam cramming) matters. 

 The suggested books cover both the "classical" ML techniques and the newer "deep learning" techniques, matching the two halves of the course. Kaggle is mentioned as a website where you can practice with real datasets, see what other learners have done, and even compete in ML challenges — a great place to apply what you learn in class.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Ye slide poore semester ka "roadmap" hai — yani kaunsa topic pehle padhenge, kaunsa baad mein, aur marks kaise milenge. 

 Course 3 phases mein baant sakte hai:
