16-08_Practical_Considerations_Scaling_D.topic_title: Practical Considerations — Scaling, Dimensionality, Speed, and Pros/Cons
16-08_Practical_Considerations_Scaling_D.source: Lecture 16, slide 5 (the issues list: computational complexity, size of training set, dimension of data) and the hidden problem in slides 13–16. **This topic is mostly enrichment from web research** — the slides name these issues but do not explain them. Research covered: feature scaling for distance-based methods, curse of dimensionality, KD-trees / ball trees, distance-weighted k-NN, strengths and weaknesses of k-NN.

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 5 lists three issues without explanation — computational complexity , size of training set , dimension of data . Here is what they mean in practice. 

 1. Feature scaling is essential 

 Distances add up squared differences of raw feature values, so a feature with a large numeric range dominates. In L16 Worked Example — Predicting a Movie's Genre ("Barbie") , duration (≈ 41–56 minute gaps) swamped rating (≈ 0.2–1.2 gaps). Fixes: 

 Min–max scaling: x′ = (x − min)/(max − min) → every feature in [0, 1]. 
 Standardization (z-score): x′ = (x − mean)/std → mean 0, std 1. 

 Both are covered earlier in the course: L7 Scaling/Normalization — Min-Max Method & Mean Normalization and L7 Scaling/Normalization — Z-score Method & Decimal Scaling Method . Fit the scaler on the training data only , then apply the same min/max or mean/std to the query. Categorical features need encoding first (or a metric suited to them). 

 2. Computational cost 

 Training: O(1) (just store data). Prediction per query: O(N·m) distance computations for N points and m features, plus selecting the k smallest. 
 Memory: must keep the entire training set. 
 Speed-ups: KD-trees and ball trees organize points spatially so far-away regions can be skipped, giving roughly O(log N) queries in low dimensions; approximate nearest-neighbor methods (e.g. locality-sensitive hashing) trade a little accuracy for large speed in big data. Also: pre-reduce data size (e.g. keep only prototype points). 

 3. Size of the training set 

 More data fills the feature space and makes neighbors truly similar — the Cover–Hart result ( L16 The Nearest Neighbor Idea and the Basic k-NN Rule ) says the 1-NN error approaches at most 2 × Bayes error as N → ∞. But more data also means slower queries and more memory. With tiny N (like the 4-sample examples) predictions are unreliable. 

 4. Dimension of data — the curse of dimensionality 

 As the number of features m grows, the feature space becomes sparse and distances concentrate : the nearest and the farthest points end up at nearly the same distance, so "nearest" loses meaning. Irrelevant features add noise to every distance. Remedies: feature selection and dimensionality reduction (PCA) — see L10 Dimensionality Reduction and the Curse of Dimensionality and L11 Principal Component Analysis — Definition, Key Facts, and Geometric Intuition and 12 — and a suitable metric ( L16 Distance Metrics Used with k-NN ). 

 5. Weighted k-NN 

 Instead of one-person-one-vote, weight each neighbor by w = 1/d (or 1/d²). This reduces the damage from choosing k too large (far neighbors count little) and breaks ties ( L16 The k-NN Algorithm, Step by Step ). 

 6. Other practical points 

 Imbalanced classes: the majority class tends to win the vote; weighting helps. 
 Outliers/noise: larger k or weighting smooths them ( L16 Issues in Nearest-Neighbor Classifiers and Choosing the Value of K ). 
 Interpretability: easy to explain a prediction ("these 3 similar examples") — a big plus. 

 Advantages vs. disadvantages 

 Advantages 
 Disadvantages 

 Very simple to understand and implement 
 Slow prediction on large data (scans everything) 

 No training phase; new data added instantly 
 Stores the whole training set (memory heavy) 

 Non-parametric: makes no assumption about decision-boundary shape 
 Sensitive to feature scale and irrelevant features 

 Works for both classification and regression 
 Suffers in high dimensions (curse of dimensionality) 

 Naturally handles multi-class problems 
 Sensitive to the choice of k and the distance metric; noisy for small k

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The slide mentions a few worries without explaining them. Here they are in everyday terms. 

 Different units fool the ruler. If one feature is "minutes" (hundreds) and another is "stars" (under 10), the minutes win every time, like comparing people by millimetres of height and years of age. Fix: squeeze every feature into the same range (like 0 to 1) before measuring distance. 
 It's slow with lots of data. k-NN has no studying phase, but every question means comparing with every stored example. 10 examples — instant. 10 million — slow. Clever filing systems (KD-trees, ball trees) help skip examples that are obviously too far away. 
 More data helps accuracy, but costs speed and memory. With only 4 examples you can't trust the answer much. 
 Too many features hurt. In a space with hundreds of features, almost everything looks equally far from everything else, so "nearest" stops being meaningful — this is the curse of dimensionality . Remove useless features or compress them first (PCA). 
 Closer friends get a louder voice. Weighted k-NN lets closer neighbors count more than far ones. 

 Good: easy to understand, no training, works for categories and numbers. Bad: slow on big data, picky about scales and about k.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Slide 5 mein kuch problems ke naam likhe hain par samjhaaye nahi gaye. Unhe yahan simple bhasha mein dekhte hain. 

 Alag-alag units ruler ko bewakoof banate hain. Agar ek feature "minutes" (sau ke upar) aur dusra "stars" (10 se kam) hai, to minutes hamesha jeetenge — jaise kisi ko "height millimetre mein" aur "age saal mein" se compare karo. Ilaaj: distance naapne se pehle sab features ko same range (jaise 0 se 1) mein kar do (min–max ya z-score scaling). Scaler sirf training data se fit karo, phir wahi query par lagao. 
 Data zyada ho to slow. k-NN mein training nahi hoti, lekin har sawaal par saare stored examples se compare karna padta hai. 10 examples — turant. 1 crore examples — slow. Isliye KD-tree / ball tree jaisi smart filing use hoti hai jo bahut door wale points ko skip kar deti hai. 
 Data zyada = accuracy behtar, lekin speed aur memory ka kharcha. Sirf 4 examples ho (jaise lecture ke examples) to answer par zyada bharosa nahi kar sakte. 
 Features bahut zyada = problem. Hazaaron features ho to har point lagbhag ek jaisa door lagta hai, "nearest" ka matlab hi khatam — isse curse of dimensionality kehte hain. Faltu features hatao ya PCA se features kam karo (Lecture 10–12 dekho). 
 Paas wale dost ki awaaz zyada. Weighted k-NN mein paas wale neighbors ko zyada weight (jaise 1/distance) milta hai — isse tie bhi toot jaate hain aur bade k ka nuksaan kam hota hai. 

 Fayde: samajhne mein aasaan, training nahi, category aur number dono ke liye kaam karta hai. Nuksaan: bade data par slow, scale aur k ke prati sensitive, high dimensions mein kamzor.

17-01_Why_System_Evaluation_and_Predicti.topic_title: Why Evaluate a Model? Predictive Modeling and Performance Evaluation
17-01_Why_System_Evaluation_and_Predicti.source: Lecture 17, slides 1–4 ("Why System Evaluation?", "Regression / classification models", "Performance evaluation"). Enriched with web research (generalization, why training-set performance is optimistic).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Why system evaluation? (slide 2). There are many models/algorithms/systems — which one is the best? The slide asks the same question for each component of a system: 

 the similarity function (cosine, correlation, …) — compare L16 Distance Metrics Used with k-NN ; 
 term selection (stop-word removal, stemming, …) and term weighting (TF, TF-IDF, …) — text-retrieval examples; 
 and, for retrieval: how far down the list will a user need to look to find some/all relevant documents? 

 So evaluation is how we compare choices objectively instead of by intuition. 

 Predictive modeling / supervised learning (slide 3). A model is a specification of the mathematical/probabilistic relationships that exist between different variables. The goal is usually to use existing data to develop models that predict outcomes for new data . The slide's examples: 

 Prediction task 
 Output type 

 Is an email spam or not? 
 Nominal (category, no order) → classification 

 Is a credit-card transaction fraudulent? 
 Nominal → classification 

 Which advertisement will a shopper most likely click? 
 Nominal → classification 

 Which football team will win the Super Bowl? 
 Nominal → classification 

 Predict the stock price of a company 
 Continuous → regression 

 Predict the number of buyers of a product 
 Continuous → regression 

 Predict user ratings of a new movie 
 Continuous/ordinal → regression 

 Predict the grade of a disease 
 Ordinal → regression/ordinal classification 

 The slide's side annotations label the target types: Nominal (categorical with no particular order) vs. Continuous / ordinal . This is the same regression-vs-classification split from L15 Linear Regression vs. Classification, and Classification Types . 

 Performance evaluation (slide 4). How predictive is the model we learned? 

 Regression: usually R² or MSE ( L17 Performance Metrics Overview and Regression Metrics (MAE, MSE, RMSE, R²) ). 
 Classification: many options ; accuracy can be used, with caution ( L17 The Confusion Matrix — TP, TN, FP, FN ). 
 Key warning: performance on the training data (data used to build models) is not a good indicator of performance on future data. 
 Q: Why? A: Because new data will probably not be exactly the same as the training data! 

 Why training performance is misleading (explained). A model can memorize its training examples — a 1-NN classifier ( L16 The Nearest Neighbor Idea and the Basic k-NN Rule ) scores 100 % on its own training data because every point is its own nearest neighbor, yet may do poorly on new points. What we truly care about is generalization error : performance on unseen data. All the techniques in this lecture (train/test split, validation set, cross-validation, bootstrap) are ways to estimate generalization performance honestly — see L17 Overfitting vs. Underfitting — Bias vs. Variance for the underlying reason.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Suppose you have several different models (or settings) and must pick one. You need a fair scorecard — that's "evaluation." 

 Prediction tasks come in two flavours: 

 Predicting a category (spam / not spam, fraud / not fraud, which team wins): this is classification . 
 Predicting a number (a stock price, how many people will buy, a movie rating): this is regression . 

 For numbers we usually score with R² or MSE ; for categories there are many scores, and "accuracy" (percentage correct) is the simplest — but use it carefully. 

 The big rule: never grade a model using the same questions it studied from. Imagine a student who memorizes last year's exam answers. Ask the same questions again and they score 100 % — but that doesn't prove they understood anything. Real life brings new questions that are never exactly like the old ones. So we must test on data the model has not seen before.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Maan lo tumhare paas kai models hain aur ek chunna hai. Iske liye ek fair scorecard chahiye — isi ko "evaluation" kehte hain. Slide 2 yahi sawaal puchhti hai: "kaun sa model/algorithm/component sabse best hai?" (jaise similarity function cosine ya correlation, ya text mein stemming/TF-IDF). 

 Prediction ke do tarah ke kaam: 

 Category predict karna (spam hai ya nahi, fraud hai ya nahi, kaun si team jeetegi) = classification . Ye "nominal" data hai (categories mein koi order nahi). 
 Number predict karna (stock price, kitne log kharidenge, movie rating) = regression . Ye "continuous / ordinal" data hai. 

 Numbers ke liye aam taur par R² ya MSE use hota hai; categories ke liye bahut options hain, aur sabse simple accuracy (kitne % sahi) hai — par isse dhyaan se use karna hai. 

 Sabse badi baat: model ko usi data par kabhi mat parkho jisse usne seekha hai. Socho ek student ne pichle saal ke paper ke answers ratt liye. Wahi sawaal dobara aaye to 100% marks, par isse ye saabit nahi hota ki usne samjha. Asli zindagi mein naye sawaal aate hain jo purane se bilkul same nahi hote. Isliye hum model ko aise data par test karte hain jo usne pehle kabhi dekha hi nahi . (Jaise 1-NN apne training data par hamesha 100% deta hai, kyunki har point ka sabse paas wala neighbor wo khud hota hai — par naye data par fail ho sakta hai.)

17-02_Overfitting_vs_Underfitting_Bias_a.topic_title: Overfitting vs. Underfitting — Bias vs. Variance
17-02_Overfitting_vs_Underfitting_Bias_a.source: Lecture 17, slide 5 ("Overfitting vs underfitting", with the instructor's "Bias vs Variance" note and the Degree 1 / Degree 4 / Degree 15 polynomial figure). Enriched with web research (bias–variance trade-off, validation curves).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Definitions (slide 5). 

 Overfitting — fitting the training data too precisely; usually leads to poor results on new data. 
 Underfitting — the model does not fit the training data well. 

 The figure. The same noisy samples (dark blue dots) come from a smooth true function (green curve). Three polynomial models (blue) are fitted: 

 Panel 
 Model 
 Behaviour 
 Bias / Variance 
 Slide's remedy 

 Degree 1 
 straight line 
 misses the curve's shape even on the training points 
 High bias, low variance → underfitting 
 Increase # of features or complexity of the model 

 Degree 4 
 gentle curve 
 follows the true function closely 
 good balance (the small top figures: "low bias, low variance") 
 — 

 Degree 15 
 very wiggly curve 
 passes through/near almost every training point but oscillates wildly between and beyond them 
 Low bias, high variance → overfitting 
 Get more training data, or reduce # of features or complexity of the model 

 The tiny top-right figures show the same story on a different dataset: "High variance" (overfitting — squiggly curve through all points), "High bias" (underfitting — flat line), "Low bias, low variance" ( good balance — smooth curve). 

 Bias vs. variance (instructor's note, with research). 

 Bias = systematic error from too-simple assumptions . A straight line can never bend to fit a parabola, no matter how much data you give it. 
 Variance = sensitivity to the particular training sample . A degree-15 curve would change drastically if a few training points changed. 
 Expected test error ≈ bias² + variance + irreducible noise . Making a model more complex lowers bias but raises variance, so there is a sweet spot — the bias–variance trade-off . 

 How to diagnose in practice (research). Compare training and validation error: 

 Symptom 
 Diagnosis 
 Fix 

 Training error high , validation error high (close together) 
 Underfitting (high bias) 
 More complex model, more/better features, less regularization 

 Training error low , validation error much higher 
 Overfitting (high variance) 
 More data, fewer features, simpler model, regularization, early stopping 

 This is exactly why training-set accuracy is untrustworthy ( L17 Why Evaluate a Model? Predictive Modeling and Performance Evaluation ): an overfit model has excellent training accuracy and poor test accuracy. Evaluation methods in the rest of this lecture exist to expose that gap. 

 Link to k-NN (Lecture 16). In k-NN, k = 1 is the overfitting end (low bias, high variance, noise-sensitive) and a very large k is the underfitting end ( L16 Issues in Nearest-Neighbor Classifiers and Choosing the Value of K ). Choosing k by cross-validation ( L17 k-Fold Cross-Validation (Stratified Ten-Fold, Repeated CV) ) finds the balance.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Imagine drawing a line through dots on a graph. 

 Underfitting: you use a plain straight ruler even though the dots clearly curve. The line is too simple — it's wrong on the dots you already have. It makes the same kind of mistake every time (that's high bias ), but it doesn't change much if you move a few dots ( low variance ). 
 Good fit: a smooth, gentle curve that follows the dots' real pattern. 
 Overfitting: you use a super-wiggly wire that touches every single dot , including the random noise. On the old dots it looks perfect, but for any new dot it swings wildly. It is too sensitive to the exact dots ( high variance ), though on average it isn't "biased" ( low bias ). 

 Cures: 

 Underfitting → make the model more powerful (more features or a more flexible model). 
 Overfitting → give it more data , or simplify it (fewer features / simpler model). 

 Think of studying: underfitting = you barely studied; overfitting = you memorized the exact practice questions including their typos; good fit = you understood the ideas.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Socho graph par kuch dots hain aur tumhe unmein se ek line/curve khinchna hai. 

 Underfitting: dots clearly curve ban rahe hain par tumne bas ek seedha scale (straight line) use kiya. Model bahut simple hai — jo dots pehle se pata hain unpe bhi galat hai. Ye hamesha ek jaisi galti karta hai ( high bias ) par dots thode idhar-udhar karo to zyada farak nahi padta ( low variance ). Slide ka Degree 1 panel. 
 Good fit: ek smooth curve jo dots ke asli pattern ko follow kare. Degree 4 panel. 
 Overfitting: tumne ek bahut wiggly taar use kiya jo har ek dot ko chhoota hai , noise ko bhi. Purane dots par perfect lagta hai, par koi naya dot aaye to wild swing karta hai. Ye dots ke exact position par bahut sensitive hai ( high variance ) par bias kam hai ( low bias ). Degree 15 panel. 

 Ilaaj (slide ke hisaab se): 

 Underfitting → model ko zyada powerful banao (zyada features ya zyada complex model). 
 Overfitting → zyada training data lo, ya model ko simple karo (kam features / kam complexity). 

 Padhai ka example: underfitting = tumne kuch padha hi nahi; overfitting = tumne practice questions typos ke saath ratt liye; good fit = tumne concepts samjhe. 

 k-NN se link (Lecture 16): k = 1 overfitting wali taraf hai, bahut bada k underfitting wali taraf. Sahi k cross-validation se milta hai.

17-03_Train_Test_Split_Large_Data_and_Va.topic_title: Evaluation on Large Data — Train/Test Split, the Three Steps, and the Validation Set
17-03_Train_Test_Split_Large_Data_and_Va.source: Lecture 17, slides 6–10 ("Evaluation on LARGE data", "Model Evaluation Step 1/2/3" diagrams, "A note on parameter tuning"). Enriched with web research (data leakage, train/validation/test roles).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Large data (slide 6). If many (thousands) of examples are available, a simple evaluation is sufficient : 

 Randomly split the data into training and test sets (e.g. 2/3 for train, 1/3 for test ). 
 For classification, make sure training and testing have a similar distribution of class labels . 
 Build a model using the train set and evaluate it using the test set. 

 The three-step picture (slides 7–9). The diagrams use a database cylinder ("Data"), a table of Results Known (the true answers, e.g. 0, 3, 2, 5, 1, …) and a "THE PAST" label (all this data comes from past, already-labelled cases): 

 Step 1 – Split the data into a Training set and a Testing set . 
 Step 2 – Build a model on the training set (the "Model Builder" box produces a model, drawn as a small decision tree). 
 Step 3 – Evaluate on the test set: the model produces Predictions (the blue column, e.g. 3, 4, 1, 2) for the held-out test cases; these are compared with the known results ("Evaluate" arrow) to compute the performance score. 

 The test set plays the role of "the future" — it must act like data the model has never seen. 

 A note on parameter tuning (slide 10). 

 It is important that the test data is not used in any way to build the model. 
 Some learning schemes work in two stages : Stage 1 builds the basic structure; Stage 2 optimizes parameter settings (for k-NN: the value of k and the distance metric — L16 Issues in Nearest-Neighbor Classifiers and Choosing the Value of K ). 
 The test data can't be used for parameter tuning! If you tune on the test set, the test score becomes an optimistic, "leaked" estimate. 
 Proper procedure uses three sets: 

 Set 
 Used for 

 Training data 
 fit the model's parameters/structure 

 Validation data 
 optimize hyper-parameters (choose k, pick between models) 

 Test data 
 final, one-time, unbiased estimate of performance 

 Worked example (illustrative). 9,000 labelled emails: take 6,000 train / 1,500 validation / 1,500 test. Train k-NN with k = 1, 3, 5, 7 on the 6,000; pick the k with the best accuracy on the 1,500 validation emails (say k = 5); finally report the accuracy of that chosen model once on the 1,500 test emails. The 2/3–1/3 split of slide 6 corresponds to 6,000/3,000 if no validation set is needed. 

 After tuning: it is common to retrain the final chosen model on train + validation data before real-world use; the test estimate then refers to that procedure.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
If you have lots of data (thousands of examples), evaluation is easy: 

 Shuffle and split your examples: roughly two-thirds to learn from (training set), one-third to be quizzed on (test set). Make sure both piles have a similar mix of answers (for example, similar numbers of spam and non-spam). 
 Teach the model using only the training pile. 
 Quiz it on the test pile: let it guess, then compare its guesses with the real answers (you already know them). 

 The test pile pretends to be "the future." 

 Important rule: the test pile must stay hidden until the very end — you may not peek at it while designing the model. Many models have settings you adjust (like how many neighbors, k). If you adjust those settings by checking the test score, you are cheating: you've indirectly studied the exam. 

 So use three piles : 

 Training – learn from it. 
 Validation – use it to choose the best settings. 
 Test – use it once , at the very end, for the honest final score.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Agar tumhare paas bahut saara data hai (hazaaron examples), to evaluation aasaan hai: 

 Data ko shuffle karke do hisson mein baanto : lagbhag 2/3 seekhne ke liye (training set) aur 1/3 test ke liye (test set) . Dhyaan rakho dono hisson mein classes ka mix similar ho (jaise spam aur non-spam dono ka ek jaisa ratio). 
 Model ko sirf training set se train karo. 
 Test set par quiz lo : model se prediction karwao aur uski guesses ko asli answers ("Results Known") se compare karo. 

 Slide 7–9 ke diagrams yahi 3 steps dikhate hain: Data → split → Model Builder → predictions → evaluate. Test set "future" ka kaam karta hai. 

 Sabse zaroori rule: test data ko model banane mein kisi bhi tarah use mat karo. Bahut se models mein settings hoti hain (jaise k-NN mein k). Agar tum test score dekh kar settings badalte ho, to ye cheating hai — jaise exam ke paper ko pehle se dekh liya. 

 Isliye teen sets use karte hain: 

 Training – isse model seekhta hai. 
 Validation – isse best settings (jaise k) chunte hain. 
 Test – sabse end mein sirf ek baar use hota hai, honest final score ke liye. 

 Example: 9,000 emails → 6,000 train, 1,500 validation, 1,500 test. Validation par k = 1,3,5,7 try karo, jo best ho (maan lo k=5) use rakho, aur phir test set par ek baar score nikaalo.

17-04_Holdout_Stratified_Sampling_and_th.topic_title: Evaluation on Small Data — Holdout, Stratified Sampling, and Why One Split Isn't Enough
17-04_Holdout_Stratified_Sampling_and_th.source: Lecture 17, slides 11–12 ("Evaluation on 'small' data, 1" and "2", with the instructor's B1…B5 block sketch and the notes "Cross-Validation → k-fold Cross Validation"). Enriched with web research (stratification, variance of a single split).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
The holdout method (slide 11). Reserve a certain amount of data for testing and use the remainder for training. Usually one third for testing, the rest for training — the same split as L17 Evaluation on Large Data — Train/Test Split, the Three Steps, and the Validation Set . 

 Problem with unbalanced datasets. With "unbalanced" data, a random sample might not be representative : there may be few or no instances of some classes in the training or test part. 

 Stratified sampling is the slide's fix — an advanced version of balancing the data : make sure each class is represented with approximately equal proportions in both subsets (i.e. the same class proportions as the full dataset). 

 Worked example (illustrative). A dataset has 90 healthy and 10 sick patients (10 % sick). A random 1/3 test set of 33 patients could by chance contain 0 sick patients, so recall on the sick class cannot even be measured. Stratified: the test set gets 33 × 0.9 ≈ 30 healthy and ≈ 3 sick; the training set gets 60 healthy and ≈ 7 sick — the 90 : 10 ratio is preserved in both. 

 Small data: one split is unreliable (slide 12). What if we have a small data set? 

 The chosen 2/3 for training may not be representative . 
 The chosen 1/3 for testing may not be representative . 

 So the score depends heavily on luck of the split : a different random split can give a quite different accuracy (high variance of the estimate). With little data we also cannot afford to waste a third of it on testing only. 

 The instructor's solution (handwriting). Draw the whole dataset as a bar cut into blocks B₁ B₂ B₃ B₄ B₅ and write → Cross-Validation → k-fold Cross Validation : let every block take a turn as the test set. This is developed fully in L17 k-Fold Cross-Validation (Stratified Ten-Fold, Repeated CV) ; a second resampling approach, the bootstrap, is in L17 The Bootstrap and Out-of-Bag Validation . 

 Summary of choices by data size. 

 Data size 
 Recommended 

 Large (thousands+) 
 Single train/test (or train/val/test) split 

 Small 
 Stratified k-fold cross-validation (often 10-fold), repeated if possible; or bootstrap 

 Imbalanced classes (any size) 
 Stratify the splits

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Holdout means: lock away a part of your data (about one third) as the "exam," and learn from the rest (two thirds). 

 Trouble 1 – uneven groups. Suppose only 10 of 100 patients are sick. If you grab a random third for the exam, by bad luck it might contain no sick patients at all — the exam can't test the one thing you care about! Stratified sampling fixes this: make sure every group (healthy, sick) appears in the same proportion in both the study pile and the exam pile. Here: roughly 30 healthy and 3 sick in the exam; 60 healthy and 7 sick in the study pile. 

 Trouble 2 – little data. If you have only a small amount of data, any single split can be unlucky: the study pile might not represent everyone, and the exam pile might be unusually easy or hard. So one score can't be trusted. 

 Solution (the teacher's sketch): cut the data into 5 blocks (B1–B5) and let each block take a turn as the exam. That's cross-validation — next topic.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Holdout ka matlab: apne data ka ek hissa (lagbhag 1/3) "exam" ke liye alag rakh do aur baaki 2/3 se seekho. 

 Pehli problem – unbalanced groups. Maan lo 100 mein se sirf 10 patients bimaar hain. Agar tum random 1/3 data test ke liye uthao, to ho sakta hai ki bad luck se usmein ek bhi bimaar patient na aaye — yaani exam us cheez ko test hi nahi kar raha jo sabse important thi! Stratified sampling iska ilaaj hai: dono hisson (train aur test) mein har class ka ratio wahi rakho jo poore data mein hai. Yahan: test mein ~30 healthy aur ~3 bimaar, train mein 60 healthy aur ~7 bimaar. 

 Doosri problem – data kam hai. Chhote data par koi bhi ek split unlucky ho sakta hai: train wala hissa sabko represent na kare, ya test wala hissa zyada aasaan/mushkil nikle. Isliye ek score par bharosa nahi kar sakte. 

 Solution (sir ne board par likha): data ko 5 blocks (B1–B5) mein todo aur har block ko ek baar test banne ka mauka do. Isi ko Cross-Validation / k-fold Cross Validation kehte hain — agla topic.

17-05_k_Fold_Cross_Validation.source: Lecture 17, slides 13–15 ("Cross-validation", "Cross-validation example" with the instructor's "10-fold CV" note, "More on cross-validation"). Enriched with web research (Kohavi 1995 study on why ten folds, leave-one-out).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Definition (slide 13). Cross-validation is more useful in small datasets ( L17 Evaluation on Small Data — Holdout, Stratified Sampling, and Why One Split Isn't Enough ). 

 Step 1: split the data into k subsets (folds) of equal size . 
 Step 2: each subset in turn is used for testing and the remainder for training — this is k-fold cross-validation . 
 For classification the subsets are often stratified before the split. 
 The error estimates are averaged to give one overall error estimate. 

 The example figure (slide 14). A row of equal boxes = the data in equal-sized groups. Hold aside one group for testing (the red box, labelled "Test") and use the rest to build the model; repeat — the red box moves one position each round (first group, …, last group). The instructor writes "10-fold CV" to mean this with k = 10. 

 Algorithm. 

 split data into k folds F1..Fk (stratified for classification)
for i in 1..k:
 train on all folds except Fi
 test on Fi -> error_i
CV error = (error_1 + ... + error_k) / k

 Worked example (illustrative, k = 5 and 10-fold sizes). 100 examples, 5-fold: each fold has 20; in every round 80 train / 20 test; every example is tested exactly once and used for training in k − 1 = 4 rounds. If the five fold accuracies are 0.80, 0.85, 0.75, 0.90, 0.80, the CV accuracy = (0.80+0.85+0.75+0.90+0.80)/5 = 0.82 . For 10-fold : 10 rounds of 90 train / 10 test. With a stratified 80 : 20 class split each fold has 8 and 2 instances of the two classes. 

 Why ten? (slide 15). Standard method for evaluation: stratified ten-fold cross-validation . Why ten? Extensive experiments have shown that this is the best choice to get an accurate estimate. (Research: this is the conclusion of Ron Kohavi's 1995 IJCAI study comparing cross-validation and bootstrap — ten-fold stratified CV gave the best bias/variance balance for model selection, even better than the more expensive leave-one-out.) The number is empirical, not a law: 5-fold is a common cheaper alternative. 

 Variance reduction (slide 15). 

 Stratification reduces the estimate's variance. 
 Repeated stratified CV is better still: e.g. ten-fold CV repeated ten times (different random fold assignments), results averaged → 100 train/test runs, reducing variance further. 

 Special case. Leave-one-out CV (LOOCV) : k = n (each fold = one instance). Nearly unbiased but costly and high-variance (research). 

 Cost and use. k-fold CV trains k models. Final deployment model is normally retrained on all the data. CV is also the standard tool for choosing hyper-parameters such as k in k-NN ( L16 Issues in Nearest-Neighbor Classifiers and Choosing the Value of K ): compute the CV error for each candidate k and keep the best. Keep any further test set separate ( L17 Evaluation on Large Data — Train/Test Split, the Three Steps, and the Validation Set ). 

 Contrast with bootstrap. CV samples without replacement — each instance sits in exactly one test fold. See L17 The Bootstrap and Out-of-Bag Validation for sampling with replacement.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
When data is scarce, a single exam can be unfair. Cross-validation gives everyone a turn . 

 Cut your data into k equal piles (say 5). 
 Round 1: pile 1 is the exam, piles 2–5 are for studying. Record the score. 
 Round 2: pile 2 is the exam, the others are for studying. Record the score. 
 … continue until every pile has been the exam once. 
 Average all the scores. That's your final, more trustworthy score. 

 Example: 100 examples in 5 piles of 20. Each round studies from 80 and is tested on 20. Scores 0.80, 0.85, 0.75, 0.90, 0.80 → average 0.82 . 

 Why 10 piles? The teacher says experiments show 10-fold gives a very reliable estimate — it's the standard choice. Two extras: stratified (every pile has the same class mix, which makes the estimate steadier) and repeated (do the whole thing 10 times with different random piles and average everything).

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Jab data kam ho to ek akela exam unfair ho sakta hai. Cross-validation mein sabko ek-ek baar mauka milta hai. 

 Data ko k barabar piles (folds) mein todo (maan lo 5). 
 Round 1: pile 1 = exam (test), piles 2–5 = padhai (train). Score likh lo. 
 Round 2: pile 2 = exam, baaki padhai. Score likh lo. 
 … jab tak har pile ek baar exam na ban jaye. 
 Saare scores ka average lo — ye hai final, zyada bharosemand score. 

 Example: 100 examples, 5 piles of 20. Har round mein 80 se seekhte hain aur 20 par test. Scores 0.80, 0.85, 0.75, 0.90, 0.80 → average = (0.80+0.85+0.75+0.90+0.80)/5 = 0.82 . Slide 14 mein lal (red) box wahi pile hai jo us round mein test hai; aage har round mein wo box khisakta jata hai. Sir ne "10-fold CV" likha hai matlab k = 10. 

 Dus hi kyun? Slide ke hisaab se bahut experiments se pata chala ki 10-fold sabse accurate estimate deta hai — isliye ye standard hai (Kohavi 1995 ki study ka bhi yahi nateeja tha). Do extra cheezein: Stratified (har pile mein class ka mix same, isse variance kam) aur Repeated (poora process 10 baar alag random piles ke saath, phir average). 

 k-NN mein sahi k chunne ke liye bhi yahi CV use hoti hai: har k ke liye CV error nikaalo, jo sabse kam ho wahi k rakho.

17-06_The_Bootstrap_and_Out_of_Bag_Valid.source: Lecture 17, slide 16 ("The bootstrap", with the instructor's "{Out of bag validation}" note, the iteration sketches and the figure comparing hold-out, K-fold and bootstrap resampling). Enriched with web research (the 63.2 % / 36.8 % result, the .632 bootstrap estimator).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Cross-validation vs. bootstrap (slide 16). 

 CV uses sampling without replacement : an instance, once selected, cannot be selected again for a particular training/test set. 
 The bootstrap uses sampling with replacement to form the training set: 
 
 Sample a dataset of n instances n times, with replacement, to form a new dataset of n instances. 
 Use this data as the training set . 
 Use the instances from the original dataset that don't occur in the new training set for testing . 

 The instructor adds "{Out of bag validation}" — those left-out test instances are called the out-of-bag (OOB) sample. His board sketch (Ist Iteration, I₂, I₃ …) shows repeating this over several iterations with different resamples. 

 The slide's figure (bottom right) contrasts three schemes: Hold-out validation (Data → Training + Validation), K-fold cross validation (Data cut into 1, 2, 3, …, K; one is the validation set each round) and Bootstrap resampling (a Data bar with a few coloured instances picked, and a "Resampled dataset" bar where those same coloured instances appear more than once ). 

 Mini-example (illustrative). Original data = {a, b, c, d, e}. Draw 5 times with replacement, e.g. b, d, b, e, a → training set {b, b, d, e, a} (b twice); out-of-bag test set = {c} (never drawn). 

 How many instances end up out-of-bag? (verified calculation + research). In one draw, an instance is not picked with probability (1 − 1/n). Over n independent draws it is never picked with probability 

 (1 − 1/n)ⁿ → e⁻¹ ≈ 0.368 as n grows. 

 Verified numerically: n = 5 → 0.328; n = 10 → 0.349; n = 100 → 0.366; n = 1000 → 0.3677. So a bootstrap training set contains on average only ≈ 63.2 % distinct original instances (1 − 0.368), and ≈ 36.8 % of the data is out-of-bag and usable for testing. 

 Because training uses only ≈ 63 % unique data , the OOB error is a bit pessimistic ; the .632 bootstrap estimator (Efron) corrects by blending: Error ≈ 0.632 × (OOB error) + 0.368 × (training/resubstitution error). Repeating the bootstrap (b = 100s of times) and averaging gives a stable estimate. Bootstrap is especially useful for very small datasets and underlies bagging / random forests , where each tree's OOB samples give a free validation score. 

 k-fold CV 
 Bootstrap 

 Sampling 
 without replacement 
 with replacement 

 Training set size 
 (k−1)/k of data 
 n draws → ≈ 63.2 % unique 

 Test instances 
 each instance tested once 
 out-of-bag ≈ 36.8 % per round 

 Typical use 
 standard accuracy/model-selection 
 very small data, ensembles 

 See also L17 k-Fold Cross-Validation (Stratified Ten-Fold, Repeated CV) .

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Another way to get "study pile" and "exam pile" from a small dataset is the bootstrap . 

 Idea: imagine your data are names written on slips in a bag. To make a study pile of the same size as your data, pull a slip, write its name down, and put it back — then repeat until you've pulled as many times as there are slips. Because you put each slip back, the same name can show up several times , and some names never show up. 

 The study pile = everything you pulled (with repeats). 
 The exam pile = the names that never got pulled (called out of bag ). 

 Example: names {a, b, c, d, e}; pulls give b, d, b, e, a → study with {b, b, d, e, a}; exam on {c}. 

 Fun fact: with a large dataset, about 63 % of the different names get picked at least once and about 37 % are left out — that's the exam pile. (The math: the chance a name is never picked is about 1/e ≈ 0.368.) 

 Cross-validation never repeats an example in a pile; the bootstrap does — that's the key difference.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Chhote data se "study pile" aur "exam pile" banane ka ek aur tareeka hai — bootstrap . 

 Idea: socho tumhare data ke naam parchiyon par likhe hain aur ek thaile mein hain. Training set banane ke liye: ek parchi nikalo, naam likho, aur parchi wapas thaile mein daal do — ye utni baar karo jitni parchiyan hain (n baar). Kyunki parchi wapas daal rahe ho, ek hi naam kai baar aa sakta hai aur kuch naam kabhi nahi aate. 

 Training set = jo bhi nikla (repeats ke saath). 
 Test set = jo naam kabhi nahi nikle — isse out-of-bag (OOB) kehte hain (sir ne "Out of bag validation" likha hai). 

 Example: data {a, b, c, d, e}; nikle b, d, b, e, a → training {b, b, d, e, a}; test {c}. 

 Interesting fact: bade data mein lagbhag 63% alag-alag examples kam se kam ek baar chun jate hain aur lagbhag 37% bach jate hain (wahi test set). Math: kisi naam ke kabhi na chunne ki probability (1 − 1/n)ⁿ ≈ 1/e ≈ 0.368 hoti hai (hamne n = 5, 10, 100, 1000 par check kiya: 0.328, 0.349, 0.366, 0.368). 

 Cross-validation vs bootstrap: CV mein koi example ek pile mein repeat nahi hota ( without replacement ); bootstrap mein hota hai ( with replacement ) — yahi asli farak hai.

17-07_Performance_Metrics_Overview_and_R.topic_title: Performance Metrics Overview and Regression Metrics (MAE, MSE, RMSE, R²)
17-07_Performance_Metrics_Overview_and_R.source: Lecture 17, slides 17–20 (the three-part "Outline" shown twice, "Metrics", and the instructor's handwritten "Regression Metrics" page: MAE, MSE, RMSE, R²). Independently re-verified with a worked example; enriched with web research (MAE vs. RMSE, negative R², normalized errors).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Outline (slides 17–18). The lecture's second half announces three parts: 1. Metrics, 2. Precision and recall, 3. Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves. (Slide 18 is a repeat of the same outline.) In this PDF only part 1 is actually delivered — precision/recall and ROC curves do not appear (the deck ends at the confusion matrix) and are presumably in the next lecture. The stray "17 /14" / "18 /14" / "19 /14" page marks on these slides are leftovers from the original deck and mean nothing. 

 Why metrics (slide 19). It is extremely important to use quantitative metrics for evaluating a machine learning model. Until now we relied on the cost-function value for regression and classification (see the least-squares cost in L13 The Least Squares Method — Formula and Worked Example (Exam Grades) ). Other metrics help to better evaluate and understand the model: 

 Classification: Accuracy / Precision / Recall / F1-score, ROC curves, … ( L17 The Confusion Matrix — TP, TN, FP, FN is the foundation). 
 Regression: Normalized RMSE, Normalized Mean Absolute Error (NMAE), … 

 Regression metrics (slide 20, handwritten). Let there be N test examples, yⱼ = actual value and ŷⱼ = predicted value , ȳ = mean of the actual values . 

 # 
 Metric 
 Formula 
 Notes 

 ① 
 MAE — Mean Absolute Error 
 (1/N) Σⱼ |yⱼ − ŷⱼ| 
 Average size of the error, in the same units as y; every error counts linearly 

 ② 
 MSE — Mean Squared Error 
 (1/N) Σⱼ (yⱼ − ŷⱼ)² 
 Squares errors, so big mistakes are penalized heavily; units are y² 

 ③ 
 RMSE — Root Mean Squared Error 
 √[ (1/N) Σⱼ (yⱼ − ŷⱼ)² ] = √MSE 
 Back in the units of y 

 ④ 
 R² (coefficient of determination) 
 1 − Σⱼ (yⱼ − ŷⱼ)² / Σⱼ (yⱼ − ȳ)² 
 "Close to 1" is good (instructor's note) 

 ⚠️ Slide-correction (flagged). The handwritten RMSE line shows √(Σ (yⱼ − ŷⱼ)²) with no 1/N . RMSE is by definition the square root of the mean squared error, i.e. with 1/N (as in ② MSE ③ = √MSE). Without 1/N the value would be inflated by √N — see the check below. Treat the 1/N as omitted by hand. 

 Worked example (our own, verified). Actual y = [3, 5, 2, 7]; predicted ŷ = [2.5, 5, 4, 8]. 

 Errors (y − ŷ) = [0.5, 0, −2, −1]; absolute = [0.5, 0, 2, 1]; squared = [0.25, 0, 4, 1]. 
 MAE = (0.5 + 0 + 2 + 1)/4 = 3.5/4 = 0.875 
 MSE = (0.25 + 0 + 4 + 1)/4 = 5.25/4 = 1.3125 
 RMSE = √1.3125 ≈ 1.1456 (without the 1/N the formula would wrongly give √5.25 ≈ 2.2913 = 1.1456 × √4) 
 ȳ = (3+5+2+7)/4 = 4.25; SS_tot = Σ(y − ȳ)² = 1.5625 + 0.5625 + 5.0625 + 7.5625 = 14.75; SS_res = 5.25 
 R² = 1 − 5.25/14.75 = 0.644 (≈ 64 % of the variance explained) 

 Reading the metrics (research). 

 MAE vs. RMSE: RMSE ≥ MAE always; the more RMSE exceeds MAE, the more the errors are dominated by a few large mistakes (RMSE is more sensitive to outliers; MAE is more robust). Here 1.1456 vs 0.875 is mostly due to the single −2 error. 
 R² = 1 → perfect; R² = 0 → no better than always predicting the mean ȳ; R² < 0 is possible on test data → worse than predicting the mean . (E.g. predicting 10 for every example above gives R² ≈ −8.97.) "Close to 1" is therefore good, but only on test data ( L17 Why Evaluate a Model? Predictive Modeling and Performance Evaluation ). 
 Normalized versions (slide 19: NRMSE, NMAE): divide RMSE or MAE by a reference scale — the range (max − min) of y, the mean of y, or the standard deviation of y — to get a unit-free number comparable across datasets. For the example above, range = 7 − 2 = 5, so NRMSE(range) = 1.1456/5 ≈ 0.229 and NMAE(range) = 0.875/5 = 0.175 . (The slide names but does not define them; the choice of normalizer must be stated.)

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Last time we said "how good is the model?" — now we need numbers for that. For predicting numbers (regression) there are four classic scores. Let "actual" be the true value and "predicted" be the model's guess. 

 MAE (Mean Absolute Error): for each example, find how far off the guess was (ignore the + or − sign) and average those gaps. "On average I'm off by 0.875." 
 MSE (Mean Squared Error): square each gap first, then average. Big mistakes become huge after squaring, so MSE punishes them. 
 RMSE: take the square root of MSE to get back to the original units. (The slide forgot to divide by N in this line; it should be square-root of the average .) 
 R²: compares your model with a lazy model that always guesses the average . R² near 1 = great; 0 = no better than the lazy average guess; negative = even worse than the lazy guess. 

 Example: actual [3, 5, 2, 7], guesses [2.5, 5, 4, 8] → gaps 0.5, 0, 2, 1. 

 MAE = 3.5 ÷ 4 = 0.875 
 MSE = (0.25 + 0 + 4 + 1) ÷ 4 = 1.3125 
 RMSE = √1.3125 ≈ 1.146 
 R² = 1 − 5.25 ÷ 14.75 ≈ 0.64 

 Normalized versions divide by a "typical size" of the data (like its range) so you can compare across problems with different units. 

 The lecture also promises two more topics ( precision/recall and ROC curves ), but they are not in this PDF.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Pehle humne kaha "model kitna accha hai?" — ab iske liye numbers chahiye. Number predict karne wale (regression) models ke liye 4 classic scores hain. "Actual" = asli value, "Predicted" = model ka guess. 

 MAE (Mean Absolute Error): har example mein guess kitna door tha (+/− sign ignore karke) nikalo aur sabka average lo. "Mera guess average mein 0.875 se galat hai." 
 MSE (Mean Squared Error): pehle har gap ka square karo, phir average. Bade errors square hone par bahut bade ho jaate hain, isliye MSE unhe zyada sazaa deta hai. 
 RMSE: MSE ka square root , taaki wapas original unit mein aa jaye. (⚠️ Sir ke handwritten formula mein 1/N likhna reh gaya hai; sahi formula √(average of squared errors) hai.) 
 R²: tumhare model ko ek aalsi model se compare karta hai jo hamesha average hi bolta hai. R² 1 ke paas = bahut accha; 0 = aalsi average se behtar nahi; negative = aalsi guess se bhi bura. 

 Example: actual [3, 5, 2, 7], guesses [2.5, 5, 4, 8] → gaps 0.5, 0, 2, 1. 

 MAE = 3.5 ÷ 4 = 0.875 
 MSE = (0.25 + 0 + 4 + 1) ÷ 4 = 1.3125 
 RMSE = √1.3125 ≈ 1.146 (agar 1/N bhool jao to galat 2.29 aata hai!) 
 R² = 1 − 5.25 ÷ 14.75 ≈ 0.64 

 Normalized versions (NRMSE, NMAE) mein error ko data ke "typical size" (jaise range = max − min) se divide karte hain taaki alag units wale problems compare ho sakein. Is example mein range = 5, to NRMSE ≈ 0.229. 

 Slide 17–18 ke outline mein precision/recall aur ROC curve ka bhi zikr hai, par wo is PDF mein nahi hain (shayad agli lecture mein).

17-08_Confusion_Matrix_TP_TN_FP_FN.topic_title: The Confusion Matrix — TP, TN, FP, FN
17-08_Confusion_Matrix_TP_TN_FP_FN.source: Lecture 17, slide 21 ("Confusion Matrix", with the instructor's red annotations: TP/TN/FP/FN, "True labels", "predicted", D = disease, ND = no disease). Enriched with a worked example and web-researched context (Type I / Type II errors, accuracy pitfall on imbalanced data).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Definition (slide 21). A confusion matrix is a table that is often used to describe the performance of a classification model (or "classifier") on a set of test data ( L17 Evaluation on Large Data — Train/Test Split, the Three Steps, and the Validation Set ). 

 The four outcomes (the slide uses a disease-test story). 

 Term 
 Meaning (slide) 

 True Positive (TP) 
 We predicted positive (they have the disease), and they do have the disease. 

 True Negative (TN) 
 We predicted negative , and they don't have the disease. 

 False Positive (FP) 
 We predicted positive , but they don't actually have the disease. Also known as a "Type I error." 

 False Negative (FN) 
 We predicted negative , but they actually do have the disease. Also known as a "Type II error." 

 The table layout (slide). Columns = Actual (the instructor writes "True labels": D = disease/positive, ND = no disease/negative). Rows = Predicted ( D / ND ): 

 Actual: Positive (D) 
 Actual: Negative (ND) 

 Predicted: Positive (D) 
 TP 
 FP 

 Predicted: Negative (ND) 
 FN 
 TN 

 The correct decisions (TP and TN) lie on the main diagonal (circled on the slide); errors (FP, FN) are off-diagonal. ⚠️ Layout conventions differ between books and libraries — some put Actual on the rows. Always read the labels, not the position. 

 Memory trick (research). Read each name as (was the prediction right?) + (what did we predict?) : "True Positive" = right, predicted positive; "False Negative" = wrong, predicted negative. 

 Which error is worse depends on the task. In disease screening a FN (missing a sick patient) is usually more dangerous than a FP (an extra test); for a spam filter a FP (real mail marked spam) is often worse than a FN. 

 Worked example (illustrative, verified). A screening test on 100 patients gives TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 5, TN = 45 (so 45 actually sick = 40 + 5; 55 healthy = 10 + 45). 

 Actual D 
 Actual ND 

 Predicted D 
 40 
 10 

 Predicted ND 
 5 
 45 

 Correct = TP + TN = 85 → accuracy = (TP + TN)/(TP + TN + FP + FN) = 85/100 = 0.85 . 
 Errors: 10 false alarms (Type I) and 5 misses (Type II). 

 Why "accuracy, with caution" (slide 4). Accuracy alone can mislead when classes are imbalanced: if only 10 of 1,000 patients are sick, a useless model that says "healthy" for everyone has TP = 0, FP = 0, FN = 10, TN = 990 → accuracy = 990/1000 = 99 % , yet it finds none of the sick patients. The confusion matrix reveals this; this is why further metrics — precision, recall, F1-score and ROC curves , announced in the outline ( L17 Performance Metrics Overview and Regression Metrics (MAE, MSE, RMSE, R²) ) but not covered in this PDF — are all built from TP, FP, FN, TN. 

 Connection. Every classifier from earlier lectures — L15 Worked Example — Logistic Regression for Exam Pass Probability (after the 0.5 threshold) and k-NN from Lecture 16 — can be evaluated with a confusion matrix on its test set; with cross-validation ( L17 k-Fold Cross-Validation (Stratified Ten-Fold, Repeated CV) ) you can sum or average the matrices across folds.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
A confusion matrix is a small 2×2 scoreboard showing how a yes/no predictor got things right and wrong. Think of a medical test for a disease. 

 True Positive (TP): test says "sick" and the person is sick. ✅ 
 True Negative (TN): test says "healthy" and the person is healthy. ✅ 
 False Positive (FP): test says "sick" but the person is healthy — a false alarm (also called Type I error). ❌ 
 False Negative (FN): test says "healthy" but the person is sick — a miss (Type II error). ❌ 

 Draw it as a table: columns = the truth , rows = the prediction . Good answers sit on the diagonal (TP and TN); mistakes are in the other two boxes. 

 Example with 100 people: 40 correctly flagged sick, 45 correctly cleared, 10 false alarms, 5 missed. Correct = 40 + 45 = 85 → accuracy 85 %. 

 Warning: accuracy can hide problems. If 99 % of people are healthy, a lazy test that says "healthy" to everyone is 99 % accurate — but misses every sick person. The scoreboard shows this at once (0 TP). That is why people also use precision, recall and other scores built from these four numbers.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Confusion matrix ek chhota 2×2 scoreboard hai jo dikhata hai ki ek yes/no predictor ne kahan sahi aur kahan galat kiya. Ek bimaari ke medical test ka example lo (slide mein bhi yahi hai). 

 True Positive (TP): test ne bola "bimaar hai" aur banda sach mein bimaar hai. ✅ 
 True Negative (TN): test ne bola "theek hai" aur banda sach mein theek hai. ✅ 
 False Positive (FP): test ne bola "bimaar hai" par banda theek hai — false alarm (ise Type I error kehte hain). ❌ 
 False Negative (FN): test ne bola "theek hai" par banda bimaar hai — chhoot gaya / miss ( Type II error ). ❌ 

 Table aise banta hai: columns = asli sach (True labels: D = disease, ND = no disease) aur rows = prediction . Sahi jawab diagonal par (TP aur TN) aate hain, galtiyan baaki do boxes mein. 

 Example (100 log): 40 bimaar sahi pakde (TP), 45 theek logon ko sahi clear kiya (TN), 10 false alarm (FP), 5 bimaar chhoot gaye (FN). Sahi = 40 + 45 = 85 → accuracy = 85% . 

 ⚠️ Dhyaan: accuracy kabhi-kabhi dhokha deti hai. Agar 99% log theek hain aur ek aalsi test sabko "theek" bol deta hai, to wo 99% accurate hai — par ek bhi bimaar nahi pakadta (TP = 0). Confusion matrix ye turant dikha deta hai. Isiliye slide 4 mein likha tha ki accuracy "with caution" use karo, aur isiliye precision, recall, F1 aur ROC jaise scores bhi hote hain (jo in chaaron numbers se hi bante hain). 

 Yaad rakhne ka trick: pehla shabd (True/False) batata hai ki prediction sahi thi ya galat , doosra shabd (Positive/Negative) batata hai ki model ne kya predict kiya .

18-00_Recap_Confusion_Matrix_and_the_Sic.topic_title: Recap — The Confusion Matrix and the "Sick People" Intuition
18-00_Recap_Confusion_Matrix_and_the_Sic.source: Lecture 18, slides 1–2 (slide 1 repeats Lecture 17's "Confusion Matrix" slide word for word; slide 2 is the instructor's handwritten re-explanation). Recap note — the full definitions already live in Topic 8 (Confusion Matrix) of Lecture 17.

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 1 = Lecture 17, slide 21, verbatim. A confusion matrix is a table often used to describe the performance of a classification model on a set of test data. The four outcomes (TP, TN, FP, FN, with FP = Type I error and FN = Type II error) and the table layout are exactly as in L17 The Confusion Matrix — TP, TN, FP, FN — not repeated here. 

 Slide 2 (new, handwritten) — what each box means in plain words. The instructor draws the matrix with Actual values across the top (+ve, −ve) and Predicted values down the side (+ve, −ve), and annotates each cell with a sentence: 

 Cell 
 Instructor's sentence 

 TP (predicted +, actual +) 
 Sick people correctly predicted as sick by the model 

 FP (predicted +, actual −) 
 Healthy people incorrectly predicted as sick by the model 

 FN (predicted −, actual +) 
 Sick people incorrectly predicted as not sick by the model 

 TN (predicted −, actual −) 
 Healthy people correctly predicted as not sick by the model 

 A second, smaller copy of the matrix at the bottom (rows "Predicted", columns "Actual") draws loops linking TP with TN (the two correct cells — the main diagonal) and the other pair FP, FN (the two errors ). 

 Rule of reading (consistent with the slide's layout). The second word (Positive/Negative) is what the model said ; the first word (True/False) says whether the model was right . This lecture builds all of its formulas from these four numbers: L18 Classification Metrics — Accuracy, Precision, Recall (Sensitivity), F1-Score .

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
This slide is a reminder of the 2×2 scoreboard from last lecture, with the teacher's plain-language labels (imagine a medical test): 

 TP: a sick person, and the test says "sick." Correct. ✅ 
 TN: a healthy person, and the test says "healthy." Correct. ✅ 
 FP: a healthy person, but the test says "sick." A false alarm. ❌ 
 FN: a sick person, but the test says "healthy." A miss. ❌ 

 The two correct boxes (TP, TN) lie on one diagonal; the two mistake boxes (FP, FN) on the other. Everything else in this lecture is just different ways of combining these four counts.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Ye slide pichli lecture ke 2×2 scoreboard ka recap hai, aur sir ne har box ko seedhi bhasha mein likha hai (medical test socho): 

 TP: banda bimaar hai aur test ne bola "bimaar" → sahi ✅ 
 TN: banda theek hai aur test ne bola "theek" → sahi ✅ 
 FP: banda theek hai par test ne bola "bimaar" → false alarm ❌ (Type I error) 
 FN: banda bimaar hai par test ne bola "theek" → chhoot gaya ❌ (Type II error) 

 Do sahi boxes (TP, TN) ek diagonal par hain, aur do galti wale boxes (FP, FN) dusre diagonal par. Is lecture ka baaki sab kuch inhi chaar counts ko alag-alag tareeke se combine karna hai. Poori definition ke liye Lecture 17 ka Confusion Matrix topic dekho. 

 Yaad rakhne ka trick: doosra shabd (Positive/Negative) = model ne kya bola ; pehla shabd (True/False) = model sahi tha ya galat .

18-01_Classification_Metrics_Accuracy_Pr.topic_title: Classification Metrics — Accuracy, Precision, Recall (Sensitivity), F1-Score
18-01_Classification_Metrics_Accuracy_Pr.source: Lecture 18, slide 3 (the instructor's handwritten page: left half "Classification Metrics" ①–④, right half "Regression Metrics"). Enriched with web research (harmonic mean, F-beta, precision–recall trade-off).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 3 is a two-column page. The right column ("Regression Metrics": MAE, MSE, RMSE, R²) is a verbatim repeat of Lecture 17, slide 20 — see L17 Performance Metrics Overview and Regression Metrics (MAE, MSE, RMSE, R²) (including the note that the handwritten RMSE is missing its 1/N). The left column is new: four classification metrics, all computed from the confusion matrix ( L18 Recap — The Confusion Matrix and the "Sick People" Intuition ). 

 # 
 Metric 
 Formula (slide) 
 In words 

 ① 
 Accuracy 
 (No. of correct predictions) / (Total no. of predictions) = (TP + TN) / (TP + FP + TN + FN) (the longer form appears on slide 6) 
 Fraction of all predictions that were right 

 ② 
 Precision (P) 
 TP / (TP + FP) 
 Of everything the model called positive , how much really was positive? 

 ③ 
 Recall (R) — "Sensitivity measure" 
 TP / (TP + FN) ; the instructor marks its range (0, 1) 
 Of everything that really is positive , how much did the model find? 

 ④ 
 F1-score 
 Harmonic mean of Precision & Recall = 2 × (P × R)/(P + R) 
 A single number that is high only when both P and R are high 

 What each denominator is. 

 Precision's denominator TP + FP = all predicted positive (the first row of the matrix). 
 Recall's denominator TP + FN = all actually positive (the first column ). 
 Accuracy's denominator = everything. 

 Why the harmonic mean (research). The F1-score uses the harmonic , not arithmetic, mean because the harmonic mean is dragged toward the smaller of the two numbers. Example: P = 1.0 and R = 0.1 → arithmetic mean = 0.55 (sounds okay), harmonic mean = 2 × 0.1 / 1.1 = 0.182 (honestly reflects a model that misses 90 % of positives). A model with P = 1, R = 0 gets F1 = 0, not 0.5. An equivalent form (verified): F1 = 2TP / (2TP + FP + FN) . 

 Precision vs. recall — they pull against each other (research). Most classifiers output a score and apply a threshold ( L15 The Sigmoid Function and the Decision Boundary , the 0.5 cut-off). Lowering the threshold flags more cases → recall rises, precision usually falls (more false alarms). Raising it does the reverse. F1 summarizes the balance; the F-beta family (F₂ weights recall more, F₀.₅ weights precision more) tilts it when one error type is costlier — see L18 Choosing the Right Metric — Imbalance, Trade-offs, and Extensions (F-beta, Balanced Accuracy, MCC) . 

 Worked check (using Lecture 17's 100-patient example, TP = 40, FP = 10, FN = 5, TN = 45). 

 Accuracy = 85/100 = 0.85 
 Precision = 40/50 = 0.80 
 Recall = 40/45 = 0.889 
 F1 = 2(0.80)(0.889)/(0.80 + 0.889) = 0.842 (= 2·40/(80 + 10 + 5) = 80/95 ✓) 

 The accuracy trap revisited. In the "say everyone is healthy" example (TP = 0, FP = 0, FN = 10, TN = 990) accuracy is 99 % but recall = 0/10 = 0 and F1 = 0 — which is exactly what these new metrics are for.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
After the 2×2 scoreboard, here are four scores built from it. Think of a doctor's test for a disease. 

 Accuracy — "Out of everyone tested, how many did the test get right?" (correct ÷ total). 
 Precision — "When the test says 'sick' , how often is it right?" = TP ÷ (TP + FP). High precision means few false alarms. 
 Recall (also called sensitivity ) — "Out of everyone who really is sick , how many did the test catch?" = TP ÷ (TP + FN). High recall means few misses. It's always between 0 and 1. 
 F1-score — one number mixing precision and recall: 2 × (P × R) ÷ (P + R). It uses a special "harmonic" average which punishes you if either score is poor. (Precision 1.0 but recall 0.1 gives only 0.18, not 0.55.) 

 Example (100 patients: TP 40, FP 10, FN 5, TN 45): accuracy 0.85, precision 40 ÷ 50 = 0.80, recall 40 ÷ 45 = 0.89, F1 = 0.84. 

 There's a tug-of-war: if you make the test "more eager" to say sick, you catch more sick people (recall ↑) but raise more false alarms (precision ↓). 

 (The right side of the slide, regression scores, was already covered last lecture.)

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
2×2 scoreboard ke baad ab chaar scores aate hain (doctor ke disease-test ka example socho): 

 Accuracy — "Jitne logon ko test kiya, unme se kitno ka test ne sahi answer diya?" = sahi ÷ total. 
 Precision — "Jab test 'bimaar' bolta hai , to kitni baar sahi hota hai?" = TP ÷ (TP + FP). Precision zyada = false alarm kam. 
 Recall (isse sensitivity bhi kehte hain) — "Jo log sach mein bimaar hain, unme se test ne kitno ko pakda?" = TP ÷ (TP + FN). Recall zyada = miss kam. Iski value hamesha 0 se 1 ke beech hoti hai (sir ne (0,1) likha hai). 
 F1-score — precision aur recall ko mila kar ek number: 2 × (P × R) ÷ (P + R). Ye harmonic mean hai, jo tab hi bada hota hai jab dono achhe hon. (Precision 1.0 par recall 0.1 ho to F1 sirf 0.18 aata hai, 0.55 nahi.) 

 Example (100 patients: TP 40, FP 10, FN 5, TN 45): accuracy 0.85, precision 40 ÷ 50 = 0.80 , recall 40 ÷ 45 = 0.89 , F1 = 0.84 . 

 Ek tug-of-war hota hai: agar test ko zyada "jaldi bimaar bolne wala" bana do, to zyada bimaar pakde jaate hain (recall ↑) par false alarm bhi badhte hain (precision ↓). 

 Slide ke daayein taraf ke regression metrics (MAE, MSE, RMSE, R²) pichli lecture (17) mein ho chuke hain.

18-02_Precision_and_Recall_Document_Retr.topic_title: Precision and Recall — The Document-Retrieval Venn Diagram
18-02_Precision_and_Recall_Document_Retr.source: Lecture 18, slide 4 ("Precision and Recall": Venn diagram over the "Space of all documents", recall and precision formulas in words). Enriched with web research (Cranfield experiments, medical vs. retrieval vocabulary).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
The picture. A rectangle = the space of all documents . Inside it two overlapping circles: 

 the Relevant circle (documents that truly match the user's need), 
 the Retrieved circle (documents the system returned), 
 their overlap = Relevant + Retrieved , 
 everything outside both circles = Not Relevant + Not Retrieved . 

 Formulas (slide). 

 recall = (Number of relevant documents retrieved) / (Total number of relevant documents) 
 precision = (Number of relevant documents retrieved) / (Total number of documents retrieved) 

 Mapping to the confusion matrix ( L18 Recap — The Confusion Matrix and the "Sick People" Intuition ): 

 Venn region 
 Confusion-matrix term 

 Relevant + Retrieved (overlap) 
 TP 

 Retrieved but not relevant 
 FP 

 Relevant but not retrieved 
 FN 

 Not relevant + not retrieved (outside both circles) 
 TN 

 Hence: relevant retrieved = TP; total retrieved = TP + FP; total relevant = TP + FN. So the slide's two formulas are exactly precision = TP/(TP + FP) and recall = TP/(TP + FN) from L18 Classification Metrics — Accuracy, Precision, Recall (Sensitivity), F1-Score — same idea, search-engine vocabulary. This also links to this course's opening question in Lecture 17 slide 2: "how far down the list will a user need to look to find some/all relevant documents?" ( L17 Why Evaluate a Model? Predictive Modeling and Performance Evaluation ). 

 Worked example (illustrative). A library holds 1,000 documents; 20 are relevant to a query. The system retrieves 40 documents, of which 15 are relevant. 

 TP = 15, FP = 40 − 15 = 25, FN = 20 − 15 = 5, TN = 1000 − 15 − 25 − 5 = 955. 
 Precision = 15/40 = 0.375 ; Recall = 15/20 = 0.75 . 
 Note TN = 955 is huge but neither formula uses it — in retrieval the vast ocean of irrelevant, unretrieved documents carries little information, which is why precision/recall (and not accuracy: (15 + 955)/1000 = 97 %) are used. 

 Origin (research). Recall and precision came out of the Cranfield experiments (1958–1966) led by Cyril Cleverdon at the College of Aeronautics, Cranfield, England — the first systematic evaluation of retrieval systems using a test collection of queries and known relevant documents. Later, C. J. van Rijsbergen (1979) derived the F-measure as a weighted harmonic mean of the two. 

 Same ideas, medical names (research). Recall = sensitivity = true-positive rate; precision = positive predictive value (PPV) . Medicine also tracks specificity (true negatives), which retrieval ignores — see L18 Worked Exercise — Predicting Man vs. Woman from a Photograph and L18 Summaries of the Confusion Matrix — The Full Table of Rates .

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Imagine a giant pile of all documents in a library. You search for "dog training." 

 Some documents truly match your need — the Relevant circle. 
 Your search engine hands you a bunch — the Retrieved circle. 
 Where the two circles overlap are the good results you actually received . 
 Everything outside both circles was both irrelevant and (rightly) not shown. 

 Two questions to judge the search engine: 

 Precision: "Of the pages it gave me, how many were actually useful?" → (useful pages given) ÷ (all pages given). 
 Recall: "Of all the useful pages that exist, how many did it manage to give me?" → (useful pages given) ÷ (all useful pages that exist). 

 Example: 20 useful documents exist; the engine shows 40 pages, 15 of them useful. Precision = 15 ÷ 40 = 0.375 (lots of junk); recall = 15 ÷ 20 = 0.75 (found three-quarters of the good ones). 

 This is the same as the confusion matrix: "useful and shown" = TP, "junk shown" = FP, "useful but hidden" = FN.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Socho ek library hai jisme saare documents ka dher hai. Tum "dog training" search karte ho. 

 Kuch documents sach mein tumhare kaam ke hain — Relevant circle. 
 Search engine ne tumhe kuch documents diye — Retrieved circle. 
 Jahan dono circles overlap karte hain, wo kaam ke results jo tumhe mile (Relevant + Retrieved) = TP . 
 Dono circles ke bahar sab kuch: na kaam ka tha, na dikhaya gaya = TN . 

 Search engine ko judge karne ke do sawaal: 

 Precision: "Jo pages mujhe diye gaye, unme se kitne kaam ke the?" = (kaam ke diye gaye pages) ÷ (kul diye gaye pages). 
 Recall: "Jitne kaam ke pages exist karte hain, unme se kitne mujhe mile?" = (kaam ke diye gaye pages) ÷ (kul kaam ke pages). 

 Example: 20 kaam ke documents hain; engine ne 40 pages dikhaye jisme 15 kaam ke. TP = 15, FP = 25, FN = 5. Precision = 15 ÷ 40 = 0.375 (kachra zyada), Recall = 15 ÷ 20 = 0.75 (3/4 achhe pages mil gaye). 

 Ye wahi confusion matrix hai: "kaam ka aur dikhaya" = TP, "kachra dikhaya" = FP, "kaam ka par nahi dikhaya" = FN. Dhyaan do: yahan TN = 955 bahut bada hai par formula mein use hi nahi hota — isiliye retrieval mein accuracy (97%) bekaar hai aur precision/recall use hote hain. 

 History: ye idea 1958–66 ke Cranfield experiments (Cyril Cleverdon) se aaya. Medical mein recall ko sensitivity aur precision ko PPV kehte hain.

18-03_Worked_Exercise_Man_vs_Woman_Photo.topic_title: Worked Exercise — Predicting Man vs. Woman from a Photograph
18-03_Worked_Exercise_Man_vs_Woman_Photo.source: Lecture 18, slides 5–9 (the exercise statement, "Woman as Positive class (P), Man as Negative class (N)", the 10-row Expected/Predicted table, Step 1 count of TP/TN/FP/FN, the confusion matrix, and the instructor's A, P, R, S / F1 notes). sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Exercise (slide 5). Consider a two-class classification problem of predicting whether a photograph contains a man or a woman. Suppose we have a test dataset of 10 records with expected outcomes and a set of predictions from our classification algorithm. (a) Compute the confusion matrix . (b) Compute the accuracy, precision, recall, sensitivity and specificity . 

 Class convention (slide 6). Woman = Positive class (P); Man = Negative class (N). (The choice is arbitrary but must be fixed first — see the swap check below.) 

 Data and Step 1 (slides 5, 8). Each row is labelled by comparing Expected with Predicted :

 TN

 woman (P)

 woman (P)

 woman (P) 
 TP 

 8 
 man (N)

 Counts (slide 9, re-verified): TP = 4 (rows 3, 6, 7, 10), TN = 3 (rows 2, 4, 8), FP = 2 (rows 1, 9), FN = 1 (row 5). Total 10 ✓. Actual women = 5 (TP + FN), actual men = 5 (TN + FP). 

 (a) Confusion matrix (the instructor's handwritten 4 / 2 / 1 / 3 grid, rows = predicted, columns = actual): 

 Actual: woman (P) 
 Actual: man (N) 

 Predicted: woman (P) 
 TP = 4 
 FP = 2 

 Predicted: man (N) 
 FN = 1 
 TN = 3 

 (b) Metrics (formulas from L18 Classification Metrics — Accuracy, Precision, Recall (Sensitivity), F1-Score ; the instructor's margin notes: "Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1" and, on slide 5, "Specificity = TN/(TN + FP)" and "Sensitivity = TP/(TP + FN) — true positive rate", "True negative rate"): 

 Metric 
 Formula 
 Calculation 
 Result 

 Accuracy 
 (TP + TN)/(TP + FP + TN + FN) 
 (4 + 3)/10 
 0.70 (70 %) 

 Precision 
 TP/(TP + FP) 
 4/(4 + 2) 
 0.667 

 Recall 
 TP/(TP + FN) 
 4/(4 + 1) 
 0.80 

 Sensitivity (TPR) 
 TP/(TP + FN) 
 4/5 
 0.80 — identical to recall 

 Specificity (TNR)

 3/(3 + 2) 
 0.60 

 F1-score 
 2PR/(P + R) 
 2(0.667)(0.8)/(1.467) 
 0.727 (= 2·4/(8 + 2 + 1) = 8/11 ✓) 

 Observations. 

 Sensitivity and recall are the same quantity under two names (medicine vs. information retrieval). The exercise asks for both only to make this point. 
 The model is better at finding women (recall 0.80) than at correctly rejecting men (specificity 0.60): of 5 men it falsely called 2 "woman". 
 Accuracy 0.70 alone hides this asymmetry — and the other 4 numbers differ a lot. 

 Swap check — the class of interest matters. If instead man is the positive class, TP/TN and FP/FN swap roles: TP = 3, TN = 4, FP = 1, FN = 2 → accuracy 0.70 (unchanged), precision = 3/4 = 0.75 , recall = 3/5 = 0.60 , specificity = 4/5 = 0.80 , F1 = 6/9 = 0.667 . Accuracy is symmetric, but precision, recall, specificity and F1 are not — always state which class is "positive" ( L18 Summaries of the Confusion Matrix — The Full Table of Rates : "depending on the class of interest"). 

 Other quantities for this exercise (from the summary table, verified). FPR = 2/5 = 0.40, FNR = 1/5 = 0.20, NPV = 3/4 = 0.75, FDR = 2/6 = 0.333, balanced accuracy = (0.8 + 0.6)/2 = 0.70.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The task: a program looks at 10 photos and says "woman" or "man." We know the real answers. We call "woman" the positive class and "man" the negative class. 

 Step 1 – mark every photo: 

 Said woman and it was a woman → TP (photos 3, 6, 7, 10) = 4 
 Said man and it was a man → TN (photos 2, 4, 8) = 3 
 Said woman but it was a man → FP (photos 1, 9) = 2 
 Said man but it was a woman → FN (photo 5) = 1 

 Confusion matrix: top row (said woman): 4 correct, 2 wrong; bottom row (said man): 1 wrong, 3 correct. 

 Scores: 

 Accuracy = 7 correct out of 10 = 0.70 
 Precision = of the 6 times it said "woman," 4 were right = 4 ÷ 6 = 0.67 
 Recall / Sensitivity = of the 5 real women, it found 4 = 4 ÷ 5 = 0.80 (these two names mean the same thing) 
 Specificity = of the 5 real men, it correctly called 3 "man" = 3 ÷ 5 = 0.60 
 F1 = mix of precision and recall = 0.73 

 Notice: if we had picked "man" as the positive class, the scores change (precision 0.75, recall 0.60, …) though accuracy stays 0.70. So always say which class is "positive."

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Task: ek program 10 photos dekhta hai aur bolta hai "woman" ya "man". Asli answers humein pata hain. "Woman" ko positive class aur "man" ko negative class maanenge. 

 Step 1 – har photo ko mark karo: 

 Bola woman aur thi woman → TP (photo 3, 6, 7, 10) = 4 
 Bola man aur tha man → TN (photo 2, 4, 8) = 3 
 Bola woman par tha man → FP (photo 1, 9) = 2 
 Bola man par thi woman → FN (photo 5) = 1 

 Confusion matrix (sir ne 4, 2, 1, 3 likha hai): upar wali row (bola woman): 4 sahi, 2 galat; neeche wali row (bola man): 1 galat, 3 sahi. 

 Scores: 

 Accuracy = 10 mein se 7 sahi = 0.70 
 Precision = jab 6 baar "woman" bola, unme se 4 sahi = 4 ÷ 6 = 0.67 
 Recall / Sensitivity = 5 asli women mein se 4 pakdi = 4 ÷ 5 = 0.80 (ye dono naam ek hi cheez ke hain; sir ne slide par "true positive rate" likha hai) 
 Specificity = 5 asli men mein se 3 ko sahi "man" bola = 3 ÷ 5 = 0.60 (ise "true negative rate" bhi kehte hain) 
 F1 = precision aur recall ka harmonic mean = 0.73 

 Dhyaan do: model women ko pakadne mein (0.80) men ko reject karne (0.60) se behtar hai — sirf accuracy 0.70 ye farak chhupa deti hai. 

 Swap check: agar "man" ko positive class bana dete, to TP = 3, TN = 4, FP = 1, FN = 2 hota. Accuracy wahi 0.70 rehti, par precision 0.75, recall 0.60, specificity 0.80, F1 0.67 ho jaate. Isliye hamesha bolo ki positive class kaun si hai.

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:

The key message: which metric you quote depends on the class of interest. (The "57 /14" at the bottom is a stray page label.)
