 Same table, two vocabularies. Information retrieval says precision, recall ; medicine and statistics say PPV, sensitivity, specificity ; ML mixes both. The summary table ties all names together ( L18 Precision and Recall — The Document-Retrieval Venn Diagram ).

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Once you have the four counts (TP, FP, FN, TN), you can make many different scores. This slide is a giant cheat-sheet of them. There is a simple way to think about it: 

 Look down each column (the real truth): 

 Recall / sensitivity (TPR): of the really-positive ones, how many did we find? 
 Miss rate (FNR): of the really-positive ones, how many did we miss? (= 1 − recall) 
 Specificity (TNR): of the really-negative ones, how many did we correctly clear? 
 Fall-out (FPR): of the really-negative ones, how many did we wrongly flag? (= 1 − specificity) 

 Look along each row (what the model said): 

 Precision (PPV): when it says "positive," how often is it right? 
 False discovery rate: when it says "positive," how often is it wrong? 
 NPV: when it says "negative," how often is it right? 
 False omission rate: when it says "negative," how often is it wrong? 

 Overall: prevalence (how common the positives are), accuracy (overall correctness), F1 (balance of precision and recall), and three "ratio" scores (LR+, LR−, DOR) that boil the quality down to one number each. 

 Using our 10-photo example: recall 0.8, specificity 0.6, precision 0.67, NPV 0.75, accuracy 0.7. Notice the pairs add to 1 (recall + miss rate = 1, and so on). 

 The slide's main hint: choose the score that matches the question you care about — which depends on which class matters.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Jab tumhare paas 4 counts (TP, FP, FN, TN) aa jaate hain, to unse bahut saare scores ban sakte hain. Ye slide unka ek bada cheat-sheet hai. Isse samajhne ka aasaan tareeka: 

 Column ke neeche dekho (asli sach ke hisaab se): 

 Recall / sensitivity (TPR): jo sach mein positive hain, unme se kitne pakde? 
 Miss rate (FNR): jo sach mein positive hain, unme se kitne chhoot gaye? (= 1 − recall) 
 Specificity (TNR): jo sach mein negative hain, unme se kitno ko sahi clear kiya? 
 Fall-out (FPR): jo sach mein negative hain, unme se kitno ko galti se positive bol diya? (= 1 − specificity) 

 Row ke saath dekho (model ne kya bola uske hisaab se): 

 Precision (PPV): jab model "positive" bole, to kitni baar sahi? 
 False discovery rate: jab "positive" bole, kitni baar galat? 
 NPV: jab "negative" bole, kitni baar sahi? 
 False omission rate: jab "negative" bole, kitni baar galat? 

 Overall: prevalence (positives kitne common hain), accuracy (kul sahi), F1 (precision-recall ka balance), aur teen ratio scores (LR+, LR−, DOR). 

 Humare 10-photo example mein: recall 0.8, specificity 0.6, precision 0.67, NPV 0.75, accuracy 0.7, FPR 0.4, FNR 0.2. Dhyaan do — jodi wale numbers 1 banate hain (recall + miss rate = 1, specificity + fall-out = 1, precision + FDR = 1). 

 Slide ka main message: wahi score chuno jo tumhare sawaal se match kare — aur wo is par depend karta hai ki class of interest kaun si hai. (Isi table ke naam alag-alag fields mein alag use hote hain: retrieval mein precision/recall, medicine mein sensitivity/specificity/PPV.)

18-05_Choosing_the_Right_Metric_Imbalanc.topic_title: Choosing the Right Metric — Imbalance, Trade-offs, and Extensions (F-beta, Balanced Accuracy, MCC)
18-05_Choosing_the_Right_Metric_Imbalanc.source: Lecture 18, slides 3, 5 and 10 (the instructor's "depending on the class of interest" point and the exercise's A, P, R, S, F1 list). **This topic is enrichment from web research** — the slides state the metrics but not when to prefer which. Research covered: precision–recall trade-off, F-beta, balanced accuracy, Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), medical vs. retrieval conventions.

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Which metric when? 

 Situation 
 Metric to emphasize 
 Why 

 Classes roughly balanced, errors equally costly 
 Accuracy 
 Simple and fine ( L18 Classification Metrics — Accuracy, Precision, Recall (Sensitivity), F1-Score ) 

 Missing a positive is very costly (cancer screening, fraud, safety defects) 
 Recall / sensitivity (also FNR) 
 A FN is the dangerous error 

 False alarms are costly (spam filter deleting real mail, legal flagging) 
 Precision 
 A FP is the dangerous error 

 Need balance of the two, positives are rare 
 F1 
 Harmonic mean punishes a weak side 

 Negatives matter too (medical devices) 
 Specificity , NPV 
 Retrieval ignores TN; diagnosis can't 

 Strongly imbalanced classes 
 Precision/recall/F1 or balanced accuracy or MCC — not plain accuracy 
 See below 

 1. The imbalance trap again. In L17 The Confusion Matrix — TP, TN, FP, FN (Lecture 17) a do-nothing model scored 99 % accuracy with 0 recall. Accuracy is dominated by the majority class. 

 2. F-beta (research). F₁ weights precision and recall equally. The generalization is
 F_β = (1 + β²)·P·R / (β²·P + R) .
β = 2 weights recall ≈ 4× more than precision (use when misses are worse than false alarms); β = 0.5 weights precision ≈ 4× more. β = 1 gives F1. (Originates with C. J. van Rijsbergen's 1979 effectiveness measure.) Check: for P = 0.667, R = 0.8 (man/woman exercise): F₂ = 5(0.667)(0.8)/(4(0.667) + 0.8) = 2.667/3.467 = 0.769 , above F1 = 0.727 because recall (0.8) is the better number and F₂ rewards it. 

 3. Balanced accuracy (research). = (sensitivity + specificity)/2 — the average per-class recall. For the exercise: (0.80 + 0.60)/2 = 0.70 (coincidentally equal to accuracy because both classes have 5 samples). For the "all healthy" model on 990 healthy/10 sick it is (0 + 1)/2 = 0.50 — correctly revealing a useless classifier, where plain accuracy said 0.99. 

 4. Matthews correlation coefficient (research). MCC = (TP·TN − FP·FN) / √((TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN)); ranges from −1 (always wrong) through 0 (no better than chance) to +1 (perfect), and uses all four cells. Exercise: (4·3 − 2·1)/√(6·5·5·4) = 10/√600 = 0.408 — a modest correlation, more sobering than 0.70 accuracy. F-scores ignore TN; MCC does not. 

 5. The precision–recall trade-off and thresholds (research). For a classifier that outputs a score or probability ( L15 The Sigmoid Function and the Decision Boundary ), changing the decision threshold moves you along a trade-off: threshold ↓ → more predicted positives → recall ↑, precision usually ↓; threshold ↑ → the reverse. Sweeping the threshold and plotting the resulting rates gives the ROC curve (TPR vs. FPR — both defined in L18 Summaries of the Confusion Matrix — The Full Table of Rates ), which Lecture 17's outline announced as part 3 but which has still not appeared in the Lecture 17 or 18 slides. 

 6. Averaging over many classes (research, beyond the slides). For more than two classes compute the metrics per class (one-vs-rest) and combine by macro average (simple mean, treats classes equally) or micro average (pool all TP/FP/FN, dominated by big classes). 

 7. Estimating these metrics honestly. Compute them on test/validation data or via cross-validation , never on training data ( L17 k-Fold Cross-Validation (Stratified Ten-Fold, Repeated CV) ). 

 Quick decision guide. Ask: What is the positive class? What does a FP cost? What does a FN cost? Are classes balanced? Then pick the metric(s) accordingly and report more than one.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
There's no single "best" score — it depends on what mistakes hurt most . 

 Balanced groups, all mistakes equal? Plain accuracy is fine. 
 Missing a positive is terrible (like a deadly disease)? Watch recall — you want to catch every sick person, even if you raise a few false alarms. 
 False alarms are terrible (like a spam filter hiding your job offer)? Watch precision . 
 Want one balanced number? Use F1 . If you want to lean toward catching more, use F2 ; toward fewer false alarms, F0.5 . 
 Very uneven groups (99 healthy, 1 sick)? Don't trust accuracy! A lazy model that always says "healthy" gets 99 %. Better: balanced accuracy (average of how well you do on each group — that lazy model scores only 50 %) or MCC (one fair score from −1 to +1 using all four counts). 

 Our 10-photo example: accuracy 0.70, but MCC is only 0.41 — a more honest picture of a modest model. 

 The tug-of-war: most models give a score , and you choose a cut-off. A low cut-off flags more things (catch more positives, more false alarms); a high cut-off flags fewer. Plotting this over all cut-offs gives the ROC curve (coming later). 

 Always judge on fresh test data , not data the model has already seen.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Koi ek "best" score nahi hota — ye isper depend karta hai ki kaun si galti zyada mehengi padti hai. 

 Groups balanced hain aur har galti barabar? Seedhi accuracy theek hai. 
 Positive ko miss karna bahut bura hai (jaise jaanleva bimaari)? Recall dekho — saare bimaar pakadne hain, chahe thode false alarm aa jaayein. 
 False alarm bahut bura hai (jaise spam filter ne tumhara job offer mail chhupa diya)? Precision dekho. 
 Ek balanced number chahiye? F1 lo. Zyada pakadne ki taraf jhukna ho to F2 , kam false alarm ki taraf jhukna ho to F0.5 . (Formula: F_β = (1 + β²)·P·R / (β²·P + R). Humare exercise ka F2 ≈ 0.77.) 
 Groups bahut uneven hain (99 healthy, 1 sick)? Accuracy par bharosa mat karo! Aalsi model jo hamesha "healthy" bole wo 99% accuracy le leta hai. Behtar: balanced accuracy (har group par performance ka average — wo aalsi model sirf 50% paata hai) ya MCC (−1 se +1 tak ek fair score jo chaaron counts use karta hai). 

 Humare 10-photo example mein accuracy 0.70 hai, par MCC sirf 0.41 — ye model ki zyada honest tasveer hai. 

 Tug-of-war: zyada tar models ek score dete hain aur tum cut-off (threshold) chunte ho. Kam cut-off = zyada cheezein positive flag hoti hain (zyada pakde, par false alarm bhi zyada); zyada cut-off = kam flag. Saare cut-offs par ye plot karne se ROC curve banta hai (ye Lecture 17 ke outline mein promise hua tha par abhi tak slides mein aaya nahi). 

 Aur hamesha score naye test data par nikaalo, us data par nahi jo model ne pehle dekha hai.

19-00_Recap_TPR_FPR_and_the_Blood_Test_T.topic_title: Recap — TPR, FPR, and the Blood-Test Threshold Idea
19-00_Recap_TPR_FPR_and_the_Blood_Test_T.source: Lecture 19, slides 1–3 (the repeated "Outline", the blood-value dataset with "Choose a classification threshold", and "Recap: Confusion matrix" with the instructor's TPR/FPR notes). Recap note — the confusion matrix itself is already covered in Lecture 17 and 18. The blood-test numbers are re-verified here.

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 1 — outline. The same three-part outline as Lecture 17: 1. Metrics, 2. Precision and recall, 3. Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves. Lectures 17 and 18 delivered parts 1 and 2; this lecture finally delivers part 3, ROC curves (the stray "68 /14" is a leftover page label). Earlier material: L17 The Confusion Matrix — TP, TN, FP, FN and L18 Classification Metrics — Accuracy, Precision, Recall (Sensitivity), F1-Score . 

 Slide 2 — a motivating example (blood test for cancer). Data from 10 people, one blood value each, with the true status:

 Step 2 — choose a classification threshold: if blood value ≥ 45 → predict Cancer; if blood value < 45 → predict Healthy. A dashed red line at Threshold = 45 separates the two groups in the scatter plot. (The slide's arrow suggests further steps, but only these two are shown in this PDF.) 

 With threshold 45 every prediction is right: all five cancer values (70, 62, 58, 52, 48) are ≥ 45 → TP = 5; all five healthy values (40, 35, 30, 25, 20) are < 45 → TN = 5; FP = FN = 0 → TPR = 5/5 = 1 , FPR = 0/5 = 0 . 

 Why it matters: this model's score (the blood value) can be cut at any threshold, and each threshold gives a different confusion matrix and different TPR/FPR. Moving the threshold — the idea the whole lecture is built on ( L19 What Is a ROC Curve? — Ranking Instead of Classifying, and How the Curve Is Built ). Our check: here the two groups don't overlap at all (lowest cancer 48 > highest healthy 40), so any threshold between 40 and 48 gives the perfect (FPR = 0, TPR = 1) point, and the ROC curve would be the ideal one with AUC = 1 ( L19 ROC Shapes, AUC, and Comparing Models ). 

 Slide 3 — recap of the confusion matrix with two new rates. 

 The confusion matrix ( easily generalizes to multi-class ). 
 Machine-learning methods usually minimize FP + FN (the total number of errors). 
 TPR (True Positive Rate) = TP / (TP + FN) = Recall (instructor writes this on the slide as "True Positive Rate (Recall) = TP/(TP+FN)"). 
 FPR (False Positive Rate) = FP / (TN + FP) — the instructor writes it out as FP over (TN + FP), i.e. FPR = FP/(TN + FP) = 1 − Specificity ( L18 Summaries of the Confusion Matrix — The Full Table of Rates ). 

 Instructor's reading trick (red notes on slide 3): "True positive: P ← P" and "False positive: N ← P" , with arrows labelling Actual class (left letter) and Predicted class (right letter). So in "True positive" the actual class is P and the predicted class is P; in "False positive" the actual class is N but the model predicted P . 

 Worked check (Lecture 18's man/woman exercise: TP 4, FP 2, FN 1, TN 3). TPR = 4/5 = 0.80; FPR = 2/(3 + 2) = 0.40 — one point (FPR, TPR) = (0.40, 0.80) that ROC analysis will treat as one dot on a curve.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The blood-test story. Ten people give a blood sample. A higher blood value tends to mean cancer. The doctor picks a cut-off (threshold) of 45: at or above 45 → "cancer", below 45 → "healthy" . In this tiny example the cancer patients all have 48–70 and the healthy people all have 20–40, so the cut-off at 45 gets everyone right : 5 cancer patients correctly flagged, 5 healthy people correctly cleared. Good — but the doctor could have used 30, or 60 as the cut-off instead, and results would change. This lecture is about studying all possible cut-offs at once . 

 Two rates to remember: 

 TPR (True Positive Rate) = of the really-sick people, what fraction did we catch? (= recall.) 
 FPR (False Positive Rate) = of the really-healthy people, what fraction did we wrongly call sick? (= false-alarm rate.) 

 Teacher's trick for the names: the first word (True/False) says whether we were right, the second word (Positive) says what we predicted. "False positive" = the person is actually N egative but we said P ositive. 

 Remember: the lecture's outline promised ROC curves in Lecture 17; here they finally arrive.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Blood-test ki kahani. 10 logon ka blood test hua. Blood value jitni zyada, cancer ke chance utne zyada. Doctor ne cut-off (threshold) 45 rakha: 45 ya usse zyada → "cancer", 45 se kam → "healthy" . Is chhote example mein cancer wale sabki value 48–70 hai aur healthy logon ki 20–40, isliye 45 ka cut-off sabko sahi pakadta hai: 5 cancer patients sahi flag hue (TP = 5) aur 5 healthy sahi clear hue (TN = 5). Par doctor 30 ya 60 ka cut-off bhi rakh sakta tha aur results badal jaate. Is lecture ka maqsad saare possible cut-offs ko ek saath dekhna hai. 

 Do rates yaad rakho: 

 TPR (True Positive Rate) = jo sach mein bimaar hain, unme se kitno ko pakda? (= recall ) = TP / (TP + FN) 
 FPR (False Positive Rate) = jo sach mein theek hain, unme se kitno ko galti se bimaar bola? (false-alarm rate) = FP / (TN + FP) = 1 − specificity 

 Sir ka trick (slide 3 ke lal notes): "True positive: P ← P" yaani actual class P aur predicted class bhi P. "False positive: N ← P" yaani actual N hai par model ne P bol diya. Left letter = Actual class, right letter = Predicted class. 

 Example: Lecture 18 ke man/woman exercise mein TPR = 4/5 = 0.80 aur FPR = 2/5 = 0.40, yaani graph par ek point (0.40, 0.80). Ek point ek threshold ka hota hai — saare thresholds ke points jodne par ROC curve banta hai. 

 Lecture 17 ke outline mein ROC curves ka promise tha — wo ab is lecture mein aa gaya.

19-01_What_Is_a_ROC_Curve_and_Ranking_In.topic_title: What Is a ROC Curve? — Ranking Instead of Classifying, and How the Curve Is Built
19-01_What_Is_a_ROC_Curve_and_Ranking_In.source: Lecture 19, slides 4, 8, 9 and 10 ("ROC Curves" definition with the instructor's "show performance of classification models", "Ranking instead of classifying" with the sliding-threshold confusion matrices, and "ROC curves" with the Observations list). Enriched with web research (origin in radar signal detection).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Definition (slide 4). 

 A receiver operating characteristic curve , i.e. ROC curve , is a graphical plot that illustrates the diagnostic ability of a binary classifier system as its discrimination threshold is varied . 
 It is used to evaluate the accuracy of a test to discriminate diseased cases from normal cases. 
 A ROC curve is a way to compare diagnostic tests . It is a plot of the true positive rate against the false positive rate . 
 Instructor's note: "Show performance of classification models." 

 Axes. x-axis = FPR = FP/(FP + TN) ; y-axis = TPR = TP/(TP + FN) ( L19 Recap — TPR, FPR, and the Blood-Test Threshold Idea ). Both lie in [0, 1], so the plot is a unit square. 

 Ranking instead of classifying (slides 8–9). Classifiers such as logistic regression can output a probability of belonging to a class (or something similar) ( L15 The Sigmoid Function and the Decision Boundary ). We can use this to rank the instances and take action on the cases at the top of the list — e.g. we may have a budget, so we must target the most promising individuals . Ranking also lets us visualize performance with many techniques (ROC being the main one). 

 One ranking → many confusion matrices (slide 9). Sort the instances by score , highest first (slide: 0.99, 0.98, 0.96, 0.90, 0.88, 0.87, 0.85, 0.80, 0.70 with true class 1 or 0). Putting the threshold at different positions in the list — "everything above the line is predicted positive (Y), everything below negative (N)" — gives a different confusion matrix each time. The slide shows five matrices (p/n are the actual positive/negative columns; Y/N the predicted rows), for a dataset of 100 positives and 100 negatives:

 FPR = FP/100

 Each row is one point (FPR, TPR) . Sliding the threshold from the top of the list to the bottom traces out the ROC curve. (The instructor's note on slide 5: threshold ↑ → fewer predicted positives; threshold ↓ → more. ) 

 ⚠️ Caveat: the slide is "adapted from [1]" and shows only 9 of the instances while the matrices count 200 (100 + 100); the last matrix (6 TP, 4 FP) does not match the 9 listed rows one-for-one (those would give 5 TP, 4 FP down to 0.70), so treat the matrices as an illustration of the idea, not a row-by-row calculation. 

 Reading the ROC plot (slide 10, "Observations"). ROC curves are a very general way to represent and compare the performance of different models (on a binary classification task). In the slide's figure an orange piece-wise curve rises from (0,0) towards the top-left star labelled "Perfection" , with a blue dashed diagonal labelled "Random guessing" ; small confusion-matrix thumbnails mark the points. 

 Point / feature 
 Meaning 

 (0, 0) 
 Threshold so high that the model predicts always negative (TP = FP = 0) 

 (1, 1) 
 Threshold so low that it predicts always positive (FN = TN = 0)

 Perfection : all positives caught, no false alarms 

 Diagonal line (TPR = FPR)

 Below the diagonal 
 Worse than random (predictions systematically inverted) 

 Curves of different classifiers 
 Can be compared on one plot 

 AUC 
 Probability that a randomly chosen positive instance will be ranked ahead of a randomly chosen negative instance — see L19 ROC Shapes, AUC, and Comparing Models 

 Origin (research). The term comes from signal detection theory developed in World War II for radar: the "receiver operator" had to decide whether a blip was an enemy aircraft or noise, and the curve described how well they traded correct detections against false alarms. It was later adopted in medicine (diagnostic tests, hence "diseased vs. normal" on the slide) and machine learning. 

 Building a ROC curve — algorithm. 

 Sort instances by score, descending; let P = number of positives, N = number of negatives. 
 Start at (0, 0). Walk down the list: for a positive instance move up by 1/P; for a negative instance move right by 1/N. 
 End at (1, 1). Worked in L19 Worked Example 1 — Building a ROC Curve from Ranked Probabilities and L19 Worked Example 2 — Computing AUC by the Trapezoid Rule (AUC = 0.64) .

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The problem: many models don't just say "yes/no"; they give a score (like a probability). To turn a score into yes/no you pick a cut-off . Pick a high cut-off → you say "yes" rarely (few false alarms, but you miss real cases). Pick a low cut-off → you say "yes" a lot (you catch most real cases, but make many false alarms). 

 Ranking: line everyone up from highest score to lowest. Drawing the cut-off line at different places gives different scoreboards (confusion matrices). Slide 9 shows five of them. 

 The ROC curve is just a picture of all those scoreboards at once: 

 Across (x-axis): false-alarm rate (FPR). 
 Up (y-axis): catch rate (TPR). 
 Each possible cut-off gives one dot; joining the dots gives the curve. 

 How to read it: 

 Bottom-left (0,0): the model says "no" to everyone. 
 Top-right (1,1): the model says "yes" to everyone. 
 Top-left corner: perfect — catches everything, no false alarms. ⭐ 
 Diagonal line: pure guessing (coin flip). 
 Below the diagonal: worse than guessing. 
 AUC (area under the curve): one number summarizing the curve; it equals the chance that a random positive person gets a higher score than a random negative person. 

 Easy way to draw it: sort by score; for each real-positive step up , for each real-negative step right . 

 History fun-fact: ROC comes from World War II radar operators who had to decide "plane or noise?"

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Problem: bahut se models sirf "haan/na" nahi bolte, wo ek score (jaise probability) dete hain. Is score ko haan/na mein badalne ke liye cut-off (threshold) chunna padta hai. Cut-off bada rakho → "haan" kam bolega (false alarm kam, par asli cases chhoot jayenge). Cut-off chhota rakho → "haan" zyada bolega (zyada asli cases pakdega, par false alarm bhi zyada). 

 Ranking: sabko highest score se lowest score tak line mein lagao. Cut-off ki line alag-alag jagah kheenchne par alag-alag scoreboard (confusion matrix) bante hain — slide 9 mein 5 aise matrices dikhaye hain. Sir ke note ke hisaab se: threshold ↑ → positive kam; threshold ↓ → positive zyada. 

 ROC curve in sab scoreboards ki ek hi tasveer hai: 

 x-axis (aage): FPR (false alarm rate) 
 y-axis (upar): TPR (catch rate / recall) 
 Har cut-off ek dot deta hai; dots jodne par curve ban jata hai. 

 Kaise padhein: 

 (0,0) neeche-baayein: model sabko "na" bolta hai (always negative). 
 (1,1) upar-daayein: model sabko "haan" bolta hai (always positive). 
 (0,1) upar-baayein corner: perfect — sab pakde, koi false alarm nahi ⭐ (slide mein "Perfection"). 
 Diagonal line: random guessing (sikka uchhalna). 
 Diagonal ke neeche: random se bhi bura . 
 AUC: curve ke neeche ka area — ek number mein poori kahani; matlab ek random positive ko random negative se zyada score milne ki probability. 

 Curve banane ka aasaan tareeka: score se sort karo; har asli positive par upar chalo (1/P), har asli negative par daayein chalo (1/N). Poora worked example aage hai. 

 Fun fact: ROC ka naam WWII ke radar operators se aaya, jinhe decide karna tha ki "jahaz hai ya noise?" 

 ⚠️ Slide 9 ke matrices schematic hain (200 examples, par table mein sirf 9 dikhaye) — isliye har matrix ko table ki rows se one-to-one match mat karo.

19-02_ROC_Shapes_AUC_and_Comparing_Model.topic_title: ROC Shapes, AUC, and Comparing Models
19-02_ROC_Shapes_AUC_and_Comparing_Model.source: Lecture 19, slides 5, 6 and 11 ("ROC Curves" with the ideal / worst / typical panels and the instructor's AUC shading, "Multiple ROC Curves", and "AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve) score" with the area formula). Enriched with web research (AUC as a ranking probability, AUC < 0.5, trapezoid rule).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Three canonical ROC shapes (slide 5). Three small plots (TPR vs. FPR, both 0–1); the instructor shades the area under each and labels it AUC , and adds "Threshold ↑Th / ↓Th". 

 Panel 
 Shape 
 Slide's description 
 AUC 

 1 
 Goes straight up the left edge to (0,1), then straight across the top 
 "This is an ideal situation . Model has an ideal measure of separability. It is perfectly able to distinguish between positive class and negative class." 
 1.0 (whole square) 

 2 
 The diagonal from (0,0) to (1,1) 
 "This is the worst situation . When AUC is approximately 0.5 , model has no discrimination capacity to distinguish between positive class and negative class. Random predictions. " 
 0.5 (a triangle = ½) 

 3 
 A smooth concave curve above the diagonal 
 A typical useful model (no caption) 
 between 0.5 and 1 

 Area Under the Curve (AUC) — slide 11. AUC = Area Under the ROC Curve — a single number summarizing performance over all thresholds. The slide's guide: 

 High AUC (close to 1): the model effectively distinguishes between positive and negative instances. 
 Low AUC (close to 0): the model struggles to differentiate between the two classes. 
 AUC around 0.5: the model doesn't learn any meaningful patterns, i.e. it is doing random guessing. 

 ⚠️ A correction on "AUC close to 0" (research). An AUC near 0 does not mean "struggles to differentiate" — it means the model separates the classes very well but with the labels reversed (it ranks negatives above positives). Flipping its predictions would give AUC ≈ 1 − AUC ≈ 1. The worst (least informative) value is 0.5 , which is what the slide says for random guessing. "Below the diagonal: worse than random" on slide 10 is the same fact ( L19 What Is a ROC Curve? — Ranking Instead of Classifying, and How the Curve Is Built ). 

 Probabilistic meaning (slide 10, verified in the worked examples). AUC = the probability that a randomly chosen positive instance is ranked ahead of (scored higher than) a randomly chosen negative instance (ties counted as ½). This equals the Wilcoxon–Mann–Whitney U statistic (research). Check: Example 1 has 5 positives × 5 negatives = 25 pairs; positive scores {0.90, 0.80, 0.60, 0.55, 0.50} vs. negative scores {0.70, 0.54, 0.53, 0.51, 0.40} → 19 of 25 pairs rank the positive higher = 0.76 , exactly the trapezoid area ( L19 Worked Example 1 — Building a ROC Curve from Ranked Probabilities ); Example 2 gives 16/25 = 0.64 ( L19 Worked Example 2 — Computing AUC by the Trapezoid Rule (AUC = 0.64) ). 

 Computing the area (slide 11 formula). Between two consecutive ROC points (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂) the area under the segment is a trapezoid : 

 Area = (x₂ − x₁)(y₁ + y₂) / 2 

 AUC = the sum of these strips over the whole curve (the instructor labels the two points "(x₁, y₁)" and "(x₂, y₂)" on the slide). Vertical moves have x₂ − x₁ = 0 and contribute nothing. 

 Multiple ROC curves (slide 6). Comparison of multiple classifiers is usually straightforward, especially when no curves cross each other. Curves close to the perfect ROC curve have a better performance level than the ones closest to the baseline. The slide's figure shows three curves with the dashed diagonal baseline: a "great model" (blue, hugging the top-left corner, AUC near 1), a "good model" (red, in between) and a "bad model" (green, only slightly above the diagonal). Rule: if one curve lies entirely above another, it is better at every threshold; if curves cross , AUC alone hides the fact that each model is better in a different region (e.g. at low FPR vs. high FPR), so pick by the operating range you care about. 

 Rough interpretation scale (research, a convention not a law). 0.5 ≈ no skill; 0.7–0.8 acceptable; 0.8–0.9 good; > 0.9 excellent. 

 Advantages of AUC: threshold-free, summarizes ranking quality, insensitive to the choice of cut-off. Limits: says nothing about calibration (are the probabilities accurate?), and can look rosy on very imbalanced data — see L19 PR Curves vs. ROC Curves .

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Imagine three models and you draw each one's ROC curve: 

 Perfect model: the line shoots straight up the left side and runs across the top. The area under it is 1 (the whole square). It never makes a mistake. 
 Coin-flip model: the line is the diagonal . The area under it is 0.5 (half the square). It knows nothing — same as guessing. 
 Normal good model: a bulging curve above the diagonal. The more it bulges towards the top-left corner, the bigger the area (somewhere between 0.5 and 1). 

 AUC = the area under the curve. One number to compare models: 

 Close to 1 → very good at telling positives from negatives. 
 Around 0.5 → just guessing. 
 Close to 0 → actually reversed (it gets things backwards — the slide says "struggles", but really you could flip its answers and get a great model). 

 Cute meaning of AUC: pick one random positive person and one random negative person. AUC is the chance that the model gave the positive person the higher score. AUC 0.76 means that's true 76 times out of 100. 

 Comparing models: draw all their curves on one graph. The curve closest to the top-left corner wins. (If two curves cross, one model is better in one region, the other elsewhere.) In the slide's picture: blue "great" > red "good" > green "bad". 

 How to compute the area: chop it into thin strips and add up. Each strip's area = width × average height = (x₂ − x₁)(y₁ + y₂) ÷ 2.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Teen models socho aur har ka ROC curve banao: 

 Perfect model: line seedhi left side se upar jaati hai aur phir top par seedhi chalti hai. Area 1 (poora square). Koi galti nahi. 
 Sikka-uchhalne wala model: line diagonal hai. Area 0.5 (aadha square). Isse kuch nahi aata — guessing ke barabar. Slide kehti hai: "no discrimination capacity, random predictions." 
 Normal accha model: diagonal ke upar ubhra hua curve. Jitna top-left corner ki taraf bulge, utna area zyada (0.5 se 1 ke beech). 

 AUC = curve ke neeche ka area. Models compare karne ke liye ek number: 

 1 ke paas → positives aur negatives ko bahut accha alag karta hai. 
 0.5 ke aas-paas → bas guessing. 
 0 ke paas → slide kehti hai "struggle karta hai", par asal mein model ulta hai (positives ko negatives se neeche rank karta hai). Uske answers flip kar do to AUC ≈ 1 ho jayega. Sabse "bekaar" value 0.5 hai, 0 nahi. 

 AUC ka cute matlab: ek random positive aur ek random negative person uthao. AUC = probability ki model ne positive ko zyada score diya. AUC 0.76 matlab 100 mein se 76 baar aisa hota hai. (Humne examples mein pairs gin kar verify kiya: Example 1 = 19/25 = 0.76, Example 2 = 16/25 = 0.64.) 

 Models compare karna (slide 6): sab curves ek graph par banao. Jo curve top-left corner ke sabse paas, wo best: blue "great" > red "good" > green "bad". Agar do curves cross karein, to ek model kisi region mein behtar hota hai aur dusra dusre region mein — tab AUC akela kaafi nahi. 

 Area nikaalne ka formula (slide 11): area ko patli strips mein kaato aur jodo. Har strip = width × average height = (x₂ − x₁)(y₁ + y₂) ÷ 2 (trapezoid). 

 Thumb rule: 0.5 = bekaar, 0.7–0.8 theek, 0.8–0.9 accha, 0.9+ bahut accha.

19-03_PR_Curves_vs_ROC_Curves.source: Lecture 19, slide 7 ("PR Curves Vs ROC Curves"). Enriched with a worked comparison and web research (Saito & Rehmsmeier, 2015, on PR plots for imbalanced data).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
What each curve plots (slide 7). 

 A ROC curve represents a relation between sensitivity (recall) and the False Positive Rate (not precision). ROC plots TPR vs. FPR . 
 The PR curve plots Precision vs. Recall (recall on the x-axis, precision on the y-axis). 

 When to use which (slide 7). 

 If your question is "How well can this classifier be expected to perform in general ?" → go with a ROC curve . 
 If true negatives are not very valuable to the problem, or negative examples are abundant , then the PR curve is typically more appropriate. For example, if the class is highly imbalanced and positive samples are very rare, use the PR curve. 
 The PR curve answers: "How meaningful is a positive result from my classifier?" (that is precision.) 

 Why the difference arises. TN appears in the ROC axis FPR = FP/(FP + TN) but not in precision = TP/(TP + FP) or recall = TP/(TP + FN) ( L18 Classification Metrics — Accuracy, Precision, Recall (Sensitivity), F1-Score ). When negatives vastly outnumber positives, TN is huge, so FPR stays tiny even when there are many false positives, making the ROC curve look excellent while the precision is poor. 

 Worked example (illustrative, verified). A test set has 10 positives and 990 negatives . A model, at some threshold, catches 8 of the 10 positives (TPR = 0.80) and wrongly flags 40 negatives. 

 FPR = 40/990 = 0.040 → the ROC point (0.04, 0.80) sits near the top-left: it looks great. 
 Precision = TP/(TP + FP) = 8/(8 + 40) = 0.167 — five out of every six alarms are false. 
 Recall = 0.80; F1 = 2·0.167·0.8/(0.967) ≈ 0.276 .
So the ROC point says "excellent", the PR point says "mostly false alarms". This is exactly the slide's point: with rare positives use PR. 

 Baselines differ. ROC's random baseline is always the diagonal (AUC = 0.5) regardless of class balance. The PR baseline is a horizontal line at the positive rate (= prevalence, here 10/1000 = 0.01), so PR AUCs are harder to read in absolute terms but more sensitive to imbalance (research: Saito & Rehmsmeier 2015 argue that the PR plot is more informative than the ROC plot for imbalanced data because it evaluates the fraction of true positives among positive predictions). 

 Practical guide. 

 Situation 
 Prefer 

 Balanced classes; both classes matter 
 ROC / AUC 

 Rare positives (fraud, rare disease); care about the quality of positive alerts 
 PR curve (average precision) 

 Compare how well models rank overall 
 ROC AUC 

 Choose an operating threshold under a precision requirement 
 PR curve 

 Both curves are built from the same sorted-score threshold sweep ( L19 What Is a ROC Curve? — Ranking Instead of Classifying, and How the Curve Is Built ); they just plot different pairs of rates. 

 PR points for Example 1 (computed from the slide's table). After the top 1, 2, 3, … instances the (recall, precision) pairs are (0.2, 1.0), (0.4, 1.0), (0.4, 0.667), (0.6, 0.75), (0.8, 0.8), (0.8, 0.667), (0.8, 0.571), (0.8, 0.5), (1.0, 0.556), (1.0, 0.5) — precision jumps up and down while recall only increases, giving the typical saw-tooth PR curve ( L19 Worked Example 1 — Building a ROC Curve from Ranked Probabilities ).

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
There are two popular "report-card pictures" for a yes/no model: 

 ROC curve: catch rate (TPR) against false-alarm rate (FPR). Answers: "Overall, how well can this model tell the two groups apart?" 
 PR curve: precision (when it says yes, how often is it right?) against recall (catch rate). Answers: "How trustworthy is a positive result?" 

 When does it matter? When almost everything is negative (say 1 sick person in 100). Then the false-alarm rate looks tiny even if you raise lots of false alarms, because it's measured against a huge number of healthy people. The ROC curve then looks wonderful. The PR curve is not fooled, because precision looks directly at "of my alarms, how many were real?" 

 Example: 10 sick, 990 healthy. The model finds 8 of the 10 sick but also wrongly flags 40 healthy people. 

 False-alarm rate = 40 ÷ 990 = 4 % → ROC point looks great. 
 Precision = 8 ÷ 48 = 17 % → five of every six alarms are false! 

 Rule from the slide: general ability to separate → ROC. Rare positives or negatives don't matter much → PR.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Yes/no model ke liye do popular "report card" graphs hain: 

 ROC curve: catch rate (TPR) vs false-alarm rate (FPR). Sawaal: "Overall ye model dono groups ko kitna accha alag kar sakta hai?" 
 PR curve: precision (jab model "haan" bole to kitni baar sahi?) vs recall (catch rate). Sawaal: "Ek positive result par kitna bharosa kar sakte hain?" (slide: "How meaningful is a positive result from my classifier") 

 Farak kab padta hai? Jab lagbhag sab negative ho (maan lo 100 mein 1 bimaar). Tab false-alarm rate bahut chhota dikhta hai chahe kitne hi false alarm ho, kyunki wo bahut saare healthy logon se divide hota hai. Isliye ROC curve bahut accha dikhta hai. PR curve dhokha nahi khaata, kyunki precision seedha dekhta hai "mere alarms mein se kitne asli the?" 

 Example: 10 bimaar, 990 healthy. Model 10 mein se 8 bimaar pakadta hai par 40 healthy ko galti se flag kar deta hai. 

 FPR = 40 ÷ 990 = 4% → ROC point accha dikhta hai. 
 Precision = 8 ÷ 48 = 17% → har 6 alarm mein se 5 jhoothe! 
 F1 sirf ≈ 0.28. 

 Slide ka rule: general separation ability → ROC . Positives bahut rare hain ya true negatives zyada kaam ke nahi → PR curve . 

 Baseline bhi alag hota hai: ROC ka random baseline hamesha diagonal (AUC 0.5); PR ka baseline ek horizontal line hai jo positive rate par hoti hai (yahan 0.01).

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The setup: a model gave 10 people a "probability of being positive." We lined them up from highest to lowest and know the truth: 5 are really P (positive) and 5 are really N (negative). 

 How to draw the ROC curve: start at the bottom-left corner. Walk down the list one person at a time: 

 If the person is really P → move up one step (each step = 1/5 = 0.2). 
 If the person is really N → move right one step (also 0.2). 

 Walking down the list: P P N P P N N N P N →
up, up, right, up, up, right, right, right, up, right. 

 That produces the points in the table: (0,0.2), (0,0.4), (0.2,0.4), (0.2,0.6), (0.2,0.8), (0.4,0.8), (0.6,0.8), (0.8,0.8), (0.8,1.0), (1,1). 

 What does each point mean? Say the teacher uses a cut-off of 0.70 — "everyone with a score of 0.70 or more is called positive." That's tuples 1, 2, 3: 2 real positives (TPR = 2/5 = 0.4) and 1 real negative wrongly included (FPR = 1/5 = 0.2). So the point is (0.2, 0.4). 

 The area under this staircase is the AUC. Add up the areas of the strips: 0.08 + 0.16 + 0.16 + 0.16 + 0.20 = 0.76 . Another way to see it: out of 25 (positive, negative) pairs, in 19 the positive got the higher score → 19/25 = 0.76. 

 Is 0.76 good? Decent (better than guessing at 0.5, far from perfect 1.0).

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Setup: ek model ne 10 logon ko "positive hone ki probability" di. Humne unhe highest se lowest tak line mein lagaya aur asli answer pata hai: 5 sach mein P (positive) hain aur 5 sach mein N (negative). 

 ROC curve kaise banate hain: bottom-left corner se shuru karo. List mein ek-ek karke neeche chalo: 

 Agar banda asli mein P hai → upar ek step (1/5 = 0.2). 
 Agar banda asli mein N hai → daayein ek step (0.2). 

 List: P P N P P N N N P N → up, up, right, up, up, right, right, right, up, right. 

 Isse table ke saare points bante hain: (0,0.2), (0,0.4), (0.2,0.4), (0.2,0.6), (0.2,0.8), (0.4,0.8), (0.6,0.8), (0.8,0.8), (0.8,1.0), (1,1). 

 Har point ka matlab: maan lo cut-off 0.70 hai — "0.70 ya usse zyada score wale sab positive." Ye tuples 1, 2, 3 hain: 2 asli positive (TPR = 2/5 = 0.4) aur 1 asli negative galti se shamil (FPR = 1/5 = 0.2). To point = (0.2, 0.4). Sir ne board par yahi likha: "Threshold ≥ 0.90 → positive, TPR = 1/5 = 0.2, FPR = 0/5 = 0", phir "≥ 0.70: TPR = 2/5 = 0.4, FPR = 1/5 = 0.2". 

 Is staircase ke neeche ka area = AUC. Strips jodo: 0.08 + 0.16 + 0.16 + 0.16 + 0.20 = 0.76 . Doosra tareeka: 25 (positive, negative) pairs mein se 19 mein positive ko zyada score mila → 19/25 = 0.76 ✅. 

 Convex hull: slide mein ek bahar wali seedhi-line wali boundary bhi hai (convex hull) — ye do thresholds ko mix karke milne wali best possible performance dikhati hai. 

 0.76 accha hai? Theek-thaak (0.5 guessing se behtar, 1.0 perfect se door). Best cut-off dhoondhna ho to Youden's J = TPR − FPR sabse bada ≥ 0.55 par hota hai (TPR 0.8, FPR 0.2).
