sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Same recipe as Example 1: line up 10 tuples by score. Real positives (P) move the curve up 0.2; real negatives (N) move it right 0.2. 

 Order: P N P P N P N N N P → up, right, up, up, right, up, right, right, right, up. 

 Finding the area under the staircase. Only the right moves add area (an up move has no width). For each right move: area = width × average height. Width is always 0.2 here: 

 First right move at height 0.2 → 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.04 
 Second right move at height 0.6 → 0.2 × 0.6 = 0.12 
 Right moves at height 0.8 (three of them) → 0.2 × 0.8 = 0.16 each → 0.48 

 Total area = 0.04 + 0.12 + 0.48 = 0.64 . That's the AUC = 0.64 the teacher circled. 

 Does 0.64 mean good? It's a bit better than a coin flip (0.5) but not great. Check by pairs: out of 25 (positive, negative) pairs, the positive had the higher score in 16 → 16/25 = 0.64. 

 Why so-so? A negative person scored 0.85 — higher than three real positives — and one real positive got the lowest score (0.40).

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Recipe wahi hai jo Example 1 mein tha: 10 tuples ko score se line mein lagao. Asli positive (P) par curve 0.2 upar jaata hai; asli negative (N) par 0.2 daayein . 

 Order: P N P P N P N N N P → up, right, up, up, right, up, right, right, right, up. 

 Area nikaalna. Sirf right moves area add karte hain (upar wale move ki width 0 hoti hai). Har right move ka area = width × average height; width yahan hamesha 0.2 hai: 

 Pehla right move height 0.2 par → 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.04 (sir ka Area₁: (0.2 − 0)(0.2 + 0.2)/2 = 0.04) 
 Doosra right move height 0.6 par → 0.2 × 0.6 = 0.12 
 Teen right moves height 0.8 par → har ek 0.2 × 0.8 = 0.16, total 0.48 

 Kul area = 0.04 + 0.12 + 0.48 = 0.64 ✅ — yahi sir ne circle kiya hai: AUC = 0.64 . 

 Ye accha hai? Sikke uchhalne (0.5) se thoda behtar, par zyada accha nahi. Pairs se check: 25 (positive, negative) pairs mein se 16 mein positive ka score zyada tha → 16/25 = 0.64. 

 Kamzori kyun? Ek negative ko 0.85 score mila jo teen asli positives se zyada hai, aur ek asli positive ko sabse kam score (0.40) mila. Example 1 (AUC 0.76) is data par behtar model tha.

19-06_Choosing_a_Threshold_Youden_J_and_.topic_title: Choosing a Threshold and Practical ROC Notes (Youden's J, Convex Hull, Multi-class, Pitfalls)
19-06_Choosing_a_Threshold_Youden_J_and_.source: Lecture 19, slides 4–6, 10, 13 (threshold idea, "Different classifiers can be compared", convex hull). **Enrichment topic from web research** — the slides show ROC curves but do not say how to pick the operating threshold or how ROC extends beyond two classes. Research covered: Youden's J, ROC convex hull, one-vs-rest AUC, AUC limitations.

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
1. A ROC curve shows all thresholds — but you must deploy one. Each point on the curve is a threshold ( L19 What Is a ROC Curve? — Ranking Instead of Classifying, and How the Curve Is Built ). Common ways to pick it: 

 Rule 
 Idea 

 Youden's J 
 Maximize J = TPR − FPR = sensitivity + specificity − 1 : the point farthest above the diagonal 

 Closest to (0, 1) 
 Minimize distance to the "Perfection" corner: √(FPR² + (1 − TPR)²) 

 Cost-based 
 Choose the point where cost(FN)·(miss rate) + cost(FP)·(false-alarm rate) is lowest; if misses are expensive, accept a higher FPR for a higher TPR (move up-right) 

 Constraint-based 
 e.g. "FPR must be ≤ 0.05" or "recall ≥ 0.9" — take the best point satisfying it 

 Worked (Example 1 from L19 Worked Example 1 — Building a ROC Curve from Ranked Probabilities , verified): J at the ten thresholds = 0.2 (≥0.90), 0.4 (≥0.80), 0.2 (≥0.70), 0.4 (≥0.60), 0.6 (≥0.55) , 0.4, 0.2, 0.0, 0.2, 0.0 → the best cut-off is 0.55 (TPR 0.8, FPR 0.2). For Example 2 ( L19 Worked Example 2 — Computing AUC by the Trapezoid Rule (AUC = 0.64) ) J at the ten thresholds = 0.2, 0.0, 0.2, 0.4 (≥ 0.66: TPR 0.6, FPR 0.2), 0.2, 0.4 (≥ 0.55: TPR 0.8, FPR 0.4), 0.2, 0.0, −0.2, 0.0 → best J is only 0.4 (a weaker model has a smaller best J than Example 1's 0.6). 

 2. ROC convex hull (slide 13). The solid outer line on the slide. Any point on a straight segment between two ROC points can be achieved by randomly choosing between the two classifiers/thresholds with suitable probabilities. So points below the hull are never optimal under any class/cost distribution; the hull is the set of potentially optimal operating points (research). 

 3. Comparing classifiers (slide 6, 10). If curve A lies above curve B everywhere → A dominates. If they cross, compare in the region of interest (e.g. low FPR) or use partial AUC ; AUC alone averages over regions you may not care about. 

 4. More than two classes (slide 3: confusion matrix "easily generalizes to multi-class"). ROC is defined for binary problems. For K classes: one-vs-rest — treat each class as positive vs. all others, draw K curves, and average the AUCs ( macro = simple mean; micro = pooled counts). 

 5. Pitfalls (research). 

 Imbalanced data: ROC/AUC can look good when precision is poor → use PR curve ( L19 PR Curves vs. ROC Curves ). 
 AUC ignores calibration: two models with the same ranking have the same AUC even if one's probabilities are nonsense. 
 AUC is not accuracy: it does not tell you performance at a particular threshold. 
 AUC < 0.5 ⇒ inverted predictions (flip them) — not "can't separate" ( L19 ROC Shapes, AUC, and Comparing Models ). 
 Tied scores create diagonal segments; use the trapezoid rule. 
 Estimate AUC on test or cross-validated predictions, never training data ( L17 k-Fold Cross-Validation (Stratified Ten-Fold, Repeated CV) ). 

 6. Connection to earlier lectures. The threshold is exactly the 0.5 cut-off of logistic regression ( L15 The Sigmoid Function and the Decision Boundary ), which can be moved; for k-NN ( L16 The k-NN Algorithm, Step by Step ) the "score" can be the fraction of the k neighbors that vote positive.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The ROC curve shows every possible cut-off at once, but in real life you must pick one . Options: 

 Best balance (Youden's J): pick the cut-off where (catch rate − false-alarm rate) is largest — the point farthest above the diagonal . In Example 1 that's cut-off 0.55 (catch 80 %, false alarms 20 %). 
 Closest to the perfect corner: pick the dot nearest the top-left. 
 Based on cost: if missing a sick person is much worse than a false alarm, accept more false alarms to catch more (move up and right on the curve). 
 Based on a rule: e.g. "false alarms must stay under 5 %". 

 Other useful facts: 

 Convex hull: by randomly switching between two cut-offs you can get any point on the straight line between them, so dots below the outer line are never the best choice. 
 Comparing two models: if one curve is above the other everywhere, it's simply better. If they cross, think about which region matters to you. 
 More than two groups: do "one group versus everyone else" for each group and average. 
 Be careful: with very rare positives the ROC looks too rosy (use PR curve); AUC doesn't tell you whether the probabilities themselves are accurate; always compute it on test data .

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
ROC curve saare possible cut-offs ek saath dikhata hai, par asli zindagi mein tumhe ek hi chunna padta hai. Tareeke: 

 Best balance (Youden's J): wo cut-off jahan (catch rate − false-alarm rate) sabse bada ho — yaani point jo diagonal se sabse upar ho. Example 1 mein ye cut-off 0.55 hai (catch 80%, false alarm 20%, J = 0.6). 
 Perfect corner ke sabse paas: top-left ke sabse nazdeek wala dot. 
 Cost ke hisaab se: agar bimaar ko miss karna false alarm se bahut bura hai, to zyada false alarm accept karke zyada pakdo (curve par upar-daayein jao). 
 Rule ke hisaab se: jaise "false alarm 5% se kam hi rahe." 

 Aur kaam ki baatein: 

 Convex hull (slide 13): do cut-offs ke beech randomly switch karke tum unke beech ki seedhi line ka koi bhi point pa sakte ho, isliye outer line ke neeche wale dots kabhi best nahi hote. 
 Do models compare karna: agar ek curve har jagah doosre se upar hai to wo seedha behtar. Agar curves cross karein, to dekho tumhe kaun sa region zyada zaroori hai. 
 2 se zyada classes: har class ke liye "wo class vs baaki sab" karke curve banao aur AUCs ka average lo. 
 Savdhaani: bahut rare positives mein ROC zyada accha dikhta hai (tab PR curve use karo); AUC ye nahi batata ki probabilities khud sahi hain ya nahi; aur hamesha test data par nikaalo. 
 AUC < 0.5 matlab predictions ulte hain — flip karo, model "bekaar" nahi hai. 

 Connection: logistic regression ka 0.5 cut-off (Lecture 15) bhi ek threshold hai jise badla ja sakta hai — ROC se pata chalta hai badalne par kya hoga.

20-01_Job_Offer_Example_and_What_Is_a_De.lecture_title: Decision Trees and the ID3 Algorithm
20-01_Job_Offer_Example_and_What_Is_a_De.topic_title: The Job-Offer Example and What a Decision Tree Is
20-01_Job_Offer_Example_and_What_Is_a_De.source: Lecture 20, slides 1–3 (title slide, "Lets see the example...", "Decision Tree"). Enriched with web research (Quinlan's ID3 paper 1986, Breiman et al. CART 1984).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 2 — the motivating example. A job seeker compares several offers that differ in commute distance, pay and benefits. They list each position's features , then derive rules that eliminate options: 

 "If my commute is longer than an hour, then I will be unhappy." 
 "If I make less than $50k, I won't be able to support my family." 

 The slide's punchline: "The difficult decision of predicting future happiness can be reduced to a series of small, but increasingly specific choices." That is exactly a decision tree: one big prediction (happy / unhappy) is broken into a chain of simple yes/no tests on features. 

 Slide 3 — the definition. 

 A decision tree is a graph that represents choices and their results in the form of a tree. 
 Nodes represent an event or choice; edges represent the decision rules / conditions . 
 It is mostly used in machine learning and data mining applications (the slide says "using Python"). 

 Mapping the example onto the vocabulary. 

 Idea 
 Job-offer example 

 Feature (attribute) 
 commute time, salary, benefits 

 Test at a node 
 "commute > 1 hour?", "salary < $50k?" 

 Edge 
 the answer (yes / no) 

 Final outcome (leaf) 
 happy / unhappy (or accept / reject) 

 Why this is "supervised learning". In ML the rules are not written by a person; they are learned from labelled training data (past offers and whether the person turned out happy). The learning algorithm (ID3 in this lecture, see L20 The ID3 Algorithm — What It Is, Who Made It, and How It Works in One Paragraph ) decides which question to ask first, which second, and so on. 

 Historical note (research). Decision-tree learning was formalised independently in the 1980s: Breiman, Friedman, Olshen & Stone's CART (1984) and J. Ross Quinlan's ID3 (paper "Induction of Decision Trees", Machine Learning , 1986). Quinlan later produced C4.5 (1993). All three build the tree top-down and greedily. Because the learned model is just a set of if–then rules, trees are among the most interpretable ML models.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The everyday story (slide 2). Imagine you have several job offers. Some are close to home, some far; some pay well, some less; some have good benefits. You don't solve this in one giant leap. You make a list of what each job offers (the features : commute, pay, benefits) and then make small rules to throw options out: 

 "If the commute is longer than an hour, I'll be unhappy" → drop that job. 
 "If it pays less than $50k, I can't support my family" → drop that job too. 

 The teacher's key sentence: a hard decision ("will I be happy?") can be cut into a series of small, increasingly specific choices . That series of small choices is a decision tree. 

 What a decision tree is (slide 3). It is a drawing that shows choices and what follows from them, shaped like a tree turned upside down: 

 Each box (node) is a question or an event, e.g. "Is the commute longer than 1 hour?" 
 Each arrow (edge) is an answer or rule, e.g. "yes" or "no". 
 The ends of the branches are the final decisions, e.g. "accept" or "decline". 

 Matching the story to the words. 

 In the story 
 Tree word 

 commute time, pay, benefits 
 features (the things we know) 

 "Is the commute > 1 hour?" 
 a test at a node 

 "yes / no" 
 an edge (branch) 

 happy / unhappy, accept / decline 
 the leaf (final answer) 

 Where "machine learning" comes in. In the story you invented the rules. In ML the computer invents them: it studies lots of past, labelled examples (jobs people took and whether they turned out happy) and works out which question to ask first, which second, and so on. The method this lecture teaches for that is called ID3 . 

 A bit of history. Two groups built these methods independently in the 1980s: CART (1984, Breiman and colleagues) and ID3 (1986, Ross Quinlan), followed by Quinlan's improved C4.5 (1993). Why trees are loved: the result is just a list of if–then rules, so a person can read and trust it.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Roz-marra ki kahani (slide 2). Maan lo tumhare paas kai job offers hain. Kisi ka office paas hai, kisi ka door; kisi ki salary achhi hai, kisi ki kam; kisi mein benefits zyada hain. Tum ek chhalaang mein decide nahi karte. Tum har job ki list banate ho ki wo kya deti hai (ye features hain: commute, pay, benefits) aur phir chhote-chhote rules se options hata dete ho: 

 "Agar commute 1 ghante se zyada hai to main khush nahi rahunga" → wo job hata do. 
 "Agar $50k se kam milta hai to ghar nahi chala paunga" → wo bhi hata do. 

 Sir ka main vaakya: ek mushkil decision ("kya main khush rahunga?") ko chhote, dheere-dheere specific hote hue choices ki series mein kaata ja sakta hai. Wahi series ek decision tree hai. 

 Decision tree kya hai (slide 3). Ye ek drawing hai jo choices aur unke natije dikhati hai, ulte tree ki shakal mein: 

 Har box (node) ek sawaal ya event hai, jaise "Commute 1 ghante se zyada hai?" 
 Har teer (edge) ek jawaab ya rule hai, jaise "haan" ya "nahi". 
 Branches ke aakhri sire final decision hain, jaise "accept" ya "decline". 

 Kahani ko shabdon se jodo. 

 Kahani mein 
 Tree ka shabd 

 commute, pay, benefits 
 features (jo humein pata hai) 

 "Commute > 1 ghanta?" 
 node par test 

 "haan / nahi" 
 edge (branch) 

 khush / naakhush, accept / decline 
 leaf (final jawaab) 

 Machine learning kahan aati hai. Kahani mein rules tumne banaye. ML mein rules computer banata hai: wo bahut saare purane, labelled examples dekhta hai (kaun si job logon ne li aur baad mein wo khush the ya nahi) aur khud decide karta hai ki pehla sawaal kaun sa, doosra kaun sa, aur aage. Is kaam ka tareeka jo is lecture mein padhaya jayega wo ID3 hai. 

 Thoda history. 1980s mein do groups ne alag-alag ye methods banaye: CART (1984, Breiman aur saathi) aur ID3 (1986, Ross Quinlan), phir Quinlan ka behtar version C4.5 (1993). Trees pasand kyun kiye jaate hain: natija bas if–then rules ki list hota hai, isliye insaan ise padh kar bharosa kar sakta hai.

20-02_Tree_Structure_Terminology_and_Whe.lecture_title: Decision Trees and the ID3 Algorithm
20-02_Tree_Structure_Terminology_and_Whe.topic_title: Tree Structure, Key Terms and Where Decision Trees Are Used
20-02_Tree_Structure_Terminology_and_Whe.source: Lecture 20, slides 4–5 ("Decision Tree" bullet list, "Example"). Enriched with web research (pruning, regression trees).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 4 — the lecture's roadmap. A decision tree is a machine-learning algorithm used for both classification and regression . The slide lists six concepts: 

 Tree structure 
 Decision nodes 
 Leaf nodes 
 Splitting 
 Entropy and information gain 
 Pruning 

 Definitions. 

 Term 
 Meaning 

 Root node 
 The topmost decision node; the first question asked, applied to the whole training set. 

 Decision (internal) node 
 A node that tests one attribute and branches into children, one per outcome/value. 

 Branch / edge 
 One outcome of a test (e.g. Outlook = Sunny). 

 Leaf (terminal) node 
 A node with no children; it holds the final prediction (a class label for classification, a number for regression). 

 Splitting 
 Dividing the set of examples at a node into subsets according to the test's outcome. 

 Entropy / information gain 
 The numbers used to decide which attribute to split on (topics 06–07). 

 Pruning 
 Cutting back branches that do not generalise (not worked out in this lecture's slides — see below). 

 Depth 
 Length of the longest root-to-leaf path. 

 Classification vs. regression trees. If the target is a category (spam / not spam) the leaf stores the majority class; if the target is a number (house price) the leaf stores the average of the training targets in that leaf. ID3, which this lecture develops, builds classification trees on categorical attributes. 

 Slide 5 — typical uses. Predicting an email as spam / not spam ; whether a tumor is cancerous ; whether a loan is a good or bad credit risk — each based on the relevant factors. 

 Slide 5 — the training workflow. 

 Build the model from observed (training) data . 
 Use a validation set to verify and improve the model. 
 For a new set of predictor variables , run the example down the tree to get the category (yes/no, spam/not spam). 

 Pruning (enrichment — the slide only names it). A tree grown until every leaf is pure will memorise noise (overfitting, see L17 Overfitting vs. Underfitting — Bias vs. Variance ). Pre-pruning stops growth early (max depth, minimum samples per leaf, minimum gain); post-pruning grows the full tree and then removes subtrees that do not improve accuracy on validation data (e.g. reduced-error pruning). Research also notes that finding the smallest possible tree is NP-hard (Hyafil & Rivest, 1976), which is why greedy construction plus pruning is used in practice ( L20 The "Play Football?" Tree and the Three Key Ideas (Splitting Criterion, Keep Splitting, Greedy Approach) ).

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The lecture's roadmap (slide 4). A decision tree is a learning method that can answer category questions (spam or not spam?) and number questions (what will the price be?). The teacher lists six ideas we will meet: the tree's structure , decision nodes , leaf nodes , splitting , entropy and information gain , and pruning . 

 The vocabulary, using one picture in your head — an upside-down tree: 

 Root — the very first question, at the top. It looks at all the examples. 
 Decision node (also called internal node) — any other question box. It asks about one feature and has one arrow for each possible answer. 
 Branch / edge — one answer to a question (e.g. "Outlook = Sunny"). 
 Leaf — a box with no arrows leaving it. It holds the final answer: a category (spam) or a number (average price). 
 Splitting — sorting the examples into smaller piles according to the answer. 
 Depth — how many questions deep the longest path goes. 
 Entropy / information gain — scores that tell us which question to ask. (Next topics.) 
 Pruning — trimming off useless twigs. 

 Where trees are used (slide 5). Is this email spam? Is this tumour cancerous? Is this loan applicant a good or bad credit risk? In each case the tree looks at the relevant facts (words in the email, test results, income and past loans) and walks down to an answer. 

 How the whole process works (slide 5). 

 Build the tree from training data — examples where the right answer is already known. 
 Use a separate validation set to check how well it does and to improve it. 
 For a brand-new case, follow the questions from the top to a leaf. The leaf's answer is the prediction. 

 Why pruning matters (not worked out on the slides). If you keep splitting until every pile is perfectly pure, the tree starts memorising random quirks of the training data, like a student who memorises last year's exam paper but can't solve new questions ( overfitting ). Two cures: stop early (limit how deep it can grow), or grow fully, then trim the branches that don't help on validation data. Finding the very smallest tree is a famously hard problem, so in practice we grow quickly and trim afterwards.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Lecture ka roadmap (slide 4). Decision tree ek learning method hai jo category wale sawaal (spam hai ya nahi?) aur number wale sawaal (price kitna hoga?) dono ka jawaab de sakta hai. Sir ne chhe cheezein likhi hain jo hum dekhenge: tree ka structure , decision nodes , leaf nodes , splitting , entropy aur information gain , aur pruning . 

 Vocabulary — ek ulte tree ki tasveer dimaag mein rakho: 

 Root — sabse upar ka pehla sawaal. Ye saare examples ko dekhta hai. 
 Decision node (internal node bhi kehte hain) — baaki saare sawaal ke boxes. Ye ek feature ke baare mein poochta hai aur har possible jawaab ke liye ek teer hota hai. 
 Branch / edge — ek sawaal ka ek jawaab (jaise "Outlook = Sunny"). 
 Leaf — wo box jisme se koi teer bahar nahi nikalta. Isme final jawaab hota hai: category (spam) ya number (average price). 
 Splitting — examples ko jawaab ke hisaab se chhoti dheriyon mein baantna. 
 Depth — sabse lambe raaste mein kitne sawaal hain. 
 Entropy / information gain — wo scores jo batate hain kaun sa sawaal poochna hai. (Agle topics mein.) 
 Pruning — faltu daaliyan kaatna. 

 Trees kahan use hote hain (slide 5). Ye email spam hai? Ye tumor cancerous hai? Ye loan lene wala good ya bad credit risk hai? Har case mein tree zaroori facts dekhta hai (email ke words, test results, income aur purane loans) aur chalte-chalte ek jawaab tak pahunchta hai. 

 Poora process kaise chalta hai (slide 5). 

 Training data se tree banao — wo examples jinka sahi jawaab pehle se pata hai. 
 Ek alag validation set se check karo ki kitna achha kaam kar raha hai aur improve karo. 
 Bilkul naye case ke liye upar se leaf tak sawaal follow karo. Leaf ka jawaab hi prediction hai. 

 Pruning kyun zaroori hai (slides mein nahi samjhaya). Agar tum tab tak split karte raho jab tak har dheri bilkul pure na ho jaye, to tree training data ki random ajeeb baatein ratt leta hai — us student ki tarah jo pichhle saal ka paper ratt leta hai par naye sawaal nahi hal kar paata ( overfitting ). Do ilaaj: jaldi ruk jao (tree ko zyada gehra mat badhne do), ya poora ugao phir kaato jo branches validation data par kaam nahi aati. Sabse chhota tree dhundhna famous mushkil problem hai, isliye practice mein jaldi ugate hain aur baad mein chhaantte hain.

20-03_Worked_Tree_Will_Vaibhav_Suryavans.lecture_title: Decision Trees and the ID3 Algorithm
20-03_Worked_Tree_Will_Vaibhav_Suryavans.topic_title: Worked Tree — "Will Vaibhav Suryavanshi Play Today's Cricket Match?"
20-03_Worked_Tree_Will_Vaibhav_Suryavans.source: Lecture 20, slides 6–11 (one infographic revealed branch by branch across six slides; slides 6–10 are progressive builds, slide 11 is the finished tree). No external research needed — this is a self-contained illustration.

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
How the slides are built. Slides 6 → 11 show one figure appearing in stages: 

 Slide 
 What is newly revealed 

 6 
 Root: Match Today? with branches Yes / No 

 7 
 No → leaf NO – He Won't Play ; Yes → new node Weather OK? 

 8 
 Weather OK? → No → node Rain? ; Yes → node Playing XI Announced? 

 9 
 Rain? → Yes → NO (He Won't Play) ; No → YES – He Plays (weather cleared) 

 10 
 Playing XI Announced? → No → NO (not in XI yet) ; Yes → node Team Combination? with branches Not Favorable / Favorable 

 11 
 Not Favorable → NO (e.g., specialist needed) ; Favorable → YES – He Plays . Tagline: "Data + Decisions = Better Outcomes" 

 The complete tree (as plain text). 

 Match Today?
├─ No → NO (won't play)
└─ Yes → Weather OK?
 ├─ No → Rain?
 │ ├─ Yes → NO
 │ └─ No → YES (weather cleared)
 └─ Yes → Playing XI announced?
 ├─ No → NO (not in XI yet)
 └─ Yes → Team combination?
 ├─ Not favorable → NO (specialist needed)
 └─ Favorable → YES

 Reading it as rules. Each root-to-leaf path is one if–then rule, e.g.
 IF Match Today = Yes AND Weather OK = Yes AND Playing XI = Announced AND Team Combination = Favorable THEN Play = Yes .
The tree has 5 decision nodes (Match Today, Weather OK, Rain, Playing XI, Team Combination) and 6 leaves (2 YES leaves, 4 NO leaves — see table). 

 Leaf 
 Path 
 Outcome 

 1 
 Match=No 
 NO 

 2 
 Match=Yes, Weather=No, Rain=Yes 
 NO 

 3 
 Match=Yes, Weather=No, Rain=No 
 YES 

 4 
 Match=Yes, Weather=Yes, XI=No 
 NO 

 5 
 Match=Yes, Weather=Yes, XI=Yes, Team=Not favorable 
 NO 

 6 
 Match=Yes, Weather=Yes, XI=Yes, Team=Favorable 
 YES 

 So: 5 decision nodes, 6 leaves, depth 4 (longest path = Match → Weather → XI → Team). 

 Observations worth noting. 

 Different branches ask different follow-up questions (the "No" side of Weather asks about Rain, the "Yes" side asks about the Playing XI). A tree is not a fixed questionnaire; the next question depends on the earlier answers. 
 The order puts the most decisive question first: if there is no match at all, nothing else matters (a cheap early exit). 
 This figure was drawn by hand/by the instructor — it is not learned from data and carries no entropy values. It introduces the shape of a tree before the lecture shows how ID3 learns one ( L20 The Steps of the ID3 Algorithm ). 
 Slight logic quirk: "Weather OK? = No" followed by "Rain? = No → YES (weather cleared)" means bad weather but no rain still lets him play — that is the instructor's design, not a general rule.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The story. We want to guess: will Vaibhav Suryavanshi play today's cricket match? The teacher draws a tree and shows it growing on six slides, one branch at a time, so you can watch the questions pile up. 

 Walk through it, question by question. 

 Is there a match today? 
 
 No → he won't play. End. (A quick exit — if there's no match, no other question matters.) 
 Yes → go on to question 2. 
 
 Is the weather OK? 
 
 No → ask Is it raining? 
 
 Yes, raining → he won't play. 
 No rain → he plays (the weather cleared). 
 
 Yes → ask Has the playing XI been announced? 
 
 No → he won't play (he's not confirmed in the team yet). 
 Yes → ask Is the team combination favourable? 
 
 Not favourable (for example the team needs a specialist) → he won't play. 
 Favourable → he plays . 

 Counting the tree. There are 5 question boxes (Match today, Weather OK, Rain, Playing XI, Team combination) and 6 answer boxes : four say "won't play" and two say "plays". The longest path has 4 questions, so the tree is 4 levels deep. 

 Every path is a rule. For example: If there is a match, the weather is OK, the XI is announced, and the team combination is favourable → he plays. 

 Three things to notice. 

 Different branches ask different next questions: the "bad weather" side asks about rain, the "good weather" side asks about the XI. A tree isn't a fixed questionnaire; the next question depends on what you already learned. 
 The most decisive question is first (no match = nothing else matters). 
 One slightly odd rule: bad weather but no rain still lets him play. That is the teacher's design for the story, not a general rule of cricket. 

 Important. This tree was drawn by the teacher to show the shape of a tree. It was not learned from data and has no entropy numbers. The next topics show how a computer learns a tree from data.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Kahani. Hume guess karna hai: kya Vaibhav Suryavanshi aaj ka cricket match khelega? Sir ek tree banate hain aur 6 slides mein ek-ek branch karke dikhate hain, taaki dikhe ki sawaal kaise jud-jud kar badhte hain. 

 Sawaal-dar-sawaal chalo. 

 Aaj match hai? 
 
 Nahi → nahi khelega. Khatam. (Jaldi nikas — match hi nahi hai to baaki sawaal ka matlab nahi.) 
 Haan → sawaal 2. 
 
 Weather theek hai? 
 
 Nahi → poocho Barish ho rahi hai? 
 
 Haan, barish → nahi khelega. 
 Barish nahi → khelega (mausam saaf ho gaya). 
 
 Haan → poocho Playing XI announce ho gayi? 
 
 Nahi → nahi khelega (abhi team mein confirm nahi). 
 Haan → poocho Team combination favourable hai? 
 
 Favourable nahi (jaise team ko specialist chahiye) → nahi khelega. 
 Favourable → khelega . 

 Tree ginti. 5 sawaal wale boxes hain (Match today, Weather OK, Rain, Playing XI, Team combination) aur 6 jawaab wale boxes : chaar "nahi khelega" aur do "khelega". Sabse lambe raaste mein 4 sawaal hain, yaani tree 4 level gehra hai. 

 Har raasta ek rule hai. Jaise: Agar match hai, weather theek hai, XI announce ho gayi aur team combination favourable hai → khelega. 

 Teen baatein dhyan do. 

 Alag branches alag agle sawaal poochti hain: "kharab weather" wali side barish poochti hai, "achha weather" wali side XI poochti hai. Tree koi fixed questionnaire nahi hai; agla sawaal is par depend karta hai ki tumne pehle kya seekha. 
 Sabse decisive sawaal sabse pehle hai (match nahi = baaki kuch matter nahi karta). 
 Ek thoda ajeeb rule: kharab weather par barish nahi ho to bhi khelta hai. Ye sir ne kahani ke liye banaya hai, cricket ka general rule nahi. 

 Zaroori. Ye tree sir ne tree ki shakal dikhane ke liye khud banaya hai. Ye data se seekha hua nahi hai aur ismein entropy ke numbers nahi hain. Agle topics mein dikhaya jayega ki computer data se tree kaise seekhta hai.

20-04_Play_Football_Tree_and_the_Three_K.lecture_title: Decision Trees and the ID3 Algorithm
20-04_Play_Football_Tree_and_the_Three_K.topic_title: The "Play Football?" Tree and the Three Key Ideas (Splitting Criterion, Keep Splitting, Greedy Approach)
20-04_Play_Football_Tree_and_the_Three_K.source: Lecture 20, slide 12 ("Play Football ?" with the instructor's red handwritten annotations). Enriched with web research (greedy vs. global optimum, NP-hardness of optimal trees, dynamic programming alternatives).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
The tree on the slide. 

 Weather
├─ Sunny → Temp.
│ ├─ Hot → No
│ ├─ Mild → Yes
│ └─ Cold → Yes
├─ Cloudy → Yes
└─ Rain → Yes

 Root = Weather (3 values). Cloudy and Rain are already decided (Yes). Only Sunny needs another question, Temp. , whose three values lead to leaves No / Yes / Yes. 

 The three handwritten points. 

 ① Splitting criteria — entropy / information gain. Before building any tree we must decide how to choose the attribute at each node . The criteria introduced are entropy and information gain ( L20 Entropy — Measuring Disorder in a Dataset , L20 Information Gain — Choosing the Best Attribute ). 

 ② Keep on splitting until all data points belong to the same (one) class. This is the stopping rule of the basic algorithm: recurse on each subset until it is pure (entropy 0, all examples share one label). In the football tree, Cloudy and Rain are already pure; Sunny is split by Temp. until each Temp value is pure. 

 ③ Greedy approach. At each node the algorithm picks the attribute that looks best right now , without looking ahead and never undoing the choice. The instructor illustrates this with a hill-climbing picture : a curve with several peaks, labelled local max , 1st best , Top , Global maximum . A greedy climber who always steps uphill ends on the nearest peak (a local maximum ) and may miss the global maximum . The note beside it reads: greedy → "Dynamic Programming Alg." — i.e. the alternative that can guarantee a global optimum is dynamic programming. (The name "Bhuvan" scribbled next to the hill appears to be a person used in the climbing analogy; the handwriting is not fully legible, so treat that detail as uncertain.) 

 Research enrichment. 

 Finding the smallest decision tree consistent with the data is NP-hard (Hyafil & Rivest, 1976), so exact search is impractical for real data. Greedy top-down induction (ID3, C4.5, CART) is the practical compromise: fast, gives good accuracy, but no guarantee of the smallest or best tree. 
 Greedy trees tend to grow large and overfit, which is why pruning is added afterwards ( L20 Tree Structure, Key Terms and Where Decision Trees Are Used ). 
 Newer research shows dynamic programming with branch-and-bound can find optimal (shallow) trees and sometimes beat greedy trees by a few % accuracy, but only for small depths — this matches the instructor's "dynamic programming" remark. 
 Strictly, greedy tree induction is a single top-down pass (no iterative improvement), so "hill climbing" is an analogy for the greedy idea, not a literal description of the procedure. 

 Where the three ideas show up later. ① is topics 06–07; ② and ③ are the loop in L20 The Steps of the ID3 Algorithm .

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The picture (slide 12): "Shall we play football?" First look at the weather: 

 Cloudy → play. 
 Rain → play (as drawn on the slide). 
 Sunny → ask one more question, the temperature : hot → don't play, mild → play, cold → play. 

 The tree has only two question boxes (Weather, Temp.). Cloudy and Rain are already settled, so only the Sunny branch needed another question. 

 The teacher then wrote three big ideas in red. 

 ① How do we choose the question? — "splitting criteria". We use two scores called entropy and information gain (explained in the next topics). Think of them as ways of asking "which question clears up the most confusion?". 

 ② When do we stop? — "keep on splitting until every group has one answer". Keep asking questions inside each group until everyone in the group has the same answer (all "play" or all "don't play"). A group like that is called pure . 

 ③ How do we build it? — the "greedy approach". At each step pick the question that looks best right now ; don't look ahead, and never go back and change a choice. 

 The hill-climbing picture explained. Imagine climbing a hilly landscape in thick fog. Your rule: always step uphill. You'll end up on top of some hill — but maybe a small one (a local maximum ), while a much higher mountain (the global maximum ) stands elsewhere and you never find it, because reaching it would have meant first going downhill . Greedy is the same: fast and usually good, but it can miss the very best tree. The teacher noted that dynamic programming is the kind of method that can find the true best — but it costs a lot more work. (The name "Bhuvan" scribbled near the hill drawing is hard to read; probably a person used in the story.) 

 What happens in practice. Finding the absolute smallest tree is known to be extremely hard (NP-hard), so real programs use the greedy method and then prune (trim) the tree. Newer research shows exact methods can win a few percent of accuracy, but only for small trees.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Picture (slide 12): "Football khelna hai ya nahi?" Pehle weather dekho: 

 Cloudy → khelo. 
 Rain → khelo (jaisa slide par bana hai). 
 Sunny → ek aur sawaal poocho, temperature : hot → mat khelo, mild → khelo, cold → khelo. 

 Tree mein sirf do sawaal wale boxes hain (Weather, Temp.). Cloudy aur Rain pehle hi tay hain, isliye sirf Sunny branch ko aur sawaal chahiye tha. 

 Sir ne laal pen se teen badi baatein likhi. 

 ① Sawaal kaise chunein? — "splitting criteria". Do scores use karte hain: entropy aur information gain (agle topics mein samjhaye jayenge). Inhe aise samjho: "kaun sa sawaal sabse zyada confusion door karta hai?" 

 ② Kab rukein? — "tab tak split karo jab tak har group mein ek hi jawaab na ho". Har group ke andar sawaal poochte raho jab tak group mein sabka jawaab ek jaisa na ho jaye (sab "khelo" ya sab "mat khelo"). Aise group ko pure kehte hain. 

 ③ Tree kaise banayein? — "greedy approach". Har step par wahi sawaal chuno jo abhi sabse achha lag raha ho; aage ka mat socho, aur pichhla choice kabhi wapas mat badlo. 

 Hill-climbing picture samjho. Socho tum ghane kohre mein pahaadi par chadh rahe ho. Tumhara rule: hamesha upar ki taraf kadam rakho. Tum kisi pahaadi ki choti par pahunch jaoge — par ho sakta hai wo chhoti pahaadi ho ( local maximum ), jabki bahut unchi choti ( global maximum ) kahin aur hai aur tum use kabhi nahi dhundh paoge, kyunki wahan jaane ke liye pehle neeche utarna padta. Greedy bhi aisa hi hai: tez aur aam taur par achha, par sabse best tree miss kar sakta hai. Sir ne bataya ki dynamic programming wo tareeka hai jo asli best dhundh sakta hai — par usmein kaam bahut zyada lagta hai. (Pahaadi ke paas likha "Bhuvan" naam dhundhla hai; shayad kahani ka koi insaan.) 

 Practice mein kya hota hai. Sabse chhota tree dhundhna bahut mushkil problem hai (NP-hard), isliye real programs greedy method use karte hain aur phir tree ko prune (chhaant) dete hain. Naye research mein exact methods kuch percent zyada accuracy dete hain, par sirf chhote trees ke liye.

20-05_ID3_Algorithm_History_and_Greedy_T.lecture_title: Decision Trees and the ID3 Algorithm
20-05_ID3_Algorithm_History_and_Greedy_T.topic_title: The ID3 Algorithm — What It Is, Who Made It, and How It Works in One Paragraph
20-05_ID3_Algorithm_History_and_Greedy_T.source: Lecture 20, slide 13 ("Example: ID3 Algorithm" / "What is Iterative Dichotomiser3 Algorithm?"). Enriched with web research (Quinlan 1986 paper, C4.5 1993, CART 1984, ID3's limitations).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 13 — definitions. 

 ID3 = Iterative Dichotomiser 3. It builds decision trees from a given dataset. Developed in 1986 by Ross Quinlan (the slide's date; the standard citation is Quinlan, "Induction of Decision Trees", Machine Learning 1(1), 1986). 
 It is a greedy algorithm that builds the tree by recursively partitioning the data into smaller and smaller subsets until all data points in each subset belong to the same class . 
 It uses a top-down approach, selecting at each step the feature to split on according to information gain . 

 The name. Dichotomiser means "divider" (splitting data into groups); the "3" is usually explained as the third in Quinlan's series of programs — this is common background knowledge, not on the slides and not verified in this session . ID3 itself branches on every value of a categorical attribute, not just two (see the Outlook split with three branches, L20 Worked Example — Entropy of Each Outlook Subset and Information Gain of Outlook ). 

 Properties of ID3 (from the slides + research). 

 Property 
 Meaning 

 Greedy 
 Picks the locally best attribute; never backtracks ( L20 The "Play Football?" Tree and the Three Key Ideas (Splitting Criterion, Keep Splitting, Greedy Approach) ) 

 Top-down, recursive 
 Starts at the root with all data and recurses on each subset 

 Split criterion 
 Information gain (based on entropy) 

 Stops when 
 The subset is pure (one class) — or no attributes are left 

 Attribute types 
 Categorical only in the original ID3 

 Pruning 
 None in the original ID3 → tends to overfit 

 Family tree of algorithms (research). 

 Algorithm 
 Year 
 Key difference from ID3 

 ID3 
 1986 (Quinlan) 
 Information gain, categorical, no pruning 

 CART 
 1984 (Breiman, Friedman, Olshen, Stone) 
 Gini index , binary splits, handles regression too 

 C4.5 
 1993 (Quinlan) 
 Gain ratio , continuous attributes, missing values, pruning 

 ID3, CART and C4.5 were developed independently but share the same greedy top-down recipe. (Sources disagree slightly on some early dates; 1986 for ID3 is the one the slide uses and the one in the primary paper.) 

 Flag — Gini vs. entropy. Slide 14 says ID3 "uses a measure of impurity, such as entropy or Gini impurity". Strictly, original ID3 uses entropy / information gain only ; Gini impurity is the criterion of CART . Both are impurity measures and behave similarly, so the slide's remark is loosely true of "decision-tree algorithms" in general, but not of ID3 itself ( L20 Entropy — Measuring Disorder in a Dataset ).

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
What ID3 is. ID3 is a recipe for building a decision tree from a table of examples. Its full name is Iterative Dichotomiser 3 . It was created by Ross Quinlan in 1986 . (The name part "Dichotomiser" roughly means "divider" — something that splits data into groups. The "3" is usually explained as "the third in Quinlan's series of programs"; that's background knowledge, not something on the slides.) 

 The recipe in plain words. 

 Put all the examples together at the top. 
 Pick the question (column) that splits them into the cleanest groups. 
 Split the examples by that question's answers. 
 Do the same thing again inside each group, and again, and again — until every group has just one kind of answer . 

 Two words that describe the style. 

 Greedy — at each step it takes whatever looks best right now. It never goes back to change an earlier choice. (Like choosing the biggest slice of cake at each turn without thinking whether a different plan would have given you more overall.) 
 Top-down — it starts with the big picture at the top and works down to small groups at the bottom. 

 What it measures to pick "the cleanest" split. It uses a score called information gain , which is built from entropy (a "messiness" number). You'll learn both in the next two topics. 

 Limits of the original ID3. 

 It works only with categories such as Sunny/Rain/Overcast, not raw numbers like 31.5 °C. 
 It never trims the tree, so it can learn the training examples too exactly (overfitting). 
 It likes columns with lots of different values too much. 

 The family it belongs to. Two cousins appeared around the same time: CART (1984) and, later, Quinlan's own improved C4.5 (1993), which fixed several of ID3's limits (numbers, missing values, trimming). All use the same greedy top-down idea. 

 One mistake on the slide. Slide 14 says ID3 uses "entropy or Gini". That's a slip: ID3 uses entropy / information gain only ; Gini belongs to the CART algorithm. Both measure messiness and behave alike, so it's a small point — but good to know for exams.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
ID3 kya hai. ID3 examples ki table se decision tree banane ki ek recipe hai. Iska poora naam Iterative Dichotomiser 3 hai. Ise Ross Quinlan ne 1986 mein banaya. ("Dichotomiser" ka matlab lagbhag "baantne wala" — jo data ko groups mein baante. "3" ko aam taur par "Quinlan ke programs ki series mein teesra" kaha jata hai; ye background knowledge hai, slides mein nahi hai.) 

 Recipe simple shabdon mein. 

 Saare examples ek saath upar rakho. 
 Wo sawaal (column) chuno jo examples ko sabse saaf-suthre groups mein baante. 
 Us sawaal ke jawaabon ke hisaab se examples baant do. 
 Har group ke andar yahi kaam dobara, phir dobara karo — jab tak har group mein sirf ek hi tarah ka jawaab na bache. 

 Iska style batane wale do shabd. 

 Greedy — har step par jo abhi sabse achha lage wahi leta hai. Pichhla choice kabhi wapas nahi badalta. (Jaise cake ka har baar sabse bada tukda le lena, ye soche bina ki doosra plan overall zyada de sakta tha.) 
 Top-down — upar ke bade picture se shuru karke neeche chhote groups tak aata hai. 

 "Sabse saaf" split chunne ke liye kya naapta hai. Ek score use karta hai jise information gain kehte hain, jo entropy ("ghalat-malat" naapne ka number) se banta hai. Dono agle do topics mein seekhoge. 

 Original ID3 ki limits. 

 Sirf categories (Sunny/Rain/Overcast) par chalta hai, 31.5 °C jaise raw numbers par nahi. 
 Tree ko kabhi chhaanta nahi, isliye training examples ko zyada hi ratt sakta hai (overfitting). 
 Bahut saari alag values wale columns ko zyada pasand karta hai. 

 Kis family ka hai. Lagbhag usi samay do cousins aaye: CART (1984) aur baad mein Quinlan ka khud ka behtar C4.5 (1993), jisne ID3 ki kai limits theek ki (numbers, missing values, chhaantna). Sab same greedy top-down idea use karte hain. 

 Slide ki ek galti. Slide 14 kehti hai ID3 "entropy ya Gini" use karta hai. Ye chook hai: ID3 sirf entropy / information gain use karta hai; Gini CART algorithm ka hai. Dono ghalat-malat naapte hain aur milte-julte chalte hain, isliye chhoti baat hai — par exam ke liye jaanna achha hai.

20-06_Entropy_Measuring_Disorder_in_a_Da.lecture_title: Decision Trees and the ID3 Algorithm
20-06_Entropy_Measuring_Disorder_in_a_Da.topic_title: Entropy — Measuring Disorder in a Dataset
20-06_Entropy_Measuring_Disorder_in_a_Da.source: Lecture 20, slide 14 ("Entropy"). Enriched with web research (Shannon 1948, bits, coin examples) and independently verified numbers.

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 14 — what it says. 

 ID3 uses a measure of impurity (the slide names entropy or Gini impurity) to compute the information gain of each attribute. Entropy is a measure of disorder in a dataset. 
 High entropy : data points are evenly distributed across the categories (very mixed). Low entropy : data points are concentrated in one or a few categories (nearly pure). 

 Formula (slide): 

 H(S) = Σ − ( P_i · log₂ P_i ) 

 where P_i = fraction of the sample in the node that belongs to class i, S = the current dataset, i ranges over the set of classes in S. Write it fully for two classes (Yes/No): 

 H(S) = − p₊ log₂ p₊ − p₋ log₂ p₋ 

 Conventions. log₂ means answers are in bits (Shannon, A Mathematical Theory of Communication , 1948). By convention 0 · log₂ 0 = 0 (the limit as p → 0). Since 0 ≤ p ≤ 1, log₂ p ≤ 0, so the leading minus makes entropy ≥ 0. 

 Range. 

 Minimum 0 : all examples in one class (pure node). 
 Maximum for two classes = 1 bit : a 50/50 split. For k equally likely classes the maximum is log₂ k (3 classes → 1.585, 4 classes → 2). 

 Verified reference values (computed). 

 Class mix (Yes, No) 
 p₊ 
 Entropy (bits) 

 (7, 0) or (0, 7) 
 1 or 0 
 0 

 (9, 1) 
 0.9 
 0.469 

 (9, 5) — the PlayTennis dataset 
 0.643 
 0.9403 

 (3, 2) or (2, 3) 
 0.6 / 0.4 
 0.9710 

 (4, 2) 
 0.667 
 0.9183 

 (3, 1) 
 0.75 
 0.8113 

 (1, 1) 
 0.5 
 1.0 

 Intuition (research). Entropy is the average surprise . A fair coin (50/50) is maximally unpredictable → 1 bit. A coin that lands heads 90% of the time is more predictable → 0.469 bits. In a decision tree we want leaves where the answer is nearly certain, i.e. low entropy . 

 Worked calculation of H(S) = H(9 Yes, 5 No). 

 −(9/14) log₂(9/14) = −0.6429 × (−0.6374) = 0.4098 
 −(5/14) log₂(5/14) = −0.3571 × (−1.4854) = 0.5305 
 Sum = 0.9403 ≈ 0.94 (the value the instructor writes on slide 18, L20 Worked Example — The PlayTennis Dataset and the Entropy of the Whole Set ). 

 Entropy vs. Gini (so the slide's "or Gini" makes sense). Gini impurity = 1 − Σ P_i². For (9, 5): 1 − (0.643² + 0.357²) = 0.459 . Gini is used by CART , entropy by ID3/C4.5 ( L20 The ID3 Algorithm — What It Is, Who Made It, and How It Works in One Paragraph ).

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Entropy = "how mixed-up is this group?" Picture baskets of fruit: 

 A basket with only apples → perfectly tidy → entropy 0 . 
 A basket with half apples, half oranges → as mixed as it can possibly be → entropy 1 (for two kinds of fruit). 
 A basket with 9 apples and 1 orange → almost tidy → entropy about 0.47 . 
 With more than two kinds the maximum is bigger: 3 equally likely kinds → 1.58, 4 kinds → 2. 

 The slide's formula in words. For each kind of thing in the group, take its share (the fraction of the group), multiply that share by log base 2 of the share, add these up, and flip the sign: H(S) = Σ − (share × log₂ share) . Here S is the group we're looking at. (By agreement, an empty share counts as 0.) You don't have to love the formula — the idea is the scale: tidy → 0, completely mixed → maximum . 

 Why the minus sign? Shares are between 0 and 1, so their logs are negative; the minus sign turns the answer positive. 

 Quick reference — yes/no groups 

 Group (Yes, No) 
 Entropy 

 (7, 0) — all the same 
 0 

 (9, 1) 
 0.47 

 (4, 2) 
 0.92 

 (3, 1) 
 0.81 

 (3, 2) 
 0.971 

 (9, 5) — our tennis table 
 0.94 

 (1, 1) — a perfect coin toss 
 1.0 

 Our tennis table, worked out. 9 "Yes" and 5 "No" out of 14 days. 

 Yes share 9/14 = 0.643 → 0.643 × 0.637 = 0.410 
 No share 5/14 = 0.357 → 0.357 × 1.485 = 0.531 
 Add: 0.94 . Very close to the maximum 1, so the table is very mixed. 

 Why we care. Building a tree means asking questions that make the groups tidier (entropy falling towards 0). Entropy is the thermometer for that. 

 About the "or Gini" on the slide. Gini impurity is a similar messiness score (for our table: 0.459). It belongs to the CART algorithm; ID3 uses entropy.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Entropy = "ye group kitna mixed-up hai?" Fal ki tokriyon ki tasveer socho: 

 Sirf seb wali tokri → bilkul saaf → entropy 0 . 
 Aadhe seb, aadhe santre → jitna mixed ho sakta hai utna → entropy 1 (do tarah ke fal ke liye). 
 9 seb aur 1 santra → lagbhag saaf → entropy lagbhag 0.47 . 
 Do se zyada tarah ke fal ho to maximum bada hota hai: 3 barabar tarah → 1.58, 4 tarah → 2. 

 Slide ka formula shabdon mein. Group ki har cheez ka hissa (group ka fraction) lo, us hisse ko hisse ke log base 2 se guna karo, sab jodo aur sign ulta kar do: H(S) = Σ − (hissa × log₂ hissa) . Yahan S wo group hai jise dekh rahe hain. (Sahmati se khaali hissa 0 maana jata hai.) Formula ratna zaroori nahi — asli baat scale hai: saaf → 0, poora mixed → maximum . 

 Minus sign kyun? Hisse 0 aur 1 ke beech hote hain, isliye unka log negative aata hai; minus laga kar jawaab positive ho jata hai. 

 Quick reference — yes/no groups 

 Group (Yes, No) 
 Entropy 

 (7, 0) — sab same 
 0 

 (9, 1) 
 0.47

 0.92

 0.81

 0.971

 Hamari tennis table, hal karke. 14 dino mein 9 "Yes" aur 5 "No". 

 Yes ka hissa 9/14 = 0.643 → 0.643 × 0.637 = 0.410 
 No ka hissa 5/14 = 0.357 → 0.357 × 1.485 = 0.531 
 Jodo: 0.94 . Maximum 1 ke bahut paas, yaani table bahut mixed hai. 

 Hume kyun parwah hai. Tree banane ka matlab hai aise sawaal poochna jo groups ko zyada saaf karein (entropy 0 ki taraf girna). Entropy us ka thermometer hai. 

 Slide par "ya Gini" ke baare mein. Gini impurity bhi milta-julta ghalat-malat score hai (hamari table ke liye: 0.459). Wo CART algorithm ka hai; ID3 entropy use karta hai.

20-07_Information_Gain_Choosing_the_Best.lecture_title: Decision Trees and the ID3 Algorithm
20-07_Information_Gain_Choosing_the_Best.topic_title: Information Gain — Choosing the Best Attribute
20-07_Information_Gain_Choosing_the_Best.source: Lecture 20, slide 15 ("Information gain", with the instructor's tick marks on the symbol definitions). Enriched with web research (information gain = mutual information; conditional entropy).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 15 — what it says. 

 Information gain assesses how much valuable information an attribute can provide. Select the attribute with the highest information gain — it contributes most to understanding the data. High gain ⇒ the attribute offers significant insight. 
 ID3 "acts like an investigator ": at each step it makes the choice that maximises information gain , aiming to minimise uncertainty and make well-informed decisions (which can be further enhanced by preprocessing the data). 

 Formula (slide): 

 IG(A, D) = H(S) − Σ_v ( |S_v| / |S| ) × H(S_v) 

 (The slide prints a stray closing bracket "]" after the last term; it is a typesetting slip, not part of the maths.) 

 Symbols (as defined on the slide). 

 |S| = total number of instances in the dataset. 
 |S_v| = number of instances for which the attribute has value v . (The slide says "attribute D"; the formula's first argument is called A — the same attribute. In the worked example on slide 20 the instructor writes Gain(S, Outlook).) 
 H(S) = entropy of the whole dataset ( L20 Entropy — Measuring Disorder in a Dataset ). 
 H(S_v) = entropy of the subset where the attribute takes value v. 

 Meaning in one line. 

 Information gain = entropy before the split − weighted-average entropy after the split . 

 The second term, Σ (|S_v|/|S|) H(S_v), is the conditional entropy H(S | A): the expected disorder left after we know the attribute's value. Each subset is weighted by its size , so a big impure subset hurts more than a tiny one. 

 Properties. 

 IG ≥ 0 always; IG = 0 means the attribute tells us nothing about the class; the largest possible IG equals H(S) (a perfect split into pure subsets). 
 Information gain equals the mutual information between the attribute and the class label (information-theory view). 
 Known bias (research): information gain favours attributes with many distinct values (e.g. an ID column would split into all-pure singletons and get maximum gain but be useless). C4.5 fixes this with gain ratio ( L20 The ID3 Algorithm — What It Is, Who Made It, and How It Works in One Paragraph ). 

 Tiny sanity example (computed). S = 4 Yes + 4 No → H = 1. An attribute splits it into {3 Yes,1 No} and {1 Yes,3 No}: each subset H = 0.8113, weights ½ and ½, so IG = 1 − 0.8113 = 0.189 . A perfect attribute splitting into {4 Yes} and {4 No} gives IG = 1 − 0 = 1.0 .

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The idea. You want to guess whether tennis will be played. Each column you could ask about (Outlook? Wind? Humidity?) helps a little. Information gain tells you how much a question reduces your confusion — the bigger the gain, the more useful the question. 

 How to compute it — four steps. 

 Measure the confusion before asking anything: that's the entropy of the whole group, H(S). 
 Ask the question and sort the examples into piles by the answer (one pile per possible answer). 
 Measure the confusion inside each pile , then take an average that gives bigger piles more weight (a pile with 10 examples should count more than a pile with 2). Each pile's weight is its size ÷ the total. 
 Gain = confusion before − average confusion after. 

 The formula, read aloud. IG(A, D) = H(S) − Σ (|S_v| / |S|) × H(S_v). In words: entropy of everything , minus the sum over each answer v of (how many examples gave that answer ÷ total examples) × entropy of those examples . Here |S| is the total number of examples, |S_v| is how many have value v, and H(S_v) is the mess score of that pile. (The slide prints a stray "]" at the end — just a typing slip.) 

 The "investigator" idea. The teacher says ID3 behaves like a detective: at every step it asks the question that clears up the most mystery. It selects the attribute with the highest gain, because that attribute offers the most insight. 

 A tiny example. A group of 8 days, 4 yes and 4 no, has confusion 1.0. Suppose a question splits it into {3 yes, 1 no} and {1 yes, 3 no}. Each pile has mess 0.81 and weight ½, so the average mess after = 0.81 and the gain = 1.0 − 0.81 = 0.19 . A perfect question that gave {4 yes} and {4 no} would have gain 1.0 − 0 = 1.0 . 

 Handy facts. 

 Gain is never negative. Gain = 0 means the question tells you nothing. 
 The biggest gain possible equals the starting entropy. 
 Beware: gain likes questions with many different answers (like a "Day number" column that gives every day its own pile). Those piles are trivially pure but useless for new days. A later version of the algorithm, C4.5, corrects this with "gain ratio".

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Idea. Tumhe guess karna hai ki tennis khela jayega ya nahi. Har column jiske baare mein poochh sakte ho (Outlook? Wind? Humidity?) thodi madad karta hai. Information gain batata hai ki ek sawaal ne tumhara confusion kitna kam kiya — gain jitna bada, sawaal utna kaam ka. 

 Kaise nikalte hain — chaar steps. 

 Kuch poochne se pehle ka confusion naapo: poore group ki entropy, H(S). 
 Sawaal poocho aur jawaab ke hisaab se examples ki dheriyan banao (har possible jawaab ke liye ek dheri). 
 Har dheri ke andar ka confusion naapo, phir aisa average lo jisme bade group ko zyada weight mile (10 examples wali dheri ka asar 2 wali se zyada hona chahiye). Har dheri ka weight = uska size ÷ total. 
 Gain = pehle ka confusion − baad ka average confusion. 

 Formula, bol kar. IG(A, D) = H(S) − Σ (|S_v| / |S|) × H(S_v). Shabdon mein: sab ki entropy , minus har jawaab v par sum ka (kitne examples ne wo jawaab diya ÷ total examples) × un examples ki entropy . Yahan |S| total examples hain, |S_v| wo jinki value v hai, aur H(S_v) us dheri ka mess score hai. (Slide ke ant mein ek faltu "]" chhapa hai — bas typing ki chook.) 

 "Investigator" wali baat. Sir kehte hain ID3 ek detective jaisa hai: har step par wo sawaal poochta hai jo sabse zyada mystery solve kare. Wo sabse bade gain wala attribute chunta hai, kyunki wahi sabse zyada insight deta hai. 

 Ek chhota example. 8 dino ka group, 4 yes aur 4 no, confusion 1.0. Maan lo ek sawaal ise {3 yes, 1 no} aur {1 yes, 3 no} mein baant deta hai. Dono dheriyon ka mess 0.81 aur weight ½, to baad ka average mess = 0.81 aur gain = 1.0 − 0.81 = 0.19 . Ek perfect sawaal jo {4 yes} aur {4 no} deta, uska gain 1.0 − 0 = 1.0 hota. 

 Kaam ki baatein. 

 Gain kabhi negative nahi hota. Gain = 0 matlab sawaal kuch nahi batata. 
 Sabse bada possible gain starting entropy ke barabar hota hai. 
 Savdhaan: gain un sawaalon ko pasand karta hai jinke bahut saare alag jawaab ho (jaise "Day number" column jo har din ko apni dheri deta hai). Aisi dheriyan aasaani se pure hoti hain par naye dino ke liye bekaar. Baad ka version C4.5 ise "gain ratio" se theek karta hai.

20-08_Steps_of_the_ID3_Algorithm.lecture_title: Decision Trees and the ID3 Algorithm
20-08_Steps_of_the_ID3_Algorithm.topic_title: The Steps of the ID3 Algorithm
20-08_Steps_of_the_ID3_Algorithm.source: Lecture 20, slide 16 ("Steps of ID3 Algorithm"). Enriched with a pseudocode expansion, stopping conditions and a preview of the full tree for the lecture's dataset (computed independently; not on the slides).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
The four steps (slide 16). 

 Determine the entropy of the overall dataset using the class distribution. 
 For each feature: calculate the entropy for each of its categorical values, then assess the information gain for the feature. 
 Choose the feature that gives the highest information gain. 
 Iteratively apply all the above steps (on each resulting subset) to build the tree structure. 

 Pseudocode (expanded). 

 ID3(S, Attributes):
 create a node
 if all examples in S have the same class: # pure
 return leaf(that class)
 if Attributes is empty: # nothing left to ask
 return leaf(majority class of S)
 for each attribute A in Attributes:
 compute IG(S, A) = H(S) − Σ_v (|S_v|/|S|)·H(S_v)
 A_best = attribute with the largest IG
 node.test = A_best
 for each value v of A_best:
 S_v = examples in S with A_best = v
 if S_v is empty: add leaf(majority class of S)
 else: add branch v → ID3(S_v, Attributes − {A_best})
 return node

 Key points. 

 Each attribute is used at most once along a path (it is removed from the list after use) — because the subsets below already all share that attribute's value. 
 Gains are recomputed inside every subset ; the best attribute at the root need not be best lower down. 
 Stopping rule: pure subset (slide 12's "keep on splitting until all data points belong to the same class", L20 The "Play Football?" Tree and the Three Key Ideas (Splitting Criterion, Keep Splitting, Greedy Approach) ), or no attributes left, or an empty subset. 
 It is greedy : no backtracking, so the final tree is not guaranteed to be the smallest. 

 Preview — where the lecture's example leads (computed here; slides stop at the Outlook gain). For the 14-day PlayTennis table ( L20 Worked Example — The PlayTennis Dataset and the Entropy of the Whole Set ): 

 Attribute 
 Information gain 

 Outlook 
 0.2467 (highest → root) 

 Humidity 
 0.1518 

 Wind 
 0.0481 

 Temp 
 0.0292 

 Outlook = Overcast is pure (4 Yes) → leaf Yes . Recursing on the two impure subsets (5 days each): Sunny → best attribute Humidity (gain 0.971, splits into pure subsets: High → No, Normal → Yes); Rain → best attribute Wind (gain 0.971: Weak → Yes, Strong → No). Resulting tree: 

 Outlook
├─ Sunny → Humidity ─ High → No ; Normal → Yes
├─ Overcast → Yes
└─ Rain → Wind ─ Weak → Yes ; Strong → No

 (Expect the next lecture to continue the instructor's own working; this preview is for orientation and was verified by direct computation.)

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The four-step recipe for growing the tree (slide 16). 

 Measure the mess of the whole table. (Entropy of everything — for our tennis table 0.94.) 
 Test every column. For each column (Outlook, Temp, Humidity, Wind): sort the days by that column's answers, measure the mess of each pile, and work out the gain. 
 Pick the winner. The column with the biggest gain becomes the next question in the tree. 
 Repeat. Inside each pile, do steps 1–3 again with the remaining columns, and keep going. 

 When do we stop growing a branch? 

 When the pile is pure (everyone has the same answer) → write that answer and stop. 
 When there are no columns left to ask about → write down the most common answer in the pile. 
 When a pile turns out to be empty → use the most common answer from the parent group. 

 Rules of the game. 

 Each column is used at most once on any path from top to bottom (after you've asked "Outlook?", everybody in a pile has the same outlook, so asking again is pointless). 
 Gains are recalculated inside every pile . The best question at the top need not be the best question further down. 
 It is greedy : it never goes back and changes an earlier choice, so it isn't guaranteed to find the smallest possible tree. 

 Preview: where our tennis example ends up (not on the slides — we worked it out). 

 At the top, the gains are: Outlook 0.2467 (winner), Humidity 0.1518, Wind 0.0481, Temp 0.0292. 
 Overcast days are all "play" → pure → leaf Yes . 
 For Sunny days the best next question is Humidity (high → no, normal → yes). 
 For Rain days the best next question is Wind (weak → yes, strong → no). 

 That gives a tree with 3 questions and 5 answers, and temperature isn't needed at all . (The next lecture does exactly this calculation on its slides.)

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Tree ugaane ki chaar-step recipe (slide 16). 

 Poori table ka mess naapo. (Sab ki entropy — hamari tennis table ke liye 0.94.) 
 Har column test karo. Har column (Outlook, Temp, Humidity, Wind) ke liye: dino ko us column ke jawaabon se baanto, har dheri ka mess naapo aur gain nikalo. 
 Winner chuno. Jis column ka gain sabse bada ho wo tree ka agla sawaal banta hai. 
 Dohraao. Har dheri ke andar bache hue columns ke saath step 1–3 phir se karo, aur chalte raho. 

 Branch ugana kab band karein? 

 Jab dheri pure ho (sab ka jawaab same) → wo jawaab likho aur ruk jao. 
 Jab poochne ke liye koi column na bache → dheri ka sabse common jawaab likh do. 
 Jab dheri khaali nikle → parent group ka sabse common jawaab use karo. 

 Khel ke niyam. 

 Har column upar se neeche ke kisi bhi raaste par zyada se zyada ek baar use hota hai ("Outlook?" poochne ke baad ek dheri ke sabka outlook same hai, dobara poochna bekaar). 
 Gains har dheri ke andar dobara nikalte hain. Upar ka best sawaal neeche ka best ho, zaroori nahi. 
 Ye greedy hai: pichhla choice kabhi wapas nahi badalta, isliye sabse chhota tree milna guaranteed nahi. 

 Preview: hamara tennis example kahan khatam hota hai (slides mein nahi — humne nikaala). 

 Sabse upar gains: Outlook 0.2467 (winner), Humidity 0.1518, Wind 0.0481, Temp 0.0292. 
 Overcast din sab "khelo" → pure → leaf Yes . 
 Sunny dino ke liye agla best sawaal Humidity (high → nahi, normal → haan). 
 Rain dino ke liye agla best sawaal Wind (weak → haan, strong → nahi). 

 Natija: 3 sawaal aur 5 jawaab wala tree, aur temperature ki zaroorat hi nahi . (Agla lecture isi calculation ko slides par karta hai.)

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
What the table is. Each row is one day. For every day someone wrote down the weather (Outlook), how hot it was (Temp), how damp the air was (Humidity), how windy (Wind) — and the answer we care about: did we play tennis that day? The goal is to learn a set of questions that predicts the last column from the first four. 

 Job 1 — count the answers. Go down the PlayTennis column: 

 "Yes" on D3, D4, D5, D7, D9, D10, D11, D12, D13 → 9 days . 
 "No" on D1, D2, D6, D8, D14 → 5 days . 
 9 + 5 = 14 days in total. (The teacher wrote exactly this on slide 17: Yes → 9, No → 5, Total → 14.) 

 We write this as S = [9+, 5−] — "9 positives, 5 negatives". 

 Job 2 — how mixed up is this? (entropy) 
Think of entropy as a "mess score": 0 means everything is the same answer, 1 means a perfect 50/50 mix (for yes/no problems). 

 Share of "Yes" days: 9 ÷ 14 = 0.643 . Share of "No" days: 5 ÷ 14 = 0.357 . 
 For each share, multiply the share by a special number (log base 2 of the share, made positive): 
 
 Yes part: 0.643 × 0.637 = 0.410 
 No part: 0.357 × 1.485 = 0.531 
 
 Add the two parts: 0.410 + 0.531 = 0.94 . 

 What 0.94 tells us. It is very close to the maximum of 1. That means the table is almost a coin-toss: if you had to guess "play or not" with no extra information you would be wrong a lot. The rest of ID3 is a hunt for questions (Outlook? Wind? …) that push this number down towards 0. 

 Why the teacher circled "Outlook" on slide 18. He is about to test Outlook as the first question. Its possible answers are {Sunny, Overcast, Rain}. For that test we first need this starting mess score, 0.94, to compare against.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Table kya hai. Har row ek din hai. Har din ke liye kisi ne likha: mausam (Outlook), kitni garmi (Temp), hawa mein kitni nami (Humidity), kitni hawa (Wind) — aur wo jawaab jo humein chahiye: us din tennis khela ya nahi? Goal hai aise sawaal seekhna jo pehle chaar columns se aakhri column ka jawaab bata sakein. 

 Kaam 1 — jawaab gino. PlayTennis column mein neeche jao: 

 "Yes" D3, D4, D5, D7, D9, D10, D11, D12, D13 par → 9 din . 
 "No" D1, D2, D6, D8, D14 par → 5 din . 
 9 + 5 = 14 din total. (Sir ne slide 17 par yahi likha: Yes → 9, No → 5, Total → 14.) 

 Ise hum likhte hain S = [9+, 5−] — "9 positive, 5 negative". 

 Kaam 2 — ye kitna mixed hai? (entropy) 
Entropy ko "mess score" samjho: 0 matlab sab ka jawaab ek hi, 1 matlab perfect 50/50 mix (yes/no wale problems ke liye). 

 "Yes" din ka hissa: 9 ÷ 14 = 0.643 . "No" din ka hissa: 5 ÷ 14 = 0.357 . 
 Har hisse ko ek khaas number (hisse ka log base 2, positive bana kar) se guna karo:
 
 Yes wala hissa: 0.643 × 0.637 = 0.410 
 No wala hissa: 0.357 × 1.485 = 0.531 
 
 Dono jodo: 0.410 + 0.531 = 0.94 . 

 0.94 ka matlab. Ye maximum 1 ke bahut paas hai. Yaani table lagbhag sikka-uchhalne jaisa hai: agar koi extra jaankari na ho aur "khelna hai ya nahi" guess karna pade to bahut baar galat honge. ID3 ka baaki kaam aise sawaal dhundhna hai (Outlook? Wind? …) jo is number ko 0 ki taraf neeche laayein. 

 Sir ne slide 18 par "Outlook" ko circle kyun kiya. Wo Outlook ko pehle sawaal ke roop mein test karne wale hain. Uske possible jawaab {Sunny, Overcast, Rain} hain. Is test ke liye pehle ye starting mess score 0.94 chahiye taaki compare kar sakein.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The question. If our very first question is "What's the outlook?", how much tidier do the 14 days become? 

 Step 1 — sort the 14 days into three piles by outlook. 

 Sunny pile (5 days: D1, D2, D8, D9, D11): 2 played, 3 didn't. 
 Overcast pile (4 days: D3, D7, D12, D13): all 4 played. 
 Rain pile (5 days: D4, D5, D6, D10, D14): 3 played, 2 didn't.
(5 + 4 + 5 = 14 ✔, and 2 + 4 + 3 = 9 played ✔) 

 Step 2 — the mess score of each pile. 

 Sunny: shares are 2/5 = 0.4 and 3/5 = 0.6. Parts: 0.4 × 1.322 = 0.529 and 0.6 × 0.737 = 0.442. Add → 0.971 . 
 Overcast: share of "played" is 4/4 = 1 and of "didn't" is 0. Nothing is mixed, so the score is 0 . (The "0 × log 0" part is counted as 0 by agreement.) 
 Rain: shares are 3/5 = 0.6 and 2/5 = 0.4 — the same two numbers as Sunny, just swapped → 0.971 . 

 Step 3 — average the three scores, giving bigger piles more say. Each pile's weight is its size ÷ 14: 

 Sunny: (5/14) × 0.971 = 0.357 × 0.971 = 0.347 
 Overcast: (4/14) × 0 = 0 
 Rain: (5/14) × 0.971 = 0.347 
 Total (the mess after asking about outlook) = 0.694 . 

 Step 4 — gain = mess before − mess after. Before we asked anything the mess was 0.94. After: 0.694. Gain = 0.94 − 0.694 = 0.2464 (the teacher's number on slide 20). With every number kept at full precision the answer is 0.2467 — only a rounding difference, nothing wrong. If an exam wants 4 decimals, use the unrounded entropies. 

 What the gain means. Asking about the outlook removes about a quarter of the confusion. A big reason is the Overcast pile: it is completely clean, so on overcast days we can already say "play" with certainty.

These slides repeat [[08_Steps_of_the_ID3_Algorithm]], [[09_Worked_Example_PlayTennis_Dataset_and_Entropy_of_the_Whole_Set]] and [[10_Worked_Example_Entropy_of_Subsets_and_Information_Gain_of_Outlook]] from Lecture 20, so this file is a short recap, not a re-explanation.

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 1 — the four ID3 steps (identical to Lecture 20, slide 16). 

 Determine the entropy of the overall dataset using the class distribution. 
 For each feature: calculate entropy for each categorical value, then assess the information gain of the feature. 
 Choose the feature with the highest information gain. 
 Iteratively apply the steps to build the tree. 

 Slide 2 — the dataset. The same 14-day PlayTennis table (Outlook, Temp, Humidity, Wind → PlayTennis): 9 Yes, 5 No . 

 Slides 3–5 — the Outlook calculation redone. 

 Entropy(S) with S = [9+, 5−]: −(9/14)log₂(9/14) − (5/14)log₂(5/14) = 0.94 (exact 0.9403). 
 values(Outlook) = {Sunny, Overcast, Rain}:
 
 S_Sunny = [2+, 3−] → 0.971 
 S_Overcast = [4+, 0−] → 0 
 S_Rain = [3+, 2−] → 0.971 (slide 3 shows the "Rain = [3+,2−] ⇒ 0.97" note written separately) 
 
 Gain(S, Outlook) = 0.94 − (5/14)(0.971) − (4/14)(0) − (5/14)(0.971) = 0.2464 (exact 0.2467, rounding explained in Lecture 20). 
 On slide 5 the instructor pencils 0.2464 and 0.029 above the Outlook and Temp columns — the gain of Outlook already known and the gain of Temp (next topic) about to be computed. 

 What is new in Lecture 21. Lecture 20 stopped after Outlook. This lecture computes the gains of Temp, Humidity and Wind ( L21 Information Gain of the Attribute Temp (Hot, Mild, Cool) , L21 Information Gain of the Attribute Humidity (High, Normal) , L21 Information Gain of Wind and Choosing Outlook as the Root ), builds the first level of the tree, then recurses into the Sunny and Rain subsets until every leaf is pure, ending with the complete tree ( L21 The Rain Subset and the Final Decision Tree ).

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
This lecture continues last time, so it starts with a reminder. 

 The four-step recipe for growing a tree (slide 1). 

 Measure how mixed-up the whole table is (entropy). 
 For every column, split the days by its answers and work out how much tidier things get (information gain). 
 Pick the column with the biggest gain. 
 Repeat inside each group until the groups are clean. 

 The table (slide 2). The same 14 tennis days: for each day we know Outlook, Temp, Humidity, Wind and whether tennis was played. Counting: 9 days played, 5 days didn't . 

 The Outlook calculation, redone (slides 3–5). 

 Mess of the whole table: 9/14 and 5/14 → entropy 0.94 (very mixed). 
 Split by Outlook into three piles: 
 
 Sunny — 5 days: 2 played, 3 didn't → mess 0.971 (mixed). 
 Overcast — 4 days: all 4 played → mess 0 (perfectly clean). 
 Rain — 5 days: 3 played, 2 didn't → mess 0.971 (mixed). 
 
 Weighted average of the three (bigger piles count more): (5/14)×0.971 + (4/14)×0 + (5/14)×0.971 = 0.694 . 
 Gain = 0.94 − 0.694 ≈ 0.25 (the slide writes 0.2464; the more exact value is 0.2467). 

 On slide 5 the teacher writes 0.2464 above the Outlook column and 0.029 above Temp — the gain we already know and the one he's about to show. 

 What's new today. Last lecture ended after Outlook. Today we (1) work out the gains for Temp, Humidity and Wind, (2) choose the winner for the top of the tree, (3) keep splitting the sunny and rainy piles, and (4) end with the complete finished tree.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Ye lecture pichhle lecture ka agla hissa hai, isliye shuru mein yaad dilate hain. 

 Tree ugaane ki chaar-step recipe (slide 1). 

 Poori table kitni mixed-up hai wo naapo (entropy). 
 Har column ke liye dino ko uske jawaabon se baanto aur nikalo ki cheezein kitni saaf hui (information gain). 
 Sabse bade gain wala column chuno. 
 Har group ke andar tab tak dohraao jab tak group saaf na ho jaye. 

 Table (slide 2). Wahi 14 tennis ke din: har din ke liye Outlook, Temp, Humidity, Wind aur tennis khela ya nahi pata hai. Ginti: 9 din khela, 5 din nahi . 

 Outlook ki calculation, dobara (slides 3–5). 

 Poori table ka mess: 9/14 aur 5/14 → entropy 0.94 (bahut mixed). 
 Outlook se teen dheriyan: 
 
 Sunny — 5 din: 2 khele, 3 nahi → mess 0.971 (mixed). 
 Overcast — 4 din: chaaron khele → mess 0 (bilkul saaf). 
 Rain — 5 din: 3 khele, 2 nahi → mess 0.971 (mixed). 
 
 Teeno ka weighted average (bade group ka weight zyada): (5/14)×0.971 + (4/14)×0 + (5/14)×0.971 = 0.694 . 
 Gain = 0.94 − 0.694 ≈ 0.25 (slide par 0.2464 likha hai; exact value 0.2467 hai). 

 Slide 5 par sir ne Outlook column ke upar 0.2464 aur Temp ke upar 0.029 likha — ek jo pehle se pata hai aur ek jo abhi dikhane wale hain. 

 Aaj kya naya hai. Pichhla lecture Outlook ke baad ruk gaya tha. Aaj hum (1) Temp, Humidity aur Wind ke gains nikaalenge, (2) tree ke sabse upar ke liye winner chunenge, (3) sunny aur rainy dheriyon ko aur split karenge, aur (4) poora finished tree banayenge.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The question we are asking. Before we ask anything, the 14 days are a jumble: 9 "played", 5 "didn't play", mess score 0.94 . If we sort the days by temperature , do the piles become tidier? Let's measure. 

 Step 1 — make three piles. 

 Hot pile: 4 days. Result: 2 played, 2 didn't. 
 Cool pile: 4 days. Result: 3 played, 1 didn't. 
 Mild pile: 6 days. Result: 4 played, 2 didn't.
(4 + 4 + 6 = 14, so every day is in exactly one pile.) 

 Step 2 — mess score of each pile (entropy: 0 = perfectly tidy, 1 = a 50/50 mix). 

 Hot: exactly half and half → the worst possible mix → 1.0 . 
 Cool: 3 of 4 played. Part for "played": 0.75 × 0.415 = 0.311. Part for "didn't": 0.25 × 2 = 0.5. Add → 0.811 . 
 Mild: 4 of 6 played. Part for "played": 0.667 × 0.585 = 0.390. Part for "didn't": 0.333 × 1.585 = 0.528. Add → 0.918 . 

 Step 3 — average the three scores, giving bigger piles more say. Weights are pile size ÷ 14: Hot 4/14 = 0.286, Cool 0.286, Mild 6/14 = 0.429. 

 Hot: 0.286 × 1.0 = 0.286 
 Cool: 0.286 × 0.811 = 0.232 
 Mild: 0.429 × 0.918 = 0.394 
 Total = 0.911 

 Step 4 — gain = mess before − mess after = 0.94 − 0.911 = 0.029 . 

 Meaning: sorting by temperature only cleaned things up by 0.03 out of a possible 0.94. Hot days are a perfect coin-toss; the others are only slightly better. Temperature is a very weak first question. (If you use the unrounded 0.9403 instead of 0.94 you get 0.0292; the teacher's 0.029 on this slide and 0.0289 on a later slide are the same number with different rounding.)

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Sawaal: abhi 14 din ek jumble hain: 9 din khela, 5 din nahi, mess score 0.94 . Agar dino ko temperature se alag-alag dheriyon mein baantein, to kya dheriyan saaf-suthri hoti hain? Chalo naapte hain. 

 Step 1 — teen dheriyan banao. 

 Hot dheri: 4 din. Natija: 2 khele, 2 nahi. 
 Cool dheri: 4 din. Natija: 3 khele, 1 nahi. 
 Mild dheri: 6 din. Natija: 4 khele, 2 nahi.
(4 + 4 + 6 = 14, yaani har din bas ek hi dheri mein hai.) 

 Step 2 — har dheri ka mess score (entropy: 0 = bilkul saaf, 1 = 50/50 ka mix). 

 Hot: theek aadha-aadha → sabse kharab mix → 1.0 . 
 Cool: 4 mein se 3 khele. "Khela" ka hissa: 0.75 × 0.415 = 0.311. "Nahi khela" ka hissa: 0.25 × 2 = 0.5. Jodo → 0.811 . 
 Mild: 6 mein se 4 khele. "Khela" ka hissa: 0.667 × 0.585 = 0.390. "Nahi khela" ka hissa: 0.333 × 1.585 = 0.528. Jodo → 0.918 . 

 Step 3 — teeno scores ka average lo, bade group ko zyada weight dekar. Weight = dheri ka size ÷ 14: Hot 4/14 = 0.286, Cool 0.286, Mild 6/14 = 0.429. 

 Hot: 0.286 × 1.0 = 0.286 
 Cool: 0.286 × 0.811 = 0.232 
 Mild: 0.429 × 0.918 = 0.394 
 Total = 0.911 

 Step 4 — gain = pehle ka mess − baad ka mess = 0.94 − 0.911 = 0.029 . 

 Matlab: temperature se baantne par mess sirf 0.03 kam hua (0.94 mein se). Hot din bilkul "sikka uchhalne" jaise hain, baaki bhi thode hi behtar. Temperature pehle sawaal ke liye bahut kamzor hai. (Agar 0.94 ki jagah exact 0.9403 lo to 0.0292 aata hai; sir ka is slide par 0.029 aur baad wali slide par 0.0289 — dono wahi number hain, bas rounding alag.)

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The question. Same 14 days (9 played, 5 didn't, mess score 0.94). Now split them by humidity — either High or Normal. Does that tidy things up? 

 Step 1 — two piles. 

 High humidity pile: 7 days → 3 played, 4 didn't. 
 Normal humidity pile: 7 days → 6 played, 1 didn't.
(7 + 7 = 14 ✔) 

 Step 2 — mess score of each pile. 

 High: 3 of 7 played (0.429) and 4 of 7 didn't (0.571). Parts: 0.429 × 1.222 = 0.524 and 0.571 × 0.807 = 0.461. Add → 0.985 . That is almost the worst possible (1.0) — the High pile is still nearly a coin-toss. 
 Normal: 6 of 7 played (0.857) and 1 of 7 didn't (0.143). Parts: 0.857 × 0.222 = 0.191 and 0.143 × 2.807 = 0.401. Add → 0.592 . Much tidier — most Normal-humidity days were "play" days. 

 Step 3 — weighted average. Both piles have 7 of the 14 days, so each counts for half: 0.5 × 0.985 = 0.493 and 0.5 × 0.592 = 0.296 → total 0.789 . 

 Step 4 — gain = 0.94 − 0.789 = 0.152 (about 0.15). 

 Meaning: humidity removes about five times as much confusion as temperature did (0.15 vs 0.03). It is a decent question, but not the best — Outlook will beat it. Remember Humidity though; it comes back later as the perfect question for sunny days.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Sawaal. Wahi 14 din (9 khele, 5 nahi, mess score 0.94). Ab inhe humidity se baanto — High ya Normal. Kya isse cheezein saaf hoti hain? 

 Step 1 — do dheriyan. 

 High humidity dheri: 7 din → 3 khele, 4 nahi. 
 Normal humidity dheri: 7 din → 6 khele, 1 nahi.
(7 + 7 = 14 ✔) 

 Step 2 — har dheri ka mess score. 

 High: 7 mein se 3 khele (0.429) aur 4 nahi (0.571). Hisse: 0.429 × 1.222 = 0.524 aur 0.571 × 0.807 = 0.461. Jodo → 0.985 . Ye lagbhag sabse kharab (1.0) hai — High wali dheri abhi bhi sikka-uchhalne jaisi hai. 
 Normal: 7 mein se 6 khele (0.857) aur 1 nahi (0.143). Hisse: 0.857 × 0.222 = 0.191 aur 0.143 × 2.807 = 0.401. Jodo → 0.592 . Kaafi saaf — Normal humidity wale zyada tar din "khelne" wale the. 

 Step 3 — weighted average. Dono dheriyon mein 14 mein se 7-7 din hain, isliye har ek ka aadha weight: 0.5 × 0.985 = 0.493 aur 0.5 × 0.592 = 0.296 → total 0.789 . 

 Step 4 — gain = 0.94 − 0.789 = 0.152 (lagbhag 0.15). 

 Matlab: humidity ne temperature se lagbhag paanch guna zyada confusion hataya (0.15 vs 0.03). Achha sawaal hai, par best nahi — Outlook isse jeet jayega. Humidity ko yaad rakhna; baad mein sunny dino ke liye ye perfect sawaal banega.
