sections.text:
Wind, step by step (the slide itself shows only the table, so this working is ours). 

 Step 1 — two piles by wind. 

 Weak wind: 8 days → 6 played, 2 didn't. 
 Strong wind: 6 days → 3 played, 3 didn't.
(8 + 6 = 14 ✔) 

 Step 2 — mess score of each pile. 

 Weak: 6 of 8 played = 0.75, 2 of 8 didn't = 0.25. Parts: 0.75 × 0.415 = 0.311 and 0.25 × 2 = 0.5 → 0.811 . 
 Strong: exactly half and half → 1.0 (the worst possible). 

 Step 3 — weighted average. Weak: 8/14 = 0.571 × 0.811 = 0.463. Strong: 6/14 = 0.429 × 1.0 = 0.429. Total = 0.892 . 

 Step 4 — gain = 0.94 − 0.892 = 0.048 . Wind helps only a tiny bit.

 Why Outlook wins. When we split by Outlook, one of its three piles (Overcast) came out perfectly tidy — all 4 days "played". That one clean pile is a huge help. None of the other questions produce a clean pile.

 Outlook kyun jeeta? Outlook se baantne par uski teen dheriyon mein se ek (Overcast) bilkul saaf nikli — chaaron din "khela". Ek saaf dheri bahut bada fayda deti hai. Baaki kisi sawaal se koi saaf dheri nahi bani. 

 Decision. Jiska score sabse bada, wahi jeetta hai, isliye tree ke sabse upar pehla sawaal hoga "Outlook kya hai?" — ise root kehte hain. (Slide ke numbers aur exact numbers mein jo chhota fark hai — jaise 0.2464 vs 0.2467 — wo sirf rounding ki wajah se hai; chaaron scores ka order kabhi nahi badalta.)

sections.text:
What the slide draws. Root node Outlook holding the whole dataset {D1, D2, …, D14}, [9+, 5−] , with three branches:

 How the subsets are formed. "Splitting" ( L20 Tree Structure, Key Terms and Where Decision Trees Are Used ) sends every row down the branch matching its Outlook value; the subset sizes 5 + 4 + 5 = 14 add back to the whole set, and the Yes/No counts add back to [9+, 5−]. 

 Applying the stopping rule ( L20 The "Play Football?" Tree and the Three Key Ideas (Splitting Criterion, Keep Splitting, Greedy Approach) : "keep on splitting until all data points belong to the same class"): 

 Overcast is pure (entropy 0) → stop; the leaf predicts Yes . 
 Sunny and Rain are impure (entropy 0.971 each) → recurse: run ID3 again on each subset, using only the remaining attributes {Temp, Humidity, Wind} — Outlook is not reused on a path because it is constant inside each subset. 

 The "?" boxes on the slide are exactly these two unfinished nodes; the next topics fill them ( L21 The Sunny Subset — Gains of Temp, Humidity, Wind and the Humidity Split and L21 The Rain Subset and the Final Decision Tree ). 

 Important: the best attribute can differ per subset — the gains must be recomputed on each subset , not reused from the root.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Where we are. The scoreboard said Outlook is the best first question, so the top of our tree is "What is the Outlook?" Now we actually use that question: every one of the 14 days walks down the arrow that matches its outlook. The teacher draws this on slide 10, writing the list of day numbers next to each box. 

 The three boxes after the split. 

 Sunny box — 5 days (D1, D2, D8, D9, D11). 2 played, 3 didn't. Still a mix, so the teacher draws a "?" — we need another question here. 
 Overcast box — 4 days (D3, D7, D12, D13). All 4 played. This one is perfectly clean , so we're done: write "Yes" . 
 Rain box — 5 days (D4, D5, D6, D10, D14). 3 played, 2 didn't. Still a mix, so another "?". 

 A good habit: check your counts. 5 + 4 + 5 = 14 days (nobody lost or doubled), and 2 + 4 + 3 = 9 "played", 3 + 0 + 2 = 5 "didn't" (matches the starting [9+, 5−]). 

 What do the two "?" boxes mean? They are the unfinished parts of the tree. For each one we repeat the same game — measure the mess, test the columns, pick the best — but with two differences: 

 We only use the days in that box (5 days each). 
 We can only use the columns not yet used on that path: Temp, Humidity, Wind . We don't ask "Outlook?" again, because everybody in a box already has the same outlook. 

 One more important point. The scores must be recomputed inside each box . The scoreboard from the top (Outlook best, then Humidity, Wind, Temp) was for all 14 days. Inside the sunny box the order will turn out to be different. 

 Rule of thumb for stopping: a box that is pure (all the same answer) becomes a leaf; a box that is still mixed gets another question.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Hum kahan hain. Scoreboard ne bataya ki Outlook sabse achha pehla sawaal hai, isliye tree ke sabse upar "Outlook kya hai?" hai. Ab hum us sawaal ko use karte hain: 14 mein se har din apne outlook wale teer par neeche jata hai. Sir ye slide 10 par banate hain aur har box ke paas day numbers ki list likhte hain. 

 Split ke baad teen box. 

 Sunny box — 5 din (D1, D2, D8, D9, D11). 2 khele, 3 nahi. Abhi bhi mix hai, isliye sir "?" banate hain — yahan aur sawaal chahiye. 
 Overcast box — 4 din (D3, D7, D12, D13). Chaaron khele. Ye bilkul saaf hai, isliye kaam khatam: "Yes" likh do. 
 Rain box — 5 din (D4, D5, D6, D10, D14). 3 khele, 2 nahi. Abhi mix hai, isliye ek aur "?". 

 Achhi aadat: apni ginti check karo. 5 + 4 + 5 = 14 din (koi gum ya double nahi hua), aur 2 + 4 + 3 = 9 "khela", 3 + 0 + 2 = 5 "nahi khela" (shuruaati [9+, 5−] se match). 

 Do "?" boxes ka matlab kya hai? Ye tree ke adhoore hisse hain. Har ek ke liye wahi khel dobara — mess naapo, columns test karo, best chuno — par do farak ke saath: 

 Sirf us box ke din use karte hain (har box mein 5 din). 
 Sirf wahi columns use kar sakte hain jo is raaste par abhi use nahi hue: Temp, Humidity, Wind . "Outlook?" dobara nahi poochte, kyunki box ke sabhi dino ka outlook pehle se same hai. 

 Ek aur zaroori baat. Scores har box ke andar dobara nikalne padte hain. Upar wala scoreboard (Outlook best, phir Humidity, Wind, Temp) saare 14 dino ke liye tha. Sunny box ke andar order alag nikalega. 

 Rukne ka rule: jo box pure hai (sab ka jawaab same) wo leaf ban jata hai; jo abhi mixed hai usse aur sawaal milta hai.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Where we are. We asked "What's the Outlook?" first. Now we look only at the sunny days — 5 of them: D1, D2, D8, D9, D11. Two played, three didn't, so this little group is still mixed. Its mess score is: 2/5 = 0.4 → 0.4 × 1.322 = 0.529; 3/5 = 0.6 → 0.6 × 0.737 = 0.442; total 0.971 . We now repeat the whole game on just these 5 days, using only the columns we haven't used yet: Temp, Humidity, Wind. 

 Question 1 — Temperature? 

 Hot: D1 and D2 → both "didn't play" → perfectly tidy → score 0. 
 Cool: only D9 → "played" → tidy → score 0. 
 Mild: D8 ("didn't") and D11 ("played") → a 50/50 mix → score 1.0. 
 Weights: Hot 2/5, Cool 1/5, Mild 2/5. Average mess = (2/5)×0 + (1/5)×0 + (2/5)×1.0 = 0.4 . 
 Gain = 0.971 − 0.4 = 0.571 . Pretty good. 

 Question 2 — Humidity? 

 High: D1, D2, D8 → all three "didn't play" → score 0. 
 Normal: D9, D11 → both "played" → score 0. 
 Average mess = 0. Both piles are perfectly clean! Gain = 0.971 − 0 = 0.971 — you can't do better than that. 

 Question 3 — Wind? 

 Weak: D1 (no), D8 (no), D9 (yes) → 1 yes, 2 no → score 0.918. 
 Strong: D2 (no), D11 (yes) → 50/50 → score 1.0. 
 Average mess = (3/5)×0.918 + (2/5)×1.0 = 0.551 + 0.4 = 0.951. Gain = 0.971 − 0.951 = 0.020 (almost nothing). 

 Winner: Humidity. So on sunny days the tree asks about humidity: High → don't play (D1, D2, D8), Normal → play (D9, D11). Both leaves are pure, so the sunny branch is finished. 

 Three small things to know. (1) The teacher's slide shows 0.570, 0.97 and 0.0192; the exact values are 0.571, 0.971 and 0.020 — only rounding. (2) On slide 11 he first wrote 0.97 for the Hot pile and then crossed it out and wrote 0, because both Hot days are "No". (3) Humidity was only second best at the very top (0.15) but is the best inside sunny days — the best question depends on which group you're looking at.

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Recap of the full ID3 run on PlayTennis. 

 Step 
 Candidate gains 
 Choice 

 Root (14 days) 
 Outlook 0.2467, Humidity 0.1518, Wind 0.0481, Temp 0.0292 
 Outlook 

 Sunny (5 days) 
 Humidity 0.971, Temp 0.571, Wind 0.020 
 Humidity

 leaf Yes 

 Rain (5 days) 
 Wind 0.971, Temp 0.020, Humidity 0.020 
 Wind 

 Result: 3 decision nodes, 5 leaves, depth 2, Temp unused ( L21 The Rain Subset and the Final Decision Tree ). 

 1. Inductive bias. ID3 searches the space of all possible trees from simple to complex, greedily. Its bias (per course notes on Mitchell's treatment) is a preference for shorter trees , and for trees that put high-information-gain attributes near the root . This is a preference bias , not a restriction of the hypothesis space. It echoes Occam's razor (prefer the simplest hypothesis that fits), although the justification is debated. Because the search is greedy ( L20 The "Play Football?" Tree and the Three Key Ideas (Splitting Criterion, Keep Splitting, Greedy Approach) ), the shortest tree is not guaranteed . 

 2. Overfitting. ID3 keeps splitting until leaves are pure, so it fits the training set perfectly (here 14/14) — including noise. On noisy data this yields large, brittle trees; remedies are pre-pruning (depth/min-samples limits), post-pruning (reduced-error pruning on validation data), and ensembles. See L17 Overfitting vs. Underfitting — Bias vs. Variance . 

 3. Limitations of original ID3. 

 Categorical attributes only (numeric ones need threshold splits → C4.5). 
 No handling of missing values. 
 Information gain favours attributes with many distinct values (a "Day" ID column would get maximal gain but is useless) → gain ratio in C4.5 ( L20 The ID3 Algorithm — What It Is, Who Made It, and How It Works in One Paragraph ). 
 Small changes in data can change the root and hence the entire tree (high variance). 

 4. Interpretability. The tree reads as five if–then rules, each root-to-leaf path being one rule — an advantage over black-box models. 

 5. In practice (Python). From general knowledge, not verified in this session: scikit-learn's DecisionTreeClassifier implements CART , not ID3; criterion="entropy" uses information gain, but trees are binary (a 3-valued attribute like Outlook is encoded/split in two-way tests) and, by default, grown until pure, so pruning parameters ( max_depth , min_samples_leaf , ccp_alpha ) are needed to control overfitting. Categorical text values must be encoded to numbers first. 

 6. Gotchas seen in these slides (all harmless). 

 Handwritten gains are rounded intermediates: Outlook 0.2464 vs exact 0.2467, Temp 0.0289 vs 0.0292, Humidity 0.1516 vs 0.1518, Sunny-Temp 0.570 vs 0.571, Sunny-Wind 0.0192 vs 0.0200. 
 Slide 13 and slide 15 show the same tree; slide 15's lower edge is cropped.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
What did building this tree teach us? 

 1. The tree is a short list of rules. 

 Sunny and high humidity → don't play. 
 Sunny and normal humidity → play. 
 Overcast → play. 
 Rain and strong wind → don't play. 
 Rain and weak wind → play.
Anyone can read these and check them. That's the big selling point of decision trees. 

 2. ID3 likes short trees. It tries to ask the most useful question first (Outlook), so that later branches need few questions. Temperature was never needed. This habit — preferring simple, short explanations — is related to an old idea called "Occam's razor": if a simple explanation fits the facts, prefer it. 

 3. It can be too perfect. Our tree gets all 14 training days right, because it keeps asking questions until each box is clean. With messy real-life data (a few wrong labels, random flukes) such a tree would memorise the flukes and then stumble on new days. This is overfitting . The usual cure is pruning : stop growing early, or grow the full tree and then trim the branches that don't really help. 

 4. Greedy means "best right now". ID3 picks the best question at each step without planning ahead. That's fast, but there might be a slightly smaller tree it never tries. 

 5. Limits of basic ID3. 

 Only works with categories (Sunny/Rain), not raw numbers. 
 Doesn't handle missing values. 
 Overrates columns with lots of different values. 
 Change a few rows of data and the top question (and so the whole tree) can change.
Later versions (C4.5, CART) fix most of these. 

 6. Using it in Python (general knowledge — not checked in this session). The popular library scikit-learn has a DecisionTreeClassifier . It is really the CART algorithm, not ID3. You can ask it to use entropy ("information gain"), but its trees are always two-way splits, and by default it grows until the boxes are pure — so you'd set limits (like a maximum depth) to avoid overfitting. Text answers like "Sunny" must first be turned into numbers. 

 Small things you may notice on the slides. The teacher's handwritten gains are slightly rounded (0.2464 instead of 0.2467, etc.). Slide 13 and slide 15 show the same tree at different stages; slide 15's bottom edge is cut off in the PDF.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Is tree ko banane se humne kya seekha? 

 1. Tree rules ki ek chhoti list hai. 

 Sunny aur high humidity → mat khelo. 
 Sunny aur normal humidity → khelo. 
 Overcast → khelo. 
 Rain aur strong wind → mat khelo. 
 Rain aur weak wind → khelo.
Koi bhi inhe padh kar check kar sakta hai. Decision trees ki sabse badi khoobi yahi hai. 

 2. ID3 chhote trees pasand karta hai. Wo sabse kaam ka sawaal pehle poochta hai (Outlook), taaki baad ki branches ko kam sawaal chahiye. Temperature ki kabhi zaroorat nahi padi. Ye aadat — simple, chhoti explanation ko pasand karna — ek purane idea "Occam's razor" se judi hai: agar simple explanation facts se match karti hai to wahi chuno. 

 3. Ye zyada hi perfect ho sakta hai. Hamara tree saare 14 training dino ko sahi pehchanta hai, kyunki jab tak har box saaf na ho wo sawaal poochta rehta hai. Gandle real-life data (kuch galat labels, random flukes) par aisa tree flukes ko ratt leta hai aur naye dino par ladkhadata hai. Ye overfitting hai. Aam ilaaj pruning hai: jaldi ruk jao, ya poora tree ugao aur phir wo branches kaat do jo sach mein kaam nahi aati. 

 4. Greedy matlab "abhi ka best". ID3 aage ki planning ke bina har step par best sawaal chunta hai. Ye tez hai, par ho sakta hai koi thoda chhota tree ho jo wo kabhi try na kare. 

 5. Basic ID3 ki limits. 

 Sirf categories (Sunny/Rain) par chalta hai, raw numbers par nahi. 
 Missing values handle nahi karta. 
 Bahut saari alag values wale columns ko zyada number deta hai. 
 Data ki kuch rows badlo to sabse upar ka sawaal (aur isliye poora tree) badal sakta hai.
Baad ke versions (C4.5, CART) inme se zyadatar theek karte hain. 

 6. Python mein use (general knowledge — is session mein verify nahi kiya). Mashhoor library scikit-learn mein DecisionTreeClassifier hota hai. Wo asal mein CART algorithm hai, ID3 nahi. Tum use entropy ("information gain") use karne ko keh sakte ho, par uske trees hamesha do-tarfa splits hote hain, aur by default wo tab tak ugta hai jab tak box pure na ho — isliye overfitting se bachne ke liye limits (jaise maximum depth) lagani padti hain. "Sunny" jaise text jawaabon ko pehle numbers mein badalna padta hai. 

 Slides par dikhne wali chhoti baatein. Sir ke haath se likhe gains thode rounded hain (0.2467 ki jagah 0.2464, wagairah). Slide 13 aur slide 15 same tree ko alag stages mein dikhati hain; slide 15 ka neeche ka hissa PDF mein kata hua hai.

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 3 — the job-offer tree (typed figure). 

 Salary at least $50,000? <- root node (decision node)
├─ no → Decline offer <- leaf
└─ yes → Commute more than 1 hour? <- decision node
 ├─ yes → Decline offer <- leaf
 └─ no → Offers free coffee? <- decision node
 ├─ yes → Accept offer <- leaf
 └─ no → Decline offer <- leaf

 The figure labels the root node , the decision nodes and the leaf nodes — exactly the vocabulary of Lecture 20. It has 3 decision nodes, 4 leaves, depth 3; only one path (salary ≥ 50k, commute ≤ 1 hr, free coffee) ends in "accept" . Instructor's red marks: ✗ on each "decline" leaf, "Yes/No" on the job-offer picture, and word-labels on the three questions — Salary , "Travel" (commute) and "Complimentary" (free coffee) — plus "FIKA" (the Swedish tradition of a coffee break; the instructor's side-remark on the coffee perk). 

 Slide 2 — handwritten recap notes (partly legible). The instructor re-uses the tree to list features that could matter in a real job decision: Salary, Distance from home, Job profile, Holiday, Working hrs. Around it are several asides that show where tree-style reasoning appears in practice or in conversation. As far as it can be read: 

 an aside on top-ranked AI venues ( NeurIPS, "A*" ranking ) and on LLM hallucination / "AI escaping" — not developed on any later slide; 
 a food-delivery flow drawn as a decision sequence (Zomato/Swiggy order vs. Domino's, "30 min"): ① order accepted, ② check order/customization/message, ③ added, ④ prepare pizza, ⑤ look for delivery partner (20 mins), ⑥ delivery in 53 mins, ⑦ completed, ⑧ payment/vendor; 
 a small box A–B–C–D "Safe order / Take risk" labelled "risky step". 

 Flag: much of this handwriting is hard to read, so the details above are best-effort; none of it is used again in the lecture's technical content. The takeaway the instructor is drawing is that a real decision is a chain of small yes/no checks on features — a decision tree. 

 Why this recap matters here. A single tree is easy to read but unstable and prone to overfitting ( L17 Overfitting vs. Underfitting — Bias vs. Variance ). Random forests, the topic of this lecture, repair that by combining many trees ( L22 What Is a Random Forest? (Breiman, 2001) ).

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
A reminder of last lecture's tree: "Should I accept this new job?" 

 Is the salary at least $50,000? If no → decline the offer. 
 If yes → Is the commute longer than 1 hour? If yes → decline. 
 If no → Does the office offer free coffee? Yes → accept. No → decline. 

 Only one path ends in "accept": good salary, short commute and free coffee. Every other path ends in "decline". On the picture the top question is the root , each question box is a decision node , and each final answer is a leaf . The teacher put a red ✗ on each "decline" leaf, labelled the three questions Salary , Travel and Complimentary (the free coffee), and wrote "FIKA" — a Swedish word for a relaxed coffee break. 

 The teacher's handwritten extras (slide 2). Around the tree he listed features that could matter in a real job decision: salary, distance from home, job profile, holidays, working hours. He also drew a few side examples to show that everyday processes are chains of checks — for instance an online pizza order: order accepted → check the customisation → added → pizza prepared → look for a delivery partner → delivered → payment. (The handwriting is hard to read, so the details of these side notes are best-effort, and a couple of other asides — about AI conferences and AI models making things up — are not developed anywhere else in the lecture.) 

 Why this recap, and why it matters today. A single decision tree is easy to read, but it is jumpy : change a few of the training examples and you may get a quite different tree; and a tree grown until every box is pure may just memorise the training data. Today's topic, the random forest , fixes this by asking many trees and taking a vote.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Pichhle lecture ke tree ki yaad: "Kya mujhe ye nayi job accept karni chahiye?" 

 Salary kam se kam $50,000 hai? Agar nahi → offer decline. 
 Agar haan → Commute 1 ghante se zyada hai? Agar haan → decline. 
 Agar nahi → Office mein free coffee milti hai? Haan → accept. Nahi → decline. 

 Sirf ek raasta "accept" par khatam hota hai: achhi salary, chhota commute aur free coffee. Baaki har raasta "decline" par. Picture mein sabse upar ka sawaal root hai, har sawaal ka box decision node hai, aur har final jawaab leaf hai. Sir ne har "decline" leaf par laal ✗ lagaya, teeno sawaalon ko Salary , Travel aur Complimentary (free coffee) naam diye, aur "FIKA" likha — Sweden ka ek shabd jiska matlab aaram wala coffee break hai. 

 Sir ke haath se likhe extras (slide 2). Tree ke aas-paas unhone wo features likhe jo asli job decision mein matter kar sakte hain: salary, ghar se doori, job profile, holidays, working hours. Saath mein kuch side examples bhi banaye ye dikhane ke liye ki roz ki cheezein bhi checks ki chain hain — jaise online pizza order: order accept → customization check → add → pizza ban raha hai → delivery partner dhoondho → delivery → payment. (Likhawat padhna mushkil hai, isliye in side notes ki details best-effort hain, aur ek-do aur baatein — AI conferences aur AI models ke jhooth bolne ke baare mein — lecture mein aur kahin develop nahi hui.) 

 Ye recap kyun, aur aaj kyun zaroori. Ek akela decision tree padhna aasan hai, par wo jumpy hota hai: training examples thode badlo to kaafi alag tree ban sakta hai; aur jo tree tab tak ugaya jaye jab tak har box pure na ho wo training data ko ratt sakta hai. Aaj ka topic, random forest , ise theek karta hai: bahut saare trees se poochho aur vote lo.

22-01_What_Is_a_Random_Forest_Breiman_20.lecture_title: Random Forest, Bagging and Ensemble Learning
22-01_What_Is_a_Random_Forest_Breiman_20.source: Lecture 22, slides 4–6 (section title "Random Forest"; "Random Forests (RF)" shown twice — slide 6 adds the source link to Breiman's paper; the left picture is a 3×3 grid of nine coloured trees with the tally "Six 1s and Three 0s → Prediction: 1"). Enriched with web research (Breiman 2001 abstract: strength and correlation of trees, comparison with AdaBoost).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
The four bullets (slides 5–6). 

 Introduced by Leo Breiman in 2001 (source cited: Random Forests , Machine Learning 45, 2001 — stat.berkeley.edu/~breiman/randomforest2001.pdf ). 
 Instead of one large tree, construct an ensemble of simpler trees . 
 A Random Forest (RF) is a classifier consisting of a collection of decision trees . 
 The prediction is obtained by majority voting over the predictions of the single trees. 

 The figure. Nine trees, each coloured differently, with predictions Predict 1, 0, 1 / 1, 1, 0 / 1, 1, 0 → six 1s and three 0s , so the forest predicts 1 . Check: row 1 = 1,0,1 (two 1s); row 2 = 1,1,0 (two 1s); row 3 = 1,1,0 (two 1s) → 2+2+2 = 6 ✔, 0s = 3 ✔. 

 Key definitions. 

 Ensemble learning: combine many models ("weak/base learners") so the group is more accurate and robust than any single member. 
 Base learner here: a decision tree ( L20 The Steps of the ID3 Algorithm ). 
 Majority vote (classification): the class predicted by the most trees; for regression the trees' outputs are averaged (the slide's later text says RF works for "classification, regression"). 

 What Breiman's paper adds (research). The abstract states that the generalisation error of a forest depends on the strength of the individual trees and the correlation between them ; using a random selection of features at each node gives error rates that compare favourably with AdaBoost and are more robust to noise . So the recipe is: make trees reasonably accurate, but as different from one another as possible ( L22 Feature Randomness — A Random Subset of Features at Each Split ). 

 A note on "simpler trees" (slide wording). In a standard random forest each tree is usually grown deep (to near-pure leaves) — individually overfit and high-variance; the averaging across many decorrelated trees is what cancels the variance. "Simpler" on the slide refers to each tree seeing only part of the data and features, not to shallow trees. 

 Verified illustration. If each tree were independently right 70% of the time: 3 trees voting → 78.4% correct; 11 trees → 92.2%; 101 trees → ≈100% (binomial calculation, L22 The "Which One Should I Choose?" Analogy — Three Friends and a Majority Vote ). Real trees are correlated, so gains are smaller — which is why feature randomness and bootstrapping exist.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The problem with one tree. A single decision tree is a bit moody . Change a few rows of your data and it grows into a quite different tree. And a tree that keeps asking questions until every box is pure may simply memorise the training examples, then stumble on new ones. 

 The idea of a random forest. Don't trust one tree. Grow a whole forest of trees and let them vote . 

 Every tree looks at the same new case and gives its own answer (spam / not spam, yes / no, a class). 
 The answer given by most of the trees is the forest's answer. 

 Think of asking nine different experts and following the majority. 

 The picture on slide 5. Nine trees, each drawn in its own colour, each saying either "1" or "0": 

 Top row: 1, 0, 1 
 Middle row: 1, 1, 0 
 Bottom row: 1, 1, 0 

 Count the 1s: 2 + 2 + 2 = six 1s and three 0s . Six beats three, so the forest says "1" . 

 What the slide says, point by point. 

 The idea was introduced by Leo Breiman in 2001 (the slide links to his paper). 
 Instead of one large tree we build an ensemble — a team — of simpler trees. 
 A random forest is a classifier made of a collection of decision trees . 
 The prediction comes from majority voting over the single trees' predictions. (For number-predicting problems the trees' numbers are averaged instead.) 

 Why a crowd of trees beats one tree. Each tree makes its own mistakes, but they make different mistakes, so when you take the vote the mistakes cancel out. Breiman's paper puts it this way: a forest's error depends on how good each tree is and how different the trees are from one another . The next topics show the tricks that make the trees different. 

 A note on the word "simpler". In practice each tree in a forest is usually grown quite deep. It is "simpler" in the sense that each tree sees only a random part of the data and the questions, not that it is tiny. 

 A quick feel for the power of voting. If each tree were right 70% of the time and they made mistakes independently, then 3 trees voting would be right 78.4% of the time, 11 trees 92.2%, and 101 trees nearly 100%. Real trees are never fully independent, so the gain is smaller — which is exactly why we work hard to make them different.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Ek tree ki problem. Ek akela decision tree thoda moody hota hai. Data ki kuch rows badlo to bilkul alag tree ban jata hai. Aur jo tree tab tak sawaal poochta hai jab tak har box pure na ho, wo training examples ko ratt sakta hai aur naye examples par ladkhada jata hai. 

 Random forest ka idea. Ek tree par bharosa mat karo. Ek poora jungle (forest) ugao aur unse vote karwao. 

 Har tree wahi naya case dekhta hai aur apna jawaab deta hai (spam / not spam, yes / no, koi class). 
 Jo jawaab zyada tar trees dete hain wahi forest ka jawaab hai. 

 Aise socho jaise tum nau alag experts se poochte ho aur majority ki baat maante ho. 

 Slide 5 ki picture. Nau trees, har ek apne rang mein, har ek "1" ya "0" bol raha hai: 

 Upar ki row: 1, 0, 1 
 Beech ki row: 1, 1, 0 
 Neeche ki row: 1, 1, 0 

 1 gino: 2 + 2 + 2 = chhe 1 aur teen 0 . Chhe teen se bade hain, isliye forest kehta hai "1" . 

 Slide kya kehti hai, point-by-point. 

 Ye idea Leo Breiman ne 2001 mein diya (slide unke paper ka link deti hai). 
 Ek bade tree ki jagah hum chhote trees ka ensemble — ek team — banate hain. 
 Random forest decision trees ke collection se bana classifier hai. 
 Prediction akele trees ke predictions par majority voting se aati hai. (Number predict karne wale problems mein trees ke numbers ka average liya jata hai.) 

 Trees ki bheed ek tree se behtar kyun. Har tree apni galtiyan karta hai, par alag-alag galtiyan, isliye vote lene par galtiyan cancel ho jaati hain. Breiman ka paper yun kehta hai: forest ki error is par depend karti hai ki har tree kitna achha hai aur trees ek-doosre se kitne alag hain . Agle topics wo tricks dikhate hain jinse trees alag-alag bante hain. 

 "Simpler" shabd ke baare mein. Practice mein forest ka har tree aam taur par kaafi gehra ugaya jata hai. Wo "simpler" is matlab mein hai ki har tree data aur sawaalon ka sirf ek random hissa dekhta hai, ye nahi ki wo chhota-sa hota hai. 

 Voting ki taakat ka andaza. Agar har tree 70% baar sahi ho aur galtiyan independent hon, to 3 trees ka vote 78.4% baar sahi hoga, 11 trees ka 92.2%, aur 101 trees ka lagbhag 100%. Asli trees poori tarah independent kabhi nahi hote, isliye fayda kam hota hai — isi wajah se hum unhe alag banane ki mehnat karte hain.

22-02_Wisdom_of_the_Crowd_Choosing_a_Pho.lecture_title: Random Forest, Bagging and Ensemble Learning
22-02_Wisdom_of_the_Crowd_Choosing_a_Pho.topic_title: The "Which One Should I Choose?" Analogy — Three Friends and a Majority Vote
22-02_Wisdom_of_the_Crowd_Choosing_a_Pho.source: Lecture 22, slides 7–9 ("I can't decide" meme; the same figure with three friends' trees; slide 8 has the instructor's handwriting, slide 9 is the clean printed version). Binomial numbers independently computed.

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
The story. A person cannot decide which product to buy (the instructor writes the choices on slide 7: OnePlus, Google Pixel, Apple, Samsung, ~~Nokia~~ — a phone purchase ). Instead of deciding alone, they ask three friends . Each friend reasons with their own decision tree and gives a decision; the person follows the majority vote . 

 Figure (slides 8–9). 

 Friend 
 Their own tree (orange path = how this case was routed) 
 Printed decision dot (slide 9) 
 Instructor's handwritten phone (slide 8, best reading) 

 Friend 1 
 tree with its own splits 
 green 
 Apple 

 Friend 2 
 a different tree 
 red 
 Apple 

 Friend 3 
 a different tree 
 green 
 Samsung 

 Majority Vote: the printed dots read green, red, green; the instructor's handwriting on slide 8 reads Apple, Apple, Samsung, and the outcome he writes is "Buy Apple" (2 friends vs 1). 

 Flag — the two readings do not line up. The printed green/red dots are generic class colours from the original picture; they do not map one-to-one onto the handwritten phone names (Friend 2's dot is red, yet the handwriting appears to say Apple). Treat the slide's own printed figure as "2 of 3 agree → majority wins" and the handwritten phone names as the instructor's story laid over it. Some handwriting beside the friends is hard to read, so the Apple/Apple/Samsung reading is best-effort. 

 What the analogy teaches. 

 Each friend = one decision tree ; the three trees differ because each friend knows different things (different data / different features). 
 Combining independent opinions beats a single opinion — the ensemble idea. 
 Voting turns many predictions into one. 

 Why it works — the condition (research/verified). Majority voting helps only if the voters are better than random and reasonably independent . For independent voters each correct with probability p = 0.7: 

 Number of voters 
 P(majority correct) 

 1 
 0.700 

 3 
 0.784 (= 3·0.7²·0.3 + 0.7³) 

 11 
 0.922 

 101 
 ≈ 1.000 

 If the friends all copy each other (perfectly correlated), voting gives no improvement. That is why a random forest deliberately makes its trees different through bootstrap sampling ( L22 Random Sampling with Replacement (the Bootstrap) ) and feature randomness ( L22 Feature Randomness — A Random Subset of Features at Each Split ). This is the "wisdom of crowds" principle (Condorcet's jury theorem in statistics).

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The story (slides 7–9). You want a new phone but can't decide. On slide 7 the teacher writes the options: OnePlus, Google Pixel, Apple, Samsung — and crosses out Nokia. The meme says "Which one should I choose? I can't decide." 

 What do you do? You ask three friends . Each friend thinks about phones in their own way — in the picture each friend has their own little decision tree (questions about price, camera, brand…) — and gives you a recommendation. Then you take a majority vote . 

 On the slide. 

 Friend 1 → one answer, Friend 2 → an answer, Friend 3 → an answer. 
 On the printed picture (slide 9) the three answers are shown as coloured dots: green, red, green . Two greens beat one red, so the majority-vote answer is green . 
 In the teacher's handwriting (slide 8), the best reading is: Friend 1 says Apple , Friend 2 says Apple , Friend 3 says Samsung — so the final decision is "Buy Apple" (two friends against one). Note: the printed green/red dots are just generic colours; they don't line up one-to-one with these phone names, so take the picture to mean "2 of 3 agree, majority wins". Some handwriting is hard to read, so this reading is best-effort. 

 What the story teaches. 

 Each friend = one decision tree. They differ because each friend knows different things. 
 Asking several people beats asking one. 
 Voting turns many answers into one final answer. 

 An important condition: the friends must think differently. Suppose each friend is right 70% of the time and their mistakes are independent. Then: 

 Number of friends 
 Chance the majority is right 

 1 
 70% 

 3 
 78.4% 

 11 
 92.2% 

 101 
 almost 100% 

 But if all your friends just copy each other, asking three people is no better than asking one. This is why a random forest deliberately makes its trees different — by giving each tree a different random sample of the data and a random choice of questions (next topics).

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Kahani (slides 7–9). Tumhe naya phone lena hai par decide nahi kar pa rahe. Slide 7 par sir ne options likhe: OnePlus, Google Pixel, Apple, Samsung — aur Nokia ko kaat diya. Meme kehta hai "Which one should I choose? I can't decide." 

 Tum kya karte ho? Tum teen dosto se poochte ho. Har dost phone ke baare mein apne tareeke se sochta hai — picture mein har dost ka apna chhota decision tree hai (price, camera, brand ke sawaal…) — aur tumhe ek recommendation deta hai. Phir tum majority vote lete ho. 

 Slide par. 

 Friend 1 → ek jawaab, Friend 2 → ek jawaab, Friend 3 → ek jawaab. 
 Printed picture (slide 9) mein teeno jawaab coloured dots ki tarah hain: hara, laal, hara . Do hare ek laal se bade hain, isliye majority-vote ka jawaab hara hai. 
 Sir ki likhawat (slide 8) ki best reading: Friend 1 kehta hai Apple , Friend 2 kehta hai Apple , Friend 3 kehta hai Samsung — to final decision "Buy Apple" (do dost vs ek). Dhyan do: printed hara/laal dots sirf generic rang hain, wo phone ke naamon se ek-ek karke match nahi karte, isliye picture ka matlab bas itna samjho: "3 mein se 2 agree, majority jeeta". Kuch likhawat dhundhli hai, isliye ye reading best-effort hai. 

 Kahani kya sikhati hai. 

 Har dost = ek decision tree. Wo alag isliye hain kyunki har dost alag cheezein jaanta hai. 
 Kai logon se poochna ek se poochne se behtar hai. 
 Voting kai jawaabon ko ek final jawaab bana deti hai. 

 Ek zaroori shart: doston ko alag tarah se sochna chahiye. Maan lo har dost 70% baar sahi hai aur unki galtiyan independent hain. Tab: 

 Doston ki sankhya 
 Majority ke sahi hone ka chance 

 1 
 70% 

 3 
 78.4% 

 11 
 92.2% 

 101 
 lagbhag 100% 

 Par agar saare dost ek doosre ki copy karein to teen logon se poochna ek se poochne jaisa hi hai. Isi liye random forest jaan-boojh kar apne trees ko alag banata hai — har tree ko data ka alag random sample aur sawaalon ka random choice dekar (agle topics).

22-03_Random_Forest_Overview_Three_Steps.lecture_title: Random Forest, Bagging and Ensemble Learning
22-03_Random_Forest_Overview_Three_Steps.topic_title: Random Forest Overview — The Three Steps and the Spam/Ham Example
22-03_Random_Forest_Overview_Three_Steps.source: Lecture 22, slides 10–11 (text slide "Random Forests (RF)" with Step 1–3; "Random Forest: Example" diagram with the instructor's handwriting: 600 samples, 200 random samples per tree, "Mail is spam or ham (not spam)", n = 40 / n = 50, Class-B). Enriched with general knowledge of how forests are built (flagged where it goes beyond the slides).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 10 — definition. Random forests (random decision forests) are an ensemble learning method for classification and regression . They correct for decision trees' habit of overfitting to their training set . 

 The three steps (slide 10). 

 Create a bootstrap dataset from the original data by randomly choosing data, repetition allowed ( L22 Random Sampling with Replacement (the Bootstrap) ). 
 Create a randomized decision tree from the bootstrap dataset ( L22 Feature Randomness — A Random Subset of Features at Each Split ). 
 Output of the forest = the class selected by most trees (majority vote). 

 Steps 1–2 are repeated for each tree (N times) — the loop is implied by the slide's diagram; each tree gets its own bootstrap dataset. 

 Slide 11 — the worked diagram. An Instance (the full dataset) feeds Tree-1, Tree-2, … Tree-n in parallel. Each tree routes the new case down its own path (orange arrows) to a leaf class; the Majority-Voting box ("most common class") produces the Final-Class . 

 Tree 
 Prediction 

 Tree-1 
 Class-A 

 Tree-2 
 Class-B 

 Tree-n 
 Class-B 

 Majority vote 
 Class-B (2 of 3 shown) 

 Instructor's handwritten numbers (as read). 

 Dataset: 600 samples ; the task: "Mail is spam or ham (not spam)" — a two-class email problem. 
 200 random samples per tree (written beside each of Tree-1, Tree-2, Tree-n). 
 n = 40, n = 50 beside the Majority-Voting box — read as the example number of trees (40 or 50) in the forest. Final answer: Class-B . 

 Flags. 

 A classic bootstrap sample is as large as the original data (here 600) ; drawing only 200 samples per tree is a sub-sampling variant (scikit-learn exposes it via max_samples ). The slide uses 200 as an illustration — noting the difference is useful: L22 Random Sampling with Replacement (the Bootstrap) . 
 The slide's definition says random forests "correct for" overfitting. More precisely, a forest reduces variance — it overfits less than a single deep tree , though it can still overfit noisy data. 
 The voting rule on a binary problem with an odd number of trees cannot tie; with an even number (40, 50) ties are possible and are broken arbitrarily or by averaged class probabilities (scikit-learn averages probabilities rather than counting hard votes — general knowledge, not on the slides). 

 Cost model. Trees are independent, so training/prediction is embarrassingly parallel (see L22 Bagging vs. Boosting ).

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
How to make a random forest — three moves (slide 10). 

 Make a practice set. Draw rows at random from your data, and allow the same row to be drawn again (like pulling numbered balls from a bag and putting each one back). 
 Grow one decision tree on that practice set — a tree with a bit of extra randomness in which questions it may ask (explained soon). 
 Repeat many times , then ask all the trees to vote on a new case. The answer chosen by most trees is the forest's answer. 

 (Steps 1 and 2 are done again for every tree, each time with a new random practice set.) 

 What the slide says a forest is good for. It's a team method ("ensemble") for both category problems (classification) and number problems (regression). It also corrects a single tree's habit of overfitting — i.e. of learning the training examples too exactly. (More precisely: a forest overfits less than one deep tree, because averaging many trees calms them down.) 

 The worked picture (slide 11). The teacher's example is an email spam filter . He wrote: 

 We have 600 emails in total. 
 Each tree gets its own random 200 emails. 
 The job: decide whether a mail is spam or ham ("ham" means "not spam"). 
 Tree-1 says Class A , Tree-2 says Class B , Tree-n says Class B → the majority vote gives Class B (for example "spam"). 
 He wrote n = 40 and n = 50 next to the voting box; this appears to mean the example forest might contain 40 or 50 trees. 

 Two small things to notice. 

 A textbook practice set is as big as the original data (here 600 emails), drawn with repeats. The teacher's 200-per-tree is a smaller-sample version. Both ideas give each tree a different view of the data. 
 With an even number of trees (40, 50) a vote can tie. In that case the library breaks the tie in a sensible way (for example by averaging each tree's confidence). 

 Good to know. The trees don't depend on each other, so they can all be trained at the same time on different processors.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Random forest banane ke teen kadam (slide 10). 

 Practice set banao. Apne data se rows random uthao, aur ek hi row dobara bhi uthne do (jaise thaile se numbered balls nikaalna aur har ek ko wapas daal dena). 
 Us practice set par ek decision tree ugao — ek tree jisme ye bhi thodi randomness hai ki wo kaun se sawaal poochh sakta hai (jaldi samjhayenge). 
 Bahut baar dohraao , phir naye case par saare trees se vote karwao . Jo jawaab zyada trees dein wahi forest ka jawaab. 

 (Step 1 aur 2 har tree ke liye dobara hote hain, har baar naye random practice set ke saath.) 

 Slide kehti hai forest kis kaam ka hai. Ye ek team method ("ensemble") hai category problems (classification) aur number problems (regression) dono ke liye. Ye ek tree ki overfitting ki aadat ko bhi theek karta hai — yaani training examples ko zyada hi exactly seekh lene ki aadat. (Zyada sahi: forest ek deep tree se kam overfit karta hai, kyunki bahut saare trees ka average unhe shaant kar deta hai.) 

 Worked picture (slide 11). Sir ka example hai email spam filter . Unhone likha: 

 Hamare paas total 600 emails hain. 
 Har tree ko apni random 200 emails milti hain. 
 Kaam: decide karna ki mail spam hai ya ham ("ham" matlab "spam nahi"). 
 Tree-1 kehta hai Class A , Tree-2 kehta hai Class B , Tree-n kehta hai Class B → majority vote Class B deta hai (jaise "spam"). 
 Voting box ke paas unhone n = 40 aur n = 50 likha; matlab lagta hai example forest mein 40 ya 50 trees ho sakte hain. 

 Do chhoti baatein. 

 Textbook practice set original data jitna bada hota hai (yahan 600 emails), repeats ke saath. Sir ka har tree ke liye 200 chhota-sample version hai. Dono idea mein har tree ko data ka alag view milta hai. 
 Trees ki sankhya even ho (40, 50) to vote tie ho sakta hai. Us case mein library tie ko sahi tareeke se todti hai (jaise har tree ke confidence ka average lekar). 

 Jaanne layak. Trees ek-doosre par depend nahi karte, isliye sab ko alag-alag processors par ek saath train kiya ja sakta hai.

22-04_Random_Sampling_with_Replacement_B.lecture_title: Random Forest, Bagging and Ensemble Learning
22-04_Random_Sampling_with_Replacement_B.source: Lecture 22, slide 12 ("Random Sampling with Replacement"). Enriched with independently computed probabilities (exact and simulated) and general statistics knowledge (out-of-bag samples, the 63.2% rule).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 12 — the idea. 

 Randomly sample from the training dataset with replacement . 
 Training set S of size m → build new training sets by drawing m samples at random from S with replacement (the same sample can be picked several times). 
 Example: training data [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] may give [1, 2, 2, 3, 6, 6] , [1, 2, 4, 4, 5, 6] , [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] , … 
 All lists have length 6 but some values repeat. We are not subsetting the data into smaller chunks — every new set is the same size as the original. 

 Check of the slide's examples. All three are valid length-6 draws with replacement. The number of equally likely ordered samples is 6⁶ = 46,656 . The "all ones" sample [1,1,1,1,1,1] has probability (1/6)⁶ = 2.1×10⁻⁵ (0.0021%) — possible but extremely rare; the chance that all six draws are the same value , whichever value, is 6·(1/6)⁶ = 1.3×10⁻⁴ (0.013%). 

 How many distinct rows does a bootstrap sample contain? (computed) 

 Probability a given row is never picked in m draws = (1 − 1/m)^m. 
 Expected fraction of distinct rows = 1 − (1 − 1/m)^m: m = 6 → 66.5% (simulation of 100,000 draws gave 66.49% ✔), m = 100 → 63.4%, m = 1000 → 63.2%, and in the limit 1 − 1/e ≈ 63.2% . 
 So a typical bootstrap sample of m rows contains about 63.2% of the original rows (some repeated) ; the remaining ≈ 36.8% are left out — called out-of-bag (OOB) rows for that tree. (Not on the slides.) OOB rows act as a free built-in validation set: each row can be predicted by only the trees that never saw it, giving an honest error estimate without a separate test set ( L22 Bootstrap Aggregation (Bagging) ). 

 Sampling with vs without replacement. 

 With replacement (bootstrap) 
 Without replacement 

 Same row repeated? 
 Yes 
 No 

 Result size m of m? 
 Yes, same size (but ~63% distinct) 
 Only a smaller subset, or the identical set 

 Independence between draws 
 Yes — each draw identical distribution 
 No 

 Use in RF 
 Standard (bagging) 
 Used by some variants / sub-sampling 

 Why do this? Each tree sees a different but similar dataset, so the trees come out different. Repeats effectively give some rows a higher weight in one tree and zero weight in another — injecting diversity that decorrelates the trees ( L22 The "Which One Should I Choose?" Analogy — Three Friends and a Majority Vote ).

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The lottery-ball picture. Imagine your six data points are six numbered balls (1 to 6) in a bag. To make a bootstrap sample : 

 Pull out one ball and write down its number. 
 Put the ball back into the bag. 
 Repeat until you've written down six numbers. 

 Because every ball goes back, the same number can come up twice, three times, or not at all. 

 Examples from the slide (data = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]). 

 [1, 2, 2, 3, 6, 6] — 2 and 6 appear twice; 4 and 5 are missing. 
 [1, 2, 4, 4, 5, 6] — 4 appears twice; 3 is missing. 
 [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] — the same ball six times! Possible, but very unlikely: the chance is 1 in 46,656 (that's 6 × 6 × 6 × 6 × 6 × 6 equally likely lists). 

 The slide's important point: it is not smaller. Every new list has exactly the same length as the original (six). We are not chopping the data into smaller pieces. Some items appear more than once and some are left out. 

 How many different items end up in a sample? For a long list, on average only about two-thirds (63%) of the original items make it in; the other one-third (37%) are left out. (Checked: for just six items it is 66.5% — about 4 distinct numbers out of 6.) The items left out for one tree are called its out-of-bag items. They're handy: they work as free "exam questions" that that tree never studied. 

 With replacement or without? 

 With replacement (the bootstrap): repeats allowed, list is the same size as the original. 
 Without replacement : no repeats, so you can only get a smaller piece of the data. 

 Why bother? Each tree in the forest gets its own bootstrap sample, so each sees a slightly different version of the data — some rows twice, some rows not at all. Different data → different trees → different mistakes → a better vote. That's the "random" in random forest.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Lottery-ball ki picture. Socho tumhare chhe data points ek thaile mein chhe numbered balls (1 se 6) hain. Bootstrap sample banane ke liye: 

 Ek ball nikaalo aur uska number likh lo. 
 Ball ko wapas thaile mein daal do. 
 Tab tak dohraao jab tak chhe numbers likh na jayein. 

 Kyunki har ball wapas jaati hai, ek hi number do baar, teen baar aa sakta hai, ya bilkul nahi bhi aa sakta. 

 Slide ke examples (data = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]). 

 [1, 2, 2, 3, 6, 6] — 2 aur 6 do-do baar; 4 aur 5 gayab. 
 [1, 2, 4, 4, 5, 6] — 4 do baar; 3 gayab. 
 [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] — wahi ball chhe baar! Ho sakta hai, par bahut mushkil: chance 46,656 mein se 1 (yaani 6 × 6 × 6 × 6 × 6 × 6 barabar-sambhav lists). 

 Slide ki zaroori baat: ye chhota nahi hota. Har nayi list ki length bilkul original jitni (chhe) hoti hai. Hum data ko chhote tukdon mein nahi kaat rahe. Kuch items ek se zyada baar aate hain aur kuch chhoot jaate hain. 

 Ek sample mein kitne alag items aate hain? Lambi list ke liye average mein sirf do-tihaai (63%) original items aate hain; baaki ek-tihaai (37%) chhoot jaate hain. (Check kiya: sirf chhe items ke liye 66.5% — chhe mein se lagbhag 4 alag numbers.) Ek tree ke liye jo items chhoot gaye unhe uske out-of-bag items kehte hain. Ye kaam ke hain: ye free "exam ke sawaal" hain jo us tree ne kabhi padhe hi nahi. 

 With replacement ya without? 

 With replacement (bootstrap): repeats allowed, list original jitni badi. 
 Without replacement : koi repeat nahi, isliye data ka sirf chhota tukda mil sakta hai. 

 Ye sab kyun? Forest ke har tree ko apna bootstrap sample milta hai, isliye har tree data ka thoda alag version dekhta hai — kuch rows do baar, kuch bilkul nahi. Alag data → alag trees → alag galtiyan → behtar vote. Random forest ka "random" yahi hai.

22-05_Bagging_Bootstrap_Aggregation.lecture_title: Random Forest, Bagging and Ensemble Learning
22-05_Bagging_Bootstrap_Aggregation.source: Lecture 22, slides 13–14 ("Bootstrap Aggregation (Bagging)" text; "Bagging: Example" two-panel figure A and B). Enriched with general knowledge (Breiman 1996, variance reduction, OOB).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 13 — the claim. 

 Decision trees are very sensitive to the data they are trained on : small changes in the training set can give significantly different tree structures (high variance). 
 Random forest takes advantage of this by letting each tree sample with replacement from the dataset, so different training sets produce different trees. 
 This process is called bagging ( B ootstrap agg regat ing ; Breiman, 1996). 

 Slide 14 — Panel A: "Bootstrap Sampling and Multiple Trees". The Training set (a 2-D scatter of green Class A and red Class B points on axes 0–3 and 0–2) is resampled into Sample 1 … Sample N ; each sample trains Tree 1 … Tree N , each producing its own row of predictions (green/red dots). 

 Panel B: "Parallel Prediction with Independent Trees". An input X goes to Tree 1, Tree 2, … Tree N in parallel . Tree 1 → Class B , Tree 2 → Class A , Tree N → Class B . Majority Vote → Random Forest Decision (2 B vs 1 A → Class B ). The legend marks root, split and leaf nodes. 

 Algorithm. 

 for b = 1..B:
 D_b = bootstrap sample of the training set (size m, with replacement)
 T_b = train a tree on D_b
prediction(x) = majority vote of T_1(x)…T_B(x) (classification)
 or average of T_1(x)…T_B(x) (regression)

 Why bagging reduces variance (standard result). If B models each have variance σ² and pairwise correlation ρ, the variance of their average is ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ²/B . Increasing B kills the second term, but the first term (ρσ²) remains — so lowering the correlation ρ between trees is the other lever. Bootstrapping lowers ρ somewhat; feature randomness lowers it further ( L22 Feature Randomness — A Random Subset of Features at Each Split ). Bagging mainly reduces variance , not bias ( L17 Overfitting vs. Underfitting — Bias vs. Variance ). 

 Bagging vs. random forest. Bagging = bootstrap + aggregate any base learner (here trees). A random forest = bagging of decision trees + random feature subsets at each split. If you bag trees but let every split consider all features you get "bagged trees", not yet a random forest. 

 Out-of-bag (OOB) estimate. Each tree leaves out ≈ 36.8% of rows ( L22 Random Sampling with Replacement (the Bootstrap) ); predicting each row using only the trees that never saw it gives a validation-like accuracy for free (scikit-learn: oob_score=True ). 

 Parallelism. Trees are independent → can be trained simultaneously ( L22 Bagging vs. Boosting ).

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The key observation (slide 13). A decision tree is very sensitive to the data it learns from: change a few of the training examples and you can get a quite different tree. Normally that's a weakness. Bagging turns it into a strength : if the trees come out different, then a crowd of them gives a more reliable answer than any one of them. 

 The recipe. 

 Make many "practice sets", each by drawing rows at random with replacement (balls pulled from a bag and put back). 
 Grow one tree on each practice set. Because the practice sets differ, the trees differ. 
 For a new case, let every tree vote and take the majority. 

 The name. Bagging is short for B ootstrap agg regat ing : "resample the data (bootstrap), then combine the answers (aggregate)". 

 Reading the picture on slide 14. 

 Left, Panel A — "Bootstrap sampling and multiple trees". At the top is the training set, a scatter of green dots (Class A) and red dots (Class B). It is resampled into Sample 1 … Sample N, and each sample grows its own Tree 1 … Tree N, each with its own list of predictions. 
 Right, Panel B — "Parallel prediction with independent trees". A new input X goes to Tree 1, Tree 2 … Tree N at the same time . Tree 1 says Class B, Tree 2 says Class A, Tree N says Class B. The majority vote is Class B (two against one), so the forest's decision is Class B . 

 Why does averaging help? Imagine measuring a table with a wobbly ruler. One measurement may be off in either direction; the average of many measurements is much closer to the truth because the errors cancel. Trees are the same: each is "wobbly" (high variance), and averaging calms the wobble. There is a catch — the errors only cancel if the trees' errors are different . If all the trees were identical copies the average would be just as wobbly as one tree. (In maths: ensemble variance = ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B, where σ² is one tree's variance, ρ how alike the trees are, and B how many trees. More trees kills the second part, but the first part remains unless ρ is small.) 

 Bagging vs. a random forest. Bagging = bootstrap samples + vote. A random forest = bagging of decision trees + a random selection of questions at each split (next topic). Bagging mostly reduces variance (the wobbliness), not bias. 

 A free bonus: out-of-bag testing. Each tree never sees about 37% of the rows. We can test each row using only the trees that never saw it, giving an honest accuracy estimate without setting aside a separate test set.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Main observation (slide 13). Decision tree apne data ke prati bahut sensitive hota hai: training examples thode badlo to kaafi alag tree ban sakta hai. Aam taur par ye kamzori hai. Bagging ise taakat bana deta hai : agar trees alag-alag bante hain, to unki bheed kisi bhi ek tree se zyada bharosemand jawaab deti hai. 

 Recipe. 

 Bahut saare "practice sets" banao, har ek rows ko random aur with replacement (thaile se ball nikaal kar wapas daal kar) uthakar. 
 Har practice set par ek tree ugao. Practice sets alag hain, isliye trees alag banenge. 
 Naye case ke liye har tree vote kare aur majority le lo. 

 Naam. Bagging = B ootstrap agg regat ing : "data ko resample karo (bootstrap), phir jawaab jodo (aggregate)". 

 Slide 14 ki picture padho. 

 Left, Panel A — "Bootstrap sampling and multiple trees". Sabse upar training set hai, hare dots (Class A) aur laal dots (Class B) ka scatter. Use resample karke Sample 1 … Sample N banaye gaye, aur har sample apna Tree 1 … Tree N ugata hai, har ek ki apni predictions ki list. 
 Right, Panel B — "Parallel prediction with independent trees". Naya input X Tree 1, Tree 2 … Tree N ko ek saath jata hai. Tree 1 kehta hai Class B, Tree 2 kehta hai Class A, Tree N kehta hai Class B. Majority vote Class B hai (do vs ek), isliye forest ka decision Class B . 

 Average se fayda kyun? Socho tum ek dagmagate ruler se mez naap rahe ho. Ek naap kisi bhi taraf galat ho sakta hai; bahut saare naapon ka average sach ke kaafi paas hota hai kyunki galtiyan cancel ho jaati hain. Trees bhi aise hi hain: har ek "dagmagata" hai (high variance), aur average dagmagahat ko shaant karta hai. Ek shart hai — galtiyan tabhi cancel hongi jab trees ki galtiyan alag-alag hon. Agar saare trees ek jaise copy hote to average bhi ek tree jitna hi dagmagata. (Maths mein: ensemble variance = ρσ² + (1−ρ)σ²/B, jahan σ² ek tree ka variance, ρ trees kitne milte-julte, aur B trees ki sankhya hai. Zyada trees doosra hissa khatam kar dete hain, par pehla hissa tab tak rehta hai jab tak ρ chhota na ho.) 

 Bagging vs random forest. Bagging = bootstrap samples + vote. Random forest = decision trees ka bagging + har split par sawaalon ka random selection (agla topic). Bagging mainly variance (dagmagahat) kam karta hai, bias nahi. 

 Free bonus: out-of-bag testing. Har tree lagbhag 37% rows kabhi nahi dekhta. Hum har row ko sirf unhi trees se test kar sakte hain jinhone use nahi dekha, aur bina alag test set rakhe ek imaandaar accuracy estimate mil jata hai.

22-06_Feature_Randomness_Random_Subset_o.lecture_title: Random Forest, Bagging and Ensemble Learning
22-06_Feature_Randomness_Random_Subset_o.topic_title: Feature Randomness — A Random Subset of Features at Each Split
22-06_Feature_Randomness_Random_Subset_o.source: Lecture 22, slide 15 ("Randomization: Feature Randomnsess" [sic]). Enriched with general knowledge of Breiman's random-feature selection and scikit-learn's `max_features` (flagged; not verified beyond what the web search confirmed about Breiman's abstract).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 15 — what it says. 

 In a normal decision tree , when it is time to split a node, we consider every possible feature and pick the one with the largest gain ( L20 Information Gain — Choosing the Best Attribute ). 
 In a random forest , each tree can pick only from a random subset of features ( feature randomness ). 
 That is, node splitting is based on a random subset of features. 
 This forces more variation amongst the trees , resulting in lower correlation across trees and more diversification . 

 Precision note (flag). The slide says "for each tree", but the standard algorithm (Breiman 2001) draws a fresh random subset at every node split , not once per tree. The slide's own second sentence ("node splitting … is based on a random subset") matches this. (Drawing one subset per tree is a different method called the random subspace method .) 

 Why it is needed. Suppose one feature is very strong (like Outlook in L20 Worked Example — Entropy of Each Outlook Subset and Information Gain of Outlook ). With bagging alone, nearly every bootstrap tree would still put that feature at the root → all trees look alike → highly correlated → voting adds little. Forcing each split to choose among a random handful means some trees must root on Humidity or Wind , producing diverse trees. (By the variance formula ρσ² + (1 − ρ)σ²/B in L22 Bootstrap Aggregation (Bagging) , lowering ρ is what lowers ensemble error.) Breiman's abstract: the forest's error depends on the strength of the individual trees and the correlation between them — random features trade a little individual strength for a big drop in correlation. 

 Illustration (our own, using the lecture-20 dataset). With 4 features (Outlook, Temp, Humidity, Wind) and a subset of 2 chosen at random at the root, Outlook is available only in some of the draws (here: 3 of the 6 possible pairs contain Outlook); in the other pairs the best available feature will be Humidity (gain 0.152) or Wind (0.048) or Temp (0.029) — so the root differs across trees. 

 How many features? (general knowledge, max_features in scikit-learn). Common defaults: √p features for classification, p/3 for regression (p = number of features). Small subset → more diverse but weaker trees; large subset → stronger but more correlated. In scikit-learn's classifier the default is max_features="sqrt" , which we confirmed on the lecture's digits data: √64 = 8 features per split ( L22 Random Forest in scikit-learn and the Handwritten-Digits Example ). 

 Summary of the two randomisations. 

 Source of randomness 
 What is random 
 Effect 

 Bootstrap (bagging) 
 Which rows each tree sees 
 Different training sets → different trees 

 Feature randomness 
 Which features each split may use 
 Different split choices → lower correlation

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
How a normal tree picks its question (slide 15). At every box a normal tree looks at all the columns and picks the one with the biggest gain (the best question). 

 How a random forest's tree picks. At every box it is only shown a few randomly chosen columns , and it must pick the best question from those . This is called feature randomness ("feature" = column). 

 Why take choices away from the trees? Suppose one column is super obvious — like Outlook in our tennis table. If every tree is allowed to see it, every tree will ask about it first, and all the trees become near-copies of each other. A vote among copies is no better than a single opinion. By hiding columns at random: 

 Some trees can't use Outlook at the top, so they build their top questions around Humidity or Wind instead. 
 The trees now ask different questions, make different mistakes, and so their vote is smarter. 

 The teacher's words: this forces more variation among the trees, giving lower correlation across trees and more diversification . Think of a committee: you want members with different backgrounds, not clones. 

 A small tennis example (ours). Our table has 4 columns. Suppose each question may see only 2 randomly chosen columns. There are 6 possible pairs; Outlook is in 3 of them. In the other 3 pairs (Temp+Humidity, Temp+Wind, Humidity+Wind) the best available top question would be Humidity or Wind — so different trees start with different questions. 

 How many columns should each box see? A common rule: about the square root of the number of columns for category problems (and about a third for number problems). Too few → trees are weak; too many → trees look alike. For the digits example later, with 64 pixel columns, a box sees √64 = 8. 

 Two kinds of randomness, side by side. 

 What is random 
 Effect 

 Bootstrap (bagging) 
 which rows each tree sees 
 different practice sets → different trees 

 Feature randomness 
 which columns each question may use 
 different questions → less alike trees 

 One caution about the slide's wording. It says "each tree" picks from a random subset. In the standard method the random choice is made fresh at every box (split) , not just once per tree — the slide's own second sentence ("node splitting … is based on a random subset") actually says this.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Normal tree apna sawaal kaise chunta hai (slide 15). Har box par normal tree saare columns dekhta hai aur sabse bade gain wala (sabse best sawaal) chunta hai. 

 Random forest ka tree kaise chunta hai. Har box par use sirf kuch random chune hue columns dikhaye jaate hain, aur use unhi mein se best sawaal chunna padta hai. Isse feature randomness kehte hain ("feature" = column). 

 Trees se choices kyun cheen lein? Maan lo ek column bahut obvious hai — jaise hamari tennis table mein Outlook. Agar har tree use dekh sakta hai, to har tree pehle usi ke baare mein poochega, aur saare trees lagbhag ek-doosre ki copy ban jayenge. Copies ke beech vote ek akeli raay jaisa hi hai. Columns random chhupa dene se: 

 Kuch trees sabse upar Outlook use nahi kar paate, to wo Humidity ya Wind ke aas-paas apne upar ke sawaal banate hain. 
 Ab trees alag sawaal poochte hain, alag galtiyan karte hain, aur isliye unka vote zyada smart hota hai. 

 Sir ke shabdon mein: isse trees ke beech zyada variation aata hai, correlation kam hota hai, aur diversification badhta hai . Committee ki tarah socho: tumhe alag-alag background wale members chahiye, clones nahi. 

 Ek chhota tennis example (humara). Hamari table mein 4 columns hain. Maan lo har sawaal sirf 2 random chune hue columns dekh sakta hai. 6 possible jodiyan hain; Outlook 3 mein hai. Baaki 3 jodiyon (Temp+Humidity, Temp+Wind, Humidity+Wind) mein sabse upar ka best sawaal Humidity ya Wind hoga — isliye alag trees alag sawaalon se shuru karte hain. 

 Har box ko kitne columns dikhein? Aam rule: category problems ke liye columns ki sankhya ka lagbhag square root (aur number problems ke liye lagbhag ek-tihaai). Bahut kam → trees kamzor; bahut zyada → trees ek jaise. Aage digits example mein, 64 pixel columns ke saath, ek box √64 = 8 dekhta hai. 

 Do tarah ki randomness, saath-saath. 

 Kya random hai 
 Asar 

 Bootstrap (bagging) 
 har tree kaun si rows dekhta hai 
 alag practice sets → alag trees 

 Feature randomness 
 har sawaal kaun se columns use kar sakta hai 
 alag sawaal → kam milte-julte trees 

 Slide ke shabdon par ek savdhani. Wo kehti hai "har tree" random subset se chunta hai. Standard method mein random choice har box (split) par naya hota hai, sirf ek baar per tree nahi — slide ka apna doosra vaakya ("node splitting … random subset par based hai") asal mein yahi kehta hai.

22-07_Bagging_vs_Boosting_Comparison.lecture_title: Random Forest, Bagging and Ensemble Learning
22-07_Bagging_vs_Boosting_Comparison.source: Lecture 22, slide 16 (comparison table; source GeeksforGeeks "Bagging vs Boosting in Machine Learning"). Enriched with general ensemble-learning knowledge (AdaBoost, gradient boosting) and one correction flagged below.

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
The slide's table (verbatim content, typos corrected). 

 Feature 
 Bagging 
 Boosting 

 Training style 
 Trains independent models 
 Trains sequential models 

 Main goal 
 Reduce variance 
 Reduce bias 

 Handling errors 
 All samples treated equally 
 Focuses on misclassified samples 

 Overfitting 
 Less sensitive to overfitting 
 More prone to overfitting 

 Parallel training 
 Yes , supports parallel computing 
 No , does not support parallel computing 

 Sensitivity to noise 
 "Not affected by noise and outliers" 
 Sensitive to noise and outliers 

 (The slide misspells "sesitive"; "supports" is also mis-conjugated in the Boosting cell.) 

 What each does. 

 Bagging (random forest is the main example): many models trained independently on bootstrap samples, outputs averaged / voted ( L22 Bootstrap Aggregation (Bagging) ). Main effect: lower variance (a high-variance, low-bias learner like a deep tree is the ideal base). 
 Boosting (AdaBoost, gradient boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM — general knowledge): build weak learners one after another ; each new model concentrates on the examples the previous ones got wrong (by up-weighting them or fitting residuals). Main effect: lower bias (a high-bias, low-variance weak learner like a shallow "stump" is the usual base). Final prediction = weighted sum of the models. 

 Reading the rows. 

 Parallel: bagging's trees don't depend on each other, so they train in parallel; boosting model k needs model k−1's errors, so it is inherently sequential (individual trees inside a boosted model can still be built with parallelism, as in XGBoost — general knowledge). 
 Overfitting: adding more trees to a forest does not make it overfit more (the error plateaus); adding too many boosting rounds can overfit, hence early stopping / learning-rate shrinkage. 

 ⚠ Correction flag — noise row. The slide says bagging "is not affected by noise and outliers". That is too strong . Bagging/random forests are more robust to label noise and outliers than boosting (Breiman 2001's abstract says random-feature forests are "more robust to noise" than AdaBoost), but they are not immune : heavy label noise still hurts, and trees can still memorise noisy points. Read the row as relatively robust . 

 Bias–variance link ( L17 Overfitting vs. Underfitting — Bias vs. Variance ): deep trees = low bias/high variance → average them (bagging); shallow trees = high bias/low variance → boost them. 

 Rule of thumb. Overfitting single model → try bagging/random forest. Underfitting weak model → try boosting. Noisy labels → prefer bagging.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Two ways to combine many simple models. 

 Bagging — "a team that votes". Many models are trained independently, at the same time , each on its own random practice set. Everyone's opinion counts equally. Its main benefit is reducing variance : it calms models that are too jumpy (like deep trees). A random forest is the best-known example. 

 Boosting — "learn from mistakes". Models are trained one after another . The next model pays extra attention to the examples the previous one got wrong . Its main benefit is reducing bias : it turns a weak, too-simple model into a strong one. Famous examples are AdaBoost and gradient boosting (including XGBoost). 

 The slide's comparison table, row by row. 

 Question 
 Bagging 
 Boosting 

 How are models trained? 
 independently 
 one after another 

 Main goal 
 reduce variance 
 reduce bias 

 How are mistakes treated? 
 every example counts equally

 Overfitting 
 less likely

 Can it run in parallel? 
 yes

 Noise and odd values (outliers) 
 copes well

 Rule of thumb for choosing. 

 Model is too jumpy / overfits → try bagging (random forest). 
 Model is too simple / underfits → try boosting . 
 Data has wrong labels or outliers → bagging is safer. 

 One thing on the slide is too strong. It says bagging is "not affected by noise and outliers". That overstates it. Bagging is more robust than boosting (Breiman's own paper says random-feature forests are more robust to noise than AdaBoost), but lots of wrong labels will still hurt it. Read the row as "copes better". 

 Links to earlier lectures. Deep trees have low bias but high variance → average them (bagging). Shallow trees have high bias but low variance → boost them. This is the bias–variance idea from the overfitting/underfitting lecture. (Slide typos: "sesitive", "supports".)

sections.text:
Bahut saare simple models ko jodne ke do tareeke.

Iska main fayda variance kam karna hai: ye jumpy models (jaise deep trees) ko shaant karta hai. Random forest iska sabse mashhoor example hai.

Iska main fayda bias kam karna hai: ye kamzor, bahut simple model ko majboot bana deta hai. Mashhoor examples AdaBoost aur gradient boosting (XGBoost samet) hain.

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 17 — ensemble methods (scikit-learn docs). Ensemble methods combine the predictions of several base estimators built with a given learning algorithm in order to improve generalisability / robustness over a single estimator. The two famous examples named are gradient-boosted trees and random forests ; more generally ensembles apply to any base learner via bagging methods, model stacking, voting, or boosting (e.g. AdaBoost) . Source: scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/ensemble.html . 

 Slide 18 — the code. 

 from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
model = RandomForestClassifier()
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

 Three lines: import the class, create the model (defaults), train on the training data ( X_train = feature matrix, y_train = labels). The displayed RandomForestClassifier() box is just the notebook echoing the fitted estimator. Prediction would be model.predict(X_test) . 

 Slide 19 — the task: handwritten-digit recognition. An 8×8 greyscale image (64 pixel values, each pixel a feature) of a handwritten "4" is classified into one of the 10 classes 0–9 (from scikit-learn's digits dataset; the slide's source link is the plot_digits_last_image example). The arrow points the image to class "4". 

 Verified experiment (ours). scikit-learn digits: 1,797 images × 64 features, 10 classes . Train/test split 75/25 (stratified, random_state=42 ). 

 Model 
 Test accuracy 

 Single decision tree (fully grown) 
 82.0% (train accuracy 100% → overfit) 

 Random forest, 1 tree 
 81.3% 

 Random forest, 10 trees 
 94.4% 

 Random forest, 50 trees 
 98.0% 

 Random forest, default (100 trees) 
 97.8% 

 Random forest, 200 trees 
 97.6% 

 The default forest's out-of-bag (OOB) accuracy was 96.6% , close to its test accuracy — OOB gives an honest estimate with no separate test set ( L22 Bootstrap Aggregation (Bagging) ). 
 Default hyper-parameters observed: n_estimators = 100 , max_features = "sqrt" (√64 = 8 features per split, L22 Feature Randomness — A Random Subset of Features at Each Split ). 
 Reading: one deep tree overfits (100% train, 82% test); a single tree from the forest is similar (≈ 81%); averaging many decorrelated trees lifts accuracy to ~98%. Gains saturate after a few dozen trees; the small dip at 200 is random noise, not overfitting (differences of ±0.3 are a handful of test images out of 450). 

 Practical hyper-parameters (general knowledge). n_estimators (number of trees), max_features , max_depth / min_samples_leaf (control tree size), bootstrap (default True), max_samples , oob_score , n_jobs (parallelism), random_state (reproducibility). model.feature_importances_ reports each feature's contribution — here, which pixels matter most. 

 Typical workflow. Load data → split train/test ( L17 k-Fold Cross-Validation (Stratified Ten-Fold, Repeated CV) for more robust validation) → fit → predict → measure accuracy / confusion matrix ( L17 The Confusion Matrix — TP, TN, FP, FN ).

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 17 — what "ensemble" means. The scikit-learn website (a popular Python toolbox for machine learning) explains: an ensemble combines the predictions of several simple models to get an answer that is more reliable than any single model. The two famous kinds are random forests and gradient-boosted trees ; the same idea also works with bagging, voting, stacking and boosting in general. 

 Slide 18 — the three lines of code. 

 from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier # 1) bring in the tool
model = RandomForestClassifier() # 2) create a forest
model.fit(X_train, y_train) # 3) teach it

 X_train = the table of examples (the columns/features); y_train = the correct answers for those examples. 
 fit means "learn from these examples". The grey/blue box you see afterwards is just the notebook showing the trained forest. 
 Afterwards you ask it for answers on new examples with model.predict(...) . 

 Slide 19 — recognising handwritten digits. The task: a computer must look at a tiny picture of a handwritten number and say which of the ten digits (0–9) it is. Each picture is an 8×8 grid of grey squares, so 64 numbers, one per square. The slide shows a "4" and an arrow pointing to the "4" box. (The last slide is just a photo of a forest.) 

 We tried it ourselves (the slides show no results). Using scikit-learn's built-in digits data — 1,797 pictures — and keeping a quarter aside for testing: 

 One fully-grown decision tree: about 82% right on the unseen pictures. (It was 100% right on the pictures it studied — a sign of overfitting.) 
 A forest of 10 trees: about 94%. 
 A forest of 50 trees: about 98%. 
 The default forest (100 trees): about 98% (97.8%). 
 A forest of just 1 tree got about 81%, similar to a single tree — it's the crowd that helps. 
 The forest also estimated its own accuracy using the left-out pictures ("out-of-bag"): about 96.6%, close to the real test result. 

 What this shows. A crowd of different trees voting beats one big tree on the same data. After a few dozen trees the improvement levels off; small ups and downs (like 98.0 → 97.6) are just luck on a few of the 450 test pictures. 

 Settings you can change (general knowledge). Number of trees, how many columns each question may see, how deep trees may grow, how many to train in parallel, and a random seed for repeatable results. A trained forest can also tell you which pixels mattered most.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Slide 17 — "ensemble" ka matlab. scikit-learn website (machine learning ke liye ek mashhoor Python toolbox) samjhati hai: ensemble kai simple models ki predictions ko jodta hai taaki jawaab kisi bhi akele model se zyada bharosemand ho. Do mashhoor kisme random forests aur gradient-boosted trees hain; wahi idea bagging, voting, stacking aur boosting ke saath bhi chalta hai. 

 Slide 18 — code ki teen line. 

 from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier # 1) tool laao
model = RandomForestClassifier() # 2) forest banao
model.fit(X_train, y_train) # 3) use sikhao

 X_train = examples ki table (columns/features); y_train = un examples ke sahi jawaab. 
 fit ka matlab "in examples se seekho". Baad mein jo grey/neela box dikhta hai wo bas notebook trained forest dikha rahi hai. 
 Baad mein naye examples par jawaab model.predict(...) se maangte hain. 

 Slide 19 — haath se likhe digits pehchanna. Kaam: computer ko haath se likhe number ki chhoti si picture dekh kar batana hai ki das digits (0–9) mein se kaun sa hai. Har picture 8×8 grey squares ki grid hai, yaani 64 numbers, har square ka ek. Slide ek "4" dikhati hai aur ek teer "4" wale box ki taraf. (Aakhri slide bas ek jungle ki photo hai.) 

 Humne khud try kiya (slides mein koi results nahi). scikit-learn ke built-in digits data (1,797 pictures) ke saath, aur ek-chauthai testing ke liye alag rakhkar: 

 Ek poora ugaya hua decision tree: unseen pictures par lagbhag 82% sahi. (Jin pictures se seekha unmein 100% sahi — overfitting ka sanket.) 
 10 trees ka forest: lagbhag 94%. 
 50 trees ka forest: lagbhag 98%. 
 Default forest (100 trees): lagbhag 98% (97.8%). 
 Sirf 1 tree ka forest lagbhag 81%, ek akele tree jaisa — madad bheed se hi hoti hai. 
 Forest ne chhodi hui pictures ("out-of-bag") se apni accuracy ka andaza bhi lagaya: lagbhag 96.6%, asli test result ke kaafi paas. 

 Isse kya dikhta hai. Alag-alag trees ki bheed ka vote, usi data par ek bade tree ko hara deta hai. Kuch darjan trees ke baad sudhaar thama jata hai; chhote upar-neeche (jaise 98.0 → 97.6) 450 test pictures mein se kuch par bas kismat hai. 

 Settings jo badal sakte ho (general knowledge). Trees ki sankhya, har sawaal kitne columns dekh sake, trees kitne gehre ugein, kitne parallel train hon, aur repeatable results ke liye random seed. Trained forest ye bhi bata sakta hai ki kaun se pixels sabse zyada matter kiye.
