 In this data, z ranges over 0.013–0.255 for inner points and 0.637–1.436 for ring points. A single threshold on z separates them perfectly, exactly as in slide 18. 
 The linear SVM on raw (x, y) is barely better than guessing, and most points become support vectors.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 15: the problem. 

 In picture A , a straight line separates green from blue. That's easy. 
 In picture B , blue dots sit in the middle and green dots surround them like a ring. No straight line can separate them. You need a circle. 
 A plain SVM only draws straight lines, so what can we do? 

 The clever idea (slides 16–19): add a new dimension. 

 Slide 17 shows green squares in the middle and blue diamonds in a ring around them. Now give every point a height : z = x² + y², which is just "how far you are from the centre, squared".
 
 Points in the middle get a small height and stay low. 
 Points on the ring get a big height and float up. 
 
 On slide 18, plotted with this height, the blue points are all up high and the green ones are down low. Now a flat horizontal line separates them perfectly. 
 When you bring that flat cut back to the original flat picture, it becomes a circle , which is exactly what we needed. 
 Slide 16 shows the same idea in 3-D. The points look tangled when flat ("complex in low dimension"). Lift them into 3-D and a flat sheet slices between them ("simple in higher dimension"). The teacher wrote "kernel transformation" on the arrow. 
 On slide 18 one blue point is circled. It was hiding among the green points near the centre, so even after lifting it stays low on the wrong side. The soft margin simply accepts it as one mistake. 

 What's a "kernel"? 

 Slide 19 says "this transformation is called kernel". 
 More precisely, the kernel is a shortcut formula that tells the SVM how similar two points would be after lifting, without actually doing the lifting. This is the famous " kernel trick ". 
 It matters because some lifts go into thousands or even infinitely many dimensions, which a computer could never build directly. 

 Checking the trick with real numbers. 

 Take points (1, 2) and (3, 4). 
 Shortcut: (1×3 + 2×4)² = 11² = 121 . 
 Long way: lift both points into 3-D, (1, 2.83, 4) and (9, 16.97, 16), and multiply matching parts: 9 + 48 + 64 = 121 . 
 Same answer, but the shortcut needed far less work. 

 The three kernels on slide 5: 

 Linear: a straight boundary, for data that is already separable. 
 Polynomial: gently curved boundaries. 
 RBF: very flexible boundaries for complicated shapes. This is the default in Python's scikit-learn. 

 Our experiment on ring-shaped data: 

 A plain straight-line SVM got only 63% right. 
 Adding the slide's height z = x² + y² gave 100% . 
 The polynomial and RBF kernels also got 100% , automatically, without us inventing the height feature ourselves.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Slide 15: problem. 

 Picture A mein seedhi line green aur blue ko alag kar deti hai. Aasaan hai (linearly separable). 
 Picture B mein blue beech mein hain aur green unke chaaron taraf ring bana rahe hain. Koi seedhi line inhe alag nahi kar sakti, circle chahiye. Ye Lecture 4 ke XOR jaisa non-linear problem hai. 
 Simple SVM sirf seedhi line kheenchta hai. Ab kya karein? 

 Smart idea (slides 16–19): ek naya dimension jodo. 

 Slide 17: green squares beech mein, blue diamonds ring mein. Har point ko ek unchai (height) do: z = x² + y² , yaani centre se doori ka square.
 
 Beech wale points ki height kam, woh neeche rahenge. 
 Ring wale points ki height zyada, woh upar uth jaayenge. 
 
 Slide 18: is height ke saath plot karo to saare blue upar aur saare green neeche. Ab ek seedhi horizontal line (orange) inhe perfectly alag kar deti hai. 
 Ye flat line jab original x–y picture mein wapas laate ho, to woh circle (x² + y² = constant) ban jaati hai. Bilkul wahi jo chahiye tha! 
 Slide 16 3-D mein yahi dikhata hai: flat picture mein points uljhe hue ("complex in low dimension"), 3-D mein uthao to ek flat sheet (hyperplane) beech se kaat deti hai ("simple in higher dimension"). Teacher ne arrow pe likha " kernel transformation ". Slide 2 ka "kernels 2D → 3D" bhi yahi hai. 
 Slide 18 pe ek blue point laal circle mein hai. Ye slide 17 mein beech mein green ke saath chhupa tha, isliye upar uthne ke baad bhi line ke neeche (galat side) hai. Ise soft margin ek galti maan ke chhod deta hai. 

 "Kernel" asal mein kya hai? 

 Slide 19 kehta hai "This transformation is called kernel". 
 Thoda precise baat: transformation φ ko feature map kehte hain. Kernel woh shortcut formula hai jo batata hai ki uthane ke baad do points kitne similar (dot product) honge, bina asal mein uthaye: K(u, v) = φ(u)·φ(v). Isi ko " kernel trick " kehte hain. 
 Kyun zaroori? Kuch transformations hazaaron ya infinite dimensions mein le jaate hain (jaise RBF). Computer unhe seedhe bana hi nahi sakta, par shortcut se kaam chal jata hai. 
 SVM ke dual form mein data sirf dot products (xᵢ·xⱼ) ke roop mein aata hai, isliye har dot product ko K(xᵢ, xⱼ) se badal do, bas. 

 Trick ko numbers se check karo. Points (1, 2) aur (3, 4) lo. 

 Shortcut: (1×3 + 2×4)² = 11² = 121 . 
 Lamba raasta: φ(v) = (v₁², √2·v₁v₂, v₂²) se 3-D mein le jao: (1, 2√2, 4) aur (9, 12√2, 16). Ab dot product: 9 + 48 + 64 = 121 ✔. 
 Same jawaab, par shortcut mein kahin kam mehnat. 

 Slide 5 ke kernels: 

 Linear (x·z): seedhi boundary, already separable data ke liye. Text jaise bahut zyada features wale data pe bhi badhiya. 
 Polynomial ((γx·z + r)^d): halki curved boundaries. Degree d se flexibility badhti hai. 
 RBF (exp(−γ‖x − z‖²)): bahut flexible, complicated shapes ke liye. scikit-learn ka default yahi hai. 
 (Sigmoid bhi hota hai, par slide pe nahi hai.) 
 Valid kernel ke liye Mercer's condition honi chahiye, yaani kernel kisi space ka dot product hona chahiye. 

 Humara experiment (ring wala data, 400 points): 

 Seedhi line wala SVM, raw (x, y) pe: test sirf 63.3% , aur 274 support vectors (lagbhag sab points). 
 Slide ki height z = x² + y² jodke linear SVM: 100% . Is data mein andar wale points ka z 0.013–0.255 aur ring wale ka 0.637–1.436 hai, to ek seedhi line saaf kaat deti hai. 
 Polynomial (degree 2) aur RBF kernel: dono 100% , apne aap, bina humare height feature banaye.

24-07_Advantages_Disadvantages_and_Appli.topic_title: Advantages, Disadvantages and Applications of SVM
24-07_Advantages_Disadvantages_and_Appli.source: Lecture 24, slides 20–22 ("Advantages", "Disadvantages", "Applications"). Enriched with general knowledge and our own timing / accuracy runs (scikit-learn 1.9.1) that test the slides' claims.

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 20: Advantages (as printed), each with a comment 

 "SVM works very well with higher-dimensional datasets ."
 
 The margin-based objective controls capacity even when d is large, even when d > n. 
 Linear SVMs are a classic strong baseline for text classification with tens of thousands of word features. 
 
 "SVM is one of the most memory-efficient classification algorithms."
 
 At prediction time only the support vectors (plus α and b) are stored. On the breast-cancer data below, 96 of 426 training points (22.5%) are support vectors. 
 Caveat: training a kernel SVM may need the n × n kernel matrix (O(n²) memory) and roughly O(n²)–O(n³) time. So "memory-efficient" applies to the trained model, not to training on large n. 
 
 "The clearer the margin of separation between the categories, the better the SVM works." A wide margin means few support vectors and good generalisation ( L24 Which Hyperplane? Maximum Margin, Good vs Bad Margin, Hard vs Soft ). 
 "Effective on datasets with multiple features , like financial or medical data." See the breast-cancer run in L24 SVM in scikit-learn: Code, Scaling, Tuning and Multiclass : 30 features, 97.9–98.6% test accuracy. 

 Other advantages (general knowledge): 

 Convex training with a unique global optimum, so no local minima, unlike k-Means (Lecture 23) or neural networks. 
 The kernel trick gives flexible non-linear boundaries ( L24 Kernels: Linear vs Non-linear Problems and the Kernel Trick ). 
 Fairly robust to overfitting when C and γ are tuned. 

 Slide 21: Disadvantage (as printed) 

 "SVM does not perform very well when the data set has more noise , i.e. target classes are overlapping ." 

 When the classes overlap heavily there is no clean margin. 
 Many points become margin violations, the number of support vectors grows, and accuracy depends heavily on C. 
 Our moons run with noise 0.3 needed careful tuning to reach about 93% ( L24 The Two Knobs: Gamma (γ) and Regularization (C) ). 

 Other well-known disadvantages (not on the slide): 

 Limitation 
 Detail 

 Slow on very large datasets 
 Kernel SVM training scales roughly quadratically or worse. Our run on random 10-feature data took 0.07 s for n = 2,000, 0.26 s for 4,000 and 0.86 s for 8,000, so doubling n costs about 3.5× the time. For millions of rows use LinearSVC or SGD. 

 Needs feature scaling 
 Distances and dot products depend on units. Breast-cancer test accuracy was 92.3% unscaled vs 97.9% scaled (our run). 

 Hyperparameters matter 
 The kernel choice, C and γ must be tuned, usually with grid search and cross-validation. 

 No native probabilities 
 The output is a signed distance. Probabilities need Platt scaling ( probability=True ), which is slower. 

 Binary by design 
 Multiclass is built from several binary SVMs (one-vs-one or one-vs-rest). 

 Hard to interpret with kernels 
 A linear SVM's w shows feature importance. An RBF model is a weighted sum of similarities to support vectors, which is hard to explain. 

 Slide 22: Applications (as printed, with notes) 

 Slide item 
 What it means / classic example 

 Hand Written Detection 
 handwriting / digit recognition . SVMs reached around 1% error on MNIST in the late 1990s. Our digits run: 99.1% test. 

 Image Classification 
 classifying images from features (e.g. HOG, SIFT) before deep learning 

 Face Detection 
 face vs non-face windows (e.g. Osuna, Freund & Girosi, 1997; HOG + linear SVM detectors) 

 Bioinformatics 
 protein classification, gene-expression analysis 

 Cancer Detection 
 tumour benign vs malignant (e.g. the Wisconsin breast-cancer dataset), microarray-based cancer typing 

 Sentimental Analysis 
 i.e. sentiment analysis : positive/negative reviews. Linear SVMs on word features are a strong baseline. 

 Spam Detection 
 spam vs ham email from word-frequency features (compare the spam example of L22 Random Forest Overview — The Three Steps and the Spam/Ham Example )

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Good things about SVM (slide 20), with our comments: 

 Works well with many features. Even when each example is described by thousands of numbers (like every word in an email), SVM copes well. 
 Memory-efficient. 
 
 Once trained, the model only needs to remember the support vectors , the few "front-line" points. 
 On a breast-cancer dataset, only 96 of 426 training patients (about 1 in 4) had to be remembered. 
 But training itself can be heavy on large datasets, because it compares points with each other. 
 
 A clear gap between the groups means great results. The wider the natural gap, the better SVM does. 
 Good for data with many measurements , like financial or medical records.
 
 On a real medical dataset (30 measurements per tumour) we got about 98% accuracy. 

 Bad things (slide 21): 

 Noisy, overlapping classes hurt it. If the two groups are mixed together with no clean gap, there's no good "road" to draw. Lots of points end up as rule-breakers, and results depend heavily on the settings. 
 Other drawbacks worth knowing:
 
 It gets slow on huge datasets . In our test, doubling the data made training about 3.5 times slower. 
 You must scale your features . On the medical data, accuracy jumped from 92% to 98% just by scaling. 
 You must tune C and gamma . 
 It doesn't naturally give probabilities like "80% sure". 
 It only does two classes at a time, so for more classes it builds many two-class SVMs. 
 With curved kernels it's hard to explain why it made a decision. 

 Where SVMs are used (slide 22): 

 Reading handwriting (digits on cheques and postcodes). Our test on handwritten digits: 99.1% correct. 
 Sorting images and finding faces in photos. 
 Biology : classifying proteins and genes. 
 Cancer detection : benign vs malignant tumours. 
 Sentiment analysis : is a review happy or angry? (The slide says "Sentimental" but means "sentiment".) 
 Spam filters .

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
SVM ke fayde (slide 20), humare comments ke saath: 

 Bahut zyada features wale data pe achha kaam karta hai. Jaise email ka har word ek feature ho (hazaaron features), tab bhi SVM sambhal leta hai, kyunki margin wala tareeka model ko control mein rakhta hai. 
 Memory-efficient. 
 
 Train hone ke baad model ko sirf support vectors (front-line points) yaad rakhne padte hain. 
 Humare breast-cancer test mein 426 training patients mein se sirf 96 (lagbhag 22.5%) yaad rakhne pade. 
 Lekin training bade data pe bhaari padti hai, kyunki points ki aapas mein tulna (n × n kernel matrix) hoti hai. To "memory-efficient" baat trained model ke liye sahi hai, training ke liye nahi. 
 
 Groups ke beech saaf gap ho to result shaandaar. Margin jitna chauda, utna achha. 
 Kai measurements wale data (financial, medical) pe effective. Real medical data (har tumour ke 30 measurements) pe humne lagbhag 98% accuracy paayi. 

 Nuksaan (slide 21): 

 Noise zyada ho ya classes overlap karein to SVM kamzor padta hai. Do groups mile-jule hon to koi saaf "sadak" nahi banti. Bahut points rule todte hain, support vectors badh jaate hain, aur result C pe bahut depend karta hai. 
 Aur bhi kamiyan jo jaanni chahiye:
 
 Bade data pe slow. Humare test mein 2,000 → 0.07 s, 4,000 → 0.26 s, 8,000 → 0.86 s. Data double karo to time ~3.5 guna. Laakhon rows ke liye LinearSVC use karo. 
 Feature scaling zaroori. Medical data pe bina scaling 92.3% , scaling ke saath 97.9% . 
 C aur gamma tune karne padte hain (grid search + cross-validation). 
 Probability seedhe nahi deta ("80% sure" jaisa). Uske liye Platt scaling ( probability=True ) chahiye, jo slow hai. 
 Naturally sirf 2 classes. Zyada classes ke liye kai binary SVMs banta hai (one-vs-one / one-vs-rest). 
 Curved kernel ke saath explain karna mushkil ki decision kyun liya. 

 Kahan use hota hai (slide 22): 

 Hand Written Detection : asal mein handwriting / digit recognition , jaise cheque aur pin code ke ank. 1990s ke end mein MNIST pe ~1% error. Humare digits test pe 99.1% . 
 Image Classification : deep learning se pehle features (HOG, SIFT) nikaal ke images classify karna. 
 Face Detection : photo ke har hisse ko "face / not face" bolna (Osuna et al. 1997, HOG + linear SVM). 
 Bioinformatics : protein aur gene classify karna. 
 Cancer Detection : tumour benign hai ya malignant (Wisconsin breast-cancer data). 
 Sentimental Analysis : sahi shabd sentiment analysis hai. Review khush hai ya gussa. 
 Spam Detection : email spam hai ya ham. Lecture 22 ke random forest wale spam example jaisa.

24-08_SVM_in_scikit_learn_Code_Scaling_a.topic_title: SVM in scikit-learn: Code, Scaling, Tuning and Multiclass
24-08_SVM_in_scikit_learn_Code_Scaling_a.source: Research enrichment, not on the slides. It puts slides 3–19 into practice. References: scikit-learn `SVC` documentation (v1.9.1, run locally) and the "RBF SVM parameters" example. Every output below is from our own runs.

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
(a) The 8-point example from Topic 3 

 import numpy as np
from sklearn.svm import SVC

X = np.array([[3,1],[3,-1],[6,1],[6,-1],[1,0],[0,1],[0,-1],[-1,0]])
y = np.array([ 1, 1, 1, 1, -1, -1, -1, -1])

svm = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e6) # huge C ≈ hard margin
svm.fit(X, y)
print(svm.coef_, svm.intercept_) # ≈ [[1. 0.]] ≈ [-2.] -> hyperplane x1 = 2 (1.0005, -2.0011: C is huge, not infinite)
print(svm.support_vectors_) # [[1,0],[3,1],[3,-1]]
print(svm.dual_coef_) # ≈ [[-0.5, 0.25, 0.25]] (alpha_i * y_i)
print(svm.decision_function([[2.5, 0]])) # ≈ [0.5] -> positive side, 0.5/||w|| = 0.5 from the line
print(svm.predict([[2.5, 0]])) # [1]

 These outputs match the hand derivation in L24 Support Vectors, Margin, Hard and Soft Margin . coef_ (that is, w) exists only for the linear kernel. With RBF the model is Σ αᵢyᵢK(xᵢ, x) + b, and there is no explicit w. 

 (b) A real dataset: breast cancer (slide 22, "Cancer Detection") 

 The Wisconsin breast-cancer data has 569 tumours, 30 numeric features, and 212 malignant vs 357 benign cases. We used a stratified 75/25 split. 

 from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, GridSearchCV
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=y)

model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel="rbf")) # scale INSIDE the pipeline
model.fit(Xtr, ytr)
print(model.score(Xte, yte))

 Model 
 Test accuracy 

 SVC() (RBF) on raw, unscaled features 
 0.923 

 StandardScaler + SVC() (RBF) 
 0.979 , with 96 support vectors (50 + 46) out of 426 training points 

 StandardScaler + SVC(kernel='linear') 
 0.986 

 Grid search (5-fold CV) over C ∈ {0.1, 1, 10, 100} and γ ∈ {'scale', 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1} 
 best C = 10, γ = 0.001; CV score 0.977; test 0.979 

 Three lessons: 

 Scaling adds about 5.6 percentage points here. 
 A linear kernel is already excellent on this data, so try the simple kernel first. 
 Tune C and γ with cross-validation ( L17 k-Fold Cross-Validation (Stratified Ten-Fold, Repeated CV) ). 

 Put the scaler inside the pipeline. That way it is fit only on training folds, and no test information leaks into training. 

 grid = GridSearchCV(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC()),
 {"svc__C": [0.1, 1, 10, 100], "svc__gamma": ["scale", 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1]},
 cv=5).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print(grid.best_params_, grid.score(Xte, yte))

 (c) Multiclass: handwritten digits (slide 22, "Hand Written Detection") 

 On the digits data (1,797 images of 8×8 pixels, classes 0–9, 75/25 split), SVC() gives 99.1% test accuracy, using 619 support vectors out of 1,347 training images. For comparison, the best random forest in Lecture 22 got 98.0% on the same dataset ( L22 Random Forest in scikit-learn and the Handwritten-Digits Example ). The splits differ, so compare loosely. 

 An SVM is inherently binary . scikit-learn's SVC handles K classes by one-vs-one : 

 It trains K(K−1)/2 binary SVMs, one per pair of classes. For 10 digits that is 10·9/2 = 45 classifiers. Our run confirmed a 45-column decision function with decision_function_shape='ovo' . 
 Prediction is by majority vote over the 45 classifiers. 
 By default the decision values are reported in one-vs-rest shape (10 columns). 
 LinearSVC uses one-vs-rest instead: K classifiers, each "class k vs all others". 

 (d) Key parameters of SVC (defaults in scikit-learn 1.9.1) 

 Parameter 
 Default

 'rbf' 
 'linear' , 'poly' , 'rbf' , 'sigmoid' , or a custom function ( L24 Kernels: Linear vs Non-linear Problems and the Kernel Trick )

 'balanced' raises C for rare classes (useful for imbalanced data, Lecture 18)

 turn on Platt-scaled probabilities, at a slower speed 

 Related estimators: 

 LinearSVC : fast linear SVM for large n. 
 SVR : regression ("SVMs … for classification and regression", slide 3). 
 OneClassSVM : novelty and outlier detection. 

 (e) SVM vs earlier classifiers in this course

 Decision tree / Random forest (L20–22)

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Using SVM in Python takes only a few lines: 

 Create the model: SVC(kernel="rbf") (or "linear" , "poly" ). 
 Train it: model.fit(X_train, y_train) . 
 Predict: model.predict(X_new) . Or check accuracy: model.score(X_test, y_test) . 

 Our small example from Topic 3. 

 Python found the dividing line x₁ = 2 with support vectors (1,0), (3,1) and (3,−1), exactly what we worked out by hand. 
 For a new point (2.5, 0) it says "+1". The point is 0.5 units on the plus side of the line. 

 A real medical test: breast-cancer data (569 tumours, 30 measurements each). 

 Without scaling the features: 92.3% correct. 
 With scaling: 97.9% . Scaling matters a lot for SVM, because measurements come in very different units. 
 A simple straight-line (linear) SVM did even better: 98.6% . Always try the simple option first. 
 Letting the computer try 20 combinations of C and gamma with cross-validation picked C = 10 and gamma = 0.001, which also gave 97.9%. 
 Put the scaler and the SVM into one "pipeline" so the scaler only ever learns from training data, never from the test data. 

 Handwritten digits (0–9). 

 SVM scored 99.1% , slightly better than the random forest of Lecture 22 (98.0%), though on a different random split. 
 An SVM can only separate two classes at a time. For 10 digits, Python quietly trains 45 mini-SVMs , one for every pair (0 vs 1, 0 vs 2, …, 8 vs 9), and lets them vote. 

 The main settings: 

 kernel : the shape of boundary (straight, polynomial, RBF). 
 C : how strict about training mistakes. 
 gamma : how far each point's influence reaches. 
 Defaults are RBF, C = 1 and gamma = "scale". 
 Related tools:
 
 LinearSVC : fast, for huge data. 
 SVR : predicts numbers instead of classes. 
 OneClassSVM : finds unusual points. 

 How SVM compares with earlier methods: 

 k-NN remembers every training point and asks the neighbours. 
 Trees and forests ask yes/no questions about features. 
 SVM draws the widest possible road between the classes and remembers only the points on the road's edges. Like k-NN, it needs scaled features. Trees don't.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Python mein SVM sirf 3 lines ka kaam hai: 

 Model banao: SVC(kernel="rbf") (ya "linear" , "poly" ). 
 Train karo: model.fit(X_train, y_train) . 
 Predict karo: model.predict(X_new) , ya accuracy dekho: model.score(X_test, y_test) . 

 Topic 3 wala chhota example. 

 SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e6) ne diya:
 
 coef_ = [1, 0] aur intercept_ = −2, yaani line x₁ = 2 . 
 Support vectors (1,0), (3,1), (3,−1). Bilkul humare haath wale jawaab jaisa. 
 
 Naya point (2.5, 0): decision value +0.5 , to prediction +1 . Line se 0.5 unit plus side pe. 
 coef_ (w) sirf linear kernel mein milta hai. RBF mein model Σ αᵢyᵢK(xᵢ, x) + b hota hai, alag se w nahi hota. 

 Real medical data: breast cancer (569 tumours, 30 measurements, slide 22 ka "Cancer Detection"). 

 Bina scaling RBF SVM: 92.3% . 
 StandardScaler + RBF SVM: 97.9% . Sirf scaling se ~5.6% ka fayda! Support vectors sirf 96 (426 mein se). 
 Scaling + linear SVM: 98.6% . Simple option pehle try karo. 
 GridSearchCV (5-fold) ne C ∈ {0.1, 1, 10, 100} aur γ ∈ {scale, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1} mein se best C = 10, γ = 0.001 chuna. Test pe 97.9%. 
 Scaler ko SVM ke saath pipeline mein daalo, taaki scaler sirf training data se seekhe aur test data ki jaankari leak na ho. 

 Handwritten digits (0–9), slide 22 ka "Hand Written Detection". 

 SVM ne 99.1% score kiya. Lecture 22 ka random forest 98.0% tha (split alag tha, isliye roughly compare karo). 
 SVM ek baar mein sirf do classes alag kar sakta hai. 10 digits ke liye scikit-learn chupchaap 45 chhote SVMs banata hai: har jodi ke liye ek (0 vs 1, 0 vs 2, …, 8 vs 9), kyunki 10×9/2 = 45. Phir voting hoti hai. Ise one-vs-one kehte hain. 
 LinearSVC one-vs-rest use karta hai: har class vs baaki sab, yaani 10 classifiers. 

 Main settings (defaults): 

 kernel='rbf' : boundary ki shape. 
 C=1.0 : galtiyon pe kitni sakhti. Bada C = patla margin = kam regularization. 
 gamma='scale' : har point ka asar kitni door tak. 
 degree=3 : polynomial kernel ki degree. 
 class_weight='balanced' : chhoti class ko zyada weight (imbalanced data ke liye, Lecture 18). 
 probability=True : probability chahiye to on karo (slow). 
 Aur tools:
 
 LinearSVC : bade data ke liye tez. 
 SVR : numbers predict karne ke liye (slide 3 ka "regression"). 
 OneClassSVM : anokhe (outlier) points dhoondhne ke liye. 

 Pichhle classifiers se tulna: 

 k-NN (L16) : saare training points yaad rakhta hai aur padosiyon se poochta hai. Scaling chahiye. 
 Tree / Forest (L20–22) : features pe haan/na sawaal poochta hai. Scaling nahi chahiye. 
 SVM (L24) : classes ke beech sabse chaudi sadak banata hai aur sirf kinare wale points (support vectors) yaad rakhta hai. Training convex hai, to ek hi best answer. k-NN ki tarah scaling chahiye . Knobs: kernel, C, γ.

25-01_Exercise_1_Problem_and_the_Six_Ste.lecture_title: SVM Numericals: Finding the Optimal Hyperplane by Hand
25-01_Exercise_1_Problem_and_the_Six_Ste.topic_title: Numerical Exercise 1: The Problem and the Six-Step Method
25-01_Exercise_1_Problem_and_the_Six_Ste.source: Lecture 25, slides 1–2 ("Numerical Exercise": question, the six solution steps, and handwritten notes "SVs (x, y) → 3D", "3D → (…, 1) → Bias", "α₁, α₂ = ?", "→ Σ wᵢ αᵢ"; slide 2 repeats the question alone). Builds directly on Lecture 24 ([[03_Support_Vectors_Margin_Hard_and_Soft_Margin]] from Lecture 24).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
The question (slides 1–2) 

 "Consider the following set of data points given, find the optimal hyperplane for these data points: 

 (1, 0.5), (1, 1), (1, −0.5), (−0.5, 0.5), (0.5, 0.5), (2, 0), (4, 0), (4.5, 1), (4.5, 0.5), (5, −1), (5.5, 0)." 

 Missing information: the class labels. The question lists 11 points but never says which are positive and which are negative. The solution (slides 3–6) implicitly treats them as two clusters: 

 Class −1 (left): (1, 0.5), (1, 1), (1, −0.5), (−0.5, 0.5), (0.5, 0.5), (2, 0). These are the six points with x₁ ≤ 2. 
 Class +1 (right): (4, 0), (4.5, 1), (4.5, 0.5), (5, −1), (5.5, 0). These are the five points with x₁ ≥ 4. 

 Because the solution sets the left support vector's equation equal to −1 and the right one's to +1, the left cluster must be the negative class. In an exam, state this assumption explicitly. 

 The six-step recipe (slide 1) 

 Step 
 Slide text 
 Meaning 

 1 
 Draw all the points on plane 
 plot them and see the two clusters and the gap 

 2 
 Find the support vectors 
 the closest point(s) of each class across the gap 

 3 
 Add the bias (b) value in vectors to convert 2D to 3D form 
 augment each support vector with a 1: s = (x₁, x₂) → s̃ = (x₁, x₂, 1). Handwritten: "SVs (x, y) → 3D", "3D → (…, 1) → Bias" 

 4 
 Consider parameters for every support vector like α₁, α₂, etc. 
 one unknown αᵢ per support vector. Handwritten: "α₁, α₂ = ?" 

 5 
 Find the linear equations and solve them to find parameter values 
 one equation per support vector: Σⱼ αⱼ (s̃ⱼ · s̃ᵢ) = yᵢ (−1 or +1) 

 6 
 Final equation for hyperplane is … 
 w̃ = Σ αᵢ s̃ᵢ. Its first entries are w, and its last entry is b. Handwritten: "→ Σ wᵢ αᵢ" (read: w̃ = Σ αᵢ s̃ᵢ) 

 The instructor ticked steps 1–3 while explaining them. 

 Why "add a 1"? With x̃ = (x₁, x₂, 1) and w̃ = (w₁, w₂, b): 

 w̃ · x̃ = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + b·1 = w·x + b 

 So the bias is absorbed into the weight vector as one extra coordinate. This is a standard trick, and it is the same "bias as a weight on a constant input of 1" used for the perceptron ( L4 Perceptron — General Architecture (N Inputs, Activation, Error) ). The slide calls it "converting 2D to 3D". This is a bookkeeping change, not the kernel lift of L24 Kernels: Linear vs Non-linear Problems and the Kernel Trick . 

 What the equations in step 5 say. For a support vector, the canonical SVM condition is w·sᵢ + b = yᵢ, i.e. exactly +1 or −1 ( L24 Support Vectors, Margin, Hard and Soft Margin ). Writing w̃ = Σⱼ αⱼ s̃ⱼ and substituting gives 

 Σⱼ αⱼ (s̃ⱼ · s̃ᵢ) = yᵢ for each support vector i, 

 a small linear system with as many equations as unknowns. 

 Important caveat. 

 In this recipe the αᵢ are signed coefficients , e.g. −6.5 and 3.5 in Exercise 1. They are not the Lagrange multipliers of SVM theory, which are always ≥ 0. 
 The recipe is a classroom shortcut . It reproduces the true maximum-margin hyperplane in both exercises of this lecture, but not for every dataset. 
 L25 Why the Classroom Shortcut Works Here, When It Fails, and the Exact Method explains when it works and gives the exact method.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The task. We are given 11 points on a graph and asked for the "optimal hyperplane", the best dividing line with the widest possible gap (Lecture 24). 

 One thing the question forgets. It never says which points belong to which class! Looking at the solution, the teacher treats: 

 the left group (six points from x = −0.5 to x = 2) as the negative class (−1) ; 
 the right group (five points from x = 4 to x = 5.5) as the positive class (+1) . 

 In an exam, write that assumption down. 

 The six-step recipe on slide 1: 

 Plot the points. You'll see two clumps with an empty strip between them. 
 Find the support vectors. These are the points from each clump that face each other across the gap, the "front-line" points. 
 Add a 1 to each support vector. (2, 0) becomes (2, 0, 1). The extra 1 is a trick that lets the "shift" number b ride along inside the vector, so we can handle the slope and the shift in one calculation. The teacher calls this "2D → 3D". 
 Give each support vector an unknown number : α₁, α₂, and so on. 
 Write one equation per support vector and solve. Each equation says "this support vector must score exactly −1 (if negative) or +1 (if positive)". 
 Build the answer : multiply each 3-D support vector by its α and add them up. The first two numbers you get are the direction of the line (w), and the last number is the shift (b). 

 Fair warning. 

 The α numbers this recipe produces can be negative. They are helper numbers, not the "official" α of SVM theory, which are never negative. 
 The recipe is a classroom shortcut. It gives the correct answer for both exercises in this lecture, and Topic 6 shows when it can go wrong and what to do instead.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Sawaal (slides 1–2). 11 points diye hain: (1, 0.5), (1, 1), (1, −0.5), (−0.5, 0.5), (0.5, 0.5), (2, 0), (4, 0), (4.5, 1), (4.5, 0.5), (5, −1), (5.5, 0). Inka optimal hyperplane dhoondhna hai, yaani woh dividing line jiska margin (khaali patti) sabse chauda ho (Lecture 24). 

 Sawaal ek cheez bhool gaya: labels! Kaunsa point kis class ka hai, ye nahi likha. Solution dekh ke pata chalta hai: 

 Left group (x = −0.5 se 2 tak, 6 points) = class −1 (negative) . 
 Right group (x = 4 se 5.5, 5 points) = class +1 (positive) . 

 Exam mein ye assumption likh dena. 

 Slide 1 ke 6 steps: 

 Saare points plot karo. Do jhund dikhenge, beech mein khaali patti. 
 Support vectors dhoondho. Har jhund ka woh point jo gap ke paar doosre jhund ke saamne hai (front-line). 
 Har support vector mein 1 jodo. (2, 0) → (2, 0, 1). Teacher ne likha "SVs (x, y) → 3D" aur "(…, 1) → Bias".
 
 Fayda: x̃ = (x₁, x₂, 1) aur w̃ = (w₁, w₂, b) lo, to w̃·x̃ = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + b = w·x + b. Bias b vector ke andar hi aa gaya. 
 Perceptron (Lecture 4) mein bhi bias ko "constant input 1 ka weight" maana tha. 
 Ye sirf hisaab ka tareeka hai, Lecture 24 wala kernel (z = x² + y²) nahi. 
 
 Har support vector ke liye ek unknown lo : α₁, α₂ … (teacher: "α₁, α₂ = ?"). 
 Har support vector ki ek equation likho aur solve karo. Equation kehti hai: "is support vector ka score exactly −1 (negative) ya +1 (positive) ho". Formula: Σⱼ αⱼ (s̃ⱼ · s̃ᵢ) = yᵢ. 
 Final hyperplane: w̃ = Σ αᵢ s̃ᵢ. Pehle do numbers = w (line ki direction), aakhri number = b (shift). Teacher ne likha "→ Σ wᵢ αᵢ". 

 Teacher ne step 1–3 pe tick lagaya hai. 

 Saavdhaan. 

 Is shortcut mein α negative bhi aa sakte hain (Exercise 1 mein −6.5 aur 3.5). Ye helper numbers hain, SVM theory ke asli Lagrange multipliers (jo hamesha ≥ 0 hote hain) nahi. 
 Ye ek classroom shortcut hai. Is lecture ke dono exercises mein sahi answer deta hai, par har data pe nahi. Kab chalta hai aur sahi general tareeka kya hai, ye Topic 6 mein hai.

25-02_Exercise_1_Full_Solution_Alphas_an.topic_title: Exercise 1, Full Solution: Support Vectors, α₁ = −6.5, α₂ = 3.5, Hyperplane x₁ = 3

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Step 1: plot (slide 3) 

 The plot "Data Points in Plane" (axes x₁ from −1 to 6, x₂ from −1.5 to 1.5) shows: 

 a left cluster : (−0.5, 0.5), (0.5, 0.5), (1, 1), (1, 0.5), (1, −0.5), (2, 0); 
 a right cluster : (4, 0), (4.5, 1), (4.5, 0.5), (5, −1), (5.5, 0). 

 The instructor drew a dashed curve in the empty band around x₁ ≈ 3 and wrote "2D to 3D". 

 Step 2: support vectors 

 The point of the left (−1) cluster closest to the right cluster is (2, 0) , circled as S₁ . 
 The point of the right (+1) cluster closest to the left cluster is (4, 0) , circled as S₂ . 
 (The handwriting labels both columns "S₂". The left one is S₁.) 
 Every other point is farther from the gap. For example, (4.5, ·) is 0.5 farther right than (4, 0), and (1, ·) is 1 farther left than (2, 0). 

 Step 3: augment with a 1 (bias coordinate) 

 S̃₁ = (2, 0, 1) , S̃₂ = (4, 0, 1) 

 Steps 4–5: equations (slide 4) 

 Unknowns α₁ and α₂, with w̃ = α₁S̃₁ + α₂S̃₂. The handwritten conditions are: 

 ① α₁ S̃₁·S̃₁ + α₂ S̃₂·S̃₁ = −1 , written "w.r.t. S₁" (S₁ is a negative support vector) 
 ② α₁ S̃₁·S̃₂ + α₂ S̃₂·S̃₂ = +1 , written "w.r.t. S₂" (S₂ is a positive support vector) 

 Dot products: 

 S̃₁·S̃₁ = 2·2 + 0·0 + 1·1 = 5 
 S̃₁·S̃₂ = 2·4 + 0·0 + 1·1 = 9 
 S̃₂·S̃₂ = 4·4 + 0·0 + 1·1 = 17 

 So the system is: 

 ③ 5α₁ + 9α₂ = −1 
 ④ 9α₁ + 17α₂ = +1 

 Solving. Multiply ③ by 9 and ④ by 5: 

 45α₁ + 81α₂ = −9 
 45α₁ + 85α₂ = 5 

 Subtract: 4α₂ = 14, so α₂ = 3.5 . Then 5α₁ = −1 − 9(3.5) = −32.5, so α₁ = −6.5 . Both values match the slide ✔. (Check with Cramer's rule: det = 5·17 − 9·9 = 4, α₁ = (−17 − 9)/4 = −6.5, α₂ = (5 + 9)/4 = 3.5.) 

 Step 6: the hyperplane (slide 5) 

 w̃ = −6.5·(2, 0, 1) + 3.5·(4, 0, 1) = (−13, 0, −6.5) + (14, 0, 3.5) = (1, 0, −3) 

 w = (1, 0) is the part the instructor marks "for orientation of line". 
 b = −3 is the part marked "for bias". 
 Hyperplane: 1·x₁ + 0·x₂ − 3 = 0, i.e. x₁ = 3 , a vertical line ✔. 

 The orientation rule on slide 5. w is the normal (perpendicular) to the line: 

 w 
 Line w·x + b = 0 
 Slide's label 

 (0, 1) 
 x₂ = −b, horizontal 
 (i) Horizontal 

 (1, 0) 
 x₁ = −b, vertical 
 (ii) Vertical (our case) 

 (1, 1) 
 x₁ + x₂ = −b, diagonal with slope −1 
 (iii) Diagonal 

 About "b + 3 = 0" on slide 5. The note "b = −3" is right, but "b + 3 = 0 plus side" is not the hyperplane equation. The equation is x₁ − 3 = 0 (x₁ = 3). 

 Points with x₁ − 3 > 0 lie on the plus side : the right cluster, class +1. 
 Points with x₁ − 3 < 0 lie on the minus side. 

 Slide 6: result, with margin 

 The hyperplane is the red line x₁ = 3. 
 The margin lines are purple dashed at x₁ = 2 (w·x + b = −1) and x₁ = 4 (w·x + b = +1). 
 The support vectors (2, 0) and (4, 0) sit on them. 
 The margin arrows show 1 unit on each side: d = 1/‖w‖ = 1, and the full width is 2/‖w‖ = 2 . 

 Every point checked (score w·x + b = x₁ − 3): 

 Point 
 Score 
 Point 
 Score 

 (−0.5, 0.5) 
 −3.5 
 (4, 0) 
 +1 (SV) 

 (0.5, 0.5) 
 −2.5 
 (4.5, 1) 
 +1.5 

 (1, 1), (1, 0.5), (1, −0.5) 
 −2 
 (4.5, 0.5) 
 +1.5 

 (2, 0) 
 −1 (SV) 
 (5, −1) 
 +2 

 (5.5, 0) 
 +2.5 

 All left points score ≤ −1 and all right points score ≥ +1, so the canonical constraints yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b) ≥ 1 hold ✔. 

 scikit-learn agrees. It gives w = (1, 0), b = −3, support vectors (2, 0) and (4, 0), and margin 2. Its true dual coefficients are αᵢyᵢ = −0.5 and +0.5, so the true multipliers are α = 0.5 each. The slide's −6.5 and 3.5 are different numbers because they come from the augmented shortcut ( L25 Why the Classroom Shortcut Works Here, When It Fails, and the Exact Method ).

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Step 1: draw. 

 On the graph, six points sit on the left (from x = −0.5 to x = 2) and five on the right (from x = 4 to x = 5.5). 
 Between x = 2 and x = 4 there is an empty strip. The best dividing line will run through it. 

 Step 2: front-line points (support vectors). 

 The left group's point closest to the gap is (2, 0) . Call it S₁. 
 The right group's point closest to the gap is (4, 0) . Call it S₂. 
 (The teacher's handwriting labels both "S₂", but the left one is S₁.) 

 Step 3: add a 1. S₁ = (2, 0, 1) and S₂ = (4, 0, 1). 

 Steps 4–5: two equations. 

 "Dot product" means multiply matching numbers and add:
 
 S₁·S₁ = 2×2 + 0×0 + 1×1 = 5 
 S₁·S₂ = 2×4 + 0 + 1 = 9 
 S₂·S₂ = 4×4 + 0 + 1 = 17 
 
 The rules are "S₁ must score −1" and "S₂ must score +1":
 
 5α₁ + 9α₂ = −1 
 9α₁ + 17α₂ = +1 
 
 Solve them like any pair of school equations:
 
 Multiply the first by 9 and the second by 5: 45α₁ + 81α₂ = −9 and 45α₁ + 85α₂ = 5. 
 Subtract: 4α₂ = 14, so α₂ = 3.5 . 
 Put it back: 5α₁ = −1 − 31.5 = −32.5, so α₁ = −6.5 . 

 Step 6: build the line. 

 −6.5 × (2, 0, 1) = (−13, 0, −6.5) 
 3.5 × (4, 0, 1) = (14, 0, 3.5) 
 Add them: (1, 0, −3) . 
 So w = (1, 0) and b = −3. The line is 1·x₁ + 0·x₂ − 3 = 0, which means x₁ = 3 : a vertical line exactly halfway between 2 and 4. 

 Reading the direction (slide 5). The w part tells you which way the line faces. w is an arrow pointing across the line, not along it. 

 w = (0, 1) → horizontal line 
 w = (1, 0) → vertical line (our case) 
 w = (1, 1) → slanted line going down to the right 

 The picture on slide 6. 

 The red line at x = 3 is the hyperplane. 
 The purple dashed lines at x = 2 and x = 4 are the edges of the "road". 
 The points (2, 0) and (4, 0) sit right on those edges; they are the support vectors. 
 The road is 1 unit wide on each side, 2 units in total. 

 Checking every point. The score of each point is just x₁ − 3. 

 Left points: −3.5, −2.5, −2, −2, −2, −1. All negative. 
 Right points: +1, +1.5, +1.5, +2, +2.5. All positive. 
 Nobody is inside the road. ✔ 

 A small slip on slide 5. It says "b + 3 = 0". The real line equation is x₁ − 3 = 0 . Points where x₁ − 3 is positive are on the "plus side".

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Step 1: plot karo (slide 3). 

 Left mein 6 points: (−0.5, 0.5), (0.5, 0.5), (1, 1), (1, 0.5), (1, −0.5), (2, 0). 
 Right mein 5 points: (4, 0), (4.5, 1), (4.5, 0.5), (5, −1), (5.5, 0). 
 x = 2 aur x = 4 ke beech khaali patti hai. Best line isi mein se jaayegi. Teacher ne wahan dashed curve bana ke "2D to 3D" likha. 

 Step 2: support vectors. 

 Left group ka gap ke sabse paas point: (2, 0) , yaani S₁. 
 Right group ka sabse paas point: (4, 0) , yaani S₂. 
 (Handwriting mein dono pe "S₂" likha hai, par left wala S₁ hai.) 

 Step 3: 1 jodo. S̃₁ = (2, 0, 1), S̃₂ = (4, 0, 1). 

 Steps 4–5: equations (slide 4). 

 Teacher ki equations:
 
 ① α₁ S₁·S₁ + α₂ S₂·S₁ = −1 (S₁ ke hisaab se, kyunki S₁ negative hai) 
 ② α₁ S₁·S₂ + α₂ S₂·S₂ = +1 (S₂ ke hisaab se, positive) 
 
 Dot product = matching numbers ka guna karke jodo:
 
 S₁·S₁ = 4 + 0 + 1 = 5 
 S₁·S₂ = 8 + 0 + 1 = 9 
 S₂·S₂ = 16 + 0 + 1 = 17 
 
 To equations ban gayi:
 
 ③ 5α₁ + 9α₂ = −1 
 ④ 9α₁ + 17α₂ = 1 
 
 Solve:
 
 ③ × 9 → 45α₁ + 81α₂ = −9, aur ④ × 5 → 45α₁ + 85α₂ = 5. 
 Ghatao: 4α₂ = 14, to α₂ = 3.5 . 
 Wapas daalo: 5α₁ = −1 − 31.5 = −32.5, to α₁ = −6.5 ✔ (slide se match). 

 Step 6: hyperplane (slide 5). 

 w̃ = α₁S̃₁ + α₂S̃₂ = −6.5(2, 0, 1) + 3.5(4, 0, 1) = (−13, 0, −6.5) + (14, 0, 3.5) = (1, 0, −3) . 
 Pehle do numbers w = (1, 0) : teacher ne likha "for orientation of line". 
 Aakhri number b = −3 : "for bias". 
 Line: 1·x₁ + 0·x₂ − 3 = 0, yaani x₁ = 3 : ek vertical line , 2 aur 4 ke theek beech. 

 Direction kaise padhein (slide 5). w line ke perpendicular (90°) wala teer hai, line ke saath nahi. 

 (i) w = (0, 1) → horizontal line 
 (ii) w = (1, 0) → vertical line (humara case) 
 (iii) w = (1, 1) → diagonal line (x₁ + x₂ = constant, slope −1) 

 Chhoti galti. Slide 5 pe "b + 3 = 0 plus side" likha hai. Sahi equation x₁ − 3 = 0 hai. Jahan x₁ − 3 > 0 ho, woh plus side (right cluster, class +1) hai. 

 Slide 6 ki picture. 

 Laal line x₁ = 3 hyperplane hai. 
 Purple dashed lines x₁ = 2 (score −1) aur x₁ = 4 (score +1) margin ki lines hain. 
 (2, 0) aur (4, 0) unpe baithe support vectors hain. 
 Margin dono taraf 1 unit hai, total 2/‖w‖ = 2 . 

 Har point check kiya (score = x₁ − 3): 

 Left: −3.5, −2.5, −2, −2, −2, −1 (SV). 
 Right: +1 (SV), +1.5, +1.5, +2, +2.5. 
 Sab apni side pe, koi margin ke andar nahi ✔. 
 scikit-learn ne bhi w = (1, 0), b = −3, margin 2 diya. Uske asli α dono 0.5 hain. Slide ke −6.5 aur 3.5 shortcut wale helper numbers hain, isliye alag hain (Topic 6).

The slide gives only the answers. The full working below (dot products, equations, solution, checks) is ours, verified with numpy and scikit-learn. This is the **same dataset** we solved in Lecture 24, Topic 3 ([[03_Support_Vectors_Margin_Hard_and_Soft_Margin]] from Lecture 24).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
The question 

 "Suppose we are given the following positively labelled data points (3, 1), (3, −1), (6, 1), (6, −1), and the following negatively labelled data points (1, 0), (0, 1), (0, −1), (−1, 0). Find the optimal hyperplane for these data points." 

 Unlike Exercise 1, the labels are given explicitly here. 

 Step 1–2: plot and support vectors 

 The negative points form a diamond around the origin. The rightmost one is (1, 0) . 
 The positive points form a rectangle at x₁ = 3 and x₁ = 6. The leftmost pair is (3, 1) and (3, −1) . 
 The gap runs from x₁ = 1 to x₁ = 3, so the support vectors are:
 
 S₁ = (1, 0), class −1 
 S₂ = (3, 1), class +1 
 S₃ = (3, −1), class +1 
 
 These match the slide's choices, marked "−", "+" and "+" in the handwriting. 

 Step 3: augment 

 S̃₁ = (1, 0, 1), S̃₂ = (3, 1, 1), S̃₃ = (3, −1, 1) 

 Step 4–5: dot products and equations 

 · 
 S̃₁ 
 S̃₂ 
 S̃₃ 

 S̃₁ 
 1+0+1 = 2 
 3+0+1 = 4 
 3+0+1 = 4 

 S̃₂ 
 4 
 9+1+1 = 11 
 9−1+1 = 9 

 S̃₃ 
 4 
 9 
 9+1+1 = 11 

 Equations (Σⱼ αⱼ S̃ⱼ·S̃ᵢ = yᵢ): 

 ① 2α₁ + 4α₂ + 4α₃ = −1 
 ② 4α₁ + 11α₂ + 9α₃ = +1 
 ③ 4α₁ + 9α₂ + 11α₃ = +1 

 Solving. 

 ② − ③ gives 2α₂ − 2α₃ = 0, so α₂ = α₃ (expected from the symmetry about the x₁-axis). 
 With α₃ = α₂:
 
 ① becomes 2α₁ + 8α₂ = −1. 
 ② becomes 4α₁ + 20α₂ = 1. 
 
 Doubling ① gives 4α₁ + 16α₂ = −2. Subtracting this from ② gives 4α₂ = 3, so α₂ = α₃ = 0.75 . 
 Then 2α₁ = −1 − 6 = −7, so α₁ = −3.5 . 

 All three match the slide ✔. 

 Step 6: hyperplane 

 w̃ = −3.5·(1, 0, 1) + 0.75·(3, 1, 1) + 0.75·(3, −1, 1)
 = (−3.5 + 2.25 + 2.25, 0 + 0.75 − 0.75, −3.5 + 0.75 + 0.75)
 = (1, 0, −2) 

 w = (1, 0) , so the line is vertical ("(i) Vertical" on the slide). 
 b = −2 ("(ii)"). 
 Hyperplane: x₁ − 2 = 0, i.e. x₁ = 2 , halfway between x₁ = 1 and x₁ = 3. 
 The slide's "(iii) b + 2 = 0" should be read as x₁ − 2 = 0 . This is the same notational slip as in Exercise 1 ( L25 Exercise 1, Full Solution: Support Vectors, α₁ = −6.5, α₂ = 3.5, Hyperplane x₁ = 3 ). 

 Margin: 2/‖w‖ = 2/1 = 2 . The margin lines are x₁ = 1 (score −1) and x₁ = 3 (score +1). 

 Checking all 8 points (score = x₁ − 2): 

 Positive points 
 Score 
 Negative points 
 Score 

 (3, 1), (3, −1) 
 +1 (SVs) 
 (1, 0) 
 −1 (SV) 

 (6, 1), (6, −1) 
 +4 
 (0, 1), (0, −1) 
 −2 

 (−1, 0) 
 −3 

 Every positive point scores ≥ +1 and every negative point scores ≤ −1 ✔. 

 scikit-learn (Lecture 24 run): w = (1, 0), b = −2, support vectors (1, 0), (3, 1), (3, −1). The true multipliers are α = 0.5, 0.25, 0.25, with αᵢyᵢ = −0.5, +0.25, +0.25. Again they differ from the shortcut's −3.5, 0.75, 0.75, but the hyperplane is identical . Why this happens is explained in L25 Why the Classroom Shortcut Works Here, When It Fails, and the Exact Method .

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The question. Plus points: (3, 1), (3, −1), (6, 1), (6, −1). Minus points: (1, 0), (0, 1), (0, −1), (−1, 0). Find the best dividing line. This time the labels are given. 

 Picture it. 

 The minus points make a small diamond around the centre (0, 0). 
 The plus points make a rectangle further right. 
 The minus point nearest the gap is (1, 0). The plus points nearest the gap are (3, 1) and (3, −1). 
 So there are three support vectors this time. The slide marks them "−", "+", "+". 

 Add a 1 to each: (1, 0, 1), (3, 1, 1), (3, −1, 1). 

 All the dot products (multiply matching numbers, then add): 

 S₁·S₁ = 2, S₁·S₂ = 4, S₁·S₃ = 4 
 S₂·S₂ = 11, S₂·S₃ = 9, S₃·S₃ = 11 

 Three equations ("minus support vector scores −1, plus ones score +1"): 

 2α₁ + 4α₂ + 4α₃ = −1 
 4α₁ + 11α₂ + 9α₃ = 1 
 4α₁ + 9α₂ + 11α₃ = 1 

 Solve step by step: 

 Subtract the third equation from the second: 2α₂ − 2α₃ = 0, so α₂ = α₃. (That makes sense: the two plus support vectors are mirror images.) 
 Replace α₃ by α₂:
 
 2α₁ + 8α₂ = −1 
 4α₁ + 20α₂ = 1 
 
 Double the first one (4α₁ + 16α₂ = −2) and subtract it from the second: 4α₂ = 3, so α₂ = α₃ = 0.75 . 
 Then 2α₁ = −1 − 6 = −7, so α₁ = −3.5 . These are exactly the numbers on the slide. 

 Build the line. 

 −3.5 × (1, 0, 1) + 0.75 × (3, 1, 1) + 0.75 × (3, −1, 1) = (1, 0, −2) . 
 So w = (1, 0) means a vertical line, and b = −2. 
 The line is x₁ = 2 , exactly halfway between the minus edge (x₁ = 1) and the plus edge (x₁ = 3). 
 The road is 2 units wide. 

 Check every point (score = x₁ − 2): 

 Plus points score +1, +1, +4, +4. 
 Minus points score −1, −2, −2, −3. 
 All are on the correct side and none is inside the road. ✔ 

 Already seen! This is exactly the example we solved in Lecture 24, Topic 3, using a different method. Python's SVM gives the same line, x₁ = 2. 

 Same small slip as before. The slide writes "b + 2 = 0", but the line's equation is x₁ − 2 = 0 .

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Sawaal (slide 7). 

 Positive points: (3, 1), (3, −1), (6, 1), (6, −1). 
 Negative points: (1, 0), (0, 1), (0, −1), (−1, 0). 
 Optimal hyperplane dhoondho. Is baar labels diye hue hain. 

 Picture socho. 

 Negative points (0, 0) ke around ek chhota diamond banate hain. 
 Positive points right mein ek rectangle. 
 Gap ke sabse paas: negative mein (1, 0) , positive mein (3, 1) aur (3, −1) . 
 Is baar teen support vectors hain. Slide pe teacher ne "−", "+", "+" mark kiya hai. 

 1 jodo: S̃₁ = (1, 0, 1), S̃₂ = (3, 1, 1), S̃₃ = (3, −1, 1). 

 Saare dot products (slide pe nahi the, humne nikaale): 

 S₁·S₁ = 1 + 0 + 1 = 2 
 S₁·S₂ = 3 + 0 + 1 = 4 , S₁·S₃ = 4 
 S₂·S₂ = 9 + 1 + 1 = 11 , S₃·S₃ = 11 
 S₂·S₃ = 9 − 1 + 1 = 9 

 Teen equations: 

 ① 2α₁ + 4α₂ + 4α₃ = −1 
 ② 4α₁ + 11α₂ + 9α₃ = 1 
 ③ 4α₁ + 9α₂ + 11α₃ = 1 

 Solve: 

 ② − ③: 2α₂ − 2α₃ = 0, to α₂ = α₃ . Dono plus SVs ek dusre ki mirror image hain, isliye barabar. 
 α₃ = α₂ daalo: ① → 2α₁ + 8α₂ = −1 aur ② → 4α₁ + 20α₂ = 1. 
 ① × 2 = 4α₁ + 16α₂ = −2. Ise ② se ghatao: 4α₂ = 3, to α₂ = α₃ = 0.75 . 
 2α₁ = −1 − 6 = −7, to α₁ = −3.5 . Slide ke answers se bilkul match ✔. 

 Hyperplane. 

 w̃ = −3.5(1, 0, 1) + 0.75(3, 1, 1) + 0.75(3, −1, 1).
 
 x₁ part: −3.5 + 2.25 + 2.25 = 1 
 x₂ part: 0 + 0.75 − 0.75 = 0 
 bias part: −3.5 + 0.75 + 0.75 = −2 
 Total: (1, 0, −2) . 
 
 w = (1, 0), to vertical line (slide ka "(i) Vertical"). b = −2 (slide ka "(ii)"). 
 Line: x₁ − 2 = 0, yaani x₁ = 2 , jo 1 aur 3 ke theek beech hai. 
 Slide ka "(iii) b + 2 = 0" asal mein x₁ − 2 = 0 hona chahiye. Ye wahi chhoti galti hai jo Exercise 1 mein thi. 
 Margin = 2/‖w‖ = 2 . Margin lines x₁ = 1 aur x₁ = 3 hain. 

 Har point check (score = x₁ − 2): 

 Positive: (3, ±1) → +1 (SV), (6, ±1) → +4. 
 Negative: (1, 0) → −1 (SV), (0, ±1) → −2, (−1, 0) → −3. 
 Sab sahi side pe ✔. 

 Ye pehle dekha hua hai! Lecture 24 Topic 3 mein humne yahi dataset doosre tareeke se solve kiya tha. scikit-learn ne bhi x₁ = 2 diya, aur asli α = 0.5, 0.25, 0.25 the. Slide ke −3.5, 0.75, 0.75 shortcut wale helper numbers hain, par line bilkul same aati hai. Kyun? Topic 6 dekho.

25-04_scikit_learn_SVM_Documentation_and.source: Lecture 25, slide 8 (screenshot of the scikit-learn User Guide, "1.4. Support Vector Machines", version 1.9.0 stable, showing the definition, the advantages list and the start of "The disadvantages of support vector machines include:"). Enriched with the rest of that documentation page (disadvantages, complexity, practical tips) and our own code run (scikit-learn 1.9.1).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
What slide 8 shows 

 Definition (as on the page): "Support vector machines (SVMs) are a set of supervised learning methods used for classification , regression and outliers detection ." 

 Classification is SVC , NuSVC and LinearSVC . 
 Regression is SVR . 
 Outlier/novelty detection is OneClassSVM . 

 Advantages (as on the page): 

 Effective in high dimensional spaces . 
 Still effective in cases where the number of dimensions is greater than the number of samples . 
 Uses a subset of training points in the decision function (called support vectors ), so it is also memory efficient . 
 Versatile : different kernel functions can be specified for the decision function. Common kernels are provided, and custom kernels are possible too. 

 These are the same points as Lecture 24's "Advantages" slide ( L24 Advantages, Disadvantages and Applications of SVM ). 

 Disadvantages (the slide cuts off at the heading; the documentation continues): 

 If the number of features is much greater than the number of samples, avoiding over-fitting by choosing the kernel and the regularization term (C) is crucial. 
 SVMs do not directly provide probability estimates. scikit-learn computes them with an expensive internal five-fold cross-validation ( probability=True ). 

 Sections listed in the page's sidebar: 1.4.1 Classification, 1.4.2 Regression, 1.4.3 Density estimation / novelty detection, 1.4.4 Complexity, 1.4.5 Tips on Practical Use, 1.4.6 Kernel functions, 1.4.7 Mathematical formulation, 1.4.8 Implementation details. 

 Complexity : kernel-SVM training time grows roughly between O(n_features·n²) and O(n_features·n³) in the number of samples n. 
 Tips : scale the data (e.g. to [0, 1] or with standardisation), tune C (and γ) by cross-validation, and consider class_weight for imbalanced data. 

 Code that reproduces both exercises 

 import numpy as np
from sklearn.svm import SVC

# Exercise 1 (labels assumed: left cluster = -1, right cluster = +1)
neg = [(1,.5),(1,1),(1,-.5),(-.5,.5),(.5,.5),(2,0)]
pos = [(4,0),(4.5,1),(4.5,.5),(5,-1),(5.5,0)]
X1 = np.array(neg + pos); y1 = np.r_[-np.ones(6), np.ones(5)]
svm1 = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e6).fit(X1, y1) # huge C ≈ hard margin
print(svm1.coef_, svm1.intercept_) # [[1. 0.]] [-3.] -> x1 = 3
print(svm1.support_vectors_) # [[2. 0.] [4. 0.]]
print(svm1.dual_coef_) # [[-0.5 0.5]] (alpha_i * y_i)
print(2 / np.linalg.norm(svm1.coef_)) # 2.0 -> margin

# Exercise 2
X2 = np.array([[3,1],[3,-1],[6,1],[6,-1],[1,0],[0,1],[0,-1],[-1,0]])
y2 = np.array([1,1,1,1,-1,-1,-1,-1])
svm2 = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e6).fit(X2, y2)
print(svm2.coef_, svm2.intercept_) # ≈ [[1. 0.]] ≈ [-2.] -> x1 = 2
print(svm2.support_vectors_) # [[1. 0.] [3. 1.] [3. -1.]]

 These outputs come from our run. 

 Exercise 1: w = (1, 0), b = −3, support vectors (2, 0) and (4, 0), margin 2. This matches slides 5–6 ( L25 Exercise 1, Full Solution: Support Vectors, α₁ = −6.5, α₂ = 3.5, Hyperplane x₁ = 3 ). 
 Exercise 2: w ≈ (1, 0), b ≈ −2, support vectors (1, 0), (3, ±1). This matches slide 7 ( L25 Exercise 2: Three Support Vectors, Hyperplane x₁ = 2 ). 

 Notes on reading the output. 

 coef_ (w) is available only for kernel="linear" . 
 dual_coef_ stores αᵢ·yᵢ for the support vectors, using the true Lagrange multipliers. These are 0.5 and 0.5 in Exercise 1, not the shortcut's −6.5 and 3.5 ( L25 Why the Classroom Shortcut Works Here, When It Fails, and the Exact Method ). 
 SVC has no separate "hard margin" switch. A very large C (here 10⁶) makes slack so expensive that the solution equals the hard-margin one when the data is separable. 

 Checking the shortcut's linear systems with numpy: 

 S = np.array([[2,0,1],[4,0,1]]) # augmented support vectors (Exercise 1)
G = S @ S.T # [[5, 9], [9, 17]]
alpha = np.linalg.solve(G, [-1, 1]) # [-6.5, 3.5]
print(alpha @ S) # [ 1. 0. -3.] = (w1, w2, b)

 Running the same code for Exercise 2 (S = [[1,0,1],[3,1,1],[3,−1,1]], y = [−1, 1, 1]) gives G = [[2,4,4],[4,11,9],[4,9,11]], α = [−3.5, 0.75, 0.75] and w̃ = (1, 0, −2) ✔.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 8 is a screenshot of the official scikit-learn help page for SVMs. scikit-learn is the Python library we've used throughout the course. 

 What the page says: 

 SVMs can do three jobs:
 
 classification : put things into groups; 
 regression : predict a number; 
 outlier detection : spot unusual points. 
 
 Good points: 
 
 They work well when each example has lots of features . 
 They still work even when there are more features than examples . 
 They only need to remember the support vectors , so they're memory efficient . 
 They're flexible : you can choose different kernels (straight, curved, RBF) or even write your own. 
 
 Weak points (the slide cuts off here, so we read the rest of the page):
 
 With far more features than examples you must pick the kernel and C carefully, or the model will overfit. 
 SVMs don't naturally give "how sure am I" probabilities. Python can compute them, but it's slow. 
 
 Practical tip from the page: always scale your data first, and tune C and gamma with cross-validation. 

 Letting the computer check our homework. 

 We typed both exercises into Python. 
 Exercise 1: Python found the line x₁ = 3 , support vectors (2, 0) and (4, 0) , and a road 2 units wide . That is exactly the slide's answer. 
 Exercise 2: Python found x₁ = 2 with support vectors (1, 0), (3, 1), (3, −1) . Again it matches. 
 We also let numpy solve the teacher's small equation systems directly. It returned α = −6.5 and 3.5 (Exercise 1) and α = −3.5, 0.75, 0.75 (Exercise 2), exactly as on the slides. 
 One thing that may confuse you: Python's own "α" values are different (0.5 and 0.5 for Exercise 1). They are the official SVM α values, while the classroom shortcut produces different helper numbers. Both lead to the same line. Topic 6 explains why.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Slide 8 scikit-learn ke official help page (User Guide 1.4, version 1.9.0) ka screenshot hai. scikit-learn wahi Python library hai jo hum poore course mein use kar rahe hain. 

 Page kya kehta hai: 

 SVM teen kaam karta hai:
 
 classification ( SVC ); 
 regression , yaani number predict karna ( SVR ); 
 outlier detection , yaani ajeeb points pakadna ( OneClassSVM ). 
 
 Fayde: 
 
 Bahut features wale data pe achha. 
 Features, samples se zyada hon tab bhi chalta hai. 
 Sirf support vectors yaad rakhta hai, isliye memory efficient . 
 Versatile : alag-alag kernels (linear, poly, RBF) ya apna custom kernel bhi de sakte ho. 

 Ye wahi points hain jo Lecture 24 ke "Advantages" slide pe the. 
 
 Nuksaan (slide pe heading ke baad kat gaya, humne page se padha):
 
 Features bahut zyada aur samples kam hon to kernel aur C dhyan se chunne padte hain, warna overfitting hogi. 
 Probability seedhe nahi deta. probability=True se milti hai, par andar 5-fold cross-validation chalta hai, isliye slow. 
 
 Tips: data ko scale karo, aur C/γ cross-validation se tune karo. 
 Complexity: training time samples ke saath n² se n³ ke beech badhta hai. 

 Computer se homework check karwaya. 

 Exercise 1 (left = −1, right = +1 maan ke): SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e6) .
 
 w = (1, 0), b = −3, yaani x₁ = 3 . 
 Support vectors (2, 0), (4, 0) , margin 2 . Slide se bilkul match ✔. 
 
 Exercise 2: w ≈ (1, 0), b ≈ −2, yaani x₁ = 2 . Support vectors (1, 0), (3, ±1) ✔. 
 C = 10⁶ kyun? SVC mein alag "hard margin" button nahi hai. Bahut bada C galti ko itna mehnga bana deta hai ki answer hard margin jaisa hi aata hai. 
 numpy se teacher ke equation systems bhi solve karwaye:
 
 Ex 1: Gram matrix [[5, 9], [9, 17]], α = [−6.5, 3.5], w̃ = (1, 0, −3) ✔. 
 Ex 2: Gram [[2, 4, 4], [4, 11, 9], [4, 9, 11]], α = [−3.5, 0.75, 0.75], w̃ = (1, 0, −2) ✔. 
 
 Confuse mat hona: scikit-learn ke dual_coef_ mein asli α·y hota hai. Ex 1 mein woh −0.5 aur +0.5 hai, yaani asli α = 0.5 dono. Slide ke −6.5, 3.5 shortcut ke helper numbers hain. Dono se line same aati hai, kyun? Topic 6 mein.

25-05_Iris_Setosa_vs_Versicolor_Choosing.topic_title: Iris Setosa vs Versicolor: Choosing the Best Line, Support Vectors and Margin

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Slides 9–10: the data 

 Slide 9 shows an iris flower. The petal (inner, upright part) and the sepal (outer, drooping part) each have a length and a width. This is the famous Iris dataset from Lecture 1 ( L1 The Iris Dataset (Case Study) ). 
 Slide 10 plots two species using two features. The x-axis is Petal Width and the y-axis is Petal Length .
 
 Setosa (green squares) sit lower-left. 
 Versicolor (blue diamonds) sit upper-right, with one versicolor point drawn far up-left. 
 
 The two classes are separable by a straight line, so this is a hard-margin linear SVM problem. 

 Slide 11: many lines separate the classes 

 Three lines are drawn: blue (shallow), black (steeper) and orange (steepest). Each one separates the training points perfectly. So "separates the data" is not enough to choose a line. This is the same question as Lecture 24's "Which hyperplane shall we use?" ( L24 Which Hyperplane? Maximum Margin, Good vs Bad Margin, Hard vs Soft ). 

 Slide 12: compare by distance to the nearest points 

 Only the black and orange lines remain. Dashed segments show the perpendicular distance from the nearest points to each line. 

 The orange line passes very close to the top-left versicolor point and to a setosa point near the bottom. Its smallest distance is tiny. 
 The black line keeps a larger distance from the nearest points of both classes. 

 The SVM picks the line whose minimum distance to the data, the margin , is largest. That is the black line. 

 Slides 13–14: support vectors and margin 

 The black line is kept. 
 The instructor's purple arrows mark " SV ": the top-left versicolor point and nearby setosa and versicolor points. 
 Slide 14 labels Support Vectors (arrows to five points near the line, from both species) and the Margin (the dashed distance from the line to a nearby point). 

 Caveat about the illustration. In an exact hard-margin solution, every support vector lies at exactly the same distance 1/‖w‖ from the hyperplane, because all of them sit on the margin lines w·x + b = ±1. In slide 14's figure the dashed segments have visibly different lengths, so it is a schematic, not a computed solution. 

 The real data, solved (our run: scikit-learn SVC(kernel='linear', C=10⁶) ) 

 The real Iris data has 50 setosa and 50 versicolor flowers. Features are (petal width, petal length) in cm. 

 Ranges: 

 Setosa: width 0.1–0.6, length 1.0–1.9. 
 Versicolor: width 1.0–1.8, length 3.0–5.1. 

 The real classes are separated by a wide gap. The real data has no versicolor flower near the setosa cluster, unlike the outlier drawn in slide 10's schematic. 

 Result: 

 w = (0.824, 1.294) , b = −3.788 . 
 Hyperplane: 0.824·width + 1.294·length − 3.788 = 0. It is a downward-sloping diagonal, like the black line on the slides. 
 Only two support vectors: setosa (0.4, 1.9) and versicolor (1.1, 3.0) . 
 Margin = 2/‖w‖ = 1.304 cm . 
 Training accuracy 100% . 

 Hand derivation (two support vectors). With one support vector per class, x₋ = (0.4, 1.9) and x₊ = (1.1, 3.0), the maximum-margin hyperplane is the perpendicular bisector of the segment between them: 

 d = x₊ − x₋ = (0.7, 1.1), ‖d‖² = 0.49 + 1.21 = 1.70 
 w = 2d/‖d‖² = (1.4, 2.2)/1.70 = (0.8235, 1.2941) ✔ 
 midpoint m = (0.75, 2.45), b = −w·m = −(0.6176 + 3.1706) = −3.788 ✔ 
 margin = 2/‖w‖ = ‖d‖ = √1.70 = 1.304 ✔ 
 Check: w·x₋ + b = 0.3294 + 2.4588 − 3.788 = −1.00 , and w·x₊ + b = 0.9059 + 3.8824 − 3.788 = +1.00 ✔ 

 Using the model. 

 A flower with petal width 0.5 and length 2.0 scores 0.412 + 2.588 − 3.788 = −0.788 , so it is setosa . 
 A flower with width 1.2 and length 4.0 scores 0.988 + 5.176 − 3.788 = +2.376 , so it is versicolor . 
 These match predict and decision_function in our run.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 9: the flower. An iris flower has inner upright petals and outer drooping sepals. For each, we can measure the length and the width. Botanists measured 150 flowers this way; that's the famous Iris dataset from Lecture 1. 

 Slide 10: the graph. 

 Petal width goes along the bottom and petal length goes up the side. 
 Setosa flowers (green squares) have small petals, so they sit in the lower-left. 
 Versicolor flowers (blue diamonds) have bigger petals, so they sit upper-right. 
 A straight line can split them. 

 Slide 11: but which line? Three different lines (blue, black, orange) all split the two groups perfectly. They're all "correct" on this data, so we need a tie-breaker. 

 Slide 12: the tie-breaker is the safety gap. 

 Look at how close each line comes to the nearest flowers (the dashed lines). 
 The orange line almost touches one blue diamond and one green square. A new flower that's slightly different could easily land on the wrong side. 
 The black line keeps a comfortable distance from both groups. 
 SVM picks the line with the biggest gap to the nearest points . That's the black one. 

 Slides 13–14: names. 

 The flowers closest to the black line are the support vectors ; the teacher wrote "SV" with arrows. 
 The gap between the line and them is the margin . 
 Small print: in a perfectly computed SVM, all support vectors sit at exactly the same distance from the line. The slide's drawing shows slightly different distances because it's a sketch, not a calculation. 

 We tried it on the real flowers. 

 In the real data, the two species are far apart:
 
 setosa petals are 1.0–1.9 cm long; 
 versicolor petals are 3.0–5.1 cm long. 
 
 (The lonely blue diamond drawn near the setosa group on the slide doesn't exist in the real data.) 
 Python's SVM found the line 0.824 × width + 1.294 × length − 3.788 = 0 , a slanted line like the black one. 
 Only two flowers turned out to be support vectors: a setosa with petal (0.4 cm wide, 1.9 cm long) and a versicolor with petal (1.1, 3.0). 
 The safety gap is 1.30 cm wide. 
 It classifies all 100 flowers correctly. 

 Checking by hand. 

 When there's one support vector on each side, the best line is simply the line that cuts the segment between them in half at a right angle . 
 The segment from (0.4, 1.9) to (1.1, 3.0) has length √1.70 ≈ 1.30. That's exactly the margin. 
 The line passes through its midpoint (0.75, 2.45). 

 Trying new flowers. 

 A flower with petals 0.5 wide and 2.0 long scores −0.79: negative, so setosa . 
 One with petals 1.2 wide and 4.0 long scores +2.38: positive, so versicolor .

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Slide 9: phool. Iris phool mein andar khade petals aur bahar latakte sepals hote hain. Dono ki length aur width naap sakte hain. Isi se bana famous Iris dataset Lecture 1 mein padha tha. 

 Slide 10: graph. 

 Neeche (x-axis) Petal Width, upar (y-axis) Petal Length. 
 Setosa (hare squares) ke petals chhote hain, to woh neeche-left mein hain. 
 Versicolor (neele diamonds) ke bade hain, to upar-right mein hain. 
 Ek seedhi line inhe alag kar sakti hai. 

 Slide 11: par kaunsi line? Teen lines (neeli, kaali, orange) teeno dono groups ko perfectly alag karti hain. Training data pe sab "sahi" hain, to tie-breaker chahiye. Ye wahi Lecture 24 wala sawaal hai: "Which hyperplane shall we use?" 

 Slide 12: tie-breaker = safety gap. 

 Har line sabse paas wale phoolon se kitni door hai (dashed lines) dekho. 
 Orange line ek neele diamond aur ek hare square ko lagbhag chhoo rahi hai. Thoda alag naya phool aaya to galat side gir sakta hai. 
 Kaali line dono groups se aaraam ki doori rakhti hai. 
 SVM wahi line chunta hai jiski sabse paas wale points se doori (margin) sabse zyada ho. Isliye kaali line. 

 Slides 13–14: naam. 

 Kaali line ke sabse paas wale phool support vectors hain (teacher ne purple arrows se "SV" likha). 
 Line aur unke beech ka gap margin hai. 
 ⚠ Chhoti baat: asli calculated SVM mein saare support vectors line se bilkul barabar doori (1/‖w‖) pe hote hain, kyunki sab margin lines (w·x + b = ±1) pe baithe hote hain. Slide 14 ki drawing mein dooriyan alag-alag dikhti hain, kyunki woh sketch hai, calculation nahi. 

 Humne asli phoolon pe chalaya (50 setosa + 50 versicolor): 

 Asli data mein dono species bahut door hain:
 
 Setosa: width 0.1–0.6, length 1.0–1.9 cm. 
 Versicolor: width 1.0–1.8, length 3.0–5.1 cm. 
 Slide 10 pe setosa ke paas jo akela neela diamond bana hai, woh asli data mein nahi hai. 
 
 scikit-learn ka answer:
 
 Line: 0.824 × width + 1.294 × length − 3.788 = 0 , ek tirchhi line, slide ki kaali line jaisi. 
 Sirf do support vectors: setosa (0.4, 1.9) aur versicolor (1.1, 3.0) . 
 Margin = 1.304 cm , aur saare 100 phool sahi ✔. 

 Haath se check (do support vectors wala shortcut). Har side ek support vector ho to best line unhe jodne wali line ka perpendicular bisector hoti hai (beech se 90° pe kaatne wali). 

 d = (1.1 − 0.4, 3.0 − 1.9) = (0.7, 1.1), aur ‖d‖² = 0.49 + 1.21 = 1.70 . 
 w = 2d/‖d‖² = (1.4, 2.2)/1.7 = (0.8235, 1.2941) ✔ 
 Midpoint = (0.75, 2.45), b = −w·midpoint = −(0.6176 + 3.1706) = −3.788 ✔ 
 Margin = ‖d‖ = √1.70 = 1.304 ✔ 
 Check: setosa SV ka score −1.00 , versicolor SV ka +1.00 ✔ 

 Naye phool: 

 Petal (0.5, 2.0): 0.412 + 2.588 − 3.788 = −0.788 → setosa . 
 Petal (1.2, 4.0): 0.988 + 5.176 − 3.788 = +2.376 → versicolor .

25-06_Why_the_Shortcut_Works_and_the_Exa.lecture_title: SVM Numericals: Finding the Optimal Hyperplane by Hand
25-06_Why_the_Shortcut_Works_and_the_Exa.topic_title: Why the Classroom Shortcut Works Here, When It Fails, and the Exact Method
25-06_Why_the_Shortcut_Works_and_the_Exa.source: Research enrichment, not on the slides. It analyses the six-step "augmented vector" method of slides 1–7 ([[01_Exercise_1_Problem_and_the_Six_Step_Method]]). Based on the standard SVM dual formulation (Boser–Guyon–Vapnik 1992; Cortes–Vapnik 1995; see Lecture 24) and our own numpy / scikit-learn checks. All numbers were computed by us.

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
What the shortcut really computes 

 The shortcut takes the chosen support vectors sᵢ with labels yᵢ ∈ {−1, +1}, augments them to s̃ᵢ = (sᵢ, 1), sets w̃ = Σ αᵢ s̃ᵢ, and solves 

 Σⱼ αⱼ (s̃ⱼ · s̃ᵢ) = yᵢ for every chosen support vector. 

 These equations say w̃·s̃ᵢ = yᵢ, i.e. w·sᵢ + b = yᵢ . That is the correct condition for a support vector: it lies on its margin line. 

 There is a catch. Forcing w̃ to be a combination of the s̃ᵢ picks, among all (w, b) that satisfy those equations, the one with the smallest ‖w‖² + b² . This is the minimum-norm solution of a linear system. 

 The real hard-margin SVM ( L24 Support Vectors, Margin, Hard and Soft Margin ) minimises ‖w‖² only , and leaves b free: 

 True SVM: minimise ½‖w‖² s.t. yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b) ≥ 1 for all points, with b unpenalised. 

 So the two methods agree only when penalising b doesn't change the answer. 

 Why it gives the right answer in both exercises 

 Exercise 2 has three support vectors in 2-D, which gives three equations in three unknowns (w₁, w₂, b): 

 (1, 0): w₁ + b = −1 
 (3, 1): 3w₁ + w₂ + b = 1 
 (3, −1): 3w₁ − w₂ + b = 1 

 These fully determine w = (1, 0), b = −2. There is no freedom left for the norm to choose, so any method that satisfies the equations gives the same line. 
 Exercise 1 has two support vectors, (2, 0) and (4, 0), which gives two equations, 2w₁ + b = −1 and 4w₁ + b = 1. 

 These fix w₁ = 1 and b = −3, and leave w₂ free. 
 Both methods minimise w₂² and set w₂ = 0. 
 Because both support vectors lie on the line x₂ = 0, the free part does not involve b, so the answers coincide. 

 A case where it fails 

 Take one support vector per class, not level with each other horizontally : x₋ = (0, 1) in class −1 and x₊ = (2, 1) in class +1. 

 True SVM: the perpendicular bisector of the segment between them, x₁ = 1 . So w = (1, 0), b = −1, margin = 2. scikit-learn confirms w = (1, 0), b = −1. 
 Shortcut: 

 Augmented vectors (0, 1, 1) and (2, 1, 1). Gram matrix [[2, 2], [2, 6]]. 
 Equations: 2α₁ + 2α₂ = −1 and 2α₁ + 6α₂ = 1, so α₁ = −1 and α₂ = 0.5. 
 w̃ = −(0, 1, 1) + 0.5(2, 1, 1) = (1, −0.5, −0.5) . 
 Line: x₁ − 0.5x₂ − 0.5 = 0. It is tilted , with margin 2/√1.25 = 1.789 < 2 . 

 It still puts both points on their margin lines, but it is not the maximum-margin hyperplane. 

 Real data example (Iris, L25 Iris Setosa vs Versicolor: Choosing the Best Line, Support Vectors and Margin ). Use the correct support vectors (0.4, 1.9) and (1.1, 3.0). 

 The shortcut gives w ≈ (2.312, 0.347), b ≈ −2.584, with margin 0.856 . 
 The true SVM gives w = (0.824, 1.294), b = −3.788, with margin 1.304 . 

 The shortcut's line is noticeably worse. 

 The exact method (dual form) for hand calculation 

 In the true dual solution, w = Σ αᵢ yᵢ xᵢ with αᵢ ≥ 0 , the extra condition Σ αᵢ yᵢ = 0 , and b is a separate unknown. For the chosen support vectors, solve: 

 Σⱼ αⱼ yⱼ (xⱼ · xᵢ) + b = yᵢ (one equation per support vector)
 Σᵢ αᵢ yᵢ = 0 

 Exercise 1 with x₋ = (2, 0) and x₊ = (4, 0): 

 Σαy = 0 forces α₋ = α₊ = α, so w = α(4, 0) − α(2, 0) = (2α, 0). 
 (4, 0): 8α + b = 1. (2, 0): 4α + b = −1. 
 So α = 0.5 , b = −3 , w = (1, 0) ✔. These are scikit-learn's values: dual_coef_ = −0.5, +0.5. 

 Exercise 2 with x₁ = (1, 0)(−), x₂ = (3, 1)(+), x₃ = (3, −1)(+): 

 Σαy = 0 gives α₁ = α₂ + α₃. By symmetry α₂ = α₃ = a and α₁ = 2a. 
 w = −2a(1, 0) + a(3, 1) + a(3, −1) = (4a, 0). 
 (1, 0): 4a + b = −1. (3, 1): 12a + b = 1. 
 So a = 0.25 , giving α = (0.5, 0.25, 0.25), b = −2 and w = (1, 0) ✔, exactly scikit-learn's values. 

 The failure case done properly: 

 α₋ = α₊ = α, so w = α((2, 1) − (0, 1)) = (2α, 0). 
 (2, 1): 4α + b = 1. (0, 1): b = −1. 
 So α = 0.5 and w = (1, 0), b = −1 , i.e. x₁ = 1 ✔. 

 Two-support-vector closed form. For one support vector per class, x₋ and x₊, let d = x₊ − x₋ and m = (x₊ + x₋)/2: 

 w = 2d/‖d‖², b = −w·m, margin = ‖d‖ 

 Exam advice 

 If the question follows the slide method, show the slide's six steps. Your marks depend on them, and they give the correct line for symmetric textbook data like Exercises 1–2. 
 Always sanity-check the final line:
 
 The support vectors must score exactly ±1. 
 Every other point must satisfy yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b) ≥ 1. If one doesn't, your choice of support vectors was wrong. 
 The line should sit midway between the classes, perpendicular to the gap. 
 
 For two support vectors that are not aligned, use the closed form above or the exact dual equations. They are just as short and always correct.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
What the shortcut does. The classroom recipe forces each support vector to score exactly −1 or +1. That part is right: support vectors should sit exactly on the edges of the "road". But the way it builds the answer, by mixing the 3-D support vectors, quietly prefers answers where the shift number b is small as well as the direction numbers. A real SVM only cares about making the road as wide as possible . It doesn't care how big b is. 

 Why it still worked in both exercises. 

 Exercise 2: three support vectors give three equations, and the line has three unknowns. There's only one possible answer, so any honest method lands on it. 
 Exercise 1: both support vectors lie on the same horizontal line (y = 0). The leftover freedom only affects the tilt, and both methods choose "no tilt". So they agree again. 

 When it goes wrong. 

 Example: one minus point at (0, 1) and one plus point at (2, 1). 
 The true best line is the vertical line x = 1 , exactly halfway, with a road 2 wide. 
 The shortcut gives a tilted line, x₁ − 0.5x₂ = 0.5, with a road only 1.79 wide. 
 It still separates the two points, but it isn't the widest road. 
 On the real Iris flowers the shortcut's road would be 0.86 cm wide instead of the true 1.30 cm. 

 The proper way, still easy by hand. The official SVM adds one extra rule: "the α's of the plus side and the minus side must balance" (Σ αᵢyᵢ = 0), and it keeps b as its own unknown. 

 Exercise 1: the balance rule makes both α's equal.
 
 Two short equations, 8α + b = 1 and 4α + b = −1, give α = 0.5 and b = −3. 
 The line is x₁ = 3, the same as the slide. 
 
 Exercise 2: 
 
 Balance plus symmetry gives α = 0.5, 0.25, 0.25 and b = −2, so the line is x₁ = 2, the same as the slide. 
 These are the α values Python reports. 

 A super-quick rule for two support vectors. The best line is the one that cuts the segment between them in half, at a right angle , and the road's width equals the length of that segment. 

 For your exam. 

 Use the teacher's steps if asked, because they give the right answer on neat textbook data. 
 Always check your final line:
 
 the support vectors score exactly ±1; 
 every other point scores at least +1 on its side (or at most −1); 
 the line sits right in the middle of the gap.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Shortcut asal mein kya karta hai? 

 Class wala recipe har support vector ko exactly −1 ya +1 score dene pe majboor karta hai. Ye sahi hai, kyunki support vectors ko margin lines pe hi hona chahiye. 
 Par jis tareeke se answer banata hai (3-D support vectors ka mix, w̃ = Σαᵢs̃ᵢ), woh chupke se aisa answer pasand karta hai jisme b (shift) bhi chhota ho. Technically ye ‖w‖² + b² ko minimum karta hai. 
 Asli SVM sirf ‖w‖ chhota (sadak chaudi) karna chahta hai. Use b ki koi parwaah nahi. 

 Dono exercises mein phir bhi sahi kyun aaya? 

 Exercise 2: 3 support vectors se 3 equations aur 3 unknowns (w₁, w₂, b). Sirf ek hi answer possible hai (w = (1, 0), b = −2), isliye koi bhi tareeka wahi dega. 
 Exercise 1: dono SVs (2, 0) aur (4, 0) ek hi horizontal line (x₂ = 0) pe hain. Equations w₁ = 1 aur b = −3 fix kar deti hain, sirf w₂ free bachta hai. Dono methods w₂ = 0 chunte hain, isliye same answer. 

 Kab galat hota hai? 

 Example: minus point (0, 1), plus point (2, 1).
 
 Asli SVM: beech mein vertical line x₁ = 1 , sadak 2 chaudi. 
 Shortcut: Gram [[2, 2], [2, 6]], α = (−1, 0.5), w̃ = (1, −0.5, −0.5). Yaani tirchhi line x₁ − 0.5x₂ − 0.5 = 0, sadak sirf 1.789 chaudi. 
 Dono points ko alag to karti hai, par sabse chaudi sadak nahi. 
 
 Asli Iris data pe: shortcut ka margin 0.856 aata hai, jabki sahi margin 1.304 hai. Kaafi kharab. 

 Sahi tareeka (dual form), haath se bhi aasaan. 

 Asli SVM mein w = Σ αᵢyᵢxᵢ, αᵢ ≥ 0 , ek extra rule Σ αᵢyᵢ = 0 (plus aur minus side ke α balance hon), aur b alag unknown. 
 Exercise 1: 
 
 Balance rule se α₋ = α₊ = α, to w = (2α, 0). 
 (4, 0): 8α + b = 1, aur (2, 0): 4α + b = −1. 
 α = 0.5, b = −3, w = (1, 0) . Line x₁ = 3 ✔. scikit-learn ke dual_coef_ (−0.5, +0.5) bhi yahi kehte hain. 
 
 Exercise 2: 
 
 α₁ = α₂ + α₃. Symmetry se α₂ = α₃ = a, to α₁ = 2a, aur w = (4a, 0). 
 (1, 0): 4a + b = −1, aur (3, 1): 12a + b = 1. 
 a = 0.25 , to α = (0.5, 0.25, 0.25), b = −2. Line x₁ = 2 ✔ (scikit-learn wale hi numbers). 
 
 Fail wala case sahi tareeke se: 
 
 w = (2α, 0). (2, 1): 4α + b = 1, aur (0, 1): b = −1. 
 α = 0.5, to x₁ = 1 ✔. 

 Do SVs ka super-shortcut formula: 

 d = x₊ − x₋ aur m = (x₊ + x₋)/2 lo. 
 w = 2d/‖d‖², b = −w·m, margin = ‖d‖ . 
 Yaani best line dono SVs ko jodne wali line ko beech se 90° pe kaatti hai. 

 Exam ke liye salaah: 

 Agar sawaal teacher ke method pe hai, to slide ke 6 steps hi dikhao. Saaf-suthre textbook data (Exercise 1, 2) pe woh sahi answer deta hai. 
 Answer hamesha check karo:
 
 SVs ka score exactly ±1 ho. 
 Baaki har point ka yᵢ(w·xᵢ + b) ≥ 1 ho. Agar nahi, to support vectors galat chune the. 
 Line dono classes ke beech mein, gap ke perpendicular ho. 
 
 Do SVs tirchhe (not aligned) hon, to upar wala closed formula ya dual equations use karo. Utne hi chhote hain aur hamesha sahi.
