26-07_Machine_Learning_and_AI_Venn_Diagr.source: Lecture 26, slides 16–17 ("Machine Learning and AI": nested Venn diagram AI ⊃ Machine learning ⊃ Representation learning ⊃ Deep learning with examples Knowledge bases, Logistic regression, Shallow autoencoders, MLPs, from the *Deep Learning* book, Fig. 1.4; "CYC Project: The project was begun in July 1984 at MCC", with Cyc's four logos from Wikipedia). Enriched with web research (Wikipedia: Cyc, Douglas Lenat; MIT Technology Review, "Cycorp: The Cost of Common Sense", 2005; Goodfellow et al., *Deep Learning*, 2016, ch. 1).

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 16: four nested circles, each with an example 

 Lecture 2's hierarchy had three circles ( L2 AI, ML, DL Hierarchy and Relationship with Data Science ). The book's version adds representation learning between ML and DL: 

 AI ⊃ Machine learning ⊃ Representation learning ⊃ Deep learning 

 Each region has an example that belongs to that circle but not to the next one inside it: 

 Region 
 Example on the slide 
 Why it sits there 

 AI but not ML 
 Knowledge bases 
 Intelligent behaviour from facts and rules written by humans. Nothing is learned from data. (Cyc, below.) 

 ML but not representation learning 
 Logistic regression 
 Learns weights from data ( L15 Worked Example — Logistic Regression for Exam Pass Probability ), but uses the features it is given. It does not learn new features. 

 Representation learning but not deep 
 Shallow autoencoders 
 Learn a new representation (the hidden code h) from data, but with only one hidden layer, so there is no hierarchy of simple → complex ( L26 Representation Learning and Factors of Variation ). 

 Deep learning 
 MLPs (multilayer perceptrons) 
 Several hidden layers, each a new representation built from the previous one ( L26 The Deep Learning Model (MLP) and the Four AI Flowcharts ). 

 How to read it: "every deep-learning model is a representation-learning model; every representation-learning model is an ML model; every ML model is an AI technique", but not the other way round. 

 Other examples (ours) for each ring: 

 AI, not ML: chess search programs like Deep Blue, route-finding with A* search, rule-based expert systems. 
 ML, not representation learning: KNN, decision trees, random forests, linear/logistic regression, linear SVM on fixed features (Lectures 13–25). 
 Representation learning, not deep: PCA ( L11 Principal Component Analysis — Definition, Key Facts, and Geometric Intuition –12), shallow autoencoders, k-means used as a feature encoder (one-hot cluster membership). 
 Deep learning: deep MLPs, CNNs, RNNs, Transformers. 

 (The slide's graphic is a re-styled version of the book's figure; the circles and examples are the same.) 

 Slide 17: the Cyc project, the classic "knowledge base" approach 

 Facts (verified): 

 Started July 1984 at MCC , the Microelectronics and Computer Technology Corporation in Austin, Texas. MCC was a US industry research consortium (about 400 people) formed partly in response to Japan's Fifth Generation Computer project. Cyc was its flagship project. 
 Led by Douglas Lenat (1950–2023). He started it after finding it frustrating to hand-code domain knowledge for his earlier AI program, EURISKO. 
 Goal: capture human common sense , the millions of everyday facts that people take for granted ("water is wet", "a person can't be in two places at once"), so that a computer could reason like a human. The name comes from "en cyc lopedia". 
 How it works: humans write facts and rules in a formal logic language called CycL . An inference engine then deduces new facts by logical reasoning. 
 Later history: spun off from MCC as the company Cycorp (1994–95; sources differ on the exact year). A subset was released free as OpenCyc in 2002. Lenat died on 31 August 2023. 

 The four logos on the slide (clockwise from top-left, per Wikipedia's caption): Cyc's Knowledge Base (KB), its Inference Engines (INF), Actionable Output (the starburst), and Intelligent Data Selection (the SKSI network logo). 

 Why Cyc appears in a deep-learning lecture 

 The Deep Learning book uses Cyc as the main example of the knowledge-base approach to AI: hard-code knowledge about the world in a formal language, then reason with logical inference rules. Its verdict: none of these projects led to a major success. People struggle to write formal rules with enough complexity to describe the world accurately. 

 The book's famous anecdote (citing Linde, 1992): Cyc failed to understand a story about a man named Fred shaving in the morning . Its inference engine found an inconsistency. It knew that people do not have electrical parts, but because Fred was holding an electric razor, it concluded that the entity "FredWhileShaving" contained electrical parts. It therefore asked whether Fred was still a person while he was shaving. 

 The lesson: hand-written rules break in endless unexpected ways, just like the hand-designed wheel detector of L26 Learning Representations, and Why Hand-Designed Features Are Hard . The difficulties of hard-coded knowledge suggest that AI systems need the ability to acquire their own knowledge by extracting patterns from raw data . That capability is machine learning, and learning the representation too is the step deep learning takes. 

 Knowledge base (Cyc) 
 Machine learning / deep learning 

 Where knowledge comes from 
 Humans write rules 
 Learned from data 

 Strength 
 Explainable, exact logical reasoning 
 Handles messy, perceptual, ambiguous data 

 Weakness 
 Brittle; impossible to write every rule 
 Needs lots of data; harder to explain

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 16: four circles inside each other. In Lecture 2 we saw three: AI, then machine learning inside it, then deep learning inside that. This slide adds a new circle, representation learning , between machine learning and deep learning. Each ring has an example that belongs to that ring but not to the smaller ring inside it: 

 AI only: knowledge bases. Humans type in facts and rules, and the computer reasons with them. Nothing is learned from data. Example: a huge database of common-sense facts (Cyc, below). 
 Machine learning, but not representation learning: logistic regression (Lecture 15). It learns its weights from examples, but it uses exactly the features we hand it. It never invents new features. 
 Representation learning, but not deep: shallow autoencoders. These do invent a new, compact description of the data (Topic 4), but in only one step. There is no ladder from simple to complex. 
 Deep learning: MLPs (multilayer perceptrons). Many layers, each building a new description on top of the previous one. 

 So every deep learning model is also representation learning, also machine learning and also AI, but not the other way round. Other examples: a chess-search program is AI but not ML; KNN and decision trees are ML but don't learn features; PCA is representation learning but not deep; image-recognition networks are deep learning. 

 Slide 17: the Cyc project. 

 Started in July 1984 at MCC (Microelectronics and Computer Technology Corporation), a big American research group in Austin, Texas. It was led by Douglas Lenat . 
 The dream: type all of human common sense into a computer, millions of facts like "water makes things wet" or "people can't be in two places at once", and let it reason like a human. The name comes from "en cyc lopedia". 
 Facts are written in a special logic language (CycL), and a reasoning program (the "inference engine") draws conclusions from them. 
 It later became a company, Cycorp , released a free part called OpenCyc in 2002, and Lenat died in 2023. 
 The four logos show its parts: the knowledge base, the inference engine, actionable output, and intelligent data selection. 

 Why mention Cyc here? It is the best-known example of the "just write all the rules by hand" approach, and of why that approach struggles. The Deep Learning book tells a famous story: Cyc read a story about Fred shaving in the morning with an electric razor. Cyc knew "people don't have electrical parts". But Fred was holding something electrical, so Cyc decided "Fred-while-shaving" contained electrical parts, and asked whether Fred was still a person while shaving! 

 The lesson: no matter how many rules you write, real life finds a case you didn't think of. This is the same problem as the hand-made wheel detector in Topic 3. The answer is to let computers learn from data instead, and deep learning goes one step further by learning the features too.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Slide 16: Chaar circles ek ke andar ek. Lecture 2 me teen the: AI ⊃ ML ⊃ DL. Is slide (Deep Learning book, Fig 1.4) me ML aur DL ke beech ek naya circle hai: representation learning . 

 AI ⊃ Machine learning ⊃ Representation learning ⊃ Deep learning 

 Har ring ka ek example, jo us ring me hai par andar wali chhoti ring me nahi: 

 Sirf AI (ML nahi): Knowledge bases. Insaan facts aur rules likhta hai, computer unse reasoning karta hai. Data se kuch seekha nahi jaata. (Jaise Cyc, neeche.) 
 ML, par representation learning nahi: Logistic regression (Lecture 15). Weights data se seekhta hai, par jo features diye wahi use karta hai. Naye features nahi banata. 
 Representation learning, par deep nahi: Shallow autoencoders. Data ka naya compact representation khud banata hai (Topic 4), par sirf ek hidden layer me. Simple → complex wali seedhi nahi hai. 
 Deep learning: MLPs (multilayer perceptrons). Kai hidden layers, har layer pichhli ke upar naya representation. 

 Matlab har deep learning model representation learning bhi hai, ML bhi, AI bhi. Ulta zaroori nahi. Aur examples: chess search program = AI par ML nahi; KNN, decision tree = ML par features nahi seekhte; PCA = representation learning par deep nahi; CNN = deep learning. 

 Slide 17: CYC Project. 

 July 1984 me MCC (Microelectronics and Computer Technology Corporation, Austin, Texas) me shuru hua. MCC lagbhag 400 logon ka American research consortium tha, aur Cyc uska flagship project tha. Leader the Douglas Lenat (1950–2023), jinhone apne pichhle program EURISKO me haath se knowledge likhne ki takleef dekh ke ye shuru kiya. 
 Sapna: insaan ka saara common sense (crore facts jaise "paani geela karta hai", "insaan ek time pe do jagah nahi ho sakta") computer me daal do, taaki wo insaan jaisa reasoning kare. Naam "en cyc lopedia" se aaya. 
 Facts ek logic language CycL me likhe jaate hain, aur inference engine unse naye conclusions nikaalta hai. 
 Baad me company Cycorp bani (1994–95), 2002 me free part OpenCyc release hua. 
 Slide ke chaar logos (clockwise): Knowledge Base , Inference Engines , Actionable Output , Intelligent Data Selection . 

 Deep learning lecture me Cyc kyun? Ye "saare rules haath se likh do" wale approach ka sabse famous example hai, aur ye bhi ki wo approach kyun fail hota hai. Deep Learning book ki famous kahani: Cyc ko ek story di gayi jisme Fred subah shave kar raha hai, electric razor se. Cyc jaanta tha "insaan me electrical parts nahi hote". Par Fred ke haath me electric razor tha, to Cyc ne socha "FredWhileShaving" me electrical parts hain, aur poochha: kya shave karte waqt Fred abhi bhi insaan hai? 

 Seekh: kitne bhi rules likh lo, real life koi aisa case le aayegi jo socha nahi tha. Ye wahi problem hai jo Topic 3 me haath se bane wheel detector ki thi. Isliye book kehti hai ki AI ko data se khud knowledge nikaalni chahiye: yahi machine learning hai. Deep learning ek kadam aage jaa ke features bhi khud seekhta hai. 

 Knowledge base (Cyc) 
 ML / Deep learning 

 Knowledge kahan se 
 Insaan rules likhta hai 
 Data se seekha 

 Fayda 
 Explain kar sakte hain, exact logic 
 Messy data (photo, awaaz) handle karta hai 

 Nuksaan 
 Brittle, har rule likhna impossible 
 Bahut data chahiye, explain karna mushkil

26-08_Conventional_Machine_Learning_Pipe.lecture_title: Introduction to Deep Learning: Representation Learning
26-08_Conventional_Machine_Learning_Pipe.topic_title: The Conventional Machine Learning Pipeline (SIFT, HOG)
26-08_Conventional_Machine_Learning_Pipe.source: Lecture 26, slide 19 ("Conventional Machine Learning": Low-level sensing → Pre-processing → Feature extraction → Feature selection → Inference: prediction, recognition; Input (motorbike photo) → Feature Representation (e.g., SIFT, HoG, etc.) → Learning algorithm; image credited to LeCun, Bengio & Hinton). Enriched with web research (Lowe, "Distinctive Image Features from Scale-Invariant Keypoints", IJCV 2004; Dalal & Triggs, "Histograms of Oriented Gradients for Human Detection", CVPR 2005; LeCun, Bengio & Hinton, *Nature* 2015). The gradient example and the descriptor-size arithmetic are ours.

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
The five-stage pipeline (top of the slide) 

 Stage 
 What happens 
 Where we studied it 

 Low-level sensing 
 A sensor records raw data: camera pixels, microphone samples, sensor readings 
 Data types: L5 Types of Data — Structured, Semi-Structured, Unstructured 

 Pre-processing 
 Clean and normalise: remove noise, fill missing values, scale, crop/resize images 
 Lectures 6–8, e.g. L6 Data Pre-processing — The Four Major Tasks Pipeline 

 Feature extraction 
 Turn raw data into informative numbers (a feature vector) using a hand-designed method 
 L10 Feature Extraction — PCA, SVD, and LDA 

 Feature selection 
 Keep only the most useful features, drop redundant/irrelevant ones 
 L10 Feature Selection Methods — Filter, Wrapper, and Embedded 

 Inference: prediction, recognition 
 A trained model (classifier/regressor) gives the answer 
 KNN, decision trees, random forest, SVM (Lectures 16–25) 

 In conventional ML, only the last stage learns from data . The middle stages are designed by people and stay fixed. 

 The bottom picture 

 Input (photo of a motorbike) → Feature Representation (e.g., SIFT, HoG) → Learning algorithm . 

 The representation is the hand-crafted part. The learning algorithm (e.g., an SVM) only sees the feature vector. If the features miss something important, no learning algorithm can recover it. LeCun, Bengio & Hinton (2015) describe this as the core limitation: for decades, building a pattern-recognition system required careful engineering and domain expertise to design a feature extractor that transformed raw pixels into a suitable representation. 

 SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform) 

 Who/when: David Lowe, ICCV 1999; full journal version IJCV 2004. 
 Idea: find distinctive keypoints (blob-like spots that stand out at some scale) and describe the patch around each one in a way that stays the same if the image is scaled, rotated or the lighting changes a little. 
 Descriptor: around each keypoint, a 4 × 4 grid of cells; in each cell, a histogram of gradient directions with 8 bins. 4 × 4 × 8 = 128 numbers per keypoint. 
 Used for: matching the same object across photos, panorama stitching, object recognition. 

 HOG (Histogram of Oriented Gradients) 

 Who/when: Navneet Dalal & Bill Triggs, CVPR 2005, for pedestrian detection . 
 Steps: 
 
 Compute the image gradient at each pixel: gₓ = I(x+1, y) − I(x−1, y), g_y = I(x, y+1) − I(x, y−1); magnitude √(gₓ² + g_y²); orientation atan2(g_y, gₓ). 
 Split the image into small cells (8 × 8 pixels). In each cell, build a histogram of orientations with 9 bins (0°–180°), each pixel voting with its gradient magnitude. 
 Group cells into blocks of 2 × 2 cells and normalise each block, which makes the feature robust to lighting changes. 
 Concatenate all block histograms into one long vector, then feed it to a linear SVM ( L24 What Is an SVM? The Hyperplane w·x + b = 0 ). 
 
 Size check (ours): the standard 64 × 128 detection window has 8 × 16 cells. Blocks of 2 × 2 cells sliding by one cell give 7 × 15 = 105 blocks. Each block has 4 cells × 9 bins = 36 numbers. Total 105 × 36 = 3,780 features . 

 Tiny gradient example (ours). A pixel whose left neighbour has brightness 50, right neighbour 200, and top and bottom neighbours both 100: 

 gₓ = 200 − 50 = 150 , g_y = 100 − 100 = 0 
 magnitude = 150 , orientation = atan2(0, 150) = 0° 

 The brightness changes left-to-right, so this pixel sits on a vertical edge . It adds 150 votes to the 0° bin of its cell's histogram. HOG describes a shape by counting how much edge there is in each direction in each small region. 

 How this compares with deep learning 

 SIFT and HOG are clever, but they are the same for every task, they were tuned by hand over years, and they capture only low-level edge statistics. Deep networks learn edge-like detectors in their first layer anyway (Topic 5), and then keep going to textures, parts and objects. On ImageNet in 2012, a CNN that learned its features (AlexNet) beat the best SIFT-plus-classifier systems by about 10 percentage points of top-5 error, which ended the era of hand-crafted vision features. HOG is often described as one of the last major hand-designed feature extractors. 

 Hand-crafted features are not obsolete everywhere: they are still used where data is small, computing power is limited (embedded devices), or explainability matters.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
The top row of the slide is the "old recipe" for machine learning, in five steps: 

 Low-level sensing: collect raw data. A camera records pixels, a microphone records sound. 
 Pre-processing: clean it up. Remove noise, fix missing values, resize photos, put numbers on the same scale (we learned this in Lectures 6–8). 
 Feature extraction: turn raw data into useful numbers. A human expert designs a method for this. 
 Feature selection: keep only the most useful numbers and throw the rest away (Lecture 10). 
 Inference: a trained model, like KNN, a decision tree or an SVM, gives the final answer: "it's a motorbike". 

 In this old recipe, only step 5 actually learns from examples. Steps 3 and 4 are fixed rules a person wrote. 

 The bottom picture says the same thing in short: photo → feature representation (made by a method like SIFT or HOG) → learning algorithm. If the hand-made features miss something important, even the best learning algorithm can't get it back. 

 Two famous hand-made image features: 

 SIFT (David Lowe, 1999/2004): finds special "landmark" points in a photo and describes the area around each with 128 numbers. The clever part is that the description stays the same if the photo is zoomed or rotated. It is used for stitching panoramas and matching the same object in different photos. 
 HOG (Dalal and Triggs, 2005): built to spot people walking in photos. It looks at every pixel and asks "which way does the brightness change here, and how strongly?" Then it divides the picture into small 8 × 8 squares and counts how much edge points in each of 9 directions. A standing person gives lots of vertical edges at the sides, for example. All the counts together (3,780 numbers for a standard 64 × 128 window) go to an SVM, which decides "person" or "not person". 

 Mini example of HOG's first step: a pixel has a dark neighbour on the left (50) and a bright one on the right (200), and the same brightness above and below (100 and 100). The left-to-right change is 200 − 50 = 150, the up-down change is 0. So the brightness changes sideways only. That means this pixel sits on an upright (vertical) edge, with strength 150. 

 Why deep learning replaced this: these methods took experts years to design and only describe simple edges. A deep network learns edge detectors by itself in its first layer, then goes on to learn textures, parts and whole objects. In 2012 such a network won the ImageNet competition by a huge margin, and most vision research switched to learned features. Hand-made features are still useful when data is small, the device is weak, or you need to explain exactly what the system looks at.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Slide ki upar wali row = conventional (purana) ML ka 5-step recipe: 

 Low-level sensing: raw data collect karo. Camera pixels record karta hai, mic awaaz. 
 Pre-processing: data saaf karo: noise hatao, missing values bharo, photo resize karo, scaling (Lectures 6–8). 
 Feature extraction: raw data ko useful numbers (feature vector) me badlo. Ye method insaan (expert) design karta hai (Lecture 10). 
 Feature selection: sirf kaam ke features rakho, baaki hatao (Lecture 10). 
 Inference (prediction, recognition): trained model (KNN, decision tree, SVM) final answer deta hai, jaise "ye motorbike hai". 

 Is recipe me sirf step 5 data se seekhta hai . Step 3 aur 4 insaan ke banaye fixed rules hain. 

 Neeche wali picture: Input (motorbike photo) → Feature Representation (SIFT, HoG jaise method se) → Learning algorithm. Agar hand-made features me koi zaroori cheez chhoot gayi, to best learning algorithm bhi use wapas nahi la sakta. LeCun, Bengio, Hinton (2015) ne bhi yahi limitation batayi. 

 SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform): David Lowe, 1999 (journal 2004). Photo me khaas keypoints (landmark jaise points) dhoondhta hai, aur har keypoint ke aas-paas ko 128 numbers se describe karta hai (4×4 grid, har cell me 8 direction bins: 4×4×8 = 128). Photo zoom ya rotate karo, description same rehta hai. Use: panorama jodna, same object alag photos me match karna. 

 HOG (Histogram of Oriented Gradients): Dalal & Triggs, 2005, pedestrian (paidal chalte log) detection ke liye. 

 Har pixel pe gradient: gₓ = right − left brightness, g_y = neeche − upar brightness. Magnitude = √(gₓ² + g_y²), direction = atan2(g_y, gₓ). 
 Photo ko 8×8 pixel ke cells me baanto. Har cell me 9 direction bins (0°–180°) ka histogram, har pixel apne magnitude jitna vote deta hai. 
 2×2 cells ka block banake normalise karo, taaki light kam-zyada hone se farak na pade. 
 Sab jod ke ek lamba vector, aur use linear SVM (Lecture 24) ko de do. 

 Size check (humara): 64×128 window me 8×16 cells. 2×2 blocks ek cell slide karke: 7×15 = 105 blocks. Har block 4 cells × 9 bins = 36. Total 105 × 36 = 3,780 features . 

 Chhota gradient example: pixel ke left me brightness 50, right me 200, upar-neeche dono 100. 

 gₓ = 200 − 50 = 150 , g_y = 100 − 100 = 0 
 Magnitude 150 , direction atan2(0, 150) = 0° 
Brightness sirf left-to-right badal rahi hai, matlab pixel ek vertical edge pe hai. Ye apne cell ke 0° bin me 150 vote daalega. 

 Deep learning ne isko kyun replace kiya? SIFT/HOG ko experts ne saalon me tune kiya, har task ke liye same rehte hain, aur sirf simple edges describe karte hain. Deep network pehli layer me edge detectors khud seekh leta hai, fir textures, parts, objects tak jaata hai (Topic 5). 2012 ImageNet me AlexNet ne SIFT-based systems ko top-5 error me lagbhag 10 percentage points se haraya, aur hand-crafted vision features ka daur khatam ho gaya. Fir bhi chhote data, kamzor device, ya jahan explain karna zaroori ho, wahan aaj bhi hand-made features use hote hain.

26-09_Deep_Learning_Model_and_the_Four_A.lecture_title: Introduction to Deep Learning: Representation Learning
26-09_Deep_Learning_Model_and_the_Four_A.topic_title: The Deep Learning Model (MLP) and the Four AI Flowcharts
26-09_Deep_Learning_Model_and_the_Four_A.source: Lecture 26, slides 20–23 ("Deep Learning Model": feed-forward deep network or multilayer perceptron, mathematical functions mapping input to output, composed of simpler functions, each layer provides a new representation, learning the right representation; "Representation learning" ×3: build-up of flowcharts for Rule-based system, Classic machine learning and Deep Learning, recreated from the *Deep Learning* book, Fig. 1.5). Enriched with web research (Goodfellow et al., *Deep Learning*, 2016, ch. 1 and ch. 6). The XOR network is our own illustration and was checked for all four inputs.

sections.heading: Technical Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 20: the deep learning model 

 "Feed-forward deep network or multilayer perceptron (MLP)." The standard example of a deep-learning model. Information flows one way, from input to output, through several layers. There are no loops ("feed-forward"). 
 "Mathematical function that maps input to output." An MLP is just a function y = f(x; θ), where θ is the set of all weights and biases. 
 "Composed of simpler functions." f(x) = f⁽ᴸ⁾(… f⁽²⁾(f⁽¹⁾(x))). Each layer is h⁽ˡ⁾ = g(W⁽ˡ⁾ h⁽ˡ⁻¹⁾ + b⁽ˡ⁾): a weighted sum (like a perceptron, L4 Perceptron — General Architecture (N Inputs, Activation, Error) ) followed by a non-linear activation g (step, sigmoid, ReLU…). 
 "Each layer provides a new representation." h⁽¹⁾ is a new description of x, h⁽²⁾ a new description of h⁽¹⁾, and so on ( L26 Deep Learning: Building Complex Concepts out of Simpler Ones ). 
 "Learning the right representation." All the W and b are learned together from labelled data, by gradient descent with back-propagation ( L26 Computational Graphs and the Depth of a Model ). The hidden representations are whatever turns out to make the final prediction accurate. 

 Worked example (ours): an MLP solves XOR where one perceptron cannot 

 XOR outputs 1 when exactly one input is 1. A single perceptron cannot compute it, because the four points are not linearly separable ( L4 Linear Separability ). Lecture 5 built OR and AND with single perceptrons ( L5 Perceptron as Logic Gates — the OR Problem & AND Problem ). Stack them: 

 Hidden unit h₁ = step(x₁ + x₂ − 0.5) → this is OR 
 Hidden unit h₂ = step(x₁ + x₂ − 1.5) → this is AND 
 Output y = step(h₁ − h₂ − 0.5) → "OR but not AND" = XOR

 0 
 +0.5 
 1 
 1 ✔ 

 1 
 1 
 1 
 1 
 −0.5 
 0 
 0 ✔ 

 Why this is representation learning in miniature. In the original (x₁, x₂) space, XOR is not linearly separable. In the hidden representation (h₁, h₂), the four inputs become (0,0) → 0, (1,0) → 1, (1,0) → 1, (1,1) → 0. Now one straight line, h₁ − h₂ = 0.5, separates them. The hidden layer changed the representation so that the last layer's simple linear rule works: the same lesson as Cartesian → polar in L26 Choice of Representation: Cartesian vs Polar Coordinates . Here we chose the weights by hand. In a real MLP, training would find weights like these automatically. 

 Slides 21–23: four kinds of AI system as flowcharts 

 The three slides build up the book's Fig. 1.5 one row at a time. In the book's version, shaded boxes are components that learn from data . 

 System 
 Flowchart 
 What is learned from data 

 Rule-based system 
 Input → Hand-designed program → Output 
 nothing 

 Classic machine learning 
 Input → Hand-designed features → Mapping from features → Output 
 only the mapping (the classifier) 

 Representation learning 
 Input → Features → Mapping from features → Output 
 features and mapping 

 Deep learning 
 Input → Simple features → Additional layers of more abstract features → Mapping from features → Output 
 all feature levels and the mapping 

 Read it as a progression. Each step down the table hands one more piece of the job from humans to data: 

 Rule-based (e.g., Cyc, expert systems, L26 Machine Learning and AI: The Venn Diagram, and the Cyc Project ): humans write the whole program. 
 Classic ML (e.g., HOG + SVM, L26 The Conventional Machine Learning Pipeline (SIFT, HOG) ; or Iris measurements + KNN): humans design the features, the model learns the mapping. 
 Representation learning (e.g., shallow autoencoder, PCA features + classifier): features are learned too, in one step. 
 Deep learning (e.g., MLP, CNN): features are learned as a hierarchy, simple → abstract, and the mapping on top. 

 Differences between the slide and the book's figure (flag) 

 The slide's redrawing differs from the book's Fig. 1.5 in three small ways: 

 In the Classic machine learning row, the second box says "Hand designed program ". The book says "Hand-designed features ". The intended meaning is features: in classic ML the human designs the features, not the whole program. Otherwise this row would not differ from the rule-based row except for the extra box. 
 The book has four labelled columns. The slide draws the last two rows inside one box labelled " Deep Learning ", and uses "Representation learning" as the slide title. In the book, the row Input → Features → Mapping → Output is labelled representation learning (not necessarily deep), and only the row with the extra "abstract features" layer is deep learning . 
 On the slide the " Abstract feature " box is not shaded. In the book, "Additional layers of more abstract features" is shaded, because those layers are learned from data. That is the whole point of deep learning. 

 For exams, use the book's version as shown in the table above.

sections.heading: Simple English Explanation
sections.text:
Slide 20: what a deep learning model looks like. 

 The standard example is the multilayer perceptron (MLP) , also called a feed-forward deep network. "Feed-forward" means information only goes one way: from the input, through several layers, to the output. 
 It is just a big mathematical function : numbers in, answer out. 
 That big function is built by chaining small simple functions . Each layer takes the numbers from the previous layer, does a weighted sum (like the perceptron from Lecture 4), and then a small "squash" or "switch" step. 
 Each layer gives a new description of the input. 
 All the weights are learned from examples , so the network finds the right descriptions by itself. 

 A tiny example: XOR. XOR means "exactly one of the two inputs is 1". One perceptron can't do it: if you plot the four cases, you can't separate the 1s from the 0s with a straight line (Lecture 4). But in Lecture 5 we built OR and AND from single perceptrons. Put them in a hidden layer: 

 h₁ = OR(x₁, x₂): 1 if at least one input is 1. 
 h₂ = AND(x₁, x₂): 1 only if both are 1. 
 Output = "h₁ is on but h₂ is off" = XOR. 

 Check all four cases: 

 (0, 0): OR = 0, AND = 0 → output 0. Correct. 
 (0, 1): OR = 1, AND = 0 → output 1. Correct. 
 (1, 0): OR = 1, AND = 0 → output 1. Correct. 
 (1, 1): OR = 1, AND = 1 → output 0. Correct. 

 The hidden layer gave a new description (OR, AND) of the input. In that new description a simple straight-line rule works. That is exactly what deep learning does, just with many more layers and with the weights found automatically instead of by hand. 

 Slides 21–23: four kinds of AI system, from "humans do everything" to "data does everything": 

 Rule-based system: input → a program a human wrote → output. Nothing is learned. (Like Cyc.) 
 Classic machine learning: input → features a human designed → a learned mapping → output. Only the last part is learned. (Like HOG + SVM, or flower measurements + KNN.) 
 Representation learning: input → features learned from data → learned mapping → output. 
 Deep learning: input → simple learned features → more abstract learned features (more layers) → learned mapping → output. 

 In the book's picture, shaded boxes are the parts learned from data. With each step down, more boxes are shaded. 

 Small mistakes in the slide's drawing: compared with the book, (1) the classic ML row should say "hand-designed features ", not "hand-designed program"; (2) the book keeps "representation learning" and "deep learning" as separate rows, while the slide puts both under "Deep Learning"; and (3) the "Abstract feature" box should be shaded, because it is learned. Use the book's version in exams.

sections.heading: Hinglish Explanation (Beginner-Friendly)
sections.text:
Slide 20: Deep Learning Model. 

 "Feed-forward deep network ya multilayer perceptron (MLP)": deep learning ka standard example. Information sirf ek direction me jaati hai: input → kai layers → output. Koi loop nahi. 
 "Mathematical function that map input to output": MLP bas ek function hai y = f(x; θ), θ = saare weights aur biases. 
 "Composed of simpler functions": f(x) = f⁽ᴸ⁾(…f⁽²⁾(f⁽¹⁾(x))). Har layer: h = g(W·h_pichhla + b), yaani weighted sum (Lecture 4 ka perceptron jaisa) + ek non-linear activation g (step, sigmoid, ReLU). 
 "Each layer provides a new representation": har layer input ka naya description deti hai. 
 "Learning right representation": saare W aur b data se ek saath seekhe jaate hain (gradient descent + back-propagation, Topic 6). 

 Humara example: XOR (jo ek perceptron nahi kar sakta). XOR = 1 jab exactly ek input 1 ho. Chaar points ko ek seedhi line se alag nahi kar sakte (Lecture 4, linear separability). Lecture 5 me OR aur AND single perceptron se banaye the. Unko hidden layer me rakho: 

 h₁ = step(x₁ + x₂ − 0.5) → OR 
 h₂ = step(x₁ + x₂ − 1.5) → AND 
 y = step(h₁ − h₂ − 0.5) → "OR hai par AND nahi" = XOR 

 (step(z) = 1 agar z > 0, warna 0) 

 Chaaron cases check: 

 (0,0): h₁=0, h₂=0, 0−0−0.5 = −0.5 → y = 0 ✔ 
 (0,1): h₁=1, h₂=0, 1−0−0.5 = +0.5 → y = 1 ✔ 
 (1,0): h₁=1, h₂=0 → +0.5 → y = 1 ✔ 
 (1,1): h₁=1, h₂=1, 1−1−0.5 = −0.5 → y = 0 ✔ 

 Ye representation learning ka chhota version hai: (x₁, x₂) space me XOR line se alag nahi hota. Hidden layer ke naye representation (h₁, h₂) me points ban gaye (0,0)→0, (1,0)→1, (1,1)→0, aur ab ek line h₁ − h₂ = 0.5 se alag ho jaate hain. Bilkul Topic 2 ke Cartesian → polar jaisa. Yahan weights humne haath se chune, asli MLP me training khud aise weights dhoondh leti hai. 

 Slides 21–23: Chaar tarah ke AI systems (Deep Learning book, Fig 1.5). Book me shaded boxes = jo data se seekhe jaate hain . 

 Rule-based system: Input → Hand-designed program → Output. Kuch nahi seekha jaata (jaise Cyc). 
 Classic machine learning: Input → Hand-designed features → Mapping from features → Output. Sirf mapping (classifier) seekhi jaati hai (jaise HOG + SVM, ya Iris measurements + KNN). 
 Representation learning: Input → Features → Mapping → Output. Features bhi seekhe jaate hain (jaise shallow autoencoder). 
 Deep learning: Input → Simple features → Aur abstract features ki extra layers → Mapping → Output. Saare feature levels + mapping seekhe jaate hain (jaise MLP, CNN). 

 Har step pe kaam ka ek aur hissa insaan se data ke paas chala jaata hai. 

 Slide ki drawing me book se teen chhote fark (flag): 

 Classic ML row me slide pe "Hand designed program " likha hai, book me "Hand-designed features ". Sahi meaning features hai: classic ML me insaan features banata hai, poora program nahi. 
 Book me chaar alag columns hain. Slide ne last do rows ek box me daal ke "Deep Learning" label diya. Book me Input → Features → Mapping → Output wali row representation learning hai, aur sirf extra "abstract features" wali row deep learning hai. 
 Slide pe "Abstract feature" box shaded nahi hai, book me shaded hai, kyunki wo layers data se seekhi jaati hain. Deep learning ka main point hi yahi hai. 

 Exam me book wala version (upar ki list) likhna.

lab-1-setup.text:
STEP 0: IMPORT THE REQUIRED LIBRARIES

The script begins by importing pandas, the standard Python library for tabular data manipulation, aliased as pd per near-universal community convention. An import statement binds an external module's namespace into the current script so its functions and classes become callable.

```python
import pandas as pd
```

The os module (Python's standard-library interface to the operating system) is imported solely to construct a filesystem path programmatically, so the script resolves the shared CSV's location correctly regardless of the process's current working directory at invocation time.

```python
import os
```

Two pandas display options are configured purely for output presentation: display.max_columns=None disables column truncation in printed DataFrames, and display.width is set to a large value so a wide row prints on a single line rather than being wrapped by pandas into stacked column blocks joined by a backslash continuation marker. Neither option affects the underlying data or any computation.

```python
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", None)
pd.set_option("display.width", 1000)


def section(title):
    """
    This is a small helper FUNCTION (a reusable mini-program) that we wrote
    ourselves, just to print a nice, easy-to-spot heading line before each
    part of the output, so the terminal output is easy to read.
    "def" is the Python keyword used to define (create) a new function.
    Whenever we call section("something") later in this file, Python jumps
    up here, runs these two print lines with "something" plugged in, and
    then jumps back to continue where it left off.
    """
    print("\n" + "=" * 90)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 90)
```

lab-1-question-2.label: Question 2: Identify the number and percentage of missing values in each column, and handle missing values using a suitable technique.
lab-1-question-2.text:
```python
section("QUESTION 2A: FINDING MISSING VALUES")
```

A "missing value" is a cell with no recorded observation for a given (row, column) pair. pandas represents this internally with the sentinel NaN (Not a Number), regardless of whether the column's other values are numeric or textual.

df.isnull() returns a boolean DataFrame of identical shape to df, where each cell is True if missing and False otherwise. Chaining .sum() aggregates each column's True count (Python's bool subtype coerces to 1/0 under arithmetic operations), yielding a per-column missing-value count.

```python
missing_count = df.isnull().sum()
```

The percentage is derived by dividing each column's missing count by len(df) (total row count), scaling by 100, and rounding to 2 decimal places via .round(2) for readability.

```python
missing_percent = (missing_count / len(df) * 100).round(2)
```

pd.DataFrame({...}) constructs a new summary DataFrame from the two previously computed Series, so both metrics can be inspected side by side in one table. The dictionary keys become that new DataFrame's column labels.

```python
missing_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Missing Count": missing_count,
    "Missing %": missing_percent
})
```

The summary is boolean-filtered to rows where Missing Count > 0 (columns with zero missing values are dropped from the view), then sorted descending so the most-affected columns surface first.

```python
missing_summary = missing_summary[missing_summary["Missing Count"] > 0]
missing_summary = missing_summary.sort_values("Missing Count", ascending=False)

print("Columns that contain missing values, and how much of each is missing:")
print(missing_summary)

print("""
INTERPRETATION (in plain English):
  - "Cabin" is missing for about 77% of all passengers. That is a HUGE
    proportion of the column - for more than 3 out of every 4 passengers,
    we simply have no cabin information at all.
  - "Age" is missing for about 20% of passengers (177 out of 891). That is
    a meaningful chunk, but still a clear minority of the data.
  - "Embarked" is missing for only 2 passengers out of 891 - a tiny, almost
    negligible amount.
  Each of these three columns is missing a very different AMOUNT of data,
  so (as the assignment hints) each one deserves a different, suitable
  technique for handling it - there is no single "one size fits all" fix.
""")

section("QUESTION 2B: HANDLING MISSING VALUES")
```

df.copy() is called before any mutation to create an independent deep copy in memory, decoupled from the original df. This is standard defensive practice: it preserves an unmodified baseline for comparison and prevents accidental in-place corruption of the source data during iterative cleaning.

```python
df_clean = df.copy()
```

Handling "Age" (a numeric column, ~20% missing)

For a numeric column with a moderate missing-value proportion, imputation is the standard technique — replacing each missing cell with a statistically derived estimate rather than discarding the entire row (which would also sacrifice every other, fully-observed feature for that record).

The median is chosen over the mean because Age's distribution contains outliers, and the median (the 50th percentile) is a robust statistic — unlike the mean, it is not pulled toward extreme values, making it the safer central-tendency estimator for imputation here.

```python
median_age = df_clean["Age"].median()
print(f"Median Age calculated from the known ages: {median_age}")
```

Series.fillna(value) replaces every NaN entry in that column with the given value while leaving all non-null entries untouched; reassigning to the same column label overwrites it with the completed version.

```python
df_clean["Age"] = df_clean["Age"].fillna(median_age)
print("-> Filled all missing 'Age' values with the median age (median imputation).")
```

Handling "Embarked" (a categorical column, 2 missing)

Embarked is categorical (its domain is restricted to {C, Q, S}), so mean or median imputation is mathematically undefined — there is no arithmetic average of categorical labels. The categorical analogue is mode imputation: filling missing entries with the modal (most frequent) category.

```python
mode_embarked = df_clean["Embarked"].mode()[0]
```

Series.mode() can return multiple values in the event of a tie, so it always returns a Series of candidates even when a unique mode exists; indexing [0] extracts the first (here, the only) modal value.

```python
print(f"Most common 'Embarked' port (the mode): '{mode_embarked}'")

df_clean["Embarked"] = df_clean["Embarked"].fillna(mode_embarked)
print("-> Filled the 2 missing 'Embarked' values with the mode (mode imputation).")
```

Handling "Cabin" (~77% missing)

Imputation is inappropriate here on two grounds: Cabin values are near-unique identifiers with no meaningful central tendency, and at ~77% missing, any imputed value would constitute fabricated signal rather than recovered information, degrading rather than improving data quality.

The appropriate remediation is column-level removal rather than row-level removal, since the unreliability is intrinsic to the column itself. Dropping the affected rows instead would discard 687 of 891 records (~77% of the dataset) purely due to one column, sacrificing otherwise complete data in every other feature.

DataFrame.drop(columns=[...]) removes the specified column(s) from the DataFrame.

```python
df_clean = df_clean.drop(columns=["Cabin"])
print("-> Dropped the entire 'Cabin' column (77% missing - too unreliable to impute, "
      "and dropping rows instead would have discarded 687 otherwise-good passenger records).")
```

A final isnull().sum() verification confirms zero remaining missing values across all columns of df_clean, closing the missing-data-handling loop.

```python
print("\nMissing value count per column AFTER cleaning (should all be 0 now):")
print(df_clean.isnull().sum())

print("""
NOTE ON THE OTHER TWO TECHNIQUES MENTIONED IN THE ASSIGNMENT
(Forward/backward filling, and Removal of rows):
  - "Forward fill" (copy the previous row's value downward) and "backward
    fill" (copy the next row's value upward) are techniques best suited to
    data that has a natural ORDER, most commonly a time series (like daily
    stock prices or hourly sensor readings), where "the next reading is
    probably close to the last one" is a reasonable assumption. In the
    Titanic dataset, the rows are just a list of unrelated passengers in
    no particular meaningful order, so copying "the previous passenger's
    Age" onto a completely different, unrelated passenger would not make
    logical sense here - which is exactly why we picked median/mode
    imputation and column removal instead, as the suitable techniques for
    THIS dataset's columns.
  - "Removal of rows" (dropping any row that has a missing value anywhere)
    was intentionally avoided for Age and Embarked, for the reason
    explained above: it would throw away good, complete information in
    every other column just because of one missing cell.
""")
```

lab-1-question-3.label: Question 3: Identify duplicate records, display them, and remove duplicate records where appropriate.
lab-1-question-3.text:
```python
section("QUESTION 3: FINDING AND REMOVING DUPLICATE RECORDS")
```

A "duplicate record" is a row whose values are identical, column for column, to another row in the table.

DataFrame.duplicated() returns a boolean mask across rows: False for a row's first occurrence, True for every subsequent identical occurrence. Chaining .sum() over this mask yields the total duplicate-row count.

```python
num_duplicates = df_clean.duplicated().sum()
print(f"Number of fully duplicate rows found: {num_duplicates}")
```

Boolean-indexing df_clean with df_clean.duplicated() filters the DataFrame down to only the flagged duplicate rows, satisfying the requirement to explicitly display them.

```python
duplicate_rows = df_clean[df_clean.duplicated()]
print("\nThe duplicate rows themselves (if any):")
print(duplicate_rows if len(duplicate_rows) > 0 else "(none - see explanation below)")
```

PassengerId is additionally checked in isolation, since it is intended as a unique identifier; a repeated PassengerId would be a strong independent signal of duplicated or corrupted data even if minor discrepancies existed elsewhere in the row.

```python
duplicate_ids = df_clean["PassengerId"].duplicated().sum()
print(f"\nNumber of repeated 'PassengerId' values (should be a unique ID per row): {duplicate_ids}")

if num_duplicates > 0:
```

DataFrame.drop_duplicates() retains only the first occurrence of each repeated row, discarding subsequent duplicates; it is invoked conditionally, only when duplicates were actually detected.

lab-1-question-4.label: Question 4: Identify columns that are Irrelevant / Redundant / Identifier / Not useful for further analysis. Remove them and explain why.
lab-1-question-4.text:
```python
section("QUESTION 4: IDENTIFYING AND REMOVING UNHELPFUL COLUMNS")

print("Columns currently remaining in the dataset:")
print(list(df_clean.columns))

print("""
Let's go column by column and classify each one. Here, "further analysis"
means: if we were later trying to study or predict something about these
passengers (for example, predicting whether a passenger survived), would
this column actually help a model or a human analyst find a genuine
PATTERN, or would it just get in the way?

  PassengerId -> IDENTIFIER COLUMN.
      It is just a running serial number (1, 2, 3, ... 891) assigned to
      each row. It carries no real-world information about the passenger
      at all (a passenger's chance of survival has nothing to do with
      which row number they happened to be listed on). Its ONLY purpose
      was to uniquely label each row, similar to a roll number - useful
      for looking a specific row up, but useless as an input for finding
      patterns. -> REMOVE.

  Name -> IDENTIFIER-LIKE / NOT USEFUL IN ITS CURRENT (RAW) FORM.
      Every single name in this dataset is unique (891 different names for
      891 rows), so it behaves just like another identifier here, not
      like a genuine descriptive feature. A person's literal name (e.g.
      "Owen Harris") does not, by itself, influence survival. (Advanced
      note, beyond this assignment's scope: analysts sometimes extract the
      person's TITLE, like "Mr./Mrs./Miss/Master", out of this column,
      because a title can hint at age/gender/social status - but that
      would be creating a brand NEW column from this one, which is a
      separate technique called "feature engineering", not part of basic
      cleaning.) As it stands, in raw form, it is not useful.
      -> REMOVE.

  Ticket -> IDENTIFIER-LIKE / NOT USEFUL IN ITS CURRENT (RAW) FORM.
      This is a messy mix of letters and numbers (like "A/5 21171" or
      "PC 17599") that mostly behaves like an internal booking-office
      code rather than a meaningful, analyzable feature - it has 681
      different values across 891 rows, so it is "nearly" a unique ID in
      practice, and its exact text format does not represent any
      measurable quantity or clean category. -> REMOVE.

  Sex, Pclass, Age, SibSp, Parch, Fare, Embarked, Survived ->
      These all describe a genuine, real-world CHARACTERISTIC of the
      passenger or their journey (their gender, travel class, age, family
      size aboard, ticket price, boarding port) or the actual OUTCOME we
      would eventually want to study/predict (Survived). None of these are
      identifiers, and none of them are duplicated/redundant copies of
      each other (each one measures something genuinely different) ->
      KEEP all of these.

  REDUNDANT COLUMNS check:
      "Redundant" would mean two columns that essentially carry the SAME
      information twice, just phrased differently. In this dataset, no
      two columns are exact duplicates of each other's meaning: Pclass
      (ticket class) and Fare (price paid) are correlated in real life
      (higher class usually costs more) but they are NOT the same
      information - Fare is a fine-grained/individual number, Pclass is
      the passenger's class category, and a person's exact fare can still
      vary even within the same class (due to discounts, family group
      bookings, etc). So no column needs to be removed purely for being
      redundant here.
""")
```

The actual removal is executed here, implementing the column-classification rationale established above.

```python
columns_to_remove = ["PassengerId", "Name", "Ticket"]
df_final = df_clean.drop(columns=columns_to_remove)

print(f"Removed columns: {columns_to_remove}")
print("\nFinal, cleaned dataset - columns remaining:")
print(list(df_final.columns))

print("\nFinal, cleaned dataset - first 5 rows:")
print(df_final.head())

print(f"\nFinal shape of the cleaned dataset: {df_final.shape[0]} rows x {df_final.shape[1]} columns")
```

lab-2-setup.text:
STEP 0: IMPORT THE REQUIRED LIBRARIES

os is the standard-library module for filesystem operations, imported here so the script can resolve paths and create directories reliably regardless of the invoking process's working directory.

```python
import os
```


matplotlib.pyplot is the standard plotting API in the Python data-science stack, used here for every chart type this assignment requires (scatter, bar, histogram, line, box plot). It is aliased as plt by the same convention pandas is aliased as pd.

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
```

From scikit-learn (imported under its conventional alias sklearn), two specific transformers required for Question 4 (Feature Scaling) are imported: MinMaxScaler, which rescales values into the [0, 1] interval, and StandardScaler, which transforms a column to zero mean and unit variance. Both are explained in full detail immediately before their use.

Two pandas display options are set purely for presentation: unrestricted column display, and a large display.width so a wide row always prints on a single line rather than being split into stacked, backslash-joined blocks.

```python
pd.set_option("display.width", 1000)

    of the output. See Lab Assignment 1's script for a full explanation of
    what a Python function/def is - the idea is identical here."""
    print("\n" + "=" * 90)
```

STEP 0b: DERIVE RELIABLE FILE PATHS AND CREATE A PLOTS DIRECTORY

os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)) resolves the absolute path of this script file and takes just its containing directory — i.e., "this script's own folder" — independent of the shell's current working directory at invocation time.

```python
this_script_folder = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
```

The cleaned CSV produced by Lab Assignment 1 resides in a sibling directory (one level up, then into "Lab Assignment 1"). os.path.join(...) concatenates path segments safely and portably, using the correct separator for the host operating system.

```python
cleaned_csv_path = os.path.join(
    this_script_folder, "..", "Lab Assignment 1", "Titanic-Dataset-Cleaned.csv"
```

This is the target directory every generated chart image will be written into.

```python

```

os.makedirs(..., exist_ok=True) creates the directory if absent; exist_ok=True suppresses the exception that would otherwise be raised if the directory already exists from a prior run.

```python
os.makedirs(plots_folder, exist_ok=True)


def save_current_plot(filename):
    """
    Small helper function: saves whatever chart matplotlib currently has
    "on screen" (in its invisible drawing canvas) to an image file inside
    our "plots" folder, then clears that canvas so the NEXT chart we draw
    starts fresh and does not accidentally overlap with this one.
    """
    full_path = os.path.join(plots_folder, filename)
```

plt.tight_layout() adjusts subplot spacing/margins so titles and axis labels are not clipped or overlapping — a purely cosmetic layout call.

```python
    plt.tight_layout()
```

plt.savefig(...) serializes the currently active figure to disk as an image file (.png here), producing a persistent artifact independent of the Python process.

```python
    plt.savefig(full_path)
```

plt.close() releases the current figure from memory, ensuring the next plt.plot(...)/plt.bar(...)/etc call begins drawing onto a fresh, empty canvas rather than accumulating onto the previous figure.

```python

    print(f"  Saved plot -> plots/{filename}")
```

lab-2-question-1.label: Question 1: Visualize the data using different plots - scatter plot, bar plot, histogram, line plot.
lab-2-question-1.text:
```python
section("QUESTION 1: VISUALIZING THE DATA WITH DIFFERENT PLOT TYPES")

print("""
Each plot type below is chosen because it is the RIGHT tool for a
particular kind of question - just like you wouldn't use a hammer to turn
a screw. We explain, for each one, WHY that plot type suits that
particular question.
""")
```

(a) Scatter plot: Age vs. Fare, coloured by survival outcome

A scatter plot maps one numeric variable to the x-axis and a second numeric variable to the y-axis, rendering one point per observation. It is the appropriate choice for examining whether an association exists between two continuous variables (e.g., does Fare correlate with Age?). Colour-encoding each point by the binary Survived label overlays a categorical dimension, letting any visual clustering of survival outcomes across the Age/Fare plane be inspected at a glance.

```python
print("1a) Scatter plot: Age vs Fare (coloured by Survived) ...")
```

plt.figure(figsize=...) initializes a new, blank figure canvas of the specified dimensions (in inches) — a display preference with no bearing on the underlying data.

```python
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
```

The data is partitioned into two subsets by boolean indexing on Survived, solely to assign each subset a distinct colour and legend label in separate plt.scatter() calls. df[df["Survived"] == 0] filters to rows where the boolean condition evaluates True.

```python
did_not_survive = df[df["Survived"] == 0]
survived = df[df["Survived"] == 1]
```

plt.scatter(x, y, ...) renders one marker per (x, y) pair. The alpha=0.6 parameter sets partial transparency, which improves legibility when many points overplot in a dense region.

```python
plt.scatter(did_not_survive["Age"], did_not_survive["Fare"],
            alpha=0.6, label="Did not survive (0)", color="firebrick")
plt.scatter(survived["Age"], survived["Fare"],
            alpha=0.6, label="Survived (1)", color="seagreen")
```

plt.xlabel/ylabel/title annotate the figure with descriptive text, so the saved image is self-explanatory without requiring the reader to consult the source code.

```python
plt.xlabel("Age (years)")
plt.ylabel("Fare (ticket price)")
plt.title("Scatter Plot: Age vs Fare, coloured by Survival")
```

plt.legend() renders the colour-key box, sourcing its labels from the label= keyword argument supplied to each preceding plt.scatter() call.

```python
plt.legend()
save_current_plot("1a_scatter_age_vs_fare.png")

print("""
   How to read this chart: most passengers cluster at low Fare values
   regardless of age, with a "tail" of higher-fare (likely 1st class)
   passengers spread across many ages. There isn't one single obvious
   straight-line relationship between Age and Fare, but you can visually
   see that a good number of the low-Fare, "everyday" passengers did NOT
   survive (more red dots low-down), which hints - just from LOOKING at
   the picture - that Fare (and by extension, ticket class) might be
   related to survival chances. A proper statistical/model-based analysis
   would come later; this plot is just a first visual clue.
""")
```

(b) Bar plot: survival counts by sex

A bar plot is the appropriate chart for comparing aggregate counts across a small number of discrete categories — unlike a scatter plot, it does not require two numeric axes. Since Sex (male/female) and Survived (0/1) are both categorical, tabulating passenger counts per combination and rendering one bar per combination is the natural visualization.

```python
print("\n1b) Bar plot: passenger counts by Sex, split by Survived ...")
```

pd.crosstab(a, b) builds a contingency table: for every unique combination of a's values (rows) and b's values (columns), it counts matching rows in the source data. Here it produces a Sex × Survived contingency table of passenger counts.

```python
counts_table = pd.crosstab(df["Sex"], df["Survived"])
counts_table.columns = ["Did Not Survive (0)", "Survived (1)"]
print("Counts table used for the bar plot:")
print(counts_table)

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5))
```

DataFrame.plot(kind="bar", ...) is a pandas convenience wrapper around matplotlib that draws one group of bars per row of the table (one group for "female", one for "male"), with one bar per column within each group.

```python
counts_table.plot(kind="bar", ax=plt.gca(), color=["firebrick", "seagreen"])
```

plt.gca() ("get current axes") directs pandas to draw onto the figure canvas already opened via plt.figure() above, rather than implicitly creating a separate figure.

```python
plt.xlabel("Sex")
plt.ylabel("Number of Passengers")
plt.title("Bar Plot: Survival Counts by Sex")
plt.xticks(rotation=0)  # keep the "male"/"female" labels horizontal, not tilted
save_current_plot("1b_bar_survival_by_sex.png")

print("""
   How to read this chart: this immediately shows a big difference between
   the two groups - far more female passengers survived than did not,
   while for male passengers it's the reverse (far more did not survive
   than did). This is one of the most well-known real patterns in the
   Titanic dataset ("women and children first").
""")
```

(c) Histogram: distribution of passenger Age

A histogram is the appropriate chart for visualizing the distribution — shape and spread — of a single numeric variable. It partitions the value range into equal-width bins and renders a bar per bin proportional to the count of observations falling within it, revealing structure (skewness, modality, spread) that a summary statistic alone cannot convey.

```python
print("\n1c) Histogram: distribution of passenger Age ...")

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
```

plt.hist(data, bins=20, ...) partitions the Age values into 20 equal-width bins spanning the full observed range, and counts observations per bin.

```python
plt.hist(df["Age"], bins=20, color="steelblue", edgecolor="black")
plt.xlabel("Age (years)")
plt.ylabel("Number of Passengers")
plt.title("Histogram: Distribution of Passenger Age")
save_current_plot("1c_histogram_age.png")

print(f"""
   How to read this chart: you should see a large spike right around
   {df['Age'].median():.0f} years old (that's the median Age value we used
   back in Lab Assignment 1 to fill in the 177 originally-missing Age
   entries - so of course a lot of passengers now share that exact value).
   Besides that artificial spike, most passengers genuinely fall between
   their late teens and about 40 years old, with far fewer very young
   children or elderly passengers above 60.
""")
```

(d) Line plot: average Fare by passenger class

A line plot is appropriate when the x-axis has a natural ordering and the goal is to depict a trend across that order — canonically a value changing over time, but any ordinal axis qualifies. Pclass (1st/2nd/3rd) is ordinal even without a time dimension, so plotting average Fare against ordered class is a valid, meaningful use of a line plot.

```python
print("\n1d) Line plot: average Fare by passenger class (Pclass) ...")
```

df.groupby("Pclass")["Fare"].mean() groups observations by their Pclass value and computes the within-group mean Fare. .sort_index() enforces ascending class order (1, 2, 3), which matters because a line plot's entire purpose is to depict a trend along an ordered axis.

```python
avg_fare_by_class = df.groupby("Pclass")["Fare"].mean().sort_index()
print("Average fare per passenger class:")
print(avg_fare_by_class)

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 5))
```

marker="o" renders an explicit marker at every actual data point along the line, making each class's exact value identifiable rather than only showing an unmarked interpolated line.

```python
plt.plot(avg_fare_by_class.index, avg_fare_by_class.values, marker="o", color="darkorange")
plt.xlabel("Passenger Class (Pclass)")
plt.ylabel("Average Fare Paid")
plt.title("Line Plot: Average Fare by Passenger Class")
```

The x-axis ticks are constrained to the actual class values (1, 2, 3) rather than allowing matplotlib to auto-generate fractional ticks (1.5, 2.5, ...), since Pclass is inherently a small set of discrete integers.

```python
plt.xticks(avg_fare_by_class.index)
save_current_plot("1d_line_avg_fare_by_class.png")

print("""
   How to read this chart: the line drops sharply from 1st class to 3rd
   class, confirming that 1st class tickets cost dramatically more on
   average than 3rd class ones - exactly what you'd expect for a "better"
   travel class, and a good sanity check that our cleaned data still makes
   real-world sense.
""")
```

   travel class, and a good sanity check that our cleaned data still makes
   real-world sense.

lab-2-question-2.label: Question 2: Identify outliers in at least two numerical variables using a Box plot. Visualize the detected outliers.
lab-2-question-2.text:
```python
section("QUESTION 2: DETECTING OUTLIERS WITH BOX PLOTS (Age and Fare)")

print("""
WHAT IS AN "OUTLIER"?
An outlier is a data point that is unusually far away from most of the
other values in its column - so extreme that it looks like it might be a
measurement mistake, a rare/unusual real case, or at least a value that
could distort calculations like the average if not handled carefully.

WHAT IS A BOX PLOT, AND HOW DOES IT FIND OUTLIERS?
A box plot is a chart built from 5 numbers taken from a sorted column:
  - the minimum "non-outlier" value
  - Q1 (the "25th percentile" - 25% of values are below this point)
  - the median (the middle value, "50th percentile")
  - Q3 (the "75th percentile" - 75% of values are below this point)
  - the maximum "non-outlier" value
It draws a box from Q1 to Q3 (this box contains the "middle 50%" of the
data, called the IQR = Interquartile Range = Q3 - Q1), a line inside the
box for the median, and "whiskers" (thin lines) extending out to the
furthest points that are still considered normal. ANY point drawn further
out than the whiskers is flagged as an outlier and shown as an individual
dot.

The standard mathematical rule a box plot uses to decide what counts as
an outlier (called the "1.5 x IQR rule") is:
    lower_bound = Q1 - 1.5 x IQR
    upper_bound = Q3 + 1.5 x IQR
Any value BELOW lower_bound or ABOVE upper_bound is flagged as an outlier.
We will calculate this ourselves below (so you can see the exact numbers
and exact outlier rows, not just look at a picture), and then also draw
the actual box plot picture that the assignment asks for.
""")


def detect_outliers_iqr(column_name):
    """
    A reusable helper function: given the NAME of a numeric column in our
    dataframe "df", this calculates Q1, Q3, the IQR, and the lower/upper
    bounds using the 1.5 x IQR rule described above, prints a summary, and
    returns the actual rows of "df" that are flagged as outliers for that
    column.
    """
```

Series.quantile(0.25) and .quantile(0.75) compute Q1 and Q3 directly, using pandas' built-in percentile-interpolation implementation, rather than requiring a manual sort-and-index computation.

```python
    q1 = df[column_name].quantile(0.25)
    q3 = df[column_name].quantile(0.75)
    iqr = q3 - q1
    lower_bound = q1 - 1.5 * iqr
    upper_bound = q3 + 1.5 * iqr

    print(f"\n--- Outlier detection for '{column_name}' ---")
    print(f"Q1 (25th percentile): {q1:.2f}")
    print(f"Q3 (75th percentile): {q3:.2f}")
    print(f"IQR (Q3 - Q1)       : {iqr:.2f}")
    print(f"Lower bound (Q1 - 1.5*IQR): {lower_bound:.2f}")
    print(f"Upper bound (Q3 + 1.5*IQR): {upper_bound:.2f}")
```

This boolean-filters df down to rows where the column value lies outside [lower_bound, upper_bound] — the "|" operator is Python's element-wise logical OR across two boolean Series.

```python
    outlier_rows = df[(df[column_name] < lower_bound) | (df[column_name] > upper_bound)]
    print(f"Number of outlier rows found in '{column_name}': {len(outlier_rows)} "
          f"out of {len(df)} total rows ({len(outlier_rows) / len(df) * 100:.1f}%)")

    return outlier_rows, lower_bound, upper_bound
```

Numeric variable 1: Age

```python
age_outliers, age_lower, age_upper = detect_outliers_iqr("Age")
print("A few of the actual outlier rows found for 'Age':")
print(age_outliers[["Survived", "Pclass", "Sex", "Age", "Fare"]].head(10))
```

Numeric variable 2: Fare

```python
fare_outliers, fare_lower, fare_upper = detect_outliers_iqr("Fare")
print("\nA few of the actual outlier rows found for 'Fare':")
print(fare_outliers[["Survived", "Pclass", "Sex", "Age", "Fare"]].head(10))

print("""
INTERPRETATION:
  - 'Age' outliers are mostly on the HIGH end (elderly passengers in their
    60s-80s) - genuinely unusual ages compared to the bulk of passengers,
    but still perfectly realistic human ages, not data-entry mistakes.
  - 'Fare' outliers are almost entirely very HIGH fares (some passengers
    paid dramatically more than most - these were likely 1st class
    passengers with large private suites/family bookings). Fare cannot go
    below 0 in a valid record, so there are no "too low" Fare outliers
    here.
  In both cases, these look like genuine, valid extreme values rather
  than data errors, so the appropriate handling here is normally to KEEP
  them but be aware of them (for example, remembering they exist is
  exactly why Question 4 below considers scaling techniques that reduce
  the influence of such extreme values).
""")
```

Rendering the box plots the assignment requires

```python
print("\nDrawing box plots for Age and Fare, side by side ...")
```

plt.subplots(1, 2, ...) constructs a single figure containing a 1×2 grid of axes, enabling the Age and Fare box plots to be rendered side by side within one image for direct visual comparison.

```python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 5))
```

axes[0].boxplot([...]) renders the Age column's box plot in the first (leftmost) axes. dropna() strips any missing values prior to plotting (a defensive no-op here, since Lab Assignment 1's cleaning already eliminated them). Box plots default to a vertical orientation, so no explicit orientation argument is required.

```python

axes[0].set_title("Box Plot: Age")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Age (years)")

axes[1].boxplot(df["Fare"].dropna())
axes[1].set_title("Box Plot: Fare")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Fare")

save_current_plot("2a_boxplots_age_and_fare.png")
```

Additionally visualizing exactly which points were flagged, overlaid on the full data

This second figure makes the flagged outliers unambiguous by plotting every passenger's Age/Fare as a faint grey point, then overplotting the flagged outlier rows in a distinct colour — making it immediately clear which specific records were flagged, and by which variable.

```python

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
plt.scatter(df["Age"], df["Fare"], color="lightgray", label="Normal passengers", alpha=0.6)
plt.scatter(age_outliers["Age"], age_outliers["Fare"], color="darkorange",
            label="Age outliers", alpha=0.8, marker="^")
plt.scatter(fare_outliers["Age"], fare_outliers["Fare"], color="crimson",
            label="Fare outliers", alpha=0.6, marker="x")
plt.xlabel("Age (years)")
plt.ylabel("Fare")
plt.title("Highlighting Detected Age and Fare Outliers")
plt.legend()
save_current_plot("2b_outliers_highlighted_scatter.png")
```

lab-2-question-3.text:
```python
section("QUESTION 3: VALIDATION CHECKS AFTER CLEANING")

print("""
The whole point of this question is to PROVE, with actual checks (not just
assume), that the cleaning we did in Lab Assignment 1 actually worked and
that the dataset is now in a trustworthy state. We go through each check
the assignment lists, one at a time.
""")
```

Check 1: Do any missing values remain?

```python
print("--- Check 1: Missing values ---")
missing_after = df.isnull().sum()
total_missing = missing_after.sum()
print(missing_after)
if total_missing == 0:
    print("PASSED: There are zero missing values left in any column.")
else:
    print(f"FAILED: There are still {total_missing} missing values remaining somewhere.")
```

Check 2: Do any duplicate records remain?

```python
print("\n--- Check 2: Duplicate records ---")
duplicate_count = df.duplicated().sum()
print(f"Number of fully duplicated rows: {duplicate_count}")
if duplicate_count == 0:
    print("PASSED: No duplicate rows remain.")
else:
    print(f"FAILED: {duplicate_count} duplicate row(s) still remain.")
```

Check 3: Are the numeric values valid (logically possible)?

```python
print("\n--- Check 3: Numerical values are valid ---")
```

A count or a monetary amount is "valid" only if non-negative. (df["Fare"] < 0) produces a boolean Series, True wherever Fare is negative; .sum() aggregates this into a count of invalid rows.

```python
invalid_fare = (df["Fare"] < 0).sum()
invalid_sibsp = (df["SibSp"] < 0).sum()
invalid_parch = (df["Parch"] < 0).sum()
invalid_age = (df["Age"] < 0).sum()
print(f"Negative Fare values (impossible - can't pay negative money): {invalid_fare}")
print(f"Negative SibSp values (impossible - can't have negative siblings/spouses): {invalid_sibsp}")
print(f"Negative Parch values (impossible - can't have negative parents/children): {invalid_parch}")
print(f"Negative Age values (impossible): {invalid_age}")
if invalid_fare == invalid_sibsp == invalid_parch == invalid_age == 0:
    print("PASSED: All numeric columns contain only logically valid (non-negative) values.")
else:
    print("FAILED: At least one numeric column contains impossible negative values.")
```

Check 4: Do categorical variables contain only valid categories?

```python
print("\n--- Check 4: Categorical variables contain only valid categories ---")
```

For each categorical column, the complete set of legitimately allowed values is defined from domain knowledge (what the Titanic dataset's documentation specifies), and the observed values are checked for anything outside that set.

```python
valid_sex_values = {"male", "female"}
valid_embarked_values = {"C", "Q", "S"}
valid_pclass_values = {1, 2, 3}
valid_survived_values = {0, 1}
```

set(df["Sex"].unique()) collects the distinct values actually present in the Sex column into a set (an unordered collection with no duplicates), enabling a direct comparison against the allowed set.

```python
actual_sex_values = set(df["Sex"].unique())
actual_embarked_values = set(df["Embarked"].unique())
actual_pclass_values = set(df["Pclass"].unique())
actual_survived_values = set(df["Survived"].unique())
```

The "-" (difference) operator between two sets returns every element of the first set absent from the second — i.e., which observed values are NOT in the allowed list. An empty result confirms validity.

```python
unexpected_sex = actual_sex_values - valid_sex_values
unexpected_embarked = actual_embarked_values - valid_embarked_values
unexpected_pclass = actual_pclass_values - valid_pclass_values
unexpected_survived = actual_survived_values - valid_survived_values

print(f"Sex      -> values found: {actual_sex_values}      | unexpected values: {unexpected_sex or 'none'}")
print(f"Embarked -> values found: {actual_embarked_values}   | unexpected values: {unexpected_embarked or 'none'}")
print(f"Pclass   -> values found: {actual_pclass_values}     | unexpected values: {unexpected_pclass or 'none'}")
print(f"Survived -> values found: {actual_survived_values}       | unexpected values: {unexpected_survived or 'none'}")

if not (unexpected_sex or unexpected_embarked or unexpected_pclass or unexpected_survived):
    print("PASSED: Every categorical column only contains its expected, valid categories.")
else:
    print("FAILED: At least one categorical column contains an unexpected value.")
```

Check 5: Are date fields correctly formatted?

```python
print("\n--- Check 5: Dates are correctly formatted ---")
print("""
This particular Titanic dataset does NOT contain any date/time column at
all (no "date of travel", "date of birth", etc. is recorded) - so this
specific check does not literally apply to this dataset. We flag this
honestly rather than skip the question, and show below the GENERAL
technique you WOULD use if a date column existed, so the method itself is
still demonstrated.

If a column called, say, "Booking_Date" existed, you would do:

    df["Booking_Date_parsed"] = pd.to_datetime(df["Booking_Date"], errors="coerce")
    invalid_dates = df["Booking_Date_parsed"].isnull().sum()

pd.to_datetime(...) tries to convert every value in that column into a
proper Python "datetime" value. Any text that does NOT look like a valid
date (e.g. "31/13/2020", or "hello", or a typo) fails to convert.
"errors='coerce'" tells pandas: "if a value can't be converted, don't
crash the whole program - just put a missing value (NaN) there instead".
Counting how many NaNs appear AFTER this conversion (that weren't already
missing BEFORE it) tells you exactly how many rows had a badly-formatted
date.
""")
```

Check 6: Do values fall within reasonable, domain-specific ranges?

```python
print("--- Check 6: Domain-specific reasonable ranges ---")
print("""
"Domain-specific" means using REAL-WORLD KNOWLEDGE about what these
numbers are allowed to realistically be - not just "is it negative or
not", but "does this number make sense for a real human being on a real
ship in 1912?".
""")
```

No verified human lifespan on record exceeds ~122 years, and this dataset describes a 1912 passenger voyage, so any Age exceeding roughly 100 would be highly implausible; Age is also, trivially, non-negative by domain definition.

```python
unreasonable_age = df[(df["Age"] < 0) | (df["Age"] > 100)]
print(f"Passengers with an unreasonable Age (below 0 or above 100): {len(unreasonable_age)}")
```

Fare cannot be negative by definition. As an additional sanity bound, the highest documented genuine Titanic fare (a first-class parlour suite) was approximately 512; a generous margin of 600 above the known historical maximum is used as the upper threshold here.

```python
unreasonable_fare = df[(df["Fare"] < 0) | (df["Fare"] > 600)]
print(f"Passengers with an unreasonable Fare (below 0 or above 600): {len(unreasonable_fare)}")
```

Pclass is constrained by domain definition to {1, 2, 3} — no fourth class exists in this schema.

```python
unreasonable_pclass = df[~df["Pclass"].isin([1, 2, 3])]
print(f"Passengers with an unreasonable Pclass (not 1, 2, or 3): {len(unreasonable_pclass)}")

if len(unreasonable_age) == 0 and len(unreasonable_fare) == 0 and len(unreasonable_pclass) == 0:
    print("PASSED: All checked columns fall within reasonable, real-world ranges.")
else:
    print("FAILED: At least one value falls outside a reasonable real-world range.")
```
