lab-2-question-4.label: Question 4: Feature Scaling - apply Min-Max Normalization AND Standardization (both, back to back, on the same chosen columns).
lab-2-question-4.text:
```python
section("QUESTION 4: FEATURE SCALING (Min-Max Normalization AND Standardization)")

print("""
WHAT IS "FEATURE SCALING" AND WHY DO IT AT ALL?
Different numeric columns in this dataset live on very different scales:
Age ranges roughly 0-80, while Fare ranges roughly 0-512 (and SibSp/Parch
are small counts, usually 0-8). Many machine learning algorithms (like
k-nearest-neighbors, or anything using distances/gradients) can end up
being unfairly dominated by whichever column happens to have the LARGEST
raw numbers - not because that column is actually more important, but
purely because of the units it happens to be measured in. Feature scaling
puts every chosen numeric column onto a comparable scale, so no column
unfairly dominates just because of its raw size.

WHICH COLUMNS ARE "APPROPRIATE" TO SCALE HERE?
We select: Age, Fare, SibSp, Parch.
  - These are all genuinely continuous/count-based NUMERIC measurements.
We deliberately do NOT scale:
  - "Survived" -> this is the outcome/label (0 or 1) we would eventually
    want to predict, not an input measurement - scaling a label doesn't
    make sense and would only confuse its meaning (0 = no, 1 = yes).
  - "Pclass" -> although stored as a number (1, 2, 3), it is really a
    CATEGORY (which class of ticket), not a measured quantity where
    "2" is meaningfully "twice as much" as "1" - scaling it numerically
    would misleadingly treat it like a true measurement.
  - "Sex", "Embarked" -> these are text categories, not numbers at all,
    so numeric scaling does not apply to them (they would first need a
    different technique entirely, called "encoding", which is outside
    this assignment's scope).
""")

columns_to_scale = ["Age", "Fare", "SibSp", "Parch"]
print(f"Columns selected for scaling: {columns_to_scale}")

print("\nOriginal (unscaled) statistics for these columns:")
print(df[columns_to_scale].describe().round(2))
```

(a) Min-Max normalization

```python
print("""
--- METHOD 1: MIN-MAX NORMALIZATION ---
Formula (applied to every value "x" in a column):
    x_scaled = (x - min(column)) / (max(column) - min(column))
This SQUEEZES every value in the column into the range [0, 1] - the
smallest original value becomes exactly 0, the largest original value
becomes exactly 1, and everything else lands proportionally in between.
It's useful when you want every feature bounded within a fixed, known
range, but it is quite sensitive to outliers (a single extreme max/min
value stretches or squashes everything else).
""")
```

MinMaxScaler() instantiates a stateful transformer object: .fit(...) learns the column's min/max from the training data, and .transform(...) applies that learned scaling. .fit_transform(...) is a convenience method performing both steps in one call.

```python
minmax_scaler = MinMaxScaler()
```

df[columns_to_scale] projects the selected 4 columns as their own sub-DataFrame. fit_transform(...) on this returns a plain NumPy array of scaled values (not a pandas object), which is immediately wrapped back into a labeled DataFrame via pd.DataFrame(..., columns=...).

```python
minmax_scaled_values = minmax_scaler.fit_transform(df[columns_to_scale])
df_minmax = df.copy()
df_minmax[columns_to_scale] = minmax_scaled_values

print("Min-Max normalized statistics (every column's min should now be 0.0, max should be 1.0):")
print(df_minmax[columns_to_scale].describe().round(3))

print("\nFirst 5 rows after Min-Max normalization (compare to the original table above):")
print(df_minmax[columns_to_scale].head())
```

(b) Standardization

```python
print("""
--- METHOD 2: STANDARDIZATION (Z-score scaling) ---
Formula (applied to every value "x" in a column):
    x_scaled = (x - mean(column)) / standard_deviation(column)
This RE-CENTRES every column so its average becomes exactly 0, and
RE-SCALES it so its standard deviation (a measure of how spread out the
values are) becomes exactly 1. Unlike Min-Max, standardized values are
NOT bounded to a fixed [0, 1] range - they can still go quite negative or
quite positive, but a value's sign and size now directly tell you "how
many standard deviations above or below the average is this value?",
which is generally LESS sensitive to a handful of extreme outliers than
Min-Max normalization is.
""")

standard_scaler = StandardScaler()
standardized_values = standard_scaler.fit_transform(df[columns_to_scale])
df_standardized = df.copy()
df_standardized[columns_to_scale] = standardized_values

print("Standardized statistics (every column's mean should now be ~0.0, std should be ~1.0):")
print(df_standardized[columns_to_scale].describe().round(3))

print("\nFirst 5 rows after Standardization (compare to the original table above):")
print(df_standardized[columns_to_scale].head())

print("""
COMPARING THE TWO METHODS SIDE BY SIDE (using 'Fare' as the example,
since it has the most extreme outliers of our 4 chosen columns):
  - The single highest Fare value in the ORIGINAL data becomes exactly
```

WHAT IS "FEATURE SCALING" AND WHY DO IT AT ALL?
Different numeric columns in this dataset live on very different scales:
Age ranges roughly 0-80, while Fare ranges roughly 0-512 (and SibSp/Parch
are small counts, usually 0-8). Many machine learning algorithms (like
k-nearest-neighbors, or anything using distances/gradients) can end up
being unfairly dominated by whichever column happens to have the LARGEST
raw numbers - not because that column is actually more important, but
purely because of the units it happens to be measured in. Feature scaling
puts every chosen numeric column onto a comparable scale, so no column
unfairly dominates just because of its raw size.

WHICH COLUMNS ARE "APPROPRIATE" TO SCALE HERE?
We select: Age, Fare, SibSp, Parch.
  - These are all genuinely continuous/count-based NUMERIC measurements.
We deliberately do NOT scale:
  - "Survived" -> this is the outcome/label (0 or 1) we would eventually
    want to predict, not an input measurement - scaling a label doesn't
    make sense and would only confuse its meaning (0 = no, 1 = yes).
  - "Pclass" -> although stored as a number (1, 2, 3), it is really a
    CATEGORY (which class of ticket), not a measured quantity where
    "2" is meaningfully "twice as much" as "1" - scaling it numerically
    would misleadingly treat it like a true measurement.
  - "Sex", "Embarked" -> these are text categories, not numbers at all,
    so numeric scaling does not apply to them (they would first need a
    different technique entirely, called "encoding", which is outside
    this assignment's scope).

--- METHOD 1: MIN-MAX NORMALIZATION ---
Formula (applied to every value "x" in a column):
    x_scaled = (x - min(column)) / (max(column) - min(column))
This SQUEEZES every value in the column into the range [0, 1] - the
smallest original value becomes exactly 0, the largest original value
becomes exactly 1, and everything else lands proportionally in between.
It's useful when you want every feature bounded within a fixed, known
range, but it is quite sensitive to outliers (a single extreme max/min
value stretches or squashes everything else).

lab-3-question-1.label: Question 1: Apply different types of Data Smoothing, with graphs: a) Using bin mean b) Using bin median c) Using bin boundaries
lab-3-question-1.text:
```python
section("QUESTION 1: DATA SMOOTHING BY BINNING (mean / median / boundaries)")

print("""
WHAT IS "DATA SMOOTHING", AND WHY DO IT?
Real-world numeric data is often "noisy" - it jitters up and down a bit
due to small random fluctuations, even though there's a genuine, smoother
underlying trend. "Smoothing" means processing the data so that this small
random jitter is reduced/flattened out, while (hopefully) keeping the
real, larger pattern intact.

"BINNING" IS ONE WAY TO SMOOTH DATA - HOW IT WORKS:
  Step 1: SORT the column's values from smallest to largest.
  Step 2: Split the sorted values into consecutive groups called "bins"
          (here we use EQUAL-FREQUENCY bins, meaning every bin gets the
          same NUMBER of values in it - e.g. with a bin size of 4, values
          1-4 form bin 1, values 5-8 form bin 2, and so on).
  Step 3: replace every value inside a bin with something calculated FROM
          that bin, so all the values in the bin become smoother/closer to
          each other. This assignment asks for 3 different ways of doing
          this last step:
            a) BIN MEAN     -> replace every value in the bin with the
                               bin's average (mean).
            b) BIN MEDIAN   -> replace every value in the bin with the
                               bin's middle value (median) instead of the
                               mean (median is less pulled around by any
                               one extreme value inside that bin).
            c) BIN BOUNDARIES -> for each value, look at just the two
                               EDGE values of its bin (the smallest value
                               in the bin, and the largest value in the
                               bin), and replace it with WHICHEVER of
                               those two edges it is numerically closer
                               to. Unlike mean/median, this technique
                               always produces one of the two original
                               boundary numbers, never a "new" invented
                               number.

WHICH COLUMN, AND WHAT BIN SIZE?
We smooth the 'Fare' column (ticket price), because it is a real,
continuous numeric measurement with plenty of natural variation - a good
candidate to demonstrate smoothing on. We use a bin size of 20 (so every
20 sorted passengers form one bin) across the full column, which is small
enough to visibly show a "staircase" smoothing effect on the graph without
creating too many tiny bins to see clearly.
""")


def smooth_by_binning(sorted_values, bin_size):
    """
    Takes a NumPy array of values that is ALREADY SORTED (smallest to
    largest), and a chosen bin_size (how many values go in each bin), and
    returns THREE new arrays of the same length and order:
        bin_mean_smoothed      - every value replaced by its bin's mean
        bin_median_smoothed    - every value replaced by its bin's median
        bin_boundary_smoothed  - every value replaced by whichever bin
                                  edge (min or max of that bin) is closer
    This directly implements the 3-technique binning method taught in
    class, just written out as reusable Python code.
    """
    n = len(sorted_values)
    bin_mean_smoothed = np.zeros(n)
    bin_median_smoothed = np.zeros(n)
    bin_boundary_smoothed = np.zeros(n)
```

range(0, n, bin_size) generates 0, bin_size, 2×bin_size, 3×bin_size, ..., up to n — i.e., the starting index of every bin.

```python
    for start in range(0, n, bin_size):
```

end marks the starting index of the next bin (or the array's true end for the final, potentially smaller, leftover bin). Python's slicing safely caps at the array's actual length even if end technically exceeds it.

```python
        end = start + bin_size
```

This slice extracts exactly the values belonging to the current bin.

```python
        current_bin = sorted_values[start:end]

        bin_mean_value = current_bin.mean()
        bin_median_value = np.median(current_bin)
        bin_min = current_bin.min()
        bin_max = current_bin.max()
```

The computed mean/median value is broadcast into every position within this bin.

```python
        bin_mean_smoothed[start:end] = bin_mean_value
        bin_median_smoothed[start:end] = bin_median_value
```

For bin-boundary smoothing, each value must be individually compared to determine whether it is nearer to bin_min or bin_max.

```python
        for i, value in enumerate(current_bin):
            distance_to_min = abs(value - bin_min)
            distance_to_max = abs(value - bin_max)
            if distance_to_min <= distance_to_max:
                bin_boundary_smoothed[start + i] = bin_min
            else:
                bin_boundary_smoothed[start + i] = bin_max

    return bin_mean_smoothed, bin_median_smoothed, bin_boundary_smoothed
```

A small, hand-calculation-style worked example first

```python
print("--- A small worked example first, on just 12 sample Fare values ---")
```

A small, sorted sample of 12 real Fare values is deliberately selected here, purely so the printed figures below stay short enough to verify by manual inspection — the same convention any textbook worked example follows.

```python
sample_fares = np.sort(df["Fare"].to_numpy())[::75][:12]  # pick 12 spread-out real values
print(f"Sample of 12 sorted Fare values: {sample_fares}")

sample_mean_smoothed, sample_median_smoothed, sample_boundary_smoothed = smooth_by_binning(
    sample_fares, bin_size=4
)
worked_example_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Original": sample_fares,
    "Bin Mean Smoothed": sample_mean_smoothed.round(2),
    "Bin Median Smoothed": sample_median_smoothed.round(2),

})

Reading this small example: within each group of 4 sorted values (one
bin), "Bin Mean Smoothed" replaces all 4 with their average, "Bin Median
Smoothed" replaces all 4 with their middle value, and "Bin Boundary
Smoothed" pulls each individual value toward whichever end of its own bin
(smallest or largest) it was originally closer to.
""")
```

```python
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
```

The plot uses a plain 0, 1, 2, 3, ... position index on the x-axis (this is just "a passenger's rank once fares are sorted", not a real-world quantity) — the standard way to visualize smoothing, since it directly shows how each technique flattens the sorted line's natural jaggedness into discrete "steps".

```python

plt.plot(x_positions, sorted_fare, label="Original (sorted)", color="lightgray", linewidth=1)
plt.plot(x_positions, mean_smoothed, label="Bin Mean Smoothed", color="steelblue")

plt.plot(x_positions, boundary_smoothed, label="Bin Boundary Smoothed", color="darkorange")
plt.xlabel("Passenger rank (after sorting by Fare)")
plt.ylabel("Fare")
plt.title("Data Smoothing by Binning: Mean vs Median vs Boundary (bin size = 20)")
```

A zoomed-in view (the first 100 sorted passengers) makes each technique's "staircase" shape substantially easier to inspect, since the full-column plot compresses all 891 points into a small image, obscuring fine detail.

```python
bin's minimum or its maximum), which is why its line looks more like sharp
up/down jumps between only two levels within a step, rather than one
perfectly flat line like mean/median smoothing.
""")
```

lab-3-question-2.label: Question 2: Identify outliers using Z-score and remove them.
lab-3-question-2.text:
```python
section("QUESTION 2: OUTLIER DETECTION AND REMOVAL USING Z-SCORE")

print("""
WHAT IS A Z-SCORE?
A Z-score tells you "how many standard deviations away from the average is
this particular value?". The formula for a value x in a column is:

    z = (x - mean_of_column) / standard_deviation_of_column

  - z = 0   means the value IS exactly the average.
  - z = 1   means the value is 1 standard deviation ABOVE the average.
  - z = -2  means the value is 2 standard deviations BELOW the average.

WHY DOES A LARGE Z-SCORE MEAN "OUTLIER"?
For data that is roughly bell-shaped (a "normal distribution"), about 99.7%
of all values naturally fall within 3 standard deviations of the mean
(this is a well-known statistics result called the "68-95-99.7 rule").
So if a value's Z-score has an ABSOLUTE VALUE greater than 3 (i.e. it is
more than 3 standard deviations away from the mean, in EITHER direction),
it is unusual enough, statistically, to be flagged as an outlier. This is
the standard, commonly used Z-score threshold, and the one we use here.

Note this is a DIFFERENT outlier-detection method than Lab Assignment 2's
box-plot/IQR method - IQR is based on percentiles/ranking (works well even
if the data is skewed), while Z-score is based on the mean and standard
deviation (works best when the data is roughly bell-shaped). Both are
valid, standard techniques; this question specifically asks us to use
Z-score.
""")


def zscore_outlier_mask(column):
    """
    Given a pandas Series of numbers, returns:
      - the Z-score of every value (as a pandas Series, same order),
      - a True/False mask that is True exactly where |z-score| > 3
        (i.e. True means "this row is an outlier for this column").
    """
    mean_value = column.mean()
    std_value = column.std()
    z_scores = (column - mean_value) / std_value
    is_outlier = z_scores.abs() > 3
    return z_scores, is_outlier
```

Both numeric columns most likely to contain genuine extreme values are checked: Age and Fare — the same two columns Lab Assignment 2 already flagged as containing IQR-based outliers, now re-examined under a different detection method.

```python
age_z, age_is_outlier = zscore_outlier_mask(df["Age"])
fare_z, fare_is_outlier = zscore_outlier_mask(df["Fare"])

print(f"Age  -> mean={df['Age'].mean():.2f}, std={df['Age'].std():.2f}, "
      f"outliers with |z|>3: {age_is_outlier.sum()}")
print(f"Fare -> mean={df['Fare'].mean():.2f}, std={df['Fare'].std():.2f}, "
      f"outliers with |z|>3: {fare_is_outlier.sum()}")
```

"|" between two boolean columns is Python's element-wise logical OR - so a row is marked an outlier if EITHER its Age Z-score OR its Fare Z-score is extreme.

```python
combined_outlier_mask = age_is_outlier | fare_is_outlier
outlier_rows = df[combined_outlier_mask]
print(f"\nTotal unique rows flagged as an outlier by Age and/or Fare Z-score: {len(outlier_rows)}")
print("\nThe flagged outlier rows:")
print(outlier_rows[["Survived", "Pclass", "Sex", "Age", "Fare"]])
```

The "~" (bitwise NOT / logical negation) operator inverts the boolean mask, retaining only rows NOT flagged as outliers — precisely the removal step the question requires. The result is assigned to a NEW variable so the original "df" (outliers still included) remains available for comparison.

```python
df_no_outliers = df[~combined_outlier_mask].copy()
print(f"\nRow count before removal: {len(df)}")
print(f"Row count after removing Z-score outliers: {len(df_no_outliers)}")
print(f"Rows removed: {len(df) - len(df_no_outliers)}")
```

WHAT IS A Z-SCORE?
A Z-score tells you "how many standard deviations away from the average is
this particular value?". The formula for a value x in a column is:

    z = (x - mean_of_column) / standard_deviation_of_column

  - z = 0   means the value IS exactly the average.
  - z = 1   means the value is 1 standard deviation ABOVE the average.
  - z = -2  means the value is 2 standard deviations BELOW the average.

WHY DOES A LARGE Z-SCORE MEAN "OUTLIER"?
For data that is roughly bell-shaped (a "normal distribution"), about 99.7%
of all values naturally fall within 3 standard deviations of the mean
(this is a well-known statistics result called the "68-95-99.7 rule").
So if a value's Z-score has an ABSOLUTE VALUE greater than 3 (i.e. it is
more than 3 standard deviations away from the mean, in EITHER direction),
it is unusual enough, statistically, to be flagged as an outlier. This is
the standard, commonly used Z-score threshold, and the one we use here.

Note this is a DIFFERENT outlier-detection method than Lab Assignment 2's
box-plot/IQR method - IQR is based on percentiles/ranking (works well even
if the data is skewed), while Z-score is based on the mean and standard
deviation (works best when the data is roughly bell-shaped). Both are
valid, standard techniques; this question specifically asks us to use
Z-score.

lab-3-question-3.label: Question 3: Perform 7 different types of data normalization on the outlier-free dataset from Question 2.
lab-3-question-3.text:
```python
section("QUESTION 3: SEVEN NORMALIZATION / SCALING TECHNIQUES")
```

Age and Fare are the columns scaled — the same two genuine continuous measurement columns used throughout this assignment series, for the reasons already established in Lab Assignment 2 (SibSp/Parch are low-cardinality integer counts with limited spread; Pclass/Sex/Embarked are categorical, not true continuous measurements).

```python
columns_to_scale = ["Age", "Fare"]
work_df = df_no_outliers[columns_to_scale].copy()

print(f"Working on the OUTLIER-REMOVED data from Question 2 "
      f"({len(work_df)} rows), columns: {columns_to_scale}\n")
print("Original (unscaled) statistics:")
print(work_df.describe().round(3))
```

This dictionary accumulates every scaled version of the data, so a final side-by-side comparison table can be printed at the end.

```python
results = {}
results["Original"] = work_df.copy()
```

(a) Min-Max normalization

```python
print("""
--- (a) MIN-MAX NORMALIZATION ---
Formula: x_scaled = (x - min) / (max - min)
Squeezes every value into the range [0, 1]. The smallest value in the
column becomes 0, the largest becomes 1.
""")
minmax_scaler = MinMaxScaler()
minmax_result = pd.DataFrame(
    minmax_scaler.fit_transform(work_df), columns=columns_to_scale
)
results["Min-Max"] = minmax_result
print(minmax_result.describe().round(3))
```

(b) Mean normalization

```python
print("""
--- (b) MEAN NORMALIZATION ---
Formula: x_scaled = (x - mean) / (max - min)
This is very similar to Min-Max, but instead of shifting by the MINIMUM
value, it shifts by the column's MEAN (average) instead. The result is
centred much closer to 0 (values below the average become negative,
values above the average become positive), while still being divided by
the same (max - min) "range" as Min-Max. scikit-learn does not have a
single ready-made function for this exact formula, so we calculate it
ourselves directly with pandas/numpy - this is a good example of how,
once you understand a formula, you don't strictly need a library function
for every single technique.
""")
mean_norm_result = pd.DataFrame()
for col in columns_to_scale:
    col_min = work_df[col].min()
    col_max = work_df[col].max()
    col_mean = work_df[col].mean()
    mean_norm_result[col] = (work_df[col] - col_mean) / (col_max - col_min)
results["Mean Normalization"] = mean_norm_result
print(mean_norm_result.describe().round(3))
```

(c) Z-score method (standardization)

```python
print("""
--- (c) Z-SCORE METHOD (Standardization) ---
Formula: x_scaled = (x - mean) / standard_deviation
This is the exact same Z-score formula from Question 2 - but this time we
apply it as a SCALING technique (to reshape the whole column), rather than
as an outlier-detection rule. After this transform, the column's mean
becomes 0 and its standard deviation becomes 1.
""")
zscore_scaler = StandardScaler()
zscore_result = pd.DataFrame(
    zscore_scaler.fit_transform(work_df), columns=columns_to_scale
)
results["Z-score"] = zscore_result
print(zscore_result.describe().round(3))
```

(d) Decimal scaling

```python
print("""
--- (d) DECIMAL SCALING ---
Formula: x_scaled = x / 10^j
where "j" is the SMALLEST whole number that makes every scaled value's
absolute size less than 1. In practice: j = the number of digits in the
largest absolute value in the column (e.g. if the biggest value is 512,
it has 3 digits, so j = 3, and every value gets divided by 10^3 = 1000).
This simply "moves the decimal point" of every number the same number of
places to the left - the simplest of all these techniques, and one
scikit-learn also has no ready-made function for, so we calculate it
ourselves.
""")
decimal_scaling_result = pd.DataFrame()
for col in columns_to_scale:
    max_abs_value = work_df[col].abs().max()
```

math.log10(max_abs_value) yields the approximate order of magnitude — roughly, the digit count — of the value (e.g., log10(512) ≈ 2.7). math.floor(...) + 1 converts this into the correct integer digit count (e.g., 3 for 512). A guard against max_abs_value being 0 prevents an undefined log10(0) call.

```python
    if max_abs_value == 0:
        j = 1
    else:
        j = math.floor(math.log10(max_abs_value)) + 1
    decimal_scaling_result[col] = work_df[col] / (10 ** j)
    print(f"  Column '{col}': max absolute value = {max_abs_value:.2f} -> "
          f"{j} digits -> dividing every value by 10^{j} = {10**j}")
results["Decimal Scaling"] = decimal_scaling_result
print(decimal_scaling_result.describe().round(3))
```

(e) Log transformer

```python
print("""
--- (e) LOG TRANSFORMER ---
Formula: x_scaled = natural_log(x)   [natural log, i.e. base "e", matching
this course's convention - see Lecture 7's Log Transformer notes]
A log transform is especially useful for columns like Fare that are
strongly "right-skewed" (most values are small/cheap, but a long tail of
expensive outliers stretches the column far to the right) - taking the log
compresses that long tail down and pulls the whole distribution closer to
a symmetric, bell-like shape, which many statistical methods work better
with.

IMPORTANT REAL DATA CAVEAT WE CHECKED FOR: natural log of 0 is undefined
(mathematically, it is negative infinity), and this Titanic dataset
genuinely contains a small number of passengers with Fare = 0 (crew/staff
travelling for free, or comped tickets). Applying a plain log(x) here
would produce invalid "-inf" results for those exact rows. The standard,
safe fix - and what we use here - is "log1p", i.e. natural_log(x + 1)
instead of natural_log(x): this keeps log(0) = log(1) = 0 (a valid,
sensible number) instead of crashing into -infinity, while barely changing
the result for any larger Fare value. Age has no zero or negative values
in this dataset, so this caveat only actually matters for Fare, but we
apply log1p consistently to both columns for safety.
""")
zero_fare_count = (work_df["Fare"] == 0).sum()
print(f"(Confirmed: {zero_fare_count} passenger(s) in this outlier-removed "
      f"data have Fare = 0, which is exactly why log1p was needed instead of a plain log.)")

log_result = pd.DataFrame()
for col in columns_to_scale:
```

np.log1p(x) computes natural_log(x + 1) directly, in a single, numerically safe operation.

```python
    log_result[col] = np.log1p(work_df[col])
results["Log Transform (log1p)"] = log_result
print(log_result.describe().round(3))
```

(f) MaxAbs transformer

```python
print("""
--- (f) MAXABS TRANSFORMER ---
Formula: x_scaled = x / max(|x|)
Divides every value by the single LARGEST ABSOLUTE value in the column.
The largest-magnitude value in the column becomes exactly +1 or -1, and
every other value lands somewhere inside [-1, 1]. Since both Age and Fare
here only ever contain positive numbers, this behaves very similarly to
Min-Max in this particular case (both end up in [0, 1]) - but MaxAbs is
the better/correct choice in general specifically WHEN a column can
contain negative numbers too, since (unlike Min-Max) it doesn't shift the
data's zero point, it only rescales around the existing zero.
""")
maxabs_scaler = MaxAbsScaler()
maxabs_result = pd.DataFrame(
    maxabs_scaler.fit_transform(work_df), columns=columns_to_scale
)
results["MaxAbs"] = maxabs_result
print(maxabs_result.describe().round(3))
```

(g) Interquartile / Robust scaler

```python
print("""
--- (g) INTERQUARTILE SCALER / ROBUST SCALER ---
Formula: x_scaled = (x - median) / (Q3 - Q1)
Instead of using the mean/min/max (all of which can be dragged around a
lot by a single extreme outlier), this technique centres the data using
the MEDIAN, and scales it using the IQR (Q3 - Q1, the width of just the
"middle 50%" of the data - see Lab Assignment 2's Q2 for a full
explanation of Q1/Q3/IQR). Because the median and IQR both ignore the most
extreme values by design, this scaler is far less affected by outliers
than any of the other 6 techniques above - which is exactly why it's
called "Robust" (robust = "not easily thrown off by unusual/extreme
values").
""")
robust_scaler = RobustScaler()
robust_result = pd.DataFrame(
    robust_scaler.fit_transform(work_df), columns=columns_to_scale
)
results["Robust (IQR)"] = robust_result
print(robust_result.describe().round(3))
```

Final side-by-side comparison (Fare only, since it is the more skewed, more outlier-prone of the two columns, making differences most visible).

```python
section("SIDE-BY-SIDE COMPARISON OF ALL 7 TECHNIQUES (Fare column, first 5 rows)")

comparison_table = pd.DataFrame({
    name: result_df["Fare"].head(5).values for name, result_df in results.items()
})
print(comparison_table.round(3))

print("""
How to read this comparison: notice how differently the SAME 5 original
Fare values end up looking depending on which technique is used - some
techniques (Min-Max, MaxAbs) force everything into a tight [0, 1] range,
Z-score and Robust can produce small negative numbers, Decimal Scaling
just shifts the decimal point without changing the overall "shape" of the
numbers at all, and Log Transform visibly compresses big values much more
aggressively than small ones. There is no single "best" technique for
every situation - which one to use depends on the shape of your data
(especially how skewed it is, and how many outliers it has) and on which
downstream machine learning algorithm you plan to use next.
""")
```

lab-4-question-2.label: Question 2: Identify Highly Correlated Features
lab-4-question-2.text:
```python
section("QUESTION 2: IDENTIFY HIGHLY CORRELATED (REDUNDANT) FEATURES")

print("""
WHAT COUNTS AS "HIGHLY CORRELATED"?
There's no single universal cutoff, but a very commonly used rule of
thumb (and the one we use here) is:

    |r| > 0.7   ->   the two features are considered "highly correlated"

The "| |" (absolute value) matters: a correlation of -0.9 is just as
"highly correlated" as +0.9 - the SIGN only tells you the DIRECTION of
the relationship (do they move together or oppositely), while the SIZE
(ignoring sign) tells you the STRENGTH of the relationship, which is what
we actually care about for spotting redundancy.

WHY DOES HIGH CORRELATION MEAN "REDUNDANT"?
If two features are highly correlated, they are carrying almost the SAME
information - so keeping both barely adds anything a model couldn't
already infer from just one of them, while still costing extra
computation and (for many models) potentially causing "multicollinearity"
problems (unstable, hard-to-trust coefficients). This is exactly the
"minimizing redundancy" driver of feature selection from the lecture
notes.
""")


def find_highly_correlated_pairs(corr_matrix, threshold=0.7):
    """
    Scans a correlation matrix (a pandas DataFrame) and returns a list of
    (feature_a, feature_b, correlation_value) tuples for every PAIR of
    DIFFERENT features whose absolute correlation exceeds the threshold.
    Each pair is only returned ONCE (we don't also return the mirror-image
    duplicate, since corr(A,B) is always equal to corr(B,A)).
    """
    columns = corr_matrix.columns
    highly_correlated = []
    for i in range(len(columns)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(columns)):  # j starts AFTER i, so no self-pairs and no duplicate mirror-pairs
            value = corr_matrix.iloc[i, j]
            if abs(value) > threshold:
                highly_correlated.append((columns[i], columns[j], value))
    return highly_correlated


threshold = 0.7
highly_correlated_pairs = find_highly_correlated_pairs(correlation_matrix, threshold)

print(f"Scanning every feature pair for |r| > {threshold} ...\n")
if highly_correlated_pairs:
    for feature_a, feature_b, value in highly_correlated_pairs:
        print(f"  '{feature_a}'  <->  '{feature_b}'   r = {value:.3f}  (|r| = {abs(value):.3f} > {threshold})")
else:
    print("  No feature pair exceeded the threshold.")

print(f"""
WHY THIS PARTICULAR PAIR SHOWS UP:
'Embarked_C' and 'Embarked_S' come from ONE-HOT ENCODING the same original
column ('Embarked'), which only has 3 possible values (C, Q, S) and every
passenger has EXACTLY ONE of them. Since the S port is by far the most
common (646 of 891 passengers) and C is the second most common, knowing
"this passenger did NOT board at S" already makes it noticeably more
likely they boarded at C (because there are only 2 remaining options, and
C is the bigger one) - hence the strong NEGATIVE correlation between the
two one-hot columns. This is a textbook example of the well-known "dummy
variable trap": whenever you one-hot-encode a category into N columns,
those N columns are never fully independent of each other, because
knowing all-but-one of them already tells you the last one for free.
""")
```

lab-4-question-3.label: Question 3: Remove Redundant Features
lab-4-question-3.text:
```python
section("QUESTION 3: REMOVE REDUNDANT FEATURES")

print("""
HOW DO WE DECIDE *WHICH* FEATURE TO DROP FROM EACH PAIR?
For each highly-correlated pair identified in Question 2, we keep the
feature that is more strongly correlated with 'Survived' (our target/
label column - the thing we'd ultimately want to predict), and drop the
other, since the one more related to the actual outcome we care about is
the more useful one to keep.
""")

target_column = "Survived"
columns_to_drop = []
for feature_a, feature_b, value in highly_correlated_pairs:
    corr_a_with_target = abs(correlation_matrix.loc[feature_a, target_column])
    corr_b_with_target = abs(correlation_matrix.loc[feature_b, target_column])
    if corr_a_with_target >= corr_b_with_target:
        drop_this_one = feature_b
        keep_this_one = feature_a
    else:
        drop_this_one = feature_a
        keep_this_one = feature_b
    columns_to_drop.append(drop_this_one)
    print(f"  Pair ('{feature_a}', '{feature_b}'): "
          f"|corr with Survived| is {corr_a_with_target:.3f} for '{feature_a}' "
          f"vs {corr_b_with_target:.3f} for '{feature_b}' "
          f"-> keeping '{keep_this_one}', dropping '{drop_this_one}'")

reduced_df = encoded_df.drop(columns=columns_to_drop)

print(f"\nColumns BEFORE removal ({len(encoded_df.columns)}): {list(encoded_df.columns)}")
print(f"Columns dropped as redundant: {columns_to_drop}")
print(f"Columns AFTER removal ({len(reduced_df.columns)}): {list(reduced_df.columns)}")

print(f"""
NOTE: Dropping 'Embarked_S' here also happens to match a second, standard
data-preparation practice independent of correlation: when one-hot
encoding a category with N values, it's normal to keep only N-1 of the
dummy columns (dropping any one of them, e.g. Embarked_S), since the
dropped column's value can always be perfectly inferred from the other
N-1 columns being all 0 - keeping all N columns is mathematically
redundant by construction, which is exactly what the correlation-based
removal above caught automatically.
""")
```

lab-4-question-4.label: Question 4: Feature Selection Using Distance/Similarity Measures
lab-4-question-4.text:
```python
section("QUESTION 4: SIX DISTANCE/SIMILARITY MEASURES BETWEEN FEATURES")

print("""
WHAT ARE WE MEASURING HERE, AND WHY?
Questions 1-3 spotted redundant features using CORRELATION. This question
uses 6 DIFFERENT formulas from the lecture notes on measuring feature
redundancy, applied the same way: to compare pairs of FEATURES (whole
columns, not individual passengers) against each other, to see if a
totally different kind of formula agrees with what correlation already
found.

We split the 10 features (from BEFORE Question 3's removal, so we can
compare against the same full set Question 1/2 used) into two groups,
since different formulas suit different kinds of data (this exact
dense-vs-sparse/binary split is in the lecture notes too):

  DENSE, CONTINUOUS features -> Pclass, Age, SibSp, Parch, Fare
      (used for Euclidean, Manhattan, and Cosine)

  BINARY (0/1) features -> Survived, Sex_male, Embarked_C, Embarked_Q,
  Embarked_S
      (used for Hamming, Jaccard, and SMC)

For the 3 dense-feature formulas, we first STANDARDIZE every column (the
same Z-score technique from Lab Assignment 3: subtract the mean, divide
by the standard deviation) - this is essential here, because otherwise
'Fare' (values up to several hundred) would completely dominate the
distance calculations over something like 'Pclass' (values only 1-3),
purely due to its bigger raw numbers, not because it's actually more
different.
""")

dense_feature_names = ["Pclass", "Age", "SibSp", "Parch", "Fare"]
binary_feature_names = ["Survived", "Sex_male", "Embarked_C", "Embarked_Q", "Embarked_S"]

scaler = StandardScaler()
standardized_dense = pd.DataFrame(
    scaler.fit_transform(encoded_df[dense_feature_names]),
    columns=dense_feature_names,
)
binary_features = encoded_df[binary_feature_names]

print("Standardized dense features (first 5 rows):")
print(standardized_dense.head().round(3))
print("\nBinary features (first 5 rows):")
print(binary_features.head())


def pairwise_matrix(feature_names, pair_function):
    """
    Given a list of feature (column) names and a function that computes
    one number for a PAIR of columns, builds and returns the full square
    matrix (as a pandas DataFrame) of that number for every pair of
    features - reused below for all 6 distance/similarity formulas so we
    don't repeat the same looping code 6 times.
    """
    n = len(feature_names)
    result = np.zeros((n, n))
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            result[i, j] = pair_function(feature_names[i], feature_names[j])
    return pd.DataFrame(result, index=feature_names, columns=feature_names)


def most_extreme_off_diagonal(matrix, find_max=True):
    """Finds the (feature_a, feature_b, value) with the largest (or, if
    find_max=False, smallest) value among all OFF-diagonal cells of a
    square matrix - used to highlight the single most notable pair for
    each of the 6 measures below."""
    best = None
    for i, row_name in enumerate(matrix.index):
        for j, col_name in enumerate(matrix.columns):
            if i == j:
                continue  # skip the diagonal (a feature compared with itself)
            value = matrix.iloc[i, j]
            if best is None or (find_max and value > best[2]) or (not find_max and value < best[2]):
                best = (row_name, col_name, value)
    return best
```

4(i) EUCLIDEAN DISTANCE

```python
print("""
--- (i) EUCLIDEAN DISTANCE ---
Formula: d(A, B) = sqrt( sum( (A_i - B_i)^2 ) )
The "straight-line" distance between two vectors, exactly as covered
(and hand-verified) in the lecture notes' worked example. Here, each
"vector" is one STANDARDIZED dense feature column (891 values long, one
per passenger) - so we're measuring how differently two entire columns
behave ACROSS ALL PASSENGERS AT ONCE, not comparing two individual
passengers to each other.
""")


def euclidean_distance(col_a, col_b):
    a = standardized_dense[col_a].to_numpy()
    b = standardized_dense[col_b].to_numpy()
    return np.sqrt(np.sum((a - b) ** 2))


euclidean_matrix = pairwise_matrix(dense_feature_names, euclidean_distance)
print("Euclidean distance matrix (dense features):")
print(euclidean_matrix.round(3))
closest_pair = most_extreme_off_diagonal(euclidean_matrix, find_max=False)
print(f"\nSMALLEST Euclidean distance (= most similar pair): "
      f"'{closest_pair[0]}' <-> '{closest_pair[1]}'  (distance = {closest_pair[2]:.3f})")
```

4(ii) MANHATTAN DISTANCE

```python
print("""
--- (ii) MANHATTAN DISTANCE ---
Formula: d(A, B) = sum( |A_i - B_i| )
Also called "city-block" distance - instead of the straight diagonal line
(Euclidean), it adds up the absolute differences directly, as if you
could only move along grid streets, never diagonally. It's less sensitive
to any single huge difference than Euclidean is (because differences
aren't squared), so it can rank feature pairs slightly differently.
""")


def manhattan_distance(col_a, col_b):
    a = standardized_dense[col_a].to_numpy()
    b = standardized_dense[col_b].to_numpy()
    return np.sum(np.abs(a - b))


manhattan_matrix = pairwise_matrix(dense_feature_names, manhattan_distance)
print("Manhattan distance matrix (dense features):")
print(manhattan_matrix.round(3))
closest_pair = most_extreme_off_diagonal(manhattan_matrix, find_max=False)
print(f"\nSMALLEST Manhattan distance (= most similar pair): "
      f"'{closest_pair[0]}' <-> '{closest_pair[1]}'  (distance = {closest_pair[2]:.3f})")
```

4(iii) HAMMING DISTANCE

```python
print("""
--- (iii) HAMMING DISTANCE ---
Formula: d(A, B) = (number of positions where A_i != B_i) / total positions
Originally designed for comparing strings/binary codes of equal length -
here, for two binary (0/1) feature columns, it simply counts, passenger
by passenger, how often the two columns DISAGREE (one is 0 and the other
is 1), then divides by the total number of passengers to get a fraction
between 0 (identical on every passenger) and 1 (opposite on every
passenger).
""")


def hamming_distance(col_a, col_b):
    a = binary_features[col_a].to_numpy()
    b = binary_features[col_b].to_numpy()
    disagreements = np.sum(a != b)
    return disagreements / len(a)


hamming_matrix = pairwise_matrix(binary_feature_names, hamming_distance)
print("Hamming distance matrix (binary features):")
print(hamming_matrix.round(3))
closest_pair = most_extreme_off_diagonal(hamming_matrix, find_max=False)
print(f"\nSMALLEST Hamming distance (= most similar pair): "
      f"'{closest_pair[0]}' <-> '{closest_pair[1]}'  (distance = {closest_pair[2]:.3f})")
```

4(iv) COSINE SIMILARITY

```python
print("""
--- (iv) COSINE SIMILARITY ---
Formula: cos(A, B) = (A . B) / (||A|| * ||B||)
Measures the ANGLE between two vectors, ignoring their magnitude/length
entirely - it asks "do these two columns point in the same DIRECTION
across passengers?", not "are their raw sizes similar?". A value of 1
means the two columns point in exactly the same direction (perfectly
similar pattern), 0 means they're at a right angle (unrelated), and -1
means they point in exactly opposite directions.
""")


def cosine_similarity(col_a, col_b):
    a = standardized_dense[col_a].to_numpy()
    b = standardized_dense[col_b].to_numpy()
    dot_product = np.dot(a, b)
    magnitude_a = np.sqrt(np.sum(a ** 2))
    magnitude_b = np.sqrt(np.sum(b ** 2))
    return dot_product / (magnitude_a * magnitude_b)


cosine_matrix = pairwise_matrix(dense_feature_names, cosine_similarity)
print("Cosine similarity matrix (dense features):")
print(cosine_matrix.round(3))
most_similar_pair = most_extreme_off_diagonal(cosine_matrix, find_max=True)
print(f"\nLARGEST Cosine similarity (= most similar pair): "
      f"'{most_similar_pair[0]}' <-> '{most_similar_pair[1]}'  (similarity = {most_similar_pair[2]:.3f})")
```

4(v) JACCARD DISTANCE

```python
print("""
--- (v) JACCARD DISTANCE ---
Formula: distance(A, B) = 1 - [ (A AND B) / (A OR B) ]
The part in [ ] brackets is the "Jaccard coefficient" from the lecture
notes: treating each binary column as a SET of passengers (the ones where
that feature = 1), it's the size of the OVERLAP (passengers where BOTH
features are 1) divided by the size of the UNION (passengers where
EITHER feature is 1). Unlike Hamming, Jaccard completely IGNORES
positions where BOTH columns are 0 together - it only cares about where
at least one of the two columns is "switched on", which is exactly why
it's the standard choice for SPARSE/binary data (see the lecture notes'
dense-vs-sparse grouping).
""")


def jaccard_distance(col_a, col_b):
    a = binary_features[col_a].to_numpy().astype(bool)
    b = binary_features[col_b].to_numpy().astype(bool)
    intersection = np.sum(a & b)
    union = np.sum(a | b)
    if union == 0:
        return 0.0  # both columns are all-zero everywhere - treat as identical (distance 0)
    jaccard_coefficient = intersection / union
    return 1 - jaccard_coefficient


jaccard_matrix = pairwise_matrix(binary_feature_names, jaccard_distance)
print("Jaccard distance matrix (binary features):")
print(jaccard_matrix.round(3))
closest_pair = most_extreme_off_diagonal(jaccard_matrix, find_max=False)
print(f"\nSMALLEST Jaccard distance (= most similar pair): "
      f"'{closest_pair[0]}' <-> '{closest_pair[1]}'  (distance = {closest_pair[2]:.3f})")
```

4(vi) SIMPLE MATCHING COEFFICIENT (SMC)

```python
print("""
--- (vi) SIMPLE MATCHING COEFFICIENT (SMC) ---
Formula: SMC(A, B) = (matches) / (total positions)
                    = (number of positions where A_i == B_i) / total positions
This is the "mirror image" of Hamming distance and the "complete"
counterpart to Jaccard: unlike Jaccard, SMC counts BOTH kinds of
agreement - positions where both columns are 1 AND positions where both
are 0 - as a "match". This makes SMC the right choice when a shared "0"
genuinely means something meaningful for both features (dense/complete
binary data), while Jaccard is better when a shared "0" is just "neither
feature happened to apply here" (sparse binary data) - exactly the
distinction drawn in the lecture notes.
""")


def simple_matching_coefficient(col_a, col_b):
    a = binary_features[col_a].to_numpy()
    b = binary_features[col_b].to_numpy()
    matches = np.sum(a == b)
    return matches / len(a)


smc_matrix = pairwise_matrix(binary_feature_names, simple_matching_coefficient)
print("Simple Matching Coefficient matrix (binary features):")
print(smc_matrix.round(3))
most_similar_pair = most_extreme_off_diagonal(smc_matrix, find_max=True)
print(f"\nLARGEST SMC (= most similar pair): "
      f"'{most_similar_pair[0]}' <-> '{most_similar_pair[1]}'  (SMC = {most_similar_pair[2]:.3f})")

embarked_c_s_hamming = hamming_matrix.loc["Embarked_C", "Embarked_S"]
embarked_c_s_jaccard = jaccard_matrix.loc["Embarked_C", "Embarked_S"]
embarked_c_s_smc = smc_matrix.loc["Embarked_C", "Embarked_S"]

print(f"""
SMC IS EXACTLY "1 - HAMMING DISTANCE":
Look closely at the two matrices above - for any pair of features, SMC
always equals 1 - Hamming_distance(that same pair) (e.g. 'Embarked_C' <->
'Embarked_Q': Hamming = 0.275, SMC = 0.725, and 0.275 + 0.725 = 1.000).
This makes sense from the formulas themselves: Hamming distance counts
the fraction of DISAGREEING positions, SMC counts the fraction of
AGREEING positions, and every position is either agreeing or disagreeing
- so the two always add up to exactly 1, and they will always rank pairs
identically (just "flipped").

AN IMPORTANT DISAGREEMENT WITH CORRELATION:
Question 2 flagged 'Embarked_C' and 'Embarked_S' as "highly correlated"
(r = -0.783). But look at how ALL THREE binary measures score that exact
same pair here: Hamming distance = {embarked_c_s_hamming:.3f} (close to
the maximum of 1 - i.e. very DISSIMILAR), Jaccard distance =
{embarked_c_s_jaccard:.3f} (the absolute maximum possible, 1.000), and
SMC = {embarked_c_s_smc:.3f} (close to the minimum of 0 - again very
DISSIMILAR). So Hamming/Jaccard/SMC all say the OPPOSITE of what
correlation said about this exact pair!

WHY THE DISAGREEMENT IS NOT A MISTAKE - IT'S A DIFFERENCE IN WHAT "SIMILAR"
MEANS: correlation treats a STRONG relationship in EITHER direction
(positive or negative) as "these two carry the same information, hence
redundant" - a passenger who is "not S" is quite predictably "C" here,
which is exactly why r is large in magnitude. Hamming/Jaccard/SMC, on the
other hand, are pure AGREEMENT measures - they only count how often the
two columns show the exact SAME value at the exact same passenger, and
'Embarked_C'/'Embarked_S' almost NEVER show the same value (whenever one
is 1 the other is 0, since a passenger can only board from one port) - so
these measures correctly call them maximally "different", even though
they're still highly (negatively) PREDICTABLE from each other. This is a
genuinely important lesson: "redundant" can mean different things under
different formulas, and a real feature-selection pipeline benefits from
checking more than one kind of measure, exactly as this question does.
""")
```
